pattern.mechanism: Each centre was a contract among a university, a group of firms and the state agency, with matched funding from all three, boards with a non-academic majority and chair, and staged three-year funding that depended on international evaluation, which kept firms engaged in the whole research agenda instead of single projects.
preconditions: Research-intensive firms prepared to commit staff and money for up to ten years
Universities willing to cede board control to non-academics
An agency able to run staged evaluations and withdraw funding from weak centres
pattern.travelled: The source notes that Austria, Hungary and Estonia started similar programmes inspired by the Swedish one; Finland's SHOKs and Austria's COMET centres are later relatives.

records.title: Doctorados Industriales (State Research Agency industrial doctorates)
records.claim: Spain's State Research Agency funds four-year contracts for doctoral candidates employed in firms and other entities to write a thesis on an industrial research or experimental development project; in the 2024-2 call, resolved in October 2025, it awarded 65 grants worth 7.6 million euros.

metric.name: Industrial doctorate grants awarded, call DIN 2024-2

secondMetric.name: Funding awarded, call DIN 2024-2

source.publisher: Agencia Estatal de Investigación (State Research Agency), news release on the award resolution for Doctorados Industriales DIN 2024-2, 24 October 2025

records.limits: The figure is one call's awards, not the stock of industrial doctorates in progress; The 2024 round was split into two calls and only the second is counted here, so the figure understates a year's awards. It is small next to France's Cifre. The release does not mention universities at all: the university side is implied by the doctoral thesis, not shown. It does not count the firms, and beneficiaries include 'other entities' as well as companies. Awards are funding decisions: the release does not say how many contracts were signed or theses completed. The start year (2014, the first call under the 2013-2016 State Plan) is not stated on the cited page. The release says funding doubled in 2024 and held in 2025, so the current scale is recent.

pattern.mechanism: The state co-funds a firm's employment of a doctoral candidate for four years on condition that the thesis is built on the firm's own research or development project, tying a university doctoral programme to a company problem through one person.
preconditions: Universities that accept company-based thesis topics and co-supervision
Firms with an R&D project long enough to carry a thesis
A national agency running regular competitive calls
pattern.travelled: The design follows France's Cifre and Denmark's Industrial PhD. Catalonia and Galicia run regional versions alongside the national one.

records.title: Office of Technology Assessment, defunded and closed in 1995
records.claim: Congress gave the Office of Technology Assessment, created under the Technology Assessment Act of 1972, the statutory function to provide early indications of the probable impacts of technology; it appropriated $21,970,000 for the office with a cap of 143 staff for fiscal year 1995, then appropriated $3,615,000 for fiscal year 1996 to carry out its orderly closure, with no more than 17 employees paid except for severance.

metric.name: Appropriation for the orderly closure of the Office of Technology Assessment

secondMetric.name: Appropriation for Office of Technology Assessment salaries and expenses, the last operating year

source.publisher: US Government Publishing Office, Public Law 104-53, Legislative Branch Appropriations Act, 1996 (109 Stat. 514)

records.limits: Technology assessment is adjacent to strategic foresight, not the same thing: the office studied technologies on request from congressional committees rather than running whole-of-government scenarios. It is filed here because its statute, 2 U.S.C. 472(c), states an anticipatory function, to provide early indications of the probable beneficial and adverse impacts of the applications of technology (govinfo, US Code 2023 edition, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title2/html/USCODE-2023-title2-chap15-sec472.htm). Both figures are appropriations, not spending or output: they show the money Congress gave, not what the office produced, and the 143 and 17 figures are statutory staff caps, not headcounts. The FY1995 figure comes from a different source, Public Law 103-283 in the Statutes at Large (108 Stat. 1423), inside a PDF on page 11 of the file (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-108/pdf/STATUTE-108-Pg1423.pdf). The authorising statute was not repealed and still appears in the US Code, so the office was ended by withdrawing funds rather than by abolishing its legal basis; it could be refunded without new legislation. The 1996 act also carried $2,500,000 of FY1995 funds forward to September 1996, so the FY1996 closure figure is not the whole of the wind-down money. Started is the year of the authorising Act, not the year the office first reported.

pattern.mechanism: Congress built its own analytic office, governed by a bipartisan board of members, to give legislators early warning on technology choices, and later closed it through the appropriations bill rather than by repeal, cutting its funding by roughly five sixths in one year and capping staff for the wind-down.
preconditions: A legislature with its own budget for in-house analytic agencies
Bipartisan support strong enough to protect a small agency through spending rounds, which failed here
A statutory mandate that survives defunding, so the function can be revived without new law
pattern.travelled: European parliaments built technology assessment offices on the model, including the German Bundestag's TAB, which cites the US office as its model; the US original closed while the copies continued.

records.title: Rządowe Centrum Studiów Strategicznych, liquidated in 2006
records.claim: Poland's Government Centre for Strategic Studies, attached to the Prime Minister, with tasks of strategic programming and forecasting of economic and social development set in article 14k of the Act of 8 August 1996 on the Council of Ministers, was liquidated as of 31 March 2006 by the Act of 17 February 2006, in the year its budget had been planned at PLN 10,016 thousand.

metric.name: Planned 2006 expenditure in budget part 47, Government Centre for Strategic Studies

source.publisher: Sejm of the Republic of Poland, government bill on the liquidation of the Government Centre for Strategic Studies (print 172, 5th term), regulatory impact assessment

records.limits: The figure is planned spending in the government's draft 2006 budget, quoted in the bill's regulatory impact assessment, not an outturn, and the same assessment expected savings of about half of it. The bill proposed liquidation on 28 February 2006; the act as passed (Dz.U. 2006 nr 45 poz. 319, ISAP, https://isap.sejm.gov.pl/isap.nsf/DocDetails.xsp?id=WDU20060450319, PDF) set 31 March 2006, and the claim uses the enacted date. The centre's statutory work was forecasting and long-term strategic programming, which sits closer to development planning than to scenario-based foresight. Its tasks did not vanish: the act moved impact assessment, foreign policy concepts and analyses ordered by the Prime Minister to the Chancellery of the Prime Minister, and the bill moved strategy and forecasting to the minister for regional development, so what ended is a dedicated unit with its own budget line, not every forward-looking task. Started is 1996, the year of the Act on the Council of Ministers whose article 14k held the centre's tasks; neither source gives the centre's founding date or first year of operation.

pattern.mechanism: Parliament gave a strategic studies centre attached to the Prime Minister its own statutory tasks and budget part, then a new government folded it into the Prime Minister's Chancellery and a line ministry as part of an administrative savings programme.
preconditions: A statute giving the unit its own budget part, which made it visible as a line to cut
A government programme of administrative consolidation that counted a separate agency as overhead
Receiving ministries willing to absorb the tasks, which let the unit be closed without a visible gap

records.title: Office of Technology Assessment at the German Bundestag (TAB)
records.claim: Since 1990 the German Bundestag has kept an Office of Technology Assessment, run under contract by the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, whose tasks include horizon scanning of scientific and technological trends at early stages; by 2026 it reported more than 200 projects and over 400 publications.

metric.name: Projects carried out by TAB since 1990 (lower bound, as stated)

secondMetric.name: Publications of TAB results since 1990 (lower bound, as stated)

source.publisher: Office of Technology Assessment at the German Bundestag (TAB), About us

records.limits: Technology assessment is adjacent to strategic foresight: most TAB projects assess specific technologies on request from the Bundestag committee for research and technology assessment. It is filed here because the same page lists horizon scanning, the observation of trends in early stages of development, among its tasks and describes its aim as forward-looking analysis, and the site carries a separate foresight section. Both figures are cumulative lower bounds (more than 200, over 400) with no date stated, so asOf is the retrieval date. TAB reports on itself, and it is operated by a university research institute (ITAS at KIT) under a contract with the Bundestag rather than by parliamentary staff, so continuity depends on contract renewal. The counts show output, not influence on legislation, and they serve parliament, not the federal executive.

pattern.mechanism: The Bundestag contracts a university technology assessment institute to run a dedicated office for parliament, steered by its research committee, which picks topics and approves reports before publication.
preconditions: A national research institute with an established technology assessment group able to host the office
A standing committee willing to act as steering client across electoral terms
A contract model that lets parliament buy analytic capacity without creating a civil service unit
pattern.travelled: The office names the US Congress's OTA as its model; Germany kept the parliamentary office when the US closed its own in 1995, but placed it with a contractor rather than inside parliament.

records.title: National Assembly Futures Institute
records.claim: Korea's National Assembly enacted the National Assembly Future Institute Act on 12 December 2017 and opened the institute on 28 May 2018 with a statutory duty to predict and analyse changes in the future environment and derive mid to long term national development strategies; its English-language research report archive listed 203 reports in 2026.

metric.name: Research reports listed in the institute's English-language report archive

source.publisher: National Assembly Futures Institute, Archive, Research Reports

records.limits: The institute reports on itself. The count is a running total shown on an archive board ("Total 203"), not a dated annual figure, so asOf is the retrieval date, and it covers the English-language listing only; the Korean site organises reports differently and may hold more. The newest report in the English listing is dated 30 December 2024, so the count shows nothing published in English since then. A report count measures output, not whether any law or budget changed. The institute serves the National Assembly, not the executive, so it says nothing about foresight inside ministries. The founding dates and the Article 1 purpose come from the institute's own History and Vision pages (https://nafi.re.kr/home/eng/contents.do?menuPos=10 and menuPos=11), not from the statute text itself.

pattern.mechanism: The National Assembly legislated a futures research institute attached to the National Assembly and gave it a statutory mandate for long-range national strategy, so parliament holds its own foresight capacity independent of the government of the day.
preconditions: Cross-party support for a statute rather than a Speaker's initiative that could lapse
A parliamentary research ecosystem (budget office, research service, library) to house it beside
A domestic research community the institute can recruit from

records.title: Federal Chancellery situation and environment analysis (Perspektivstab)
records.claim: Switzerland's Federal Chancellery runs a long-term, continuous situation and environment analysis for the Federal Council that looks 10 to 15 years ahead; it produced Herausforderungen in 2007 with expertise from 30 federal offices, Perspektiven 2025 in 2011, Perspektiven 2030 in 2014, the Schweiz 2030 and Schweiz 2035 reports and the scenario report Perspektiven Schweiz 2040, which feed the Federal Council's legislature planning.

metric.name: Reports in the Chancellery situation and environment analysis series named on the page

secondMetric.name: Federal offices whose expertise fed the 2007 report Herausforderungen

source.publisher: Swiss Federal Chancellery, Lage- und Umfeldanalyse

records.limits: The report count is ours, made from the six titles the page names (Herausforderungen, Perspektiven 2025, Perspektiven 2030, Schweiz 2030, Schweiz 2035, Perspektiven Schweiz 2040). Both numbers describe the process, not its effect: six reports and 30 contributing offices show the analysis was made, not that a decision changed because of it. The Chancellery describes its own work and states that the reports serve as a basis for legislature planning; the source does not show how. The page gives publication years only up to 2014 and does not date Schweiz 2030, Schweiz 2035 or Perspektiven Schweiz 2040, so the series after 2014 is shown as existing, not as dated. Started is the year of the earliest report the page names, not the founding of the Perspektivstab, which the page does not date. The 30 offices figure belongs to the 2007 report only. The Chancellery is the Federal Council's staff office, so this is a staff function, not a minister's unit.

pattern.mechanism: The Federal Chancellery, as staff office of the Federal Council, pools experts from across the federal offices into a standing interdepartmental staff that writes a futures report timed to each legislature planning cycle.
preconditions: A collegial executive whose four-year legislature planning gives the report a fixed customer and date
A neutral staff office above the departments that can convene them without belonging to one
Federal offices willing to lend analysts to a cross-cutting exercise

records.title: Senate foresight delegation (Délégation sénatoriale à la prospective)
records.claim: The Bureau of the French Senate created a foresight delegation in April 2009, succeeding the planning delegation set up by the 1982 planning reform law, with a mandate to study changes in society and the economy and to build scenarios; it has 36 senators appointed in proportion to the political groups and adopted reports in every year from 2010 to 2022 listed on its page.

metric.name: Members of the Senate foresight delegation

source.publisher: Sénat (France), Présentation de la délégation à la prospective

records.limits: Membership measures size, not influence: 36 senators on a delegation say nothing about whether a report changed a law, and the delegation has no legislative power by design. It informs the Senate only; the National Assembly has no equivalent, as the page itself says, and the figure says nothing about foresight in the executive. The page's report list stops at 2022, although the delegation's main page shows a report dated June 2026, so the list is incomplete and no report count is given here. After the 2026 Senate renewal the main page states the delegations will be reconstituted, so the current membership is pending. It is filed against the foresight construct because its rules instruct it to draw up scenarios of change, which is foresight practice rather than technology assessment (France's technology assessment office, OPECST, is a separate body).

pattern.mechanism: A chamber's governing bureau turned an existing planning delegation into a standing foresight body of members with free choice of topics and a duty to write scenarios, which keeps it outside the legislative calendar.
preconditions: An earlier planning delegation whose seat and staff could be repurposed
A chamber with longer terms and partial renewal, which suits long-horizon work
Freedom from bill work, which lets members choose topics without committee pressure
pattern.travelled: The page names Finland's and Lithuania's committees for the future as the only European parliamentary equivalents; the French version is a delegation of senators served by Senate staff rather than a research institute.

records.title: Senate Commission on Future Challenges, Science, Technology and Innovation
records.claim: Chile's Senate created the Commission on Future Challenges, Science, Technology and Innovation in April 2012, modelled on Finland's Committee for the Future, with the Academy of Sciences, National Prize winners and university rectors as permanent members; by July 2024 more than 700 scientists had worked in more than 20 of its expert tables.

metric.name: Scientists who worked in the commission's expert tables (lower bound, as stated)

secondMetric.name: Expert tables convened by the commission (lower bound, as stated)

source.publisher: Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional de Chile, Serie Minutas Nº 62-24, Comisión Desafíos del Futuro, Ciencia, Tecnología e Innovación del Senado, antecedentes de trabajo legislativo

records.limits: Both figures are lower bounds (más de) and sit inside a four-page PDF, on page 3. They count participation, not influence: the same note lists five bills in the commission's legislative work, four members' motions and one government bill, all still in their first or second constitutional stage in July 2024, including two to create a national strategic foresight agency (Boletín 16.061-07) and a new foresight institution (Boletín 16.441-19). That means Chile had a parliamentary foresight committee but, as of the note's date, no statutory executive foresight body, and this record does not claim one. The commission is a standing Senate committee; the note does not count its sessions or reports. The figures are compiled by the Congress library at a director's request and are not independently audited. The Senate's own committee page (https://www.senado.cl/actividad-legislativa/comisiones/941) still lists the commission in 2026.

pattern.mechanism: A Senate committee co-opts the national science establishment as permanent members and runs expert tables that turn scientific frontiers into draft strategies and bills, giving parliament a standing futures agenda without a research staff of its own.
preconditions: A science academy and university rectors willing to sit with legislators
A senator who chaired it for a decade, which gave it continuity
A public outreach event, Congreso Futuro, that keeps the agenda visible
pattern.travelled: It was modelled on Finland's Committee for the Future; Chile kept the committee and replaced the Finnish government's duty to report with expert tables drawn from academia.

records.title: CFPB Compliance Assistance Sandbox, rescinded in 2022 and withdrawn again in 2025
records.claim: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau opened a national Compliance Assistance Sandbox in September 2019, issued two sandbox approval orders in December 2020, terminated one of them in June 2022 and rescinded the policy with effect from 30 September 2022; a reissued version of January 2025 was withdrawn in May 2025.

metric.name: Compliance Assistance Sandbox approval orders listed as granted

source.publisher: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, Innovation: granted applications

records.limits: The count of two is ours, made by counting the approval orders the CFPB lists as granted (Payactiv and Synchrony Bank); the page also lists one template (Build Commonwealth) and separate No-Action Letters and Trial Disclosure waivers, which are not counted here. The rescission and the 2025 withdrawal are read from Federal Register notices on govinfo.gov (87 FR 58439, 90 FR 1974 and 90 FR 20086), not from the cited page. The CFPB page is blocked to some automated clients. Two approvals over three years is evidence that the federal consumer-finance sandbox barely operated before it was ended, not that it failed on its merits: the Bureau's stated reasons were that the policies did not advance consumer-beneficial innovation and failed to meet standards for transparency and stakeholder participation. State sandboxes (Arizona, Utah and others) are subnational and are not counted.

pattern.mechanism: A federal consumer-finance regulator offered firms a statutory safe harbour and a written approval that a described product complied with named laws, in exchange for sharing data during the test. A later leadership judged that the policies did not advance innovation and lacked transparency, let the information-collection authority lapse and rescinded the policy.
preconditions: Statutory safe-harbour provisions the agency could invoke for good-faith reliance on its approval
Leadership continuity across administrations, which this sandbox did not have
Guardrails stopping a firm from marketing an approval as an endorsement
pattern.travelled: Sandboxes that rest on an agency policy statement rather than a statute can be switched off by the next director; the CFPB's was rescinded, reissued and withdrawn within three years.

records.title: CSA Regulatory Sandbox, succeeded by the Financial Innovation Hub
records.claim: Canada's provincial securities regulators, acting jointly as the Canadian Securities Administrators, authorised 13 firms through the CSA Regulatory Sandbox between 2016 and 2021, before it was succeeded by the CSA Financial Innovation Hub and its decision list stopped being updated in December 2023.

metric.name: Firms listed as authorised in the former CSA Regulatory Sandbox

source.publisher: Canadian Securities Administrators, Former CSA Regulatory Sandbox decisions

records.limits: The 13 is ours, counted from the firms the page lists under 'Former CSA Regulatory Sandbox'; the crypto trading platform decisions on the same page belong to a separate pre-registration process and are not counted. Most authorisations were crypto funds and token offerings from 2017 to 2019, and the page says nothing about outcomes. The sandbox was succeeded by the CSA Financial Innovation Hub, whose page lists research, workshops and 'testing environments' among possible activities, so the testing function may not be wholly gone; what ended is the named regime and its public register, which is why the record is concluded rather than dismantled. The earliest listed decision (AngelList, October 2016) predates the sandbox's 2017 start and is listed under it by the CSA. The site sits behind a JavaScript challenge that blocks simple scripted fetches.

pattern.mechanism: Thirteen provincial and territorial securities regulators agreed to process fintech registrations and exemptive relief faster and on a time-limited basis through a shared sandbox, then folded it into a broader innovation hub once crypto platforms moved to their own registration track.
preconditions: A passport-style system letting one principal regulator's decision apply across provinces
A wave of novel business models (crypto funds, token offerings) that did not fit existing categories
Regulators willing to publish each decision so the sandbox could be audited
pattern.travelled: Canada shows a sandbox absorbed once its main user group gets a dedicated rulebook: the crypto platforms that filled it moved to a pre-registration undertaking regime.

records.title: ASIC enhanced regulatory sandbox
records.claim: Australia's government introduced the enhanced regulatory sandbox on 1 September 2020, letting firms test financial services and credit activities for up to 24 months without a licence, and ASIC's register lists 23 users, four current and 19 past.

metric.name: Entities listed as current or past users of the enhanced regulatory sandbox exemption

source.publisher: Australian Securities and Investments Commission, Enhanced regulatory sandbox (ERS)

records.limits: The 23 is ours, counted from the two expandable lists ('Current users' 4, 'Past users' 19) on the day of retrieval; the page carries no headline total or reference date, and the lists change as exemptions start and lapse. Users notify ASIC rather than being selected, so the count measures take-up of an exemption, not supervised trials, and the page does not say how many past users went on to obtain a licence or simply stopped. Twenty-three users in six years is small for Australia's financial sector. ASIC's earlier sandbox, which the ERS superseded, is not counted.

pattern.mechanism: Parliament and Treasury put a licensing exemption into regulation, so an eligible firm can notify ASIC and start testing within set client and exposure limits, rather than applying for case-by-case relief.
preconditions: A statutory power to exempt from the licensing regime by regulation
Hard caps on clients and exposure so a notification regime stays safe without vetting
A public register so customers can check that a firm is a sandbox user
pattern.travelled: Australia moved from a regulator-run sandbox to a legislated notification exemption; low take-up suggests automatic entry does not by itself create demand.

records.title: SINTEG-Verordnung, the energy-transition experimentation clause
records.claim: Germany's federal government ran a time-limited regulatory experimentation clause for the SINTEG smart-energy showcases from June 2017 to June 2022, under which the Federal Network Agency received 49 notifications of experiments but only two claims for compensation of regulatory costs.

metric.name: Notifications to the Bundesnetzagentur under § 3 SINTEG-V

secondMetric.name: Applications for compensation of economic disadvantages under the clause

source.publisher: Bundesregierung (BMWK), Erfahrungen mit der SINTEG-Verordnung, Bericht nach § 13 SINTEG-V

records.limits: Both figures are inside a PDF (pages 4 and 5). The clause was open only to participants in the five funded SINTEG showcases, not to every firm in the country. A notification is an announcement of intent, not a completed trial, and the government's own report says use of the compensation mechanism fell well short of expectations because participants had to bear losses first and faced high administrative cost. The regulation expired by design in 2022. Because its core was ex post compensation, the report says the general legal framework applied essentially unchanged to participants, apart from the § 5 derogation for flexibility platforms.

pattern.mechanism: The federal government wrote a time-boxed ordinance letting showcase participants trial flexible grid use and be compensated afterwards for network charges and levies they would otherwise have lost, with the network regulator verifying each claim.
preconditions: A large funded demonstration programme to supply the experimenters
A regulator able to verify claims against network operators
State-aid clearance from the European Commission for the compensation
pattern.travelled: The lesson in the report is that ex post compensation with audited claims deters use, so a clause must waive rules up front to be taken up.

records.title: Experimenten Elektriciteitswet 2015-2018, and its erosion
records.claim: The Dutch economy ministry let energy cooperatives and owners' associations deviate from the Electricity Act 1998 through 19 exemptions granted in four rounds between 2015 and 2018, then closed the scheme to new entrants; by 2024 only 10 of the experiments were operational.

metric.name: Experiments operational under the exemption scheme

secondMetric.name: Exemptions granted 2015 to 2018 (peak)

source.publisher: Rijksdienst voor Ondernemend Nederland, Tussentijdse evaluatie Besluit experimenten decentrale duurzame elektriciteitsopwekking (January 2025)

records.limits: Both figures are inside a PDF (section 3, page labelled 4 of 12, PDF page 5). Nineteen is the total ever granted, used as the peak because no entry was possible after 2018. It counts exemptions and the 10 counts operating experiments, so the gap mixes projects that never started with ones that stopped; the sources do not show 19 operating at once. The only same-unit loss they document is from 19 exemptions granted to 15 still held. RVO's scheme page gives a third figure, 15 current exemption holders, which counts exemptions still held rather than experiments running. The minister closed the scheme on the advice of the Raad van State pending the new Energiewet (in force 1 January 2026), so part of the fall is a planned run-down rather than failure. The experiments are small local grids, and the report itself says their number and size limit what can be concluded.

pattern.mechanism: The ministry used a decree under the Electricity Act to let local cooperatives run their own project grids and supply members for up to ten years, testing whether the full act needed to apply to local renewable generation.
preconditions: An enabling article in the Electricity Act permitting time-limited derogations
Energy cooperatives able to carry grid-operator duties
An agency (RVO) to vet applications and monitor results
pattern.travelled: The Dutch case shows a sandbox closed to entry while a successor law was drafted; experiments outside the new law's scope must either fit it or end when their exemption expires.

records.title: Bac à sable réglementaire in the energy sector
records.claim: Under the 2019 energy and climate law, France's energy regulator CRE and the energy directorate DGEC granted temporary derogations from network access rules to 30 projects, 25 by CRE and 5 by DGEC, of which six were running and reporting indicators in May 2025 and two had been generalised into regulation in 2024.

metric.name: Projects granted derogations under the energy regulatory sandbox

source.publisher: Commission de régulation de l'énergie, Rapport n°2025-03 sur l'avancement des projets bénéficiant de dérogations

records.limits: The figure is inside a PDF (page 3). A derogation granted is not a trial run: the same report says only six of the 30 were in progress and producing indicators, and 14 further requests were awaiting a decision, mostly at DGEC. Progress data come from project holders and network operators. The sandbox covers network access and use in electricity and gas only, so it says nothing about experimentation elsewhere in French regulation.

pattern.mechanism: Parliament gave the energy regulator and the ministry a power to grant time-limited derogations from network access conditions, first through application windows and since November 2022 on a rolling basis, with annual public progress reports.
preconditions: A statutory derogation power covering named titles of the energy code
An independent regulator able to assess projects and publish follow-up
Network operators willing to host and measure non-standard arrangements
pattern.travelled: Two experiments (Enedis Reflex and an EDF project) were generalised by regulation in 2024, the route from sandbox to rule that many sandboxes lack.

records.title: State-administered adult education under the Adult Education and Family Literacy Act, and its erosion
records.claim: Federally funded, state-administered adult basic, adult secondary and English language programmes served 2,629,643 participants in fiscal year 2000, and by fiscal year 2021 served 770,179, after a fall through every year the table shows up to fiscal year 2020 (627,728) and a partial rebound in 2021.

metric.name: Participants in state-administered adult basic, adult secondary and English language acquisition programmes

secondMetric.name: Participants in the same programmes in fiscal year 2000, the highest year the table shows

source.publisher: U.S. Department of Education, National Center for Education Statistics, Digest of Education Statistics 2022, table 507.20 (from the OCTAE National Reporting System)

records.limits: The table starts in fiscal year 2000, so the second metric is the highest year it shows, not a proven all-time peak. FY2021 is a pandemic year and a partial rebound from FY2020's 627,728; FY2019, before the pandemic, already stood at 948,934, so most of the fall predates it. The fall is computed from two published table cells (about 71 percent), and part of it may reflect tighter participant definitions and federal performance reporting rather than lost provision; the table carries no note on definitional changes. The count covers only programmes reporting to the federal National Reporting System, not community college, employer or private adult learning, so it is not a national adult participation rate. Funding is shared between federal and state governments and the record does not attribute the decline to a single decision.

pattern.mechanism: The federal government funds states by formula to run adult basic education, high school equivalency preparation and English classes through local providers, and requires every state to report participants and outcomes into one national reporting system.
preconditions: A federal formula grant with a state match that keeps every state in the system
A national reporting system that defines a participant the same way across states
Local providers, from school districts to community colleges, willing to run low-margin classes
pattern.travelled: Formula-funded adult basic education is common across OECD countries; the American series shows how a stable statute can still deliver a shrinking service when appropriations flatten and accountability rules raise the bar for who counts.

records.title: STAP-budget training grant, abolished in 2024
records.claim: The Dutch employee insurance agency UWV paid individual training grants of up to 1,000 euros from 2022, approved more than 214,000 applications in five rounds that year, and stopped the scheme on 1 January 2024.

metric.name: STAP-budget applications approved in 2022

source.publisher: UWV (Uitvoeringsinstituut Werknemersverzekeringen), press release on the first 2023 STAP round

records.limits: The figure is the executing agency reporting on its own scheme, counts approved applications rather than courses completed, and is a lower bound ('ruim 214.000'); the same release puts people with a grant at more than 200,000. Approval is not participation: the release does not say how many approved grants were used, and the record does not show whether the courses improved anyone's position in the labour market. The end date comes from a second UWV page (https://www.uwv.nl/nl/stap-budget), not from the source page. Against a Dutch labour force of roughly ten million, one year of grants is around two percent of workers, so the scheme never moved the national participation share by itself. UWV's page gives no reason for the end, and the 2023 release reports that the cabinet had to tighten the scheme against misuse; the record documents the loss of this channel, not a collapse of Dutch adult learning, which other instruments still fund.

pattern.mechanism: The state replaced a tax deduction for training costs with a first-come grant that any worker or jobseeker could claim once a year from UWV, paid directly to a registered training provider, in fixed application windows with a capped budget.
preconditions: A national register of eligible training providers and courses
An agency with an online portal and identity check able to process tens of thousands of claims in hours
A fixed annual budget, which made demand visible as queues and exhausted windows
pattern.travelled: Individual training budgets also run in France (CPF) and Singapore (SkillsFuture Credit). The Dutch version shows the failure mode of open first-come windows: budgets ran out within hours, and the scheme was ended after two years.

records.title: INEA adult basic education
records.claim: Mexico's Instituto Nacional para la Educación de los Adultos certified 651,473 young people and adults as having completed a level of literacy, primary or secondary education in 2024, with 352,600 learners in its services at the close of the year.

metric.name: People who completed a level (literacy, primary or secondary) with INEA

secondMetric.name: Learners in INEA services at the close of the year

source.publisher: Instituto Nacional para la Educación de los Adultos, Programa Institucional 2025-2030, published in the Diario Oficial de la Federación

records.limits: The figures are INEA reporting on itself from its own tracking system (SASA). A completed level is a credential, often obtained by examination after self-study, and says nothing about how much was learned; one person can complete more than one level in a year. Against 27.5 million people aged 15 and over who, by the same document, have not finished basic education, a year's completions are about two percent of the backlog. The same document's indicator series shows completions fell sharply in 2019 and 2020 and rebounded from 2021, and it notes a fall in people served in 2024; chaining those published rates back from the 538,741 completions the document gives for 2023 puts 2019 at about 680,000 and 2018 at about 853,000, so 2024 is below both, by about 4 and 24 percent (our computation, from rounded rates).

pattern.mechanism: A federal institute and state adult education institutes run a semi-open model in which volunteers with a small stipend tutor adults in community spaces, and learners sit module examinations when ready, so a credential can be earned without a classroom timetable.
preconditions: A modular curriculum and an examination system recognised as equivalent to school certificates
A large network of subsidised volunteer tutors and community learning spaces
Federal and state co-financing, since delivery runs through state institutes
pattern.travelled: The semi-open, examination-at-will model resembles Brazil's ENCCEJA and Spain's adult graduation tests. The Mexican case shows the dependence on volunteer tutors, whose numbers rise and fall with the stipend budget.

records.title: Hello Training, public vocational training
records.claim: Japan's national and prefectural governments trained 225,176 people through public vocational training in fiscal year 2023, 95,752 of them jobseekers and 114,552 people in work, and a further 44,699 through job-seeker support training.

metric.name: Trainees in public vocational training (national and prefectural)

secondMetric.name: Trainees in job-seeker support training

source.publisher: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, policy evaluation sheet for policy goal VI-1-1 (public vocational training)

records.limits: The figures sit in a table on page 10 of a PDF. The 225,176 total includes 14,872 school-leaver trainees who are mostly young people entering work, not adults returning to learning. Against a labour force of roughly 69 million, public training reaches well under one percent of workers a year; most adult learning in Japan is employer-provided and is not counted here. Trainee counts say nothing about the quality of training beyond the employment rates the same table reports for jobseeker courses.

pattern.mechanism: The national government, through polytechnic centres run by its employment support agency, and the prefectures run free vocational courses for jobseekers and fee-based upskilling for employees, contract much of the jobseeker training to accredited private providers, and route trainees through Hello Work offices.
preconditions: A national network of public vocational schools and polytechnic centres
Unemployment insurance and a training allowance so jobseekers can afford to attend
Employment offices that refer trainees and track whether they find work
pattern.travelled: Korea's employer training system and Germany's Federal Employment Agency vouchers do similar work. The Japanese model is distinctive for keeping a large public provider of its own beside contracted private training.

records.title: CRADLE, DOST's collaborative R&D grant for academe and companies
records.claim: From 2017 the Department of Science and Technology's CRADLE programme funded 82 projects in which a university or research institute did R&D on a problem set by a Filipino company, worth 373.6 million pesos and involving 36 HEIs or RDIs and 83 companies by early 2022.

metric.name: CRADLE projects funded since 2017

secondMetric.name: Value of CRADLE projects funded since 2017

source.publisher: Department of Science and Technology (DOST), Science for Change Program, CRADLE call for proposals for CY 2023 funding

records.limits: The figures are DOST's own, stated in a call for proposals rather than an audited annual report, and they are cumulative from 2017 to the date of the call (March 2022), so no single year can be read off them. The number sits inside a PDF, on page 1. A funded project is an input: the document does not say how many were completed, how many technologies the partner companies adopted, or what the companies paid as their required counterpart of at least 20 percent. 82 projects over five years is small against the size of the Philippine economy, and the partner pool includes public research institutes as well as universities. No newer official count was found: the operating status rests on DOST's undated S4CP programme page, which still describes CRADLE as being implemented, so the 2022 figures may understate the programme's current size.

pattern.mechanism: DOST pays for an R&D project only when a Filipino company names the problem, commits counterpart funding and agrees to adopt the result, and a university or research institute does the research.
preconditions: University and RDI researchers able to work on applied industrial problems
Companies willing to co-fund and commit to adopting the result
A public grant line, here the Science for Change Program, that can contract with both sides
pattern.travelled: The design is close to Turkey's TÜBİTAK 1505 and Malaysia's PPRN: the firm states the problem and shares the cost. DOST later added an industry-led variant, iCRADLE, for larger consortia.

records.title: Public-Private Research Network (PPRN) matching grants
records.claim: Malaysia's Ministry of Higher Education approved 680 Public-Private Research Network projects involving 634 companies by the end of 2022, with a total allocation of RM27.7 million, and 469 of them had closed as successfully completed.

metric.name: PPRN projects approved, cumulative

secondMetric.name: Companies involved in approved PPRN projects, cumulative

source.publisher: Ministry of Higher Education Malaysia (KPT), Deputy Minister's speech at the PPRN 2.0 briefing and exhibition, 22 February 2023

records.limits: The figures come from a ministerial speech published on the ministry's site, not from an annual report or audit, and the page is in Malay with no English translation. They are cumulative since the programme began, so they do not show the annual rate. The projects are small: RM27.7 million across 680 projects is roughly RM41,000 of public money each, and the speech describes them as demand-driven projects to raise company productivity rather than joint research of the kind the indicator's survey item imagines. The productivity gain the speech quotes comes from a 2019 study by the Malaysia Productivity Corporation that is not cited here. The page writes the amount as 'RM 27,797,149.25 juta', a typo for RM27.8 million, and the record uses the rounded RM27.7 million the same sentence gives. The start year is not stated in the speech, which places PPRN under the 2015-2025 higher education blueprint.

pattern.mechanism: The ministry matches a company's own contribution, on a sliding scale by company size, to pay a university or public research institute researcher to solve a problem the company brings, and pays the researcher's fee only after the project is certified complete.
preconditions: University researchers allowed and rewarded to do consultancy-style projects for firms
A register of viable SMEs and agencies such as SME Corp that can vouch for them
A small grant line run centrally with a single online application system
pattern.travelled: PPRN 2.0 widened the original scheme after 2021. The same firm-states-the-problem design appears in the Philippines' CRADLE and Turkey's TÜBİTAK 1505.

records.title: TIA Technology Stations Programme, and its erosion
records.claim: South Africa's Technology Innovation Agency runs a network of university-based Technology Stations that gave 2,907 small firms science, engineering and technology services in 2024/25, against 3,167 at the five-year high in 2021/22, while the programme's budget fell from R105.9 million in 2020 to R93.98 million in 2025 and only 80 percent of the stations were operational.

metric.name: SMMEs accessing SET services through the Technology Stations network

secondMetric.name: SMMEs accessing SET services through the Technology Stations network, five-year peak

source.publisher: Technology Innovation Agency (TIA), Annual Report 2024/25

records.limits: The numbers sit inside a 188-page PDF, in the outcome table on PDF page 41 (printed page 39), and the budget figures in the Outcome 3 narrative on PDF page 42. The peak is the highest of the five years TIA reports, not a long-run maximum, and the fall from it is about 8 percent, which is computed here. The yearly count is noisy (1,990, 3,167, 2,671, 3,114, 2,907), and 2024/25 sits above two of the five years, so the erosion rests on what TIA reports about capacity: the budget cut, a fifth of the stations not functioning and no new high-end equipment, rather than on the count alone; the budget cut is in nominal rand and larger in real terms. A count of firms served measures university-to-firm technical service, testing and prototyping, which is a thinner form of research collaboration than joint projects: the same report says 73 percent of station equipment time goes to firms. The agency also reports a separate SMME figure (3,775) across all its programmes; this record uses only the Technology Stations line. A 2022 National Treasury spending review recommended moving the programme out of TIA altogether. The start year is taken from the programme's establishment under the former Department of Science and Technology and is not stated in the cited report.

pattern.mechanism: The state funds equipped technology stations inside universities, mostly universities of technology, whose staff and students sell subsidised testing, prototyping and process improvement to small firms that could not afford the equipment.
preconditions: Universities of technology with engineering staff and laboratory space
Steady operating and capital budgets, since stations with ageing equipment stop functioning
Small manufacturers close enough to a station to use it
pattern.travelled: The model resembles Canada's college applied research centres and Germany's Steinbeis transfer centres. Here the erosion came from flat budgets and no new capital equipment rather than from a decision to close it.

records.title: CORFO Programas y Consorcios Tecnológicos
records.claim: Chile's development agency CORFO had 49 technology programmes and consortia in execution during 2024, 38 technology programmes and 11 technology consortia, the consortia joining firms with universities and technology centres in multi-year R&D portfolios, after awarding six new consortia in 2023 with 1,500 million pesos of co-financing each.

metric.name: Technology programmes and consortia in execution

secondMetric.name: New technology consortia funded in the 2023 call

source.publisher: Corporación de Fomento de la Producción (CORFO), Dirección de Programas y Consorcios Tecnológicos, results presentation at the VI Encuentro de Programas y Consorcios Tecnológicos, January 2025

records.limits: The count is CORFO's own, from a slide deck hosted on CORFO's asset store, not an audited report, and it is a stock of initiatives in execution, including six new and ten finished in the year, not a flow of research output. The figure sits inside a PDF (page 13, footnote; the 38 and 11 split on page 9). Not every technology programme is led by a university: several of the 38 programmes are executed by a single company with no university partner named in the deck, so only the 11 consortia are collaborative by design and the 49 overstates university-firm collaboration. The second metric comes from a separate Ministry of Economy press release of 12 December 2023 announcing the 2023 awards, which is an award notice rather than evidence of delivery. The deck also gives figures for participating firms and private co-funding whose layout in the PDF does not make clear which label each number belongs to, so they are not used. The instrument began as the 2004 Consorcios Tecnológicos Empresariales and has been redesigned since; that start year is not stated in either cited source.

pattern.mechanism: CORFO co-finances long-lived consortia and programmes, for up to six years per award, at about 30 percent of cost for new consortia, inside a stated horizon of more than ten years, in which firms in one sector and universities or technology centres share a portfolio of R&D projects and the intellectual property they produce.
preconditions: Export sectors such as fruit, wine and aquaculture with firms that face shared technical problems
Universities with applied research groups in those sectors
An agency able to commit funding over a horizon longer than a political term
pattern.travelled: Chile's first-generation consortia of 2004 drew on Australia's Cooperative Research Centres; several, such as Biofrutales, still run.

records.title: Manufacturing USA innovation institutes
records.claim: In fiscal 2023 the 16 reporting Manufacturing USA institutes, public-private consortia sponsored by the Departments of Commerce, Defense and Energy, managed 929 applied research and development projects and held 2,921 memberships, 655 of them universities, community colleges and other academic members alongside 1,315 small and 493 large manufacturers.

metric.name: Ongoing applied research and development projects across the institutes

secondMetric.name: Academic members (universities, community colleges, etc.) of the institutes

source.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology, Advanced Manufacturing National Program Office, Manufacturing USA Report to Congress 2025 (covering FY 2023)

records.limits: The figures are the institutes' own reports aggregated by the program office, in Table 2 on PDF page 13 (printed page 11) of the report, and they cover fiscal 2023 although the report was posted in March 2026, so they are about three years old. Sixteen of the 17 institutes report; EPIXC joined mid-year and is excluded. The counts are memberships, not distinct organisations: a university that belongs to three institutes counts three times. The academic count mixes research universities with community colleges, which join mainly for workforce training, and the report does not say how many of the 929 projects actually pair a university with a firm; some are workforce or firm-only projects. Federal base funding was 160.4 million dollars in the year against 379.5 million of cost share and other funding, all as reported by the institutes, with no counterfactual for what members would have done anyway. The start year is the first institute, America Makes, established August 2012 per the report's Appendix B; the program's statute is the Revitalize American Manufacturing and Innovation Act of 2014.

pattern.mechanism: Federal agencies fund a standing consortium per manufacturing technology for a fixed term; firms, universities and colleges pay membership and cost share to sit on a shared applied research and workforce agenda that no single member would fund alone.
preconditions: Multi-year federal base funding with an expectation of non-federal cost share
Research universities and manufacturers in the same technology area willing to share pre-competitive IP
A national program office that sets common metrics across institutes run by different agencies
pattern.travelled: The model borrowed explicitly from Germany's Fraunhofer institutes, but institutes are member consortia with term-limited federal money rather than permanent contract-research labs, which leaves each one to find a sustainable funding model after its federal term.

records.title: Mitacs Accelerate research internships
records.claim: Mitacs, the federally and provincially funded not-for-profit, placed 4,859 students, recent graduates and postdoctoral fellows in Accelerate research internships with 2,314 host organisations under 2,406 professors in 2024-25, out of 20,885 internships across all its programmes that year.

metric.name: Interns in the Accelerate program

secondMetric.name: Host organisations in the Accelerate program

source.publisher: Mitacs, 2024-2025 Annual Report for Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada

records.limits: This is Mitacs reporting on itself to its federal funder: the Accelerate counts are on PDF page 28 and the 20,885 total on PDF page 2. Mitacs is a not-for-profit rather than a government body; ISED funding was 48 percent of its income in 2024-25 and the rest came from provinces and partners. Host organisations include not-for-profits, hospitals and municipalities as well as firms, so 2,314 overstates the firms involved. An internship is a funded unit of four to six months and one intern can hold several, so internships and interns are different counts; the 20,885 total also includes Globalink internships that bring international students to Canadian labs with no firm involved. The next report (2025-26, July 2026) gives 20,819 internships in total, against 21,432 in 2022-23. The capacity is now shrinking by plan: in 2024-25 Mitacs capped Accelerate units per university for lack of federal money, and its 2026-27 corporate plan (PDF page 9) foresees 12,540 internships on a 120 million dollar ISED grant, against more than 200 million of federal support in 2022-23. If that plan is delivered this record becomes an erosion. The 2003 start year, the first Mitacs research internship program, comes from ISED's evaluation of its funding to Mitacs, not from the cited report.

pattern.mechanism: A national intermediary splits the cost of a graduate student's or postdoc's research project inside a firm with the firm, using federal and provincial money, and uses the student's supervisor as the university link.
preconditions: A large pool of graduate students whose supervisors accept industry-defined projects
Firms willing to pay a fixed partner contribution per internship unit
Stable federal and provincial co-funding, since unit caps follow budget cuts directly
pattern.travelled: Close relatives are France's Cifre and Spain's Doctorados Industriales, which fund a whole doctorate inside a firm; Mitacs uses short, stackable units instead, which scale fast but tie volume closely to each year's budget.

records.title: COI-NEXT, co-creation centres for industry, academia and government
records.claim: Japan Science and Technology Agency ran 42 COI-NEXT co-creation centres in April 2023, 30 full-scale and 12 in a development stage, most led by universities and some by national research institutes, which in fiscal 2022 counted 1,073 participating organisations, 256 universities and research institutes and 817 companies and others, with 2,566 participants from the company side.

metric.name: Companies and other non-academic organisations participating in COI-NEXT centres

secondMetric.name: COI-NEXT centres supported (30 full-scale, 12 development-stage)

source.publisher: Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT), Science and Technology Policy Bureau, briefing for the 2023 autumn administrative project review (JST operating grant for co-creation programmes)

records.limits: The source is the funding ministry's own briefing, written to defend the programme's budget before a government spending review, and the participant counts are its self-reported totals. The counts are on PDF page 13 (printed page 12) and the centre counts on PDF page 10 (printed page 9). The organisation counts are for fiscal 2022 alone and are now more than three years old. The category is 'companies and others' (企業等), which can include municipalities and other non-academic bodies, so 817 is an upper bound on firms. The ministry's claim that external income of about 15.4 billion yen already exceeds about 14 billion yen of support counts resources the firms provided at their own valuation. The 2020 start year is inferred from the heading 'activities FY2020 to FY2022' on the same page. MEXT's fiscal 2026 budget sheet plans support for about 37 centres in the main fields, fewer than 42, which partly reflects centres graduating from support.

pattern.mechanism: JST funds a university-led centre for up to ten years around a stated vision for society, requires the university's leadership to commit and firms to contribute resources, and steps down its funding in the final years so the centre must find its own.
preconditions: Universities with industry-liaison offices able to run a multi-partner centre
Firms willing to second staff and contribute in kind over years
A funding agency able to commit to a ten-year horizon with stage-gate reviews
pattern.travelled: COI-NEXT succeeds the 2013 to 2021 Center of Innovation programme (COI STREAM) and carries over its centre format, adding regional centres led by local universities with municipalities and local firms.

records.title: MAI/DAI, innovation scholarships for research with partner companies
records.claim: Brazil's research council CNPq, with CAPES co-funding the 2024 call, has run four calls of its Mestrado e Doutorado Acadêmico para Inovação programme (2018, 2020, 2022 and 2024), in which about 80 science and technology institutions and more than 200 companies had taken part and at least 5,000 scholarships had been granted by 2024 for undergraduate and graduate student research on projects defined with partner firms.

metric.name: Scholarships granted across MAI/DAI calls

secondMetric.name: Companies that have taken part in MAI/DAI

source.publisher: Conselho Nacional de Desenvolvimento Científico e Tecnológico (CNPq), news release on the preliminary result of the first round of the 2024 MAI/DAI call

records.limits: (append) The 2018 start year is also stated on the cited page, which lists the earlier calls as 2018, 2020 and 2022.

pattern.mechanism: The national research council pays scholarships for students whose thesis or initiation project is a research project defined with a partner firm, run through a university that must have a technology transfer office and an innovation policy, and since 2024 asks the firm for a financial counterpart.
preconditions: Graduate programmes willing to accept industry-defined thesis topics
University technology transfer offices able to manage firm agreements and IP
Firms with enough R&D activity to host and co-supervise students
pattern.travelled: The design follows industrial doctorate schemes such as France's Cifre, but pays the scholarship to the student through the university rather than as a salary from the firm, which lowers the firm's commitment.

records.title: NWO Perspectief, ended by the 2026 spring budget
records.claim: NWO's Perspectief programme, funded mainly by the Ministry of Economic Affairs, awarded 12 public-private technology consortia in 2025 with 46.4 million euros of subsidy, each joining at least three knowledge institutions with at least four companies or other users paying at least 30 percent of costs; the ministry's own page records that the last Perspectief round started in July 2026.

metric.name: Perspectief projects awarded

secondMetric.name: Perspectief subsidy awarded

source.publisher: Ministerie van Economische Zaken, Bedrijvenbeleid in beeld, NWO Perspectief programma (data from NWO)

records.limits: The counts are NWO's awards as published by the ministry, and an award is a project starting, not a result: projects run for up to six years, so awarded consortia will continue until the early 2030s although no new ones will be funded after the 2026-27 round. 2025 was an unusually large year: the same table gives 4 projects in 2024 and 5 to 9 in most years since 2016, so 12 is the peak, not the norm. The page's table of participating companies has two columns whose labels do not make clear which is total and which is SMEs (70 and 79 in 2025), so company counts are not used. The termination is stated on the cited page only as 'the last round started in July 2026'; the reason, the end of ministry funding in the first supplementary budget to the 2026 Spring Memorandum, is in NWO's news release of 2 April 2026, which also states NWO's objection. The final round has 26.5 million euros by NWO's account. The start year is approximate: NWO's release says the programme has run for twenty years, and the ministry's series begins in 2016.

pattern.mechanism: The research council runs a yearly competition for multi-year consortia in which universities receive the subsidy and companies and civil-society users co-fund in cash and kind, sit on a user committee and get first access to the results.
preconditions: A ministry willing to route industrial policy money through the research council
Firms willing to co-fund early-stage (TRL 1 to 6) research with no exclusive claim to it
Universities of technology able to assemble multi-group consortia
pattern.travelled: Perspectief was the Dutch counterpart of collaborative programmes such as the competence centres in Sweden; the Netherlands ended it while announcing a new national agency for disruptive innovation, so the bridging function moves to an instrument not yet built.

records.title: Inland Rail, and its consolidation at Parkes
records.claim: The Australian Government began building Inland Rail, a Melbourne to Brisbane freight railway, in 2018 through the Australian Rail Track Corporation, which passed delivery to its subsidiary Inland Rail Pty Ltd in May 2024; a verification report delivered to the infrastructure department in November 2025 reported the company's estimate at completion of A$45.6 billion (P90, Target scenario, estimate current as of December 2024) with completions finalised in May 2036, and the 2026-27 Budget then consolidated the project at Parkes and returned $4.4 billion in equity.

metric.name: Estimate at completion of the full Inland Rail programme, Target scenario (P90)

secondMetric.name: Month in which completions are finalised under the Target scenario schedule

source.publisher: ACIL Allen for the Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts, Verification and assurance of Inland Rail scope, design, delivery and cost, final report of 20 November 2025, tabled at Senate Rural and Regional Affairs and Transport Budget Estimates 2026-27

records.limits: Both numbers are forecasts, not outturn: they are Inland Rail Pty Ltd's own December 2024 estimate as reviewed by a consultancy (ACIL Allen) for the department, and the report itself says IRPL's core assumptions have not been met and the cost is likely to increase with further delay. The faster Stretch scenario is A$44.7 billion with completions by June 2035. Both figures are in Table 1.1 on PDF page 12; the 2018 start and the 2015 business case are on page 8. The truncation is not in this report: it comes from Budget Paper No. 2, 2026-27 (https://budget.gov.au/content/bp2/download/bp2_2026-27.pdf, PDF page 139, printed page 124), which says the government will 'consolidate the Inland Rail project at Parkes and preserve the remaining rail corridor and intermodal sites for future investment, with $4.4 billion in equity to be returned to the Budget'. The 2015 business case cost and the estimates in the 2023 Schott review are published on infrastructure.gov.au, which did not answer from the machine used for this record, so no original baseline is given here and the overrun against it is not stated. The erosion is to planned scope: Beveridge to Parkes is still being built and nothing in service was lost, and no section of the full line has opened to double-stacked through traffic.

pattern.mechanism: The Commonwealth committed to a 1,700 km freight line through a government-owned track company and started construction before the route ends, approvals and designs were settled; when successive reviews put the cost far above the budget, it moved delivery into a dedicated subsidiary, commissioned independent cost assurance and then cut the line back to the sections already under way.
preconditions: A government-owned rail company able to take Commonwealth equity and build without a separate procurement for each section
Construction started on sections whose environmental approvals and designs were immature
A budget process willing to recognise a reversal and return equity rather than keep funding the full scope
pattern.travelled: The pattern matches gbr-hs2 in this corpus: a national line cut back to its first sections after its cost estimate tripled, with the corridor preserved for later.

records.title: Kehärata airport rail loop, and its cost overrun
records.claim: The Finnish state, with the City of Vantaa paying part of the cost, began building the Kehärata (Ring Rail Line) through Helsinki Airport in Vantaa in 2009; construction costs came in above estimate, a glycol leak found at the airport took a year to resolve and reset the schedule, passenger service began on 1 July 2015, and the construction cost finally came to 770 million euros.

metric.name: Final construction cost of Kehärata

secondMetric.name: Delay attributed to resolving the glycol leak at the airport

source.publisher: Väylävirasto (Finnish Transport Infrastructure Agency), news article 'Kehärata on ollut ilonamme jo viisi vuotta', 1 July 2020

records.limits: The 770 million euro figure is stated by the delivery agency in an anniversary news article ('Hankkeen rakennuskustannukset olivat lopulta 770 miljoonaa euroa'), not taken from an audited final account, and the page flags itself as an old article. The page says only that costs were higher than estimated; the size of the overrun comes from a different source: the Ministry of Transport and Communications release of 10 March 2008 (https://lvm.fi/-/keharadan-kustannukset-ylittyvat-770641) put the forecast at 590 million euros, 75 million more than the estimate before it, so the final cost is about 30 percent above the 2008 forecast and about 50 percent above the earlier one. Those percentages are computed here, and neither source states the price basis, so part of the gap is inflation over 2008 to 2015. The originally planned opening date is not on either page, so the schedule slip is given only as the one year the agency attributes to the glycol problem. The state and the City of Vantaa shared the cost (73 and 27 percent under the original agreement, per the 2008 release). The same article says population growth along the line has been slower than forecast, especially in Kivistö, and that not all of the line's targets had been met by 2020. One line is not a national delivery record.

pattern.mechanism: The state rail administration and the City of Vantaa cofunded an airport loop tied to new housing zoned along the line; when the cost forecast rose before construction, the ministry renegotiated the cost split and kept the start date, then absorbed a further overrun from ground contamination at the airport.
preconditions: A municipality willing to share capital cost in exchange for land-use value along the line
A state budget able to absorb an overrun on a single project without stopping it
Airport ground conditions that were not fully surveyed before tunnelling

records.title: Chixoy hydroelectric project, and its cost and time overrun
records.claim: Guatemala's state electricity institute INDE built the 300 MW Chixoy hydroelectric project under contracts signed in 1977 and 1978; after the power-tunnel lining collapsed in late 1983 it entered commercial operation in November 1985, 41 months later than originally planned, at a final cost of US$823.1 million excluding finance charges against an appraisal estimate of US$372.7 million, an increase of 120 percent.

metric.name: Final project cost excluding finance charges, as estimated by INDE

secondMetric.name: Appraisal cost estimate excluding finance charges

source.publisher: World Bank, Project Completion Report, Guatemala Chixoy Hydroelectric Power Project (Loan 1605-GU), Report No. 10258-GU, 31 December 1991

records.limits: The final cost is INDE's own figure as reported in the World Bank's completion report, which says INDE's data 'reflect shortcomings' and could not reconcile cost increases with physical quantities (para. 4.26, PDF page 32). Both costs and the 120 percent increase are in the table under para. 4.04 (PDF page 25), in para. 4.24 (PDF pages 31 to 32) and in Table 3 (PDF page 71); the 41-month delay against the original plan is in para. 4.04 (PDF page 24) and the summary's 'about 3.5 years' on PDF page 8; para. 3.18 (PDF page 19) records that the bids implied commercial operation by October 1981 while the appraisal team judged it unlikely before June 1982; the November 1985 start of operation is in para. 2.08 (PDF page 13). The text is OCR of a scanned 1991 document. The appraisal estimate is dated to the March 1977 appraisal; its exact price basis is not stated, and price increases account for US$141.1 million of the overrun by INDE's breakdown. The power tunnel's lining remained structurally unreliable after repair, so 'concluded' means built and operating, not sound. The project was co-financed by the World Bank, the IDB and others, though INDE owned and built it. The PCR records that the resettlement programme was judged flawed in conception; the 1980 to 1982 killings of Río Negro residents displaced by the reservoir, documented elsewhere, are outside what this cost figure measures and are the larger failure of this project. This is a 1977 to 1985 build and says little about Guatemala's delivery capacity now.

pattern.mechanism: The state utility chose a single-stage scheme with a 26 km power tunnel through poorly understood geology, contracted the works on winning bids before the seismic redesign that followed the 1976 earthquake was settled, and financed the doubling of cost with supplementary loans and local funds.
preconditions: A state utility with a monopoly on generation and access to multilateral loans
Cost estimates built from bid prices with contingencies sized for ordinary geology
Lenders willing to add supplementary financing rather than stop a half-built dam

records.title: Abuja-Kaduna-Zaria-Kano dual carriageway, and the termination of its 2017 contract
records.claim: Nigeria's Federal Ministry of Works awarded the rehabilitation of the Abuja-Kaduna-Zaria-Kano dual carriageway to Julius Berger on 20 December 2017 at an initial N155.7 billion with a 36-month completion period; after repeated variations and augmentations, the Federal Executive Council cut the contract sum under Section I from N797.3 billion to N740.8 billion on 23 September 2024, and the ministry issued a 14-day termination notice on 4 November 2024 after the contractor rejected the reviewed sum and stopped work.

metric.name: Contract sum (Contract No. 6350) before the September 2024 downward review

secondMetric.name: Initial contract sum at award

source.publisher: Federal Ministry of Works (Nigeria), press release 'Notice of Termination of Contract for the Rehabilitation of the Abuja-Kaduna-Zaria-Kano Dual Carriageway, Section I (Abuja-Kaduna)', 4 November 2024

records.limits: The source is the ministry's own statement in a dispute with the contractor, so it carries the government's side. Figures are nominal naira across years of high inflation and a large devaluation, so most of the roughly fivefold growth may be price change rather than poor delivery; the ministry also re-scoped Section I to concrete pavement and gave 38 km of it to Dangote, so the 2024 sum buys a different road from the 2017 one. The termination release frames the N797.3 billion review as concerning 'Section I' while the N155.7 billion award covered all three sections; a ministry release of 7 October 2024 (https://www.fmw.gov.ng/index.php/read/3233) describes the same N740 billion as the total contract sum within Julius Berger's scope, with N391 billion already paid, so the two sums may or may not cover identical scope. What ended is the 2017 contract, not the road: Sections II and III were partly completed and handed over before 2023, and a ministry update dated 9 September 2026 (https://www.fmw.gov.ng/index.php/read/3425, also shown as a banner on the source page) says the government took over the project, finished 118 km of lot 1, has lot 2 over 60 percent complete and schedules completion for December 2026. Earlier ministry pages (https://fmw.gov.ng/index.php/read/2352) give a 36-month completion period from 21 May 2018, so the road is at least five years late; a 2018 ministry release (https://fmw.gov.ng/index.php/read/1299) states the award sum as N155.47 billion, slightly different from the N155.75 billion here. No audit or Bureau of Public Procurement document was opened.

pattern.mechanism: The federal government let one large contract for a 375 km corridor, paid for it through repeated variations and augmentations, and when a new minister demanded a lower fixed price the contractor refused and the ministry terminated, split the work among other contractors and took direct control.
preconditions: Award and variation approvals routed through the Federal Executive Council rather than a fixed-price baseline
A naira devaluation and inflation shock that made earlier contract sums unenforceable
Political will to terminate a dominant contractor on a flagship route

records.title: Educação de Jovens e Adultos (EJA), and its erosion
records.claim: Brazil's Educação de Jovens e Adultos, the second-chance basic education modality delivered mostly by public school networks, enrolled 2,962,322 students in 2021 and 2,252,069 in 2025, a fall of about 24 percent in four years, according to INEP's School Census.

metric.name: Enrolments in Educação de Jovens e Adultos (EJA), total of public and private networks

secondMetric.name: Enrolments in EJA in 2021, the highest year of the 2021 to 2025 series in this release

source.publisher: Instituto Nacional de Estudos e Pesquisas Educacionais Anísio Teixeira (INEP), Censo Escolar da Educação Básica 2025, results presentation (Gráfico 24)

records.limits: Both numbers are read off a bar chart in a PDF slide deck (Gráfico 24, PDF page 25), not a table, and the chart labels the totals as public plus private. The deck's window only starts in 2021, so the 'peak' is the first year shown and not EJA's historical peak: INEP's 2024 presentation (PDF page 35) shows 3,002,749 enrolments in 2020, and the decline is older than either window. The real loss from the modality's peak is therefore understated, not overstated. Enrolment counts registrations in the census reference week, not adults who attend or complete. A falling count is not by itself a capability loss: part of the fall reflects more young people finishing regular school on time, so fewer need a second chance, and INEP's own 2024 deck notes that EJA also absorbs teenagers who left regular school after repeated failure, so EJA is not purely adult learning. The source gives no count of the adults who lack completed basic education, so the 2,252,069 enrolments cannot be turned into the share of adults the indicator asks for. The 1996 start is the Lei de Diretrizes e Bases (Lei 9.394) that set EJA as a modality; it is not stated at the source URL, and adult schooling in Brazil predates it.

pattern.mechanism: The federal education law makes basic education for youths and adults a modality of the public school system, and state and municipal networks deliver it in evening classes, funded through the per-pupil FUNDEB transfers with a lower weight than regular schooling. Enrolment has fallen every year since at least 2020 as networks close evening classes and fewer young adults enter.
preconditions: A national school census that counts every enrolment by modality each year
State and municipal school networks with buildings and teachers free in the evening
A per-pupil federal-state funding formula that includes the modality, which also sets the incentive to keep or cut it

records.title: Government-funded adult further education in England, and its erosion
records.claim: Participation of adults aged 19 and over in government-funded further education and skills in England fell from a recent peak of nearly 3.3 million learners in 2012/13 to 1.6 million in 2020/21, and stood at 1,798,970 in 2024/25, according to the Department for Education.

metric.name: Adult (19+) further education and skills participation, education and training plus adult apprenticeships, England

secondMetric.name: Adult (19+) further education and skills participation at the most recent peak, as published (rounded, 'nearly 3.3 million')

source.publisher: Department for Education, Further education and skills, academic year 2024/25 (accredited official statistics), section 'Total adult (19+) activity in further education and skills (including apprenticeships)'

records.limits: The peak is published only as rounded prose ('nearly 3.3 million learners in 2012/13'), so the second metric is a rounded figure and the fall to 1,798,970 (about 45 percent) is approximate. The department calls 2012/13 the 'most recent peak', which implies earlier years may have been higher; the record does not claim the series' all-time high. The release also warns that the 2024/25 introduction of the Adult Skills Fund and tailored learning breaks the long-running Education and Training time series, although it says total further education and skills volumes are unaffected. Participation counts learners on government-funded or loan-funded provision recorded on the Individualised Learner Record, so adults in employer-paid, private or university learning are outside it, and it is England only, not the United Kingdom. The total includes adult apprenticeships, whose own funding reforms moved volumes independently of the adult skills budget. A headcount cannot show course length or level, so some of the fall may reflect a change in the mix of courses rather than fewer adults learning. The rise to 1.8 million in 2022/23 and 2023/24 came mostly from Multiply and Skills Bootcamps, according to the release, and Multiply funding stopped in March 2025. The 1992 start date is the Further and Higher Education Act that created the funded further education sector; it is not stated at the source URL.

pattern.mechanism: The Department for Education funds colleges, local authorities and training providers through a national adult skills budget and later loans and apprenticeship levy funding, and counts every funded learner through a single administrative return.
