pattern.mechanism: After its external co-financing package changed, the government kept the Bridge Authority as executing agency and paid for the bridge from its own budget. The Authority revised the project document as costs rose and opened the road deck in 2022, with rail running on the lower deck since.
preconditions: A fiscal position able to absorb a multi-billion-dollar project without concessional lenders
A specialised bridge authority with a design and supervision record from the earlier Jamuna Bridge
Political commitment strong enough to carry repeated cost and schedule revisions
pattern.travelled: Self-financing a flagship after donors withdraw is rare. Where it has been tried, the usual result is the one here: the asset was delivered, and its cost and schedule were judged against shifting baselines.

records.title: eRecovery (єВідновлення) housing compensation programme
records.claim: Ukraine's government, through the Ministry for Development and the Diia digital platform, paid war-damage housing compensation to 231,681 families totalling UAH 119.1 billion by 10 July 2026. Of these, more than 153,000 families received repair payments, and more than 74,000 received certificates to buy replacement housing for homes that were destroyed.

metric.name: Families that received eRecovery compensation, cumulative

secondMetric.name: Total eRecovery compensation paid, cumulative

source.publisher: Ministry for Development of Communities and Territories of Ukraine (Ministry for Recovery): eRecovery programme results

records.limits: These are the ministry's own running totals, published as press releases and not as a statistical series, and nothing independent audits them. The page shows recovery for households whose claims were accepted, not the share of all damaged housing compensated. For destroyed homes, more than 161,000 applications produced certificates for about 74,000 families, and only about 33,000 had bought a home, so most of the destroyed-housing caseload is unresolved. The page ties the repair payments to the World Bank HOPE project and the own-plot rebuilding payments to the Council of Europe Development Bank HOME project, and does not say who funds the certificates for destroyed homes, so how much of the delivery rests on external money is not shown here. The record evidences recovery after a war shock and says nothing about preparedness before one. Amounts are nominal hryvnias. The figure is the ministry's results update of 10 July 2026.

pattern.mechanism: The Rada created a statutory right to compensation for war-damaged housing. The ministry and the Ministry of Digital Transformation then ran claims, damage inspection and payment through the Diia app and the state register of damaged property, paying repair grants to bank accounts and issuing purchase certificates for destroyed homes.
preconditions: A national digital identity and services app that most households already used
Property and damage registers that could be linked to verify claims
External concessional finance willing to fund payouts through government systems during a war

records.title: Brave1 defence technology cluster
records.claim: Ukraine's government set up the Brave1 cluster in 2023 under the Ministry of Digital Transformation. By September 2026 it had awarded more than 1,000 non-repayable grants worth UAH 6.2 billion to private defence-technology developers, whose products it tests with the armed forces and moves toward serial production.

metric.name: Defence technology development funded by Brave1 since 2023

secondMetric.name: Grants awarded to Ukrainian defence developers since 2023

source.publisher: Brave1 defence innovation cluster (state institution under the Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine): news release

records.limits: The source is the cluster reporting on itself in a news release, with a minister's quote. Neither the 6.2 billion nor the grant count is broken down by year or audited. The figures measure money and grants going out, not what was delivered: they do not show how many funded products reached serial production or the front. The impact claims on the page, a 1.7-point gain in technology readiness and 79 percent of firms saying they had no alternative, come from a survey of defence-tech manufacturers in a study by the BRDO Office for Effective Regulation and are self-reported. Grants are one-way subsidies, so the record evidences public funding of private developers plus joint testing, which is a thin reading of joint delivery. The standard grant programme accounts for UAH 2.3 billion of the total; most of the rest, UAH 3.7 billion, went to 34 competition projects for missiles, air defence and autonomy, so the money is concentrated in a few large awards. Wartime urgency and secrecy limit what can be verified.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Digital Transformation, with the Ministry of Defence and the General Staff, set up a state cluster. It registers private developers, funds them through tiered grants, arranges battlefield testing and military feedback, and steers money toward priority areas the military defines.
preconditions: An acute, shared national objective that private firms and the state both accept
A large pool of small engineering and software firms able to iterate quickly
A military willing to test immature products and return field data to developers

records.title: Noor-Ouarzazate solar complex
records.claim: Morocco's solar agency MASEN had the Noor-Ouarzazate I, II and III concentrated solar plants (510 MW) built, grid-connected and fully operational by October 2018, at a completed capital cost of US$1,962 million, about 7 percent below the appraisal estimate of US$2,093 million. Noor II and III then generated an average of 739 GWh a year in 2019 to 2023, against the 1,144 GWh expected at appraisal.

metric.name: Completed capital cost of the Noor-Ouarzazate complex (appraisal estimate US$2,093 million)

secondMetric.name: Average annual generation of Noor-Ouarzazate II and III, against 1,144 GWh expected at appraisal

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR00043, Morocco Noor Solar Power Project (P131256, P164288), March 2025

records.limits: The lender graded its own project here. The World Bank financed it, and the report rates the outcome 'Moderately Unsatisfactory', with efficacy and efficiency both 'Modest'. The cost figure is the Bank's economic-analysis number for the Ouarzazate plants. A footnote says it nets a 14 percent saving at Noor I against an overrun at Noor III. On schedule the report gives no figure, only that Noor II and III were built 'with a delay of just a few months'. Cost was on budget, but output was not. Generation ran about 35 percent below the appraisal expectation. Noor II missed its peak-hour share, at 32 percent against a 41 percent target. The Noor III tower plant had two prolonged outages caused by cracks in its molten salt tank: September 2021 to December 2022, and April 2024 to at least October 2024, when the report says it was still offline. The second phase financed under the same operation, Noor-Midelt, had not started construction by the June 2024 closing date. The project therefore delivered 510 MW against a 1,310 MW target. The economic rate of return was negative without carbon benefits. Generation-mix forecasts did not materialise either: coal's share rose to almost 70 percent by 2020. The capital came largely from concessional international lenders, with about US$4.1 billion disbursed from all financiers. A copy of this design would need that finance. All figures are read from a 40-page PDF.

pattern.mechanism: MASEN, the state agency set up for the Moroccan Solar Plan, tendered the plants to private developers under power purchase agreements and sat between them and the national utility ONEE. A World Bank-financed cost mitigation mechanism covered the gap between the solar tariff and what the utility paid.
preconditions: Concessional finance pooled from the World Bank, KfW, AfDB, EIB, the EU and AFD, coordinated by one national agency
A state buyer willing to absorb a tariff above the cost of grid power for the life of the contracts
A site with high direct irradiation where the state delivered land, access, water and grid evacuation before the developers arrived
pattern.travelled: Morocco tried the same structure at Noor-Midelt. Construction had not started by June 2024, and Noor-Midelt II was redesigned as photovoltaic plus battery storage, because PV and battery costs fell while CSP costs did not.

records.title: Catastrophe insurance regime and the Solidarity Fund against Catastrophic Events (FSEC)
records.claim: Morocco's dual catastrophe insurance regime under Law 110-14 took effect in January 2020. It offered private cover to close to 9 million insured people and set up the FSEC, financed by a parafiscal levy, for the uninsured. After the September 2023 Al Haouz earthquake, the government deployed the FSEC for the first time, and it mobilised US$300 million to compensate uninsured victims.

metric.name: Compensation funding mobilised by the FSEC for uninsured victims of the Al Haouz earthquake (US$25 million from reserves plus US$275 million from sovereign reinsurance)

secondMetric.name: People insured against bodily injury in catastrophic events under the private scheme

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR00006503, Morocco Disaster Risk Management Development Policy Loan with a Catastrophe Deferred Drawdown Option (P168580), June 2024

records.limits: Both sources are the World Bank reporting on reforms it financed: an FSEC programme-for-results loan and a Cat DDO whose prior actions were these reforms. The US$300 million is money mobilised, not money paid to households. The ICR says the compensation process was still under way in June 2024 and gives no count of victims compensated. Nothing here shows what share of the earthquake's losses the regime covered. The 9 million and 6 million figures are coverage estimates from a 2022 results brief, not counts of policies or payouts. The regime's one real test is a single earthquake. One of the Cat DDO's own result indicators was missed by a wide margin: Interior ministry officials trained on victim registration stood at 7.4 percent against a 90 percent target. The audit of the FSEC's internal controls had not been completed. The two World Bank documents disagree on the law's date: the ICR says Law 110-14 was promulgated in 2016, while the brief says it was adopted in 2018. Started is therefore the year the regime took effect. The headline figures are read from a 45-page PDF and a web page.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Interior and the Ministry of Economy and Finance legislated a two-tier regime. Private insurers carry catastrophe cover for people who already hold policies. A public fund, paid for by a parafiscal levy and backed by sovereign reinsurance, gives basic compensation to the uninsured once the government declares an event a catastrophe.
preconditions: An insurance market with a policy base wide enough to carry catastrophe cover, and a levy base to fund the public tier
An Interior ministry able to declare a catastrophe and register uninsured victims through local agents and an online portal
International reinsurance capacity and World Bank technical and financial backing for the design

records.title: Government Resolution 218 complex projects for high-tech production
records.claim: Under Government Resolution 218 of 9 April 2010, Russia's Ministry of Science and Higher Education subsidised 41 joint firm-university complex projects in their R&D stage in 2024, from the 14th and 15th selection rounds. Federal funding was 2.708 billion rubles, and firms put in 4.14 billion rubles of their own (156 percent of the budget funds). The ministry reports 161 technologies developed and handed over to production by January 2025.

metric.name: Complex projects receiving state support in the year (14th and 15th selection rounds)

secondMetric.name: Extrabudgetary funds raised from participating firms (156% of budget funds)

source.publisher: Ministry of Science and Higher Education of the Russian Federation, report on the ministry's results for 2024 (June 2025)

records.limits: The ministry is reporting on its own programme in its own annual report, and none of it is audited. The figures are counts of subsidised projects and money, not a measure of how much research firms and universities do together. The 156 percent co-funding largely reflects the rule itself, which requires each firm to match the subsidy at least one for one. The report's cumulative total of 133 projects cannot be reconciled, from this document, with 15 selection rounds since 2010, so the programme's scale over time is unclear. Whether output or new projects per year have grown or shrunk is not shown. The '161 technologies transferred' figure is self-defined and does not show sales. The terms of the scheme and the 2010 to 2020 funding total come from the operator's site, which a private contractor runs. That site says that from 2025 the projects run inside a departmental project of the state programme for scientific and technological development. That reorganisation could change the scheme, and this record does not track it. The figures are read from a 3 MB Russian-language PDF. The figures say nothing about the effect of post-2022 sanctions on the firms involved.

pattern.mechanism: The Russian government subsidises the manufacturer rather than the university. A firm wins a competitive subsidy to commission R&D from a Russian university or state research institute, co-funds it at least one for one, and must build the production line and sell the product from its own resources.
preconditions: Manufacturers with enough capital to match the subsidy and build production
Universities and state institutes with applied R&D capacity that firms are willing to contract
A federal budget line sustained across 15 selection rounds since 2010

records.title: Takaful and Karama cash transfer programme
records.claim: Egypt's Ministry of Social Solidarity launched the Takaful and Karama cash transfers in early 2015 and expanded coverage from an initial 1.5 million to 4.675 million households (about 17 million people) by project close in 2024, revising the eligibility threshold and adding top-ups in response to COVID-19 and later inflation, while the cash transfer budget rose from EGP 3.5 billion in 2015 to EGP 41 billion in 2024.

metric.name: Households receiving Takaful and Karama cash transfers

secondMetric.name: Budget allocation for cash transfers in 2024 (from EGP 3.5 billion in 2015)

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Strengthening Social Safety Net Project (P155558)

records.limits: The construct is the speed of rule and programme change, and the headline number is coverage, which is scale rather than speed. The ICR describes the COVID-19 response (a revised proxy-means-test threshold, wider coverage, Meeza cards, top-ups) in prose without dates or a count of households added by the revision, so how fast the rules moved is not measured here. The 4.675 million includes legacy Daman social pension beneficiaries absorbed into the programme by consolidation, so part of the growth is relabelling rather than new reach. The budget figure is nominal Egyptian pounds across years of high inflation and two large devaluations, so the 12-fold rise overstates the real increase. Coverage still reaches only about 28 percent of the poorest quintile. The source is the World Bank's own completion report on a project it financed with US$900 million, read from a PDF, and the counts are administrative figures reported by the ministry.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Social Solidarity built a proxy-means-tested registry and a cash transfer programme with World Bank financing, then used the registry's threshold and benefit levels as the levers it moved when COVID-19, inflation and devaluation hit.
preconditions: A national social registry, which reached 11.3 million registered households, to retarget against
A payment rail through post offices and later Meeza cards that could absorb more beneficiaries without a new system
Fiscal room created by the 2014 energy subsidy reform, which the programme was launched to offset

records.title: Renewable energy feed-in tariff programme and Benban
records.claim: Egypt's Ministry of Electricity and Renewable Energy took private sector-owned renewable generation from 0 MW in October 2015 to 1,500 MW at financial closure by the end of FY2017/18 under its feed-in tariff programme, with about US$2 billion of private investment, much of it in the Benban solar park.

metric.name: Private sector-owned renewable energy capacity reaching financial closure

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Egypt First, Second and Third Fiscal Consolidation, Sustainable Energy and Competitiveness Programmatic DPF

records.limits: The indicator was softened mid-programme: DPF1 asked for 1,500 MW commissioned, and DPF2 redefined it as 1,500 MW at financial closure, so the number shows contracts financed, not plants generating, and the ICR's statement that Benban was then the world's fourth-largest solar plant sits in a footnote that says it 'promises' capacity. Most developers and lenders were foreign, and the deal flow leaned on IFC debt (US$653 million) and MIGA risk insurance (US$210 million), so how much of the collaboration was the Egyptian state's own capacity and how much was World Bank Group de-risking cannot be separated. The figure does not show the tariff cost carried by the state offtaker, or that the feed-in tariff was later replaced by other procurement. The source is the World Bank's own evaluation of operations whose results framework included this indicator, and the number is read from a PDF results table.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Electricity and Renewable Energy legislated a renewable energy law in 2014, set a feed-in tariff by cabinet decree, licensed private developers through the regulator and allocated land in one desert park, Benban, so many small IPPs could share grid connection and permitting.
preconditions: A power deficit (5,540 MW in FY15) that made new private capacity politically urgent
A state offtaker whose payment risk international guarantors were willing to cover
Desert land under state control with high irradiation, allocated as one park

records.title: Pap-Angren railway and Kamchik tunnel
records.claim: Uzbekistan's government and its state railway UTY began building the 124 km Pap-Angren line with a 19 km tunnel in mid-2013 and finished the works within nine months of the World Bank loan's 2015 effectiveness, with the main infrastructure costing US$1,475.68 million against an estimate of US$1,438.75 million, about 2.6 percent over, and benefits flowing about 18 months earlier than appraisal assumed.

metric.name: Actual cost of railway main infrastructure (line and tunnel)

secondMetric.name: Original estimated cost of railway main infrastructure

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Pap-Angren Railway Project (P146328)

records.limits: The overrun of 2.6 percent is our computation from two figures in the ICR's cost table. The baseline is weak: construction ran simultaneously with detailed design and cost estimation, and by the Bank's appraisal in late 2014 the works were already very advanced, so the estimate was set when much of the cost was known, which flatters the overrun. The ICR gives no planned and actual completion dates for the line itself, only that works finished within nine months of loan effectiveness and benefits began about 18 months early. The 19 km tunnel was built by China Rail and Tunnel Company with China Exim Bank financing, so not all of the delivery was Uzbek institutional capacity, though the rail line was built by UTY's own workforce. The World Bank's own components went badly: the signaling contract was cancelled for misprocurement, US$72.87 million of the loan was cancelled, resettlement compliance was downgraded to moderately unsatisfactory, and UTY declined a second user survey. Passenger demand came in lower than projected. The source is the World Bank evaluating a project it part-financed (about 12 percent of cost), read from a PDF.

pattern.mechanism: The Cabinet of Ministers decreed the line and put it on a fast track, with the state railway UTY building the track with its own crews and equipment while design proceeded, and a Chinese contractor driving the tunnel in parallel.
preconditions: A state railway that had already built 640 km of new line with its own workforce
Central authority able to order design and construction to run at once, and to compel the railway to share data
Concessional tunnel financing from China Exim Bank

records.title: Competitive renewable IPP programme, from Navoi Scaling Solar
records.claim: Uzbekistan's government signed its first competitively tendered solar PPP in November 2019 at US¢2.679 per kWh, the 100 MW Navoi plant began commercial operation in December 2021, and by January 2024 operational solar PV capacity in the country stood at 1,497 MW, with agreements for a further 5,677 MW of solar and 5,100 MW of wind by 2030.

metric.name: Total operational solar PV generation capacity in Uzbekistan

secondMetric.name: Winning fixed offtake tariff in the first competitive solar PPP (Navoi, 25 years)

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Uzbekistan Navoi Scaling Solar IPP Project (P170598)

records.limits: The 1,497 MW is all operational solar, and the ICR's own table of operating projects includes 400 MW from Gezhouba procured non-competitively, so not every megawatt came through the competitive PPP route. One foreign developer, Masdar, holds most of the competitive capacity listed (Navoi, Scaling Solar 2, Sherobod), so the collaboration is concentrated. Most deals carry World Bank Group, ADB or EBRD payment guarantees, so the state and multilateral lenders carry offtake risk and the number cannot separate Uzbek institutional capacity from multilateral de-risking. Capacity is nameplate, not generation, and solar remains a small share of a system of roughly 14 GW of mostly gas-fired plant. The 5,677 MW and 5,100 MW are agreements, not delivery. The source is the World Bank evaluating its own guarantee operation.

pattern.mechanism: The government, through the energy ministry and a new PPP agency, ran a World Bank Group Scaling Solar tender with standard contracts and a sovereign support agreement, and used the record low tariff it produced to raise its renewable target and repeat the tender model.
preconditions: A PPP law and a PPP agency created in 2019 to sign and manage the contracts
Multilateral payment guarantees covering a state offtaker with below-cost-recovery tariffs
An electricity tariff reform commitment that made long-term offtake credible to bidders

records.title: Pro-Routes high-priority road reopening and maintenance
records.claim: Between October 2008 and June 2020 the Ministry of Infrastructure's Cellule Infrastructure reopened 2,752 of a targeted 2,762 km of high-priority earth roads across five provinces and maintained 3,335 km, finishing 3.6 percent over the financing-agreement total and 28 months behind the combined original schedule.

metric.name: Total project cost at closure against the values in the financing agreements (parent project plus two additional financings)

secondMetric.name: Implementation delay against the combined original timeline of the three financings (113 months planned, about 141 actual)

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, High Priority Reopening and Maintenance Project (P101745)

records.limits: The source is the World Bank's own completion report on a project it financed, and the PDF has to be read (table 3 and paragraph 50, pages 19-20). IDA carried 61.6 percent of the money and DFID, through World Bank-administered trust funds, 24.2 percent; the government's own Road Maintenance Fund put in 14.2 percent, so the delivery is Congolese institutions spending donor money under Bank supervision. The 3.6 percent total overrun is measured against financing agreements that were enlarged twice, so it does not compare with the 2008 appraisal cost (US$123 million for 1,800 km); the road works came in 22.6 percent under budget while institution building ran 1,656 percent and the environmental and social programme 235 percent over. The 28-month delay includes a 12-month suspension of disbursements in 2017-18 for non-compliance with environmental and social obligations, including gender-based violence, after an Inspection Panel investigation. The roads are low-standard reopened earth roads, about one fifth of the 15,800 km priority network; the ICR says ten kilometres are unaccounted for, rates M&E quality Modest, and says road-sector management and the maintenance fund's allocation remain opaque. Nothing in the report shows whether the roads stayed open after June 2020.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Infrastructure's project unit (Cellule Infrastructure) bought the cheapest passable standard, spot-improved earth roads, through output-based contracts and the Office des Routes, so that mileage, not finish quality, set the pace and kept civil works inside budget.
preconditions: Concessional donor finance covering most of the cost and a donor willing to extend the closing date four times
A road maintenance fund created in 2009 to keep reopened sections passable
Enough security on the selected corridors for contractors to work

records.title: Emergency Operation for Development, reconstruction of areas affected by terroristic operations
records.claim: From September 2015 Iraqi ministries, governorates and the Reconstruction Fund for Areas Affected by Terroristic Operations used two World Bank loans totalling US$750 million (IBRD-85200, US$350 million, and IBRD-87930, US$400 million), of which US$610 million was disbursed by 30 November 2024, to rebuild water, power, roads, bridges and railway in five governorates, reaching 5 million direct beneficiaries by March 2024, with the first loan's closing date pushed six years past the original June 2020.

metric.name: Direct project beneficiaries

secondMetric.name: Extension of the first loan's closing date beyond the original (30 June 2020 to 30 June 2026), computed

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Status and Results Report, Emergency Operation for Development (P155732), sequence 19, archived 12 January 2025

records.limits: The figures come from a World Bank supervision report on its own loan, compiled from implementing agencies' reporting; procurement and M&E are rated Moderately Unsatisfactory in the same report, and the beneficiary count is a 'direct beneficiaries' definition that counts everyone in a served area, so it can overlap across water, power and road indicators. The project is still open, so nothing here is a completion figure, and the 72-month extension is our computation from the table, not a published delay figure. The shock is war, not a natural hazard, and the record evidences recovery, not preparation. The money is World Bank lending the government must repay, implemented by Iraqi agencies under Bank supervision, and the US$68 million repurposed to railway works in 2024 shows the scope moved with time. It covers five governorates, not the country, and the report gives no measure of whether rebuilt services were kept running after handover.

pattern.mechanism: The federal government channelled World Bank loans through line ministries, governorates and a dedicated reconstruction fund, rebuilding basic services in retaken cities sub-project by sub-project rather than through one master plan.
preconditions: Military recovery of the territory before any rebuilding could start
Sovereign borrowing capacity and an international lender willing to extend the closing date repeatedly
A reconstruction fund and planning ministry able to register and approve hundreds of sub-projects

records.title: Targeted Subsidy Reform cash transfer, and its erosion
records.claim: Iran's government replaced universal fuel and bread subsidies with a universal cash transfer of 455,000 rials (about US$40) per person per month from late 2010, then left the transfer unindexed, so that by 2019 its purchasing power had fallen to less than US$6 per person before a top-up was added in late 2019.

metric.name: Purchasing power of the per-person cash transfer, 2019 (published as 'less than')

secondMetric.name: Cash transfer per person per month at launch
secondMetric.unit: US$ per person per month (about 455,000 rials)

source.publisher: World Bank, Poverty Global Practice, Middle East and North Africa: Islamic Republic of Iran poverty diagnostic (November 2023)

records.limits: The World Bank restates every figure here from secondary sources (Salehi-Isfahani et al. 2015, Enami and Lustig 2018, UNICEF 2019). It does not compute them, and no Iranian official series is cited. The two dollar figures are not comparable: US$40 converts at the 2010 rate, the 2019 figure is undated within the year and published only as 'less than US$6', and the rial's collapse after 2018 inflates the fall in dollar terms. The 'nearly in half' real decline from 2012 to 2016 is the cleaner measure, but it is published as prose and not as a number. The reversal is partial. The transfer still reached about 90 percent of households, and the government added a top-up in late 2019 and COVID-19 payments in 2020. The construct asks how fast rules change. This record shows a fast rule change in 2010 followed by about nine years in which the transfer was not changed as inflation rose. It is evidence of the second half, not a measure of speed. The figures are read from a PDF.

pattern.mechanism: The Iranian government raised domestic energy and bread prices in one move and paid the savings back as a flat universal cash transfer. It then left the transfer nominal, so inflation dissolved the benefit while energy prices drifted back toward subsidy.
preconditions: A national population and household register able to pay nearly every resident within months
Large implicit energy subsidies whose removal freed fiscal room for a transfer
A fiscal position, later hit by sanctions and inflation, that made indexing the transfer unaffordable
pattern.travelled: Cited by the World Bank as a model for Angola's 2023 fuel subsidy reform (Policy Research Working Paper 10939). The retellings stress the 2010 compensation and rarely the later erosion.

records.title: Earthquake Emergency Recovery after the 2002 Changureh-Avaj earthquake
records.claim: After the April 2002 earthquake in Kermanshah and the June 2002 earthquake in Qazvin, Zanjan and Hamedan, Iran's Ministry of Interior project unit and the Housing Foundation repaired or rebuilt about 24,000 damaged houses to seismic standards by June 2009, using government funds and a US$180 million World Bank loan, of which US$174.9 million was disbursed.

metric.name: Damaged housing units repaired and reconstructed in compliance with seismic standards

secondMetric.name: Houses damaged by the June 2002 earthquakes

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR00001192, Earthquake Emergency Recovery Project (P080802, Loan IBRD-46970)

records.limits: The figure is self-reported by the Bank and the borrower's project unit in a completion report, and no independent audit of the houses is cited. The report contradicts itself: the results table gives 24,000 actual against a 24,200 target, the narrative says around 24,200, and a footnote gives an appraisal estimate of 29,232. The project financed materials (steel, cement and equipment) for reconstruction rather than building every house, so the count is of houses it supplied. About 59 percent of the 40,727 damaged houses are covered. The response was regional, in four provinces. It was not national, and it is not the Bam 2003 reconstruction that Iranians would name first. Schedule slipped: the loan closing moved from June 2007 to June 2009, and the indicator was achieved six months after its target date. The disaster insurance component was dropped from Bank financing at the government's request. The evidence of preparedness is limited to seismic-code training for 350 staff against a target of 200 and a public awareness campaign, with no later test against a subsequent earthquake. The figures are read from a PDF.

pattern.mechanism: Iran's Ministry of Interior set up a project unit and handed housing reconstruction to the Housing Foundation, which tied reconstruction materials to compliance with seismic codes and trained local engineers and masons to enforce them.
preconditions: A standing national housing body (the Housing Foundation) with rural reach and a reconstruction mandate
Government funds already committed before external finance arrived
Access to multilateral lending, which later sanctions closed off
pattern.travelled: The Housing Foundation reused the model of owner-driven rebuilding to code after Bam in 2003, with a World Bank loan approved in 2004.

records.title: Fuel subsidy removal, and its erosion
records.claim: Angola's government removed gasoline and diesel subsidies by raising retail prices at the end of 2015, but subsidies returned as costs rose, reaching 3.7 percent of GDP in 2023 from 1.5 percent in 2019. A second reform raised gasoline prices 87.5 percent in June 2023, but the kwanza's depreciation took the gasoline subsidy from 39 percent of the market price in June back to 65 percent by October 2023.

metric.name: Gasoline subsidy as a share of the market price, after depreciation

secondMetric.name: Gasoline subsidy as a share of the market price, after the June 2023 price rise

source.publisher: World Bank, Policy Research Working Paper 10939, Fuel Subsidy Reforms: Lessons from the Literature and Assessing the Price Shock for Different Sectors through an Input-Output Table in the Case of Angola (October 2024)

records.limits: This is a World Bank working paper, which disclaims representing the Bank's view. Every subsidy share is the authors' own estimate from IGAPE and INE data, not a published government series. No figure is given for the 2015 removal itself: the source only says subsidies were removed and then reemerged. The 2019 to 2023 rise is in part an oil price and exchange rate effect, so it measures exposure as much as inaction. The October 2023 figure reflects a 40 percent depreciation in May and June 2023, which no price rule could have tracked. The government did act again: the gasoline rise in June 2023, a 1 June 2023 decree setting out a multiphase reform, and a diesel rise from 135 to 200 kwanzas in April 2024. Between the two steps retail prices remained constant until May 2023, and the June 2023 decree was the first since 2016. The figures are read from a PDF.

pattern.mechanism: Angola's government raised administered fuel prices in discrete steps, in 2015 and again from June 2023, while leaving them fixed in kwanza between steps. Each devaluation or oil price rise then rebuilt the subsidy the step had removed.
preconditions: Administered retail fuel prices set by decree with no automatic adjustment
A currency exposed to oil price shocks and sharp devaluation
Fuel subsidies acting as the de facto social spending before a cash transfer (Kwenda) could reach the poor
pattern.travelled: The 2023 reform drew on the 2010 Iranian and Indonesian lessons cited in the same paper: compensate before raising prices. Kwenda was meant to be that compensation, but the same paper says it has failed to reach enough people.

records.title: Lobito Corridor rail concession
records.claim: Angola's Ministry of Transport signed a 30-year concession with Lobito Atlantic Railway, in which Mota-Engil holds equity, on 4 November 2022 to rehabilitate, operate and maintain about 1,300 km of the Benguela line from Lobito to Luau and the Lobito mineral terminal. By September 2026 the concessionaire was operating the corridor with about 945 workers, 529 of them transferred from state rail and port operators.

metric.name: Rail infrastructure operated, maintained and modernised under the concession

secondMetric.name: Workers employed by the concessionaire, of whom 529 transferred from state-owned operators

source.publisher: Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (World Bank Group), press release of 10 September 2026

records.limits: Neither figure measures delivery. 1,300 km is the length of an asset handed over, and the press release does not say what was rehabilitated, what freight moved or what the concessionaire invested. The publisher is a guarantor promoting its own transaction, and the April 2024 summary that dates the contract was written by the concessionaire. 2022 is the contract date, and the source does not say when operations passed to the concessionaire. The concession is four years into 30, so it shows that the state handed over operations, not that the partnership delivered. Passenger service stays with the state operator. The corridor is driven by DRC and Zambian copper exports and by US and EU strategic finance, so the national objective it serves is as much foreign as Angolan. It is one contract, and the construct asks for the frequency and scale of public-private delivery across the country.

pattern.mechanism: Angola's Ministry of Transport tendered the freight operation of a state railway to a private consortium for 30 years, keeping passenger service public and moving state rail and port staff into the concession company.
preconditions: Mineral traffic from the DRC and Zambia large enough to attract a commodity trader as operator
Political risk cover and development finance (MIGA, DFC, AfDB) to make a 30-year private commitment bankable

records.title: Functional Adult Literacy programme, and its decline
records.claim: Uganda's Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development enrolled 434,664 adult learners in its government-funded Functional Adult Literacy programme in 2004, and enrolment fell to 88,533 by 2007.

metric.name: Learners enrolled in government-funded Functional Adult Literacy (FAL)

secondMetric.name: Learners enrolled in government-funded FAL in 2004, the high of the 1997-2007 table

source.publisher: Republic of Uganda, Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development, national report on adult learning and education for CONFINTEA VI, hosted by the UNESCO Institute for Lifelong Learning

records.limits: The series stops in 2007. The report is a 2008 ministry submission to UNESCO, and no later official FAL enrolment series was found or checked. Whether it recovered later, under this or another name, is not shown, so the eroded status describes 2004 to 2007 and nothing after. 2004 is the high of one eleven-year table, and the jump from about 149,000 in 2001 to 358,000 in 2002 suggests a one-off funding push rather than a stable peak. The table's printed total (2,090,340) does not match the 2,091,340 in the text above it. The figures are the ministry's own administrative counts, taken from a PDF, with no independent check. A count of literacy learners is much narrower than the indicator's construct, the share of all adults in any education or training. The report's national figures show 43% of adults had some primary schooling, so not every enrolee was starting from zero. It also says FAL relied on UNICEF, UNESCO and DVV funding that stopped around 1999, so part of the swing may come from donor funding rather than from state delivery. The same report's release table shows government FAL releases of Shs 3.61bn a year in 2002/03-2004/05 and 3.08bn in 2005/06-2006/07, a cut of about 15% against a fall in enrolment of about 80%, so the cause of the decline is not shown. Elsewhere the report dates the government's re-launch budget to 1991. The start year is a re-launch: there was adult literacy work before 1992, and FAL began as a pilot in eight districts.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development ran adult literacy classes through district community development officers and volunteer instructors. Enrolment fell after 2004 while government releases fell only from Shs 3.61bn to 3.08bn a year, so the source does not explain the fall.
preconditions: District community development staff in every local government
Volunteer instructors willing to teach for little or no pay
A protected budget line that outlasts donor and poverty-fund cycles

records.title: Karuma Hydropower Project
records.claim: Uganda began building the 600 MW Karuma hydropower station in August 2013 against a 60-month plan. By the end of June 2023 the Auditor General reported it 54 months late at 99.9 percent physical progress, and UEGCL records commercial operation from 12 June 2024.

metric.name: Schedule overrun of Karuma HPP at the end of FY2022/23 (actual duration 114 months against a 60-month plan)

secondMetric.name: Planned construction duration of Karuma HPP

source.publisher: Office of the Auditor General of Uganda, Report of the Auditor General to Parliament for the Financial Year ended 30th June 2023

records.limits: The record carries schedule performance only. No official baseline-against-outturn cost figure was found: UEGCL's page states a project cost of US$1.398 billion with no original budget beside it, so cost overrun is unknown. The Auditor General names USD 30 million of interest claims on delayed payments, which is one cost of the delay and not the overrun. The 54-month figure is measured at June 2023, when the plant was not yet in commercial operation. Commercial operation on 12 June 2024 implies a total overrun near 66 months, more than double the plan, but that figure is our computation from two sources. The 60-month plan is the Auditor General's statement of the plan, and the contract itself was not checked. The same report finds that the community development projects promised with the dam were largely unfunded (UGX 3 billion of 38.3 billion received) and that resettlement lagged, so the delivery is incomplete beyond the powerhouse. The record says nothing about how the plant has performed since commissioning.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development and UEGCL let the dam as a single turnkey EPC contract to a foreign state contractor, financed mostly by an export-credit loan. That handed design and construction to the contractor, and land, resettlement and transmission stayed with Ugandan agencies, where much of the delay arose.
preconditions: An export-credit lender willing to finance most of the cost against a sovereign guarantee
A state land acquisition and resettlement process able to keep pace with an EPC contractor, which it did not
Transmission lines built in step to evacuate the power

records.title: Integrated Community-Based Adult Education (MEMKWA), and its decline
records.claim: Tanzania's Ministry of Education ran Integrated Community-Based Adult Education in all 25 mainland regions from 1993. Enrolment peaked at 1,900,255 learners in 2005 and fell to 786,602 by 2014.

metric.name: Learners enrolled in ICBAE learning centres

secondMetric.name: Learners enrolled in ICBAE learning centres at the 2005 high of the 2000-2014 table

source.publisher: UNESCO Institute for Lifelong Learning, LitBase effective practices database: Integrated Community-Based Adult Education (ICBAE), United Republic of Tanzania

records.limits: The table exists only as an image on the UNESCO page, so the numbers were read off a picture and a machine cannot check them. UNESCO's page is a case-study write-up that presents the programme as good practice, and the figures are ministry figures republished without a stated source. The ministry's own 2008 CONFINTEA report prints 1,900,225 for 2004/05, but its male and female columns sum to UNESCO's 1,900,255, so the difference is a ministry arithmetic slip; the ministry's 1999/2000 and 2000/2001 rows reappear as UNESCO's 2000 and 2001, so UNESCO's year labels may be the second year of a school year. The ministry labels its table 'participation in literacy programmes', so UNESCO may have attached the ICBAE name to all adult literacy participation. The series has gaps (2002 to 2004 are missing) and ends in 2014, and later years were not checked, so the eroded status describes 2005 to 2014 only. 2014 ticked up from 734,950 in 2013, and the fall is not monotonic. A count of literacy learners is far narrower than the indicator's construct, the share of all adults in any education or training. The programme had no standardized tests, so the count says nothing about what learners gained.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Education ran literacy circles of up to 30 learners in primary school buildings in the evenings, staffed by facilitators and coordinated through local government. Enrolment fell by more than half within a decade as funding and facilitator support thinned.
preconditions: A primary school in every village to host evening classes
A local government coordinator for adult education in each ward and district
Recurrent funding for facilitators that survives the end of a campaign, which is what eroded
pattern.travelled: Tanzania's 1970s mass literacy campaign is the earlier, larger version of the same move. The literacy gains it is credited with were also reported to slip back in the 1980s and 1990s.

records.title: Julius Nyerere Hydropower Project
records.claim: TANESCO contracted the 2,115 MW Julius Nyerere hydropower dam on the Rufiji in December 2018 for TZS 6.56 trillion over 42 months to June 2022. The contractor completed it on 31 March 2025, and claims settled in the contractor's favour raised the cost to TZS 7.44 trillion.

metric.name: Adjusted cost of the Julius Nyerere Hydropower Project after USD 400 million of contractor claims

secondMetric.name: Original EPC contract price of the Julius Nyerere Hydropower Project

source.publisher: National Audit Office of Tanzania, Controller and Auditor General, Annual General Audit Report on Public Authorities and Other Bodies for FY 2024/25 (Ripoti Kuu ya Mwaka ya Ukaguzi ya Mashirika ya Umma kwa Mwaka wa Fedha 2024-25)

records.limits: The sources are Swahili PDFs. The quotes are from extracted text with spacing artifacts removed, and the English in the claim is our translation. Neither overrun is published as a percentage. The cost overrun of about 13.4 percent (6.56 to 7.44 trillion) and the schedule overrun of about 33.5 months against a 42-month plan (roughly 80 percent) are our computations from the Auditor General's dates and figures. The cost figure counts only the USD 400 million of claims the dispute board awarded. Price adjustment, financing costs, transmission, resettlement and supervision are not shown, so the true overrun is likely larger. The Auditor General adds that the contractor was granted two ex-gratia extensions to 14 January 2024, that TZS 327.03 billion of liquidated damages had not been deducted by November 2025, and that the contractor was released from TZS 262.34 billion of community projects. At completion, three of nine turbines had not been tested because the reservoir was too low, and the full-capacity test was not done on time because TANESCO lacked transmission capacity. Completion of the civil contract therefore does not mean the plant delivers 2,115 MW. The record says nothing about the dam's environmental cost in the Selous (Nyerere) protected area.

pattern.mechanism: The government had TANESCO let the whole dam as one EPC contract to an Egyptian joint venture and financed it from the domestic budget rather than concessional loans. That kept the project moving and kept it in national hands, but left contract management and the transmission build with TANESCO, where the audited losses arose.
preconditions: A treasury able to fund a multi-trillion-shilling project from domestic revenue over several budget years
A utility with the contract-management capacity to enforce delay damages and resist claims, which the Auditor General found lacking
Transmission lines built in step with generation

records.title: Beira railways concession, and its termination
records.claim: Mozambique's government concessioned the Sena and Machipanda railways for 25 years in 2004 to a joint company in which the state rail enterprise CFM held 49 percent; the Sena line reopened to Moatize more than two years late, carried 266,000 tonnes against a target of one million, and the government terminated the concession on 7 December 2011.

metric.name: Freight carried on the Sena line by the end of the project

secondMetric.name: Target freight on the Sena line by the end of the project

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Beira Railway Project (P082618)

records.limits: The source is the World Bank's own completion report on a project it financed, so the lender is grading a failure it shares, and the independent review of that report found its cost tables mutually inconsistent: the text claims a cost overrun of more than US$50 million while the annex shows actual cost below appraisal, which is why no cost figure is used here. The ICR also dates the termination both to September and to December 2011. The 266,000 tonnes is coal moved in the months after the line opened in August 2011, against a target set for 2009, so it measures lateness as much as capacity. The concession covered two lines in the centre of the country, not the national network. The termination ended the partnership but not the asset: CFM kept operating the rehabilitated Sena line, and later coal traffic on it is not in this record. Blame is contested: the report faults the concession design, the state's 49 percent stake and ineffectual Bank supervision as well as the private operator.

pattern.mechanism: The government of Mozambique, through CFM, handed rehabilitation and operation of two state railways to a private concessionaire in a 51 to 49 joint company, financed largely by an IDA credit, and took the lines back when rehabilitation ran late and traffic did not materialise.
preconditions: A state rail enterprise able to supervise a concessionaire, which a 49 percent shareholding in the same company undercut
A traffic forecast tied to coal mines whose own concessions were being negotiated in parallel by another ministry
A dispute mechanism or independent arbiter, which the concession lacked

records.title: Instituto Nacional de Gestao de Calamidades (INGC)
records.claim: Mozambique's National Disaster Management Institute, created in 1999 after a new national disaster policy, evacuated around 150,000 people with two days of warning in the 2007 floods, and by 2011 had ten days of warning for an event of similar scale and spent under US$1 million on evacuation, against about US$5 million in 2007.

metric.name: People evacuated by INGC ahead of the 2007 floods

secondMetric.name: Advance warning INGC had before a 2011 flood event similar in scale to 2007/2008

source.publisher: World Bank, Global Facility for Disaster Reduction and Recovery, Recovery from Recurrent Floods 2000-2013: Mozambique, Recovery Framework Case Study

records.limits: Every figure here is a round number in a GFDRR case study, a conference version that says it aims to learn from country experience rather than evaluate it and carries a disclaimer on accuracy; the evacuation counts and costs are INGC's own, with no underlying series published. 'Similar in scale' is the case study's judgement, not a measured comparison of hazards. The same document's comparison of the 2000 and 2013 floods (700 and 117 deaths) does not show a falling death rate once divided by the population affected (4.5 million and 478,892, our computation), and its own text gives 30 direct deaths for 2013, so mortality is not used as the metric. The record says nothing about the cyclone seasons after 2014. Much of the system was built with donor money.

pattern.mechanism: The government replaced a relief department with a standing disaster agency, INGC, gave it a national emergency operations centre and a civil protection unit, and paired forecasting with district and community risk committees that carry warnings to people who then move.
preconditions: A flood catastrophe in 2000 that made preparedness a political priority
Hydrological and meteorological forecasting with enough lead time to act on
Donor funding and an annual contingency budget line for evacuation

records.title: A1 motorway, Bucharest to Nadlac
records.claim: Romania's national road administration has built the 582 km A1 motorway in sections, and construction of the sections the auditors timed began in 2009, and in November 2025 the European Court of Auditors found its latest cost estimate 11 percent below the original estimate in real terms, while one EU co-funded section had run 79 months, or 263 percent of its planned time, late.

metric.name: Change in the A1 motorway's latest cost estimate against the original estimate, 2019 prices

secondMetric.name: Longest delay on an EU co-funded A1 motorway action against its planned completion

source.publisher: European Court of Auditors, Special report 02/2026, EU transport infrastructure (update of special report 10/2020)

records.limits: The cost figure is the auditors' aggregate of many sections planned and priced in different years, reindexed to 2019 values from an original estimate whose own date the auditors do not give, and it excludes the Bucharest-Pitesti section; the 2020 report warned that the unfinished Pitesti-Sibiu and Deva-Lugoj stretches left the figures subject to significant change. A real-terms fall can come from cheaper design, deferred scope or optimistic pricing of unbuilt sections, and the report does not say which. The auditors did not compute a schedule delay for the A1 as a whole because its timeline varies by section, and the 2020 report took 2030 as the original opening date only because the TEN-T regulation sets it, so the motorway's schedule performance cannot be read from the cost row. The 2026 update was a desk review of figures supplied by the Commission, national authorities and project promoters, with no site visits. The 79 months is one EU co-funded action, not the whole road, and it compares the Lugoj-Deva lots 2-4 action's planned end of May 2016 with an end date of December 2022 that was still a forecast in 2020. The 2020 report also found €3.7 million of EU co-funding wasted, a finished Lugoj-Deva stretch left unused and 800 metres of built motorway demolished, and one building permit needed for every 7 km.

pattern.mechanism: Romania's national road company split a 582 km corridor into many small procurement lots and financed most of them with EU cohesion and connecting-Europe funds, which kept unit prices visible and auditable but multiplied permits and interfaces.
preconditions: EU co-financing with audit and use-it-or-lose-it deadlines that discipline cost reporting
A national road agency able to tender and supervise dozens of separate lots
A permitting regime that, here, required a building permit every 7 km and slowed delivery

records.title: National Functional Literacy Programme, and its erosion
records.claim: Ghana's Non-Formal Education Division enrolled 312,907 adults in a single National Functional Literacy Programme batch in 2003-2005, and after donor funding ended in 2006 the government-funded batches shrank to 14,029 learners in the 2014-2016 batch.

metric.name: Learners enrolled in NFLP local-language Batch 19 (2014/16)

secondMetric.name: Learners enrolled in NFLP Batch 9 (Feb 2003/2005), the largest single batch

source.publisher: Ministry of Education, Ghana, Education Sector Performance Report 2018 (hosted by the National Development Planning Commission)

records.limits: The two numbers come from two different Ministry of Education reports, and both are administrative enrolment counts reported upward by district supervisors; the 2013 report says monitoring visits to verify figures had not been possible since 2010 for lack of funds, and the 2018 report restates Batch 18 at 44,730 where the 2013 report had 51,257, so the series is revised without explanation. A batch runs about 21 months and batches overlap (Batch 10 ran November 2003 to 2005 alongside Batch 9), so a per-batch count is not a 12-month participation rate, and the peak-year total across overlapping batches was higher than the single batch quoted. The programme teaches basic literacy, which is one narrow slice of the adult learning the indicator asks about, and even the peak batch was a few percent of Ghana's adults. The 2003-2005 peak was financed mostly by an IDA credit: US$33.86 million of US$44.94 million in project costs (World Bank ICR535, IDA-3246, P000974), so the erosion partly measures a donor exit rather than a domestic choice. The 2018 report also shows a separate Basic English Literacy track (17,647 learners in 2016/18) that partly offsets the fall. The record carries no figure after the 2014-2016 batch.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Education's Non-Formal Education Division ran 21-month local-language literacy classes in every region through volunteer facilitators, scaled them with an IDA credit to about 200,000 to 300,000 enrolments per batch, and then carried the programme on a government budget line that funded a fraction of that after 2006.
preconditions: A volunteer facilitator network and primers in 15 Ghanaian languages
External credit financing most of the cost at peak
A domestic budget line large enough to replace the donor share, which is what did not happen

records.title: Sankofa Gas Project (Offshore Cape Three Points)
records.claim: Ghana structured the Sankofa offshore gas development as a public-private deal in which Eni and Vitol invested and the state oil company GNPC bought the gas under take-or-pay terms backed by an IDA payment guarantee, mobilising US$4,653 million of private capital and bringing first gas to power plants in 2018.

metric.name: Private sector capital mobilized for the Sankofa gas field development

secondMetric.name: Average daily gas off-take in 2019, against take-or-pay volume of 170 mmscfd
secondMetric.unit: million standard cubic feet per day

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR 147538-GH, Ghana Sankofa Gas Project (P152670)

records.limits: The capital was private and the build was done by the Eni-Vitol consortium; Ghana's institutional move was the deal structure and the offtake, and that side performed worst. GNPC could not pay: arrears reached US$192 million by March 2020 and the sponsors drew US$191.6 million on the letter of credit backed by the IDA guarantee, so the public half of the partnership needed a World Bank backstop within two years of first gas. Off-take in 2018 and 2019 was a fraction of the 170 mmscfd the state contracted to take or pay for, because the pipeline interconnector to the eastern market was late and demand in the west was too small, which means Ghana paid for gas it did not use. The source is the World Bank's own completion report on its own guarantee, written in 2020, and its figures are not published as a machine-readable series; the source stops in mid-2020. One deal, however large, says little about the frequency of public-private delivery the indicator asks for.

pattern.mechanism: The Government of Ghana and GNPC contracted to buy domestic gas from a privately financed offshore field on take-or-pay terms, and the World Bank guaranteed those payments so that private sponsors and banks would commit capital to a sub-Saharan gas project.
preconditions: A proven offshore gas discovery and an international operator willing to develop it
A multilateral guarantee to cover the sovereign's payment risk
A power sector able to pay for the gas, which Ghana's state utilities could not do on time

records.title: Bank of Ghana Regulatory Sandbox
records.claim: The Bank of Ghana, which launched a regulatory and innovation sandbox pilot in 2021, admitted six firms into its Regulatory Sandbox for one year in January 2026 to test the exchange, custody, administration and issuance of virtual assets.

metric.name: Entities admitted into the Bank of Ghana Regulatory Sandbox (virtual assets cohort)

source.publisher: Bank of Ghana, press release 'List of participants - Regulatory Sandbox', 22 January 2026

records.limits: The metric is a count of six firms in one cohort, taken from a press release rather than a statistical series; divided by Ghana's population it is well under one firm per million people. It counts admissions only, not completions or exits. The 2021 launch was a pilot run with EMTECH Service LLC, not a documented admission, so the start year is the first documented admission, 2026. The indicator sums every regulator in the country, and this record covers the Bank of Ghana only. A sandbox at this scale is evidence that the instrument exists and is used, not that it operates at national scale in the sense of a mass programme.

pattern.mechanism: The Bank of Ghana's FinTech and Innovation Office admits named firms for a fixed one-year test under supervision, using each cohort to validate rules it has not yet issued, here for virtual assets.
preconditions: A central bank FinTech office with staff to supervise individual tests
A legal basis to grant time-limited, conditional permission outside existing licences
A pending regulatory question concrete enough to define a cohort around

records.title: South-West Roads: Western Europe-Western China corridor (CAREC 1b and 6b)
records.claim: Kazakhstan's Committee for Roads upgraded 1,281 km of the Western Europe-Western China corridor and connecting roads under a US$2.5 billion programme between 2009 and 2024, for an actual cost of US$2,468.6 million against US$2,500 million appraised, but over 15 years against a planned four and a half.

metric.name: Implementation duration, actual (planned at appraisal: 4.5 years)

secondMetric.name: Actual total project cost (appraised: US$2,500 million)

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR00317, South-West Roads Project (P099270)

records.limits: The cost line looks on budget only because the scope was moved to fit the money: bid prices came in low and the tenge depreciated, and the savings bought 219 km of extra road, so the total says nothing about cost per km against plan. The schedule figure is the honest one, and it is poor: the closing date was extended four times, the first three to absorb added scope and the last for COVID-19 and the termination of several civil works contracts, and a 42 km Otar-Uzynagash section was still unfinished at closing after two contractors were terminated for non-performance. The source is the lender's own completion report; the World Bank financed 85 percent of the cost, so this is a borrowed-money build supervised by the lender, though executed and repaid by Kazakhstan. Traffic came in about a third below forecast. It is one corridor programme, not a portfolio, so it cannot stand for Kazakhstan's average project performance.

pattern.mechanism: Kazakhstan's Committee for Roads borrowed from the World Bank to rebuild its stretch of the Western Europe-Western China corridor to dual carriageway, procured it in large international civil works packages, and used the savings from low bids to extend the scope across three oblasts.
preconditions: Sovereign borrowing capacity backed by oil revenue
A road agency able to run international competitive bidding under lender rules
A corridor with transit demand that neighbours and lenders also wanted built

records.title: AFSA FinTech Lab at the Astana International Financial Centre
records.claim: The Astana Financial Services Authority granted five FinTech Lab sandbox licences in 2022, saw the first participant graduate to a full licence that year, and had 18 licensed firms in its sandbox at the end of 2022.

metric.name: FinTech Lab licences granted (firms admitted to the sandbox) in 2022

secondMetric.name: Licensed companies in the FinTech Lab at end of year

source.publisher: Astana Financial Services Authority, 2022 Annual Report

records.limits: The regulator is reporting on itself in an annual report, and the counts stop at 2022. Admissions plus completions in 2022 come to six firms, which is well under one per million people. AFSA regulates only the Astana International Financial Centre, a special jurisdiction under English-style common law, so the sandbox sits outside Kazakhstan's ordinary financial regulation; the indicator sums every regulator in the country, and the National Bank and the Agency for Regulation and Development of Financial Markets are not counted here. Many participants are crypto exchanges drawn by the AIFC regime, and eight licences were withdrawn in the same year five were granted, so the counts measure churn as much as successful testing. The start year is inferred from 'fifth year' rather than stated.

pattern.mechanism: The Astana Financial Services Authority grants individual, time-limited FinTech Lab licences with requirements tailored to each firm, and graduates a firm to full authorisation when its test succeeds.
preconditions: A financial centre with its own regulator and rulebook separate from the national one
Demand from foreign fintech and crypto firms for a regional base
Supervisory staff able to write firm-specific requirements

records.title: Reseau Ferroviaire Rapide de Tunis, lines D and E, and its overruns
records.claim: Tunisia's transport ministry and the Societe du RFR built the first two lines of the Tunis rapid rail network, about 18 km plus 28 trains, financed from December 2010; the EIB's approximate total cost for the same scheme rose from EUR 550 million at the 2009 appraisal to EUR 653 million at the 2017 appraisal, Line E opened in March 2023 and Line D on 25 January 2025, against a 2015 project study that scheduled construction of the Line E viaduct for 2014 to 2017.

metric.name: Approximate total cost of RFR lines D and E (EIB appraisal, operation 2015-0288)

secondMetric.name: Approximate total cost of RFR lines D and E (EIB appraisal, operation 2009-0154)

source.publisher: European Investment Bank, project summary sheet 20150288 (RESEAU FERROVIAIRE RAPIDE II)

records.limits: The cost figures are the EIB's approximate appraisal totals, not an audited out-turn: the 18.7 percent rise from 550 to 653 million EUR is our computation across two appraisals whose scope wording differs slightly (the 2017 sheet names a maintenance facility and 28 trains, the 2010 sheet only rolling stock), and in January 2025 the French Treasury still quoted a total of 550 million EUR including rolling stock, so the publishers do not agree on the out-turn. The cost is in euros and says nothing about dinar costs after the currency's depreciation. The record has no official original line-opening date: the only official schedule is a 2015 impact study placing the Line E viaduct's construction in 2014 to 2017, so the roughly six-year slip to the March 2023 Line E opening is a comparison of one structure's plan against the line's opening, not a published overrun. The EIB suspended disbursements in 2016 over construction companies' failures to implement safeguards (ESDS 18 July 2017), and works at Bardo were halted by the municipality until an administrative court annulled the stop on 29 December 2023 (EIB register 236943929), so part of the delay is litigation rather than delivery. About 60 percent of financing came from foreign lenders and French and Korean firms supplied engineering and trains. This is a city network, not a national programme, and it records poor delivery rather than good: it is evidence of the construct's weak end.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Transport created a dedicated project company, the Societe du RFR, assembled a 40 percent state and 60 percent multi-donor financing package, and built the first two lines through civil works contracts while SNCFT took the operating role; when the Bardo municipality stopped the works, the company went to the administrative court and the cabinet chose a design variant in December 2023.
preconditions: Concessional lenders (EIB, AFD, KfW, EU) willing to stay in for more than a decade and to suspend and restart disbursement rather than exit
A rail right of way partly owned by SNCFT, so most of the route did not need fresh land
An administrative court able to overrule a municipality that blocked works on a national project
pattern.travelled: The same multi-lender package financed Line A in 2013 and is meant to carry the remaining lines of the planned 85 km network; the Tunis case is usually retold as a delay story, and the part that drops out is that the lines did open.

records.title: Banque Centrale de Tunisie regulatory sandbox, first cohort
records.claim: The Banque Centrale de Tunisie launched a regulatory sandbox in January 2020, admitted four fintech solutions to its first cohort in September 2020, ran tests with real customers and partner banks for 13 months, notified exit in September 2022, and drafted a circular on digital enrolment and remote bank account opening from the results (BCT Rapport annuel 2022).

metric.name: Fintech solutions admitted to the first cohort of the BCT regulatory sandbox

source.publisher: Banque Centrale de Tunisie, Rapport annuel 2020 (June 2021)

records.limits: The count is the regulator's own report of its own programme. The number does not say how many of the four completed, only that exit plans were validated. Only one regulator is covered; capital markets and insurance regulators are not. Four solutions in one cohort over 2020 to 2022 is about 0.33 admissions per million people (our computation against the World Bank's 2020 population of 11,974,057), and the record shows one cohort only.

pattern.mechanism: The central bank set up a fintech committee, published an access guide, selected four solutions against its own strategic priorities, exempted them from specified rules for a bounded test with partner banks, and then wrote the tested remote-onboarding practice into a banking circular.
preconditions: A central bank with rule-making power over the banks the fintechs had to test through
Partner banks willing to embed outside firms in a protected test environment
A strategic plan that named innovation as an objective, so staff time was allocated to it
pattern.travelled: The design follows the cohort model of the UK FCA and Bahrain's central bank; what did not travel was the cadence, since Tunisia ran one cohort and stopped.

records.title: FID crisis response transfers, including Fiavota
records.claim: Madagascar's Fonds d'Intervention pour le Developpement turned its safety net project into a shock-response channel from December 2016, delivering crisis-response unconditional cash transfers to 622,961 people and crisis cash-for-work to 155,649 people after droughts in the South and the 2022 cyclones, by the project's close in October 2024.

metric.name: People who benefited from crisis response unconditional cash transfers

secondMetric.name: People who benefited from cash-for-work under the crisis response mechanism

source.publisher: World Bank Independent Evaluation Group, ICR Review ICRR0024665, MG-Social Safety Net Project (P149323)

records.limits: The figures are cumulative over 2016 to 2024 and come from the World Bank's own evaluation of a project it financed, which draws on the implementing agency's reporting; they count people reached, not whether households recovered, and say nothing about speed of delivery after each shock. Almost all the money was IDA credit and grants (US$305.9 million actual), so the record shows the state's agency delivering donor-financed transfers, not domestic fiscal capacity to respond. Targets were set and raised repeatedly in emergency conditions, and IEG notes that some reach targets were not scaled up as financing grew (its remark about targets set quickly and with limited clarity concerns the emergency nutrition targets), so exceeding them is weak evidence. The response was reactive, reallocating funds after each shock rather than drawing on a pre-arranged trigger, which is recovery more than preparedness. Security problems in the South forced FID to sign an agreement with the police to deliver cash. The project closed in October 2024, so the status is concluded.

pattern.mechanism: FID, a government agency with field staff and a beneficiary registry from the regular safety net, repeatedly restructured the project to redirect funds to drought and cyclone victims, paying unconditional transfers and cash-for-work through the channels it already ran.
preconditions: An implementing agency with a targeting method and payment channels already operating before the shock
A financier willing to restructure a project within weeks rather than design a new one
Enough security in affected districts to move cash, here secured by an agreement with the police

records.title: Southern Expressway (Southern Transport Development Project)
records.claim: Sri Lanka's Road Development Authority built the country's first access-controlled expressway, about 126 km from Kottawa to Godagama. Sections I to III opened on 26 November 2011 and section IV on 15 March 2014. The project took 13 years against a planned six. Its total cost rose from US$295.9 million at the 1999 appraisal to US$906.5 million at completion in 2014, partly because it was widened from two to four lanes.

metric.name: Actual total project cost at completion

secondMetric.name: Total project cost estimated at the 1999 appraisal (two-lane design)

source.publisher: Asian Development Bank, Completion Report, Sri Lanka: Southern Transport Development Project (Project 26522, Loans 1711 and 2413), August 2014

records.limits: The cost growth is not a like-for-like overrun. In 2008 the scope was widened from a two-lane road to four lanes, and against the 2008 re-appraisal of $757.7 million the overrun is about 20 percent, not about 206 percent. Both ratios are our computation from the report's figures. The cost table is sourced to the borrower's own completion report (Government of Sri Lanka, 2011), and ADB, as lender, judges a project it financed. The PCR's cost-by-financier table puts China Exim at $159.48 million within the $906.47 million total, so the section it financed is included. The schedule figure (13 years against six) runs from the 1999 approval and includes four years of design and land acquisition before construction.

pattern.mechanism: The Road Development Authority ran one project management unit for an expressway financed in sections by ADB, JICA, the Nordic Development Fund and later China Exim. When prices rose and the design changed, it went back to the lenders for a supplementary loan instead of cutting the scope.
preconditions: Several concessional lenders willing to finance one corridor in parallel and to top up after a cost overrun
Land acquisition and resettlement capacity, whose absence caused most of the early delay
A design finalized before contract award, which this project lacked and which ADB names as its main lesson
pattern.travelled: The same Road Development Authority model was reused for the Colombo-Katunayake Expressway (2013), the Outer Circular Highway and the Southern Expressway extension to Hambantota (2020), mostly with Chinese loans instead of multilateral ones.

records.title: Centres d'alphabétisation, and their erosion
records.claim: Côte d'Ivoire's education ministry ran a national network of literacy centres. It counted 75,275 learners in 2,828 centres in 2015-16 and 53,311 learners in 2,707 centres in 2024-25, a fall of about 29 percent in learners over the decade.

metric.name: Learners enrolled in literacy centres, all levels, 2024-2025 school year

secondMetric.name: Learners enrolled in literacy centres, all levels, 2015-2016 school year, the highest of the years checked

source.publisher: Ministère de l'Education Nationale et de l'Alphabétisation, Direction des Stratégies, de la Planification et des Statistiques (DESPS), Statistiques scolaires de poche 2024-2025

records.limits: The numbers are enrolments in literacy centres, not a participation rate. At about 53,000 learners against an adult population in the millions, the network reaches well under 1 percent of adults. So it shows little about adult learning participation at national scale. The erosion is measured between two of the ministry's pocket yearbooks. The yearbooks give 2015-16 (75,275), 2016-17 (57,299), 2017-18 (59,111), 2022-23 (55,405), 2023-24 (52,554) and 2024-25 (53,311). 2015-16 is the highest of these years, not a confirmed all-time peak. Most of the fall happened in one year, 2015-16 to 2016-17, which could be a change in coverage or method rather than in delivery. The yearbooks do not explain it. The centres include those run by NGOs, religious bodies and communities as well as the state, and the yearbook does not split them by operator. The age chart in 2024-25 shows some learners under 15. The figures are administrative counts collected through the ministry's own IEPP and DRENA offices. The publisher's domain (mena-desps.org) is the DESPS statistics site, not a gouv.ci address. The start year is when the service that runs the network was created, not when the first literacy class was held.

pattern.mechanism: The education ministry ran adult literacy through a dedicated service and a network of centres staffed by volunteer or low-paid animateurs. That network contracted by about a quarter in the decade after 2015 while primary enrolment expanded.
preconditions: A standing budget line for animateurs and materials, which a volunteer-based network lacks
Partner NGOs and donors whose project cycles keep centres open, so closures follow funding cycles
Demand from adults who can take time out of informal work, which literacy alone rarely pays for

records.title: Henri Konan Bédié toll bridge
records.claim: The Ivorian government let a third Abidjan lagoon crossing as a toll-bridge concession to SOCOPRIM, the project company formed in 1997, whose investors include Bouygues Travaux Publics, after a 1996 tender. It funded initial works from October 2011 after the conflict. Private equity and loans, insured by MIGA guarantees of $145 million, built the 1.5 km bridge and 6.7 km road at a cost of about $282 million, and the bridge opened on 16 December 2014.

metric.name: Approximate construction cost of the bridge

secondMetric.name: MIGA guarantees covering the private investment

source.publisher: World Bank Group (MIGA / IFC), Public-Private Partnerships Briefs: Côte d'Ivoire Toll Bridge, April 2015

records.limits: The source is a two-page promotional brief from the World Bank Group, whose agency MIGA guaranteed the deal. It is an interested party describing its own transaction. The cost is given as approximate, with no baseline budget, so the record shows no cost or schedule performance against plan. The 100,000 vehicles a day is a forecast ('will use'), not observed traffic. No toll revenue, traffic or state guarantee and payment figures are published here, so the fiscal risk the state kept (minimum revenue guarantees, its own up-front works) is not visible. The brief is from 2015. This is one PPP.
