It does not show how often or at what scale Côte d'Ivoire delivers national objectives jointly with the private sector, which is the construct, and the 18 years from tender to opening were spent mostly in conflict, not in delivery.

pattern.mechanism: The government kept a 1990s concession alive through a decade of conflict and then restarted it in 2011, funding the first works itself. A political-risk guarantee from MIGA let a French contractor and development lenders put equity and debt into a toll bridge in a post-conflict country.
preconditions: A concessionaire and sponsor willing to hold a dormant contract through 15 years of instability
Multilateral political-risk cover that lenders accept as a substitute for sovereign creditworthiness
Urban traffic dense enough to carry tolls, which only Abidjan offers in the country

records.title: Melamchi Water Supply Project, and its erosion after the 2021 flood
records.claim: Nepal's government built the Melamchi River diversion tunnel and headworks to pipe an additional 170 million litres a day into the Kathmandu Valley, closing the project in June 2021, more than 14 years after its original March 2007 closing date; the 2021 flood then damaged the headworks, and water has since been diverted for about eight months a year.

metric.name: Delay of project closing beyond the originally planned closing date (March 2007 planned, June 2021 actual)

secondMetric.name: Months per year Melamchi water could be diverted after the 2021 flood damaged the headworks

source.publisher: Asian Development Bank, Independent Evaluation Department, Validation Report PVR-1165 (Melamchi Water Supply Project and Kathmandu Valley Water Services Sector Development Program)

records.limits: The 14 years is the gap between two loan closing dates, which is a lender's administrative milestone, not a measured completion date for the tunnel; the source gives no physical completion schedule against a baseline. The cost figure is not usable as an overrun: appraisal was $464 million and completion $345.3 million, but the 2008 scope change and the exit of the World Bank, NORAD and Sida mean the two totals price different projects, and ADB says separately that a 2014 additional loan covered tunnel cost overruns without stating the overrun in percent. The erosion is stated in words and one current number: the source publishes no figure for the year-round flow before the 2021 flood, so the secondMetric holds the post-flood level, not a measured peak. The flood is an exogenous shock, though ADB attributes the vulnerability to design that did not fit the terrain. The validation rests on the project completion report written by the lender and the executing agency, and ADB was itself a party to the project's design. The delay mixes national causes (slow decisions, leadership turnover, poor contractor management) with contractor failure, the cancelled and re-bid contracts of nonperforming contractors.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Physical Planning and Works and later the Ministry of Water Supply, with ADB as lead financier, tied a trans-basin water diversion to a reform of Kathmandu's water utility in a single loan. The infrastructure was delivered and the institutional reforms largely were not.
preconditions: Concessional finance from several lenders willing to stay through repeated contractor failure and the exit of three co-financiers
An executing agency able to cancel and re-tender a failed tunnel contract in mountainous, flood-prone terrain
A utility (KUKL) whose tariff and water-levy reforms the project assumed but could not compel
pattern.travelled: ADB's own lesson is that bundling a major physical build with a governance overhaul in one operation was over-ambitious; the remaining reforms were moved into separate pipeline programmes.

records.title: Earthquake housing reconstruction programme (National Reconstruction Authority)
records.claim: After the April 2015 Gorkha earthquake, Nepal's National Reconstruction Authority ran an owner-driven housing grant programme that, by 23 September 2021, had paid the third and final tranche of the reconstruction grant to 704,341 of 866,207 eligible households across 32 districts, with the World Bank-financed share revised to 309,335 houses.

metric.name: Eligible beneficiary households that had received the third tranche of the housing reconstruction grant

secondMetric.name: Houses whose safer reconstruction was supported by the IDA-financed Earthquake Housing Reconstruction Project, final revised count

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Status and Results Report, Earthquake Housing Reconstruction Project (P155969), Sequence No. 13

records.limits: A grant tranche is a payment, not a finished house: in the programme's rules the third tranche is released on completion of construction up to the roof band, so 704,341 counts households verified to that stage, not occupied, completed homes. The figures are reported by the government agencies to the lender and published by the lender, which financed about $700 million of the programme and rates its own operation; the 309,335 count was itself revised in 2023 after the project clarified that its reported total had included 3,766 houses financed by a trust fund grant (TF0A4783). About 162,000 eligible households had not received the final tranche at the reporting date, and the World Bank's ICR for the MDTF Funding for Earthquake Housing Reconstruction project (P162067, TF0A4783) notes the average rebuilding cost was about three times the NPR 300,000 grant, and one third of households used loans to close the gap. The number shows recovery after one shock; it says nothing about preparedness before the next one, and the NRA was a temporary body dissolved in December 2021, with its residual work passed to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. The record documents the national programme's scale through a single donor's monitoring report; there is no independent national statistical series behind it.

pattern.mechanism: Parliament created a time-limited National Reconstruction Authority that enrolled every damaged household, paid a flat grant in three tranches, and released each tranche only after engineers verified that the house met a seismic building code, so the payment schedule enforced the standard.
preconditions: A damage census that enumerated eligible households district by district before money flowed
Concessional and pooled donor finance large enough to fund a uniform grant for most of the caseload
Enough trained masons and inspecting engineers in remote districts to verify construction stage by stage
pattern.travelled: The tranche-on-verification model is the owner-driven reconstruction approach also used after the 2005 Pakistan earthquake; Nepal's version is distinguished by its scale and by tying each tranche to a code-compliance inspection.

records.title: Harare-Masvingo-Beitbridge highway rehabilitation, behind schedule
records.claim: Zimbabwe's government, funding the works from the budget, set out in its 2021 Budget to finish upgrading the roughly 580 km Harare-Beitbridge highway by 2022; it had opened 355 km to traffic by October 2022, and in July 2025 the Finance Ministry still reported 88 km outstanding, more than two and a half years past the 2022 target.

metric.name: Kilometres of the Harare-Masvingo-Beitbridge highway still outstanding, against a 2022 completion target

secondMetric.name: Kilometres of the 580 km Harare-Beitbridge highway opened to traffic

source.publisher: Ministry of Finance, Economic Development and Investment Promotion of Zimbabwe, 2025 Mid-Term Budget and Economic Review

records.limits: This is a schedule record with no cost figure: the ministry publishes allocations in a currency that was redenominated twice in the period (ZWL to ZiG) and gives no baseline budget for the whole road, so no cost overrun can be computed. The schedule slip of more than two and a half years (end of 2022 to July 2025) is our arithmetic from targets and progress the same ministry wrote in successive budget documents. It is not an audited figure, and the ministry itself kept moving the target (2022, then 2023, then 2025). The documents give the road's length as 560 km in 2020 and 580 km from 2022 onward without explaining the change. Kilometres 'opened to traffic' are self-reported and say nothing about pavement quality. The start year is that of the earliest official progress note, July 2020. Delivery used several local contractors under a national emergency programme, so this is evidence about a fiscally funded, multi-contractor build, not a single tender.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Transport split the corridor into sections and paid local contractors from the national budget, opening the road section by section as money arrived.
preconditions: Budget space for a large capital programme during high inflation and currency redenomination
Domestic contractors able to build trunk-road sections to regional standards
A political commitment to a flagship corridor strong enough to survive successive missed targets

records.title: Beitbridge Border Post modernisation (Zimborders build-operate-transfer concession)
records.claim: Zimbabwe's government contracted the Zimborders consortium under a build-operate-transfer concession to rebuild the Beitbridge Border Post with a US$300 million investment; works began in March 2019 and the President commissioned the modernised post in September 2022.

metric.name: Investment in the Beitbridge Border Post upgrade

source.publisher: Zimbabwe Revenue Authority (ZIMRA), news release 'Beitbridge Border upgrade takes shape'

records.limits: The US$300 million is a headline project value stated in a revenue authority news release during construction, not an audited outturn, and the release itself credits 'the government' with the investment, which blurs how much the concessionaire financed. The concession's term, tariff and risk allocation are not given in the official sources behind this record. One concession, however large, says little about the frequency of public-private delivery, which is half of what the indicator asks; the Treasury's own text shows the model only 'being considered' for other border posts. The record has no official series on clearance times or traffic before and after, so it shows that the facility was built and commissioned, not that it performs better.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Finance concessioned the rebuild of the country's busiest port of entry to a private consortium under build-operate-transfer, so the consortium financed construction and recovers it from user fees before handing the facility back.
preconditions: A border post whose traffic volume can repay private capital through user fees
A government willing to cede fee revenue for a fixed concession term
Financial closure achievable despite sovereign arrears that cut the state off from most concessional lenders

records.title: Solar powered milling plants contract, and its erosion
records.claim: Zambia's government contracted Shandong Dejian Group for a fixed-price US$200 million national programme of solar powered milling plants, financed in 2016 and due 24 months after the March 2016 deposit. The Auditor General found it still incomplete at 31 March 2022, 38 months after the scheduled completion date, and found 555 of the completed plants non-functional at audit in January 2024.

metric.name: Solar powered milling plants found non-functional at audit

secondMetric.name: Units contracted (1,553 solar powered milling plants plus 30 solar powered rice mills)

source.publisher: Office of the Auditor General of Zambia, Special Audit Report of the Auditor General on Public Debt for the period 1 January 2006 to 31 December 2022, section 7.6.4

records.limits: The Auditor General never publishes the peak number of working plants. The secondMetric is the contracted count, not the peak installed or working count. The 555 non-functional plants are counted among the 1,553 milling plants, about 36 percent; that share is our inference. The audit inspected selected sites, so the 555 figure may rest partly on progress reports rather than visits to every plant. The report is internally inconsistent: the loan paragraph describes 1,000 plants for US$200 million, while the finding counts 1,583 contracted units. It also dates the deposit (March 2016) before the China Development Bank loan (July 2016). The section gives no final cost and no completion date, so neither a cost overrun nor a final schedule overrun can be computed. 38 months is the delay at 31 March 2022 against the revised January 2019 date; against the original 6 March 2018 date it is about 49 months. The plants are distributed small units rather than a single structure, which makes the record a weaker fit for major public infrastructure. The Zambia Co-operative Federation, the implementing agent, is a federation and not a ministry. The audit also found K15.5 million in lease fees that were never paid into the Treasury. Nothing here shows how many households used the mills, or whether the non-functional plants were later repaired.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Finance borrowed from China Development Bank to buy a turnkey national programme of off-grid milling plants from one Chinese contractor, and appointed the Zambia Co-operative Federation to run them through local co-operatives. No public body was funded to maintain the equipment, so delivery slipped for years and a third of the completed plants stopped working.
preconditions: A maintenance and spare-parts budget for battery-based equipment spread across rural districts
An implementing agent with the technical staff to accept, commission and service the plants
Contract management able to enforce the fixed-price completion clause against the supplier

records.title: Drought Emergency Cash Transfer through the Social Cash Transfer
records.claim: After the President declared the 2024 El Niño drought a national disaster, Zambia's Ministry of Community Development and Social Services enumerated households in all 116 districts within four to eight weeks. From May 2024 to April 2025 it paid a drought emergency cash transfer to 1,631,007 households in 84 districts through the Social Cash Transfer, and paid a nationally funded price-shock transfer to 632,664 households in the other 32 districts.

metric.name: Households supported by the drought emergency cash transfer (D-ECT) in 84 drought-affected districts

secondMetric.name: Households paid the government-funded indirect price shock emergency cash transfer in the remaining 32 districts

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Zambia Scaling-up Shock Responsive Social Protection Project (P179095)

records.limits: The source is the World Bank's own completion report on a project it financed, written with the implementing ministry, and the household counts are programme administrative data, not an independent survey. The 1.63 million drought transfers were financed by IDA grants and a donor trust fund. Only the 632,664 price-shock transfers were paid from national funds, so the record shows government delivery capacity more than government financing. Payment timeliness fell to 17 percent in the first half of 2025, at the height of the drought, and averaged 29 percent over the project against a 90 percent target. Households counted as supported were not necessarily paid on time. The consumption and coping effects the report cites come from evaluations it says should be interpreted cautiously. The report's own footnote 51 puts enumeration at about eight weeks, against four weeks in the main text. The report dates the disaster declaration to 28 February 2024 in one place and 29 February in another. The record shows a response after a shock was declared. It does not show forecasting or contingent financing in place before the drought, and the report says the government began strengthening disaster risk financing, with contingent financing instruments, only from 2024, after the drought. The transfer ended in April 2025 and the caseload returned to its pre-drought level, so nothing here shows recovery outcomes.

pattern.mechanism: Once the drought was declared, the Cabinet chose the existing Social Cash Transfer instead of a parallel humanitarian pipeline to deliver emergency aid. The Ministry of Community Development and Social Services then used enumerators already on retainer in every district and a simplified proxy-means test to enrol drought-hit households in weeks and pay them through the same digital rails.
preconditions: A national cash transfer already running in all 116 districts, with a beneficiary information system and digital payments
Enumerators kept on retainer and a targeting questionnaire that could be adapted in weeks
Donor crisis financing available at short notice to fund the expansion while the treasury was in debt restructuring

records.title: Urban Water Supply Project (PEMU), part of the Kabala programme for Bamako
records.claim: Mali's water assets company SOMAPEP-SA built the reservoirs, transmission mains and 1,016 km of distribution networks that brought water services to 803,000 people in Bamako and six other towns, alongside the Kabala treatment plant that came into service in June 2019. Of the US$130 million approved, US$119.6 million was spent, and the project closed in December 2022 against an original closing date of December 2018.

metric.name: Actual project cost disbursed at closing

secondMetric.name: Approved project cost, original 2013 credit plus 2016 additional financing

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Mali Urban Water Supply Project (P122826)

records.limits: The source is the World Bank's self-evaluation of its own credit. Spending US$119.6 million of an approved US$130 million is not a cost underrun against a fixed scope. The approved amount grew from US$80 million to US$130 million in 2016, when six towns were added. The report says savings were used to raise targets, and it publishes no unit cost or contract-level overrun. The four-year schedule slip, from a December 2018 to a December 2022 closing, is our reading of the key dates. Three of those years were added with the 2016 scope expansion and one year in 2021 for COVID-19 and the disbursement suspensions that followed the 2020 and 2021 coups, so most of the slip was planned. Targets outside Bamako were not met because distribution networks were finished late. The Kabala treatment plant itself was financed by AFD, the EU and the EIB, and its cost and schedule are not in this record. The project was designed to make the urban water sector financially sustainable, and that objective failed: tariffs were frozen for eight years, and the indicator was removed in 2021. The project was IDA-financed throughout. The national contribution was implementation by SOMAPEP-SA and SOMAGEP-SA, not money.

pattern.mechanism: Mali's government split urban water into an asset-holding company (SOMAPEP-SA) that builds and a utility (SOMAGEP-SA) that operates, under a regulator (CREE). SOMAPEP-SA then used an IDA credit to build the transmission and distribution side of an eleven-donor Kabala programme, while other donors financed the treatment plant.
preconditions: A standing asset company and utility able to procure and supervise works through two coups and a pandemic
Donor co-financing coordinated through one programme, so the plant and the networks were built in step
Tariffs set high enough to keep the system running, which Mali did not do

records.title: Adult literacy centres financed through FONAENF, and their erosion
records.claim: Burkina Faso's adult literacy and non-formal education centres, financed through FONAENF and run by contracted operators under the faire-faire strategy, enrolled 178,021 adult learners in 2015. Enrolment fell to 113,721 in 2018 and 86,405 in 2021, when 1,885 adult centres opened against 3,094 in 2018.

metric.name: Young people and adults enrolled in non-formal education centres (apprenants jeunes et adultes)

secondMetric.name: Adults enrolled in non-formal education centres at the 2015 high point of the 2015 to 2019 series (ENF des adultes)

source.publisher: Ministère de l'Education nationale, de l'Alphabétisation et de la Promotion des Langues nationales (MENAPLN), Burkina Faso, Rapport de suivi annuel 2021 du Programme de développement stratégique de l'éducation de base (PDSEB), version provisoire, May 2022, from DGESS annuaires statistiques de l'ENF, hosted by the Global Partnership for Education

records.limits: The figures are counts of people enrolled in literacy and non-formal education centres, not the share of adults that the gap asks for. The ministry publishes no participation rate, and on any plausible adult population the 2021 count is around one percent of adults or less, so even the 2015 level was a small programme against the construct. The 2021 figure comes from a ministry monitoring report marked 'version provisoire' (provisional), and the copy used is hosted by the Global Partnership for Education, a funder of the plan. The 2015 figure comes from a different ministry document, the SNDENF 2021-2025, and the copy used is on a third-party site (mojaafrica.net), not a government domain. The two documents do not fully agree: the SNDENF prints 2016 adult enrolment as 86,001 in one table and 88,770 in the next. 2015 is the high point of the published 2015 to 2019 series and may not be the programme's true peak, and the series is volatile: it dropped by half in 2016 and partly recovered in 2018, which shows enrolment following each year's funding, not a steady decline. The 2021 figure is up from a 2020 low of 81,350, and the ministry credits the rise to a slight increase in budget programme 060. The 2021 level matches 2016 (86,001), so the decline is from the 2015 and 2018 highs, not a steady fall. The centre counts in Tableau V-4 are for 'jeunes et adultes' centres. 'Jeunes et adultes' covers learners aged 15 and over, and the adolescent centres are counted separately and excluded here. The counts are compiled from forms filled in by the operators the fund pays, so the people delivering the programme are reporting their own enrolment. The ministry attributes the fall to reduced budget allocations, and its own reports say the security crisis since 2016 closed many education facilities, but the series cannot separate the two causes. The record has no figure after 2021, so it cannot say whether the decline continued after the 2022 coups.

pattern.mechanism: The ministry created FONAENF in 2002 to pool state and donor money and pay NGOs and associations to run literacy centres under the faire-faire strategy, so the state finances and supervises while operators deliver. Because each year's allocation decides how many centres open, cuts in the budget line and the spread of insecurity reduced the number of centres and learners almost immediately.
preconditions: A pooled fund with donor co-financing and a pipeline of contracted local operators in every region
An annual budget allocation large enough to open thousands of centres each campaign
Enough security in rural areas for centres to open and learners to attend, which the country lost after 2016

records.title: Ouagadougou Water Supply Project (Ziga)
records.claim: Between 2001 and 2007, ONEA, Burkina Faso's national water utility, delivered the Ziga project through a dedicated project unit. The project built the Ziga earth dam and its transmission main to Ouagadougou, plus 56,000 subsidised connections and 400 standpipes. Eleven external financiers and the government paid US$269.37 million, 131 percent of the US$205.88 million estimated at appraisal, and the project closed on its original date of 31 December 2007.

metric.name: Actual total financing of the Ouagadougou Water Supply Project, all financiers

secondMetric.name: Total financing estimated at appraisal

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Burkina Faso Ouagadougou Water Supply Project (P000306), ICR705, April 2008

records.limits: The 31 percent overrun is in US dollars, and much of it is exchange rate. The ICR's own note puts the dollar at 640 CFA francs at appraisal and 506 at closing. Converted at those two rates, the appraisal total of about CFAF 132 to 134 billion and the actual total of about CFAF 136 billion are within a few percent of each other. Spending happened between the two dates, so neither conversion is exact, and the ICR prints both 640 and 650 for the appraisal rate. The real cost overrun in local currency is therefore unknown and probably small, and the dollar figure overstates it. The schedule figure only covers the 2001 to 2007 financing window. The project was conceived in the early 1990s and launched in 1994, so on-time closing says nothing about the decade of preparation before it. The ICR is the World Bank grading an operation it financed and supervised, and it relies on the borrower's reporting. The people-served figure is an estimate the ICR computes at 10 people per connection and 120 per standpipe, not a count. Donors provided almost all of the money, and the borrower's share was about US$8.8 million, so the record shows execution by ONEA, not national financing. The data are from 2007 and say nothing about Burkina Faso's delivery of large projects since then.

pattern.mechanism: The government gave ONEA a mandate by decree in 1996 to set up a dedicated Ziga project unit. That unit ran one investment programme for eleven external financiers and the government, with joint annual supervision meetings, while the government adjusted tariffs and paid its own water bills so the utility stayed solvent.
preconditions: A national utility already financially sound enough to borrow and to recover costs through tariffs
Donor coordination under one project unit and one supervision committee rather than parallel projects
Political backing for tariff adjustments and for the state paying its own utility bills
pattern.travelled: The ONEA model, a public utility under a performance contract with its own project units, became a West African reference case for urban water reform. Later Burkina Faso programmes extended it to sanitation and secondary towns.

records.title: Guinea's 2021 Ebola outbreak response
records.claim: Guinea's Ministry of Health announced an Ebola outbreak in N'Zérékoré Prefecture on 14 February 2021 and declared it over on 19 June 2021. It activated national and district emergency committees, vaccinated 10,873 people and followed 1,031 of 1,110 contacts daily, and held the outbreak to 23 confirmed and probable cases and 12 deaths, five years after the 2014 to 2016 West African epidemic.

metric.name: Ebola cases in the 2021 outbreak, confirmed and probable

secondMetric.name: People vaccinated against Ebola in the response, including 885 contacts and 2,779 frontline workers

source.publisher: World Health Organization, Disease Outbreak News, Ebola virus disease - Guinea (DON328), 19 June 2021

records.limits: This is one outbreak in one prefecture, so it shows a response to one shock and not a standing national capacity, and a single outcome cannot separate preparedness from luck. Detection was slow: WHO reports the index case, a health worker, fell ill on 15 January and died on 28 January after visiting two health facilities and a traditional practitioner. She was buried without safe burial practices, and the outbreak was announced only on 14 February. Five cases were health workers, which points to infection-control failures. A second cluster of community deaths surfaced in late March after more than three weeks with no cases. One confirmed case was lost to follow-up from 1 April until 18 June, and 79 of the 1,110 contacts were not followed daily. WHO notes that only nine (39%) of the 23 cases were known contacts at detection, and that the alert system reported a suboptimal number of alerts. The response was not purely national: WHO reports the MoH acted together with WHO and other partners, and their contribution cannot be separated from that of the national institutions. The figures are WHO restating Ministry of Health reports, so the government is reporting on its own response. The page gives no figures for the 2014 to 2016 epidemic, so the record makes no quantitative comparison with it.

pattern.mechanism: Guinea's Ministry of Health activated national and district emergency management committees within days of the announcement. It deployed case-search, contact-tracing, burial and community-engagement teams, set up PCR testing in N'Zérékoré, and ran ring vaccination of contacts and frontline workers with WHO and partner support. It declared the outbreak over after the 42-day count.
preconditions: Response structures, trained staff and community networks left in place from the 2014 to 2016 epidemic
A licensed Ebola vaccine and therapeutics that partners could ship within days
A laboratory able to confirm cases near the outbreak, here a PCR capacity stood up in N'Zérékoré
pattern.travelled: The ring-vaccination and emergency-committee model from the 2018 to 2020 eastern DRC response, applied in a country that had lived through the 2014 to 2016 epidemic.

records.title: Private-led coffee sector governance through InterCafe, and its dismantling
records.claim: Burundi had run its coffee value chain through a public regulator, ARFIC, beside private-led bodies: InterCafe, whose members were producers, millers, roasters and exporters, and the growers' consortium CNAC with about 109,000 members. The government named all three as joint implementing agencies of the Coffee Sector Competitiveness Project. In January 2020 it replaced them by decree with ODECA, an office under state control. The project closed early in 2021, and 44 percent of the grant was cancelled.

metric.name: Share of the IDA Coffee Sector Competitiveness grant cancelled after the government returned the coffee sector to state control

secondMetric.name: Individual members of CNAC, the national coffee growers' consortium, one of the three private-led implementing bodies

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR00004849, Burundi Coffee Sector Competitiveness Project (P151869), March 2022

records.limits: The only source is the lender's own completion report, and it is written from the side that lost the argument: the World Bank calls the 2020 decision unilateral and made without advance warning. The 44 percent is the share of one donor project cancelled. It measures what the dismantling cost that project, not how much public-private delivery Burundi lost. The ICR publishes no series on the scale of the private-led arrangement, such as the private share of washing stations, InterCafe's budget or the volumes it governed. The 109,000 CNAC members is a membership count at appraisal, not a delivery figure. The liberalisation began under structural adjustment in the 1980s and was pushed by donors (IFC advised on the third phase), so how far the arrangement was Burundi's own institutional choice is contestable. The 2005 start year rests on a decree the ICR names as the one that reformed the sector. The ICR does not say in which year InterCafe itself was created. Nothing here shows whether coffee output, quality or grower prices fell after ODECA took over. The ICR reports the share of AA/A/FW+ grade coffee rising from 59 to 66 percent, 70 percent of the incremental target. No data exists for the second quality indicator, the specialty share of exports, because ARFIC was removed and ODECA provided none.

pattern.mechanism: Over two decades the Government of Burundi handed coffee sector governance to an independent public regulator alongside a private interprofessional association and a growers' consortium, and wrote them into a donor project as co-implementers. In January 2020 it took the value chain back by presidential decree under a new state office, without consulting the partners.
preconditions: Private and cooperative operators organised enough to run washing stations, sector data and an interprofessional body
A state willing to share control of the main export crop, a commitment that here rested on donor conditionality more than on domestic consensus
Legal footing that can survive a change of government, which a decree-based arrangement did not have

records.title: Jiji and Mulembwe hydropower project
records.claim: The Government of Burundi, through REGIDESO and a World Bank project unit, built the 49.5 MW Jiji (32.5 MW) and Mulembwe (17 MW) run-of-river plants with their transmission lines and substations. The project was approved in 2014 at US$270.3 million with an original closing date of December 2019. Construction began only in February 2020, after the 2015 political crisis. The World Bank put the estimated cost at US$319.1 million in November 2024. Jiji was inaugurated in June 2025 and Mulembwe in June 2026.

metric.name: Estimated total cost of the Jiji and Mulembwe Hydropower Project, all financiers

secondMetric.name: Appraised total cost at Board approval

source.publisher: World Bank, Project Paper for Additional Financing, Burundi Jiji and Mulembwe Hydropower Project (P133610), December 2024

records.limits: The cost figure is the World Bank's estimate in November 2024, before either plant was commissioned. At that date it reported a financing gap of US$41.7 million still to close. The 18 percent is the Bank's own ratio in its cost table, set against the 2014 appraisal. It excludes a further estimated US$19 million lost to currency depreciation on the 2014 pledges. The schedule slip is not published as a figure. The original closing date of 31 December 2019 against inauguration in June 2025 (Jiji) and June 2026 (Mulembwe) is our reading of a 6.5-year slip. Much of it comes from the 2015 to 2020 political crisis, which delayed hiring the owner's engineer to 2017 and the contractor's mobilisation to 2020, so it is not purely an execution failure. The project was financed and supervised by IDA, the EU, the EIB and the AfDB. Delivery was shared, and the Bank reports weak contract management in the project unit. Completion rests on press releases: the Presidency's June 2025 release for Jiji, and the EIB's June 2026 release for Mulembwe. Neither release shows that the plants deliver the planned 235 GWh a year.

pattern.mechanism: Burundi bundled two run-of-river plants, transmission and utility reform into one donor-pooled project under a World Bank-supervised implementation unit. It held the scheme together through a political crisis and two additional financings until both plants were commissioned.
preconditions: Concessional co-financiers willing to top up a stalled grant rather than cancel it
An owner's engineer and contractors able to work in a fragile state with fuel and foreign-exchange shortages
A utility (REGIDESO) able to absorb and operate new generation capacity

records.title: Shock-responsive social cash transfers and the Cat DDO
records.claim: From 2019 the Government of Malawi identified every household it registered for shock-responsive cash transfers through its Unified Beneficiary Registry. It expanded the Social Cash Transfer Programme to give drought and COVID-19 aid to more than 300,000 rural households, and it drew US$30 million of pre-arranged contingent financing on 10 April 2020, three weeks after declaring a state of disaster.

metric.name: Rural households given drought and COVID-19 aid through shock-responsive expansions of the Social Cash Transfer Programme, identified through the Unified Beneficiary Registry

secondMetric.name: Catastrophe Deferred Drawdown Option disbursed after the COVID-19 state of disaster

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR00006189, Malawi Disaster Risk Management Development Policy Financing with Cat DDO (P165056), June 2023

records.limits: The source is the lender's self-evaluation of its own policy operation, and the 300,000 is a floor ('more than') summed over about four years and two kinds of shock. It is not a per-event count and has no denominator of affected households. The money behind the transfers was largely external: a World Bank project's contingency window, ARC sovereign drought insurance whose premiums donors financed in full (ICR Annex), and IDA's Cat DDO. The evidence is that the national system routed aid, not that Malawi financed it. The Cat DDO was triggered by a pandemic, not a natural hazard, and its US$30 million was budget support with no traceable link to households. The ICR says fewer than 10 percent of the households receiving transfers were registered before the protocols. It rates the operation moderately satisfactory and reports that resilient transport standards were never developed. The source is dated June 2023; the operation itself closed in 2022. Cyclone Freddy (February and March 2023) and the 2024 El Nino drought fell after the operation closed and are not assessed. 'Operating' assumes the registry and the scale-up mechanism are still in use, which this source does not confirm beyond 2023.

pattern.mechanism: Malawi's Ministry of Finance and its social protection agencies built one registry of rural households and set protocols that every shock-response transfer must use it. They paired the registry with financing pre-arranged before a disaster (a contingent credit line, a project contingency window and sovereign drought insurance), so cash could reach households without a new appeal each time.
preconditions: A census-style household registry covering most of the rural population and kept current
Contingent financing agreed before the shock, which here depended on concessional lenders and an insurance pool
A legal trigger, a declared state of disaster under the 1991 Disaster Preparedness and Relief Act, that releases the funds

records.title: National Adult Literacy Programme
records.claim: Malawi's Ministry of Gender, Community Development and Social Welfare has run the National Adult Literacy Programme since 1986 through volunteer-taught community classes. Enrolment in Adult Literacy and Education reached 171,434 learners in the 2024/25 financial year, against about 82,000 participants in 2006.

metric.name: Learners enrolled in Adult Literacy and Education

secondMetric.name: Adult literacy participants, public and NGO classes combined

source.publisher: Malawi Government, Ministry of Finance and Economic Affairs, Annual Economic Report 2025 (Budget Document No. 2), section 15.2.2.1

records.limits: The gap asks for a share of adults, and this is a count of learners in one literacy programme. Against Malawi's adult population, roughly 10 million people aged 15 and over, it is under 2 percent. That ratio is our rough computation and is not published. The figure is the ministry's administrative report, carried without method in a budget document. It does not say whether NGO and faith-based classes are included. The series is inconsistent: the Annual Economic Report 2024 gives the same 158,048 as learners who 'graduated' in 2023/24, and the 2025 report uses it as the previous year's enrolment. The 2006 comparison comes from a different ministry, the department's earlier home, and counts public and NGO participants together, so the two numbers may not measure the same thing. Literacy classes are one narrow kind of non-formal adult education. They say nothing about vocational, workplace or tertiary adult learning. The 2008 report records that the programme aimed to reach 2 million of 4.6 million illiterate adults by 2000 but had reached about 860,000 by 2006. It also records 'magnitude of failure', volunteer instructors whose minimum qualification is primary school grade 8, and inadequate funding. The 2025 report names the National Strategy on Adult Literacy and Lifelong Learning, not NALP, so treating the 2024/25 enrolment as the same programme begun in 1986 is our reading. Enrolment says nothing about completion or literacy gained.

pattern.mechanism: The ministry responsible for community development runs adult literacy as a standing national programme. It organises classes of about 25 learners through district community development officers and volunteer instructors that communities choose, and NGOs and churches run parallel classes under the same policy.
preconditions: A field network of district community development staff to open and supervise classes in every district
Volunteers with at least primary schooling willing to teach for little or no pay
A recurrent budget line, however small, that survives changes of ministry

records.title: Sandbox Regulatório do Banco de Moçambique
records.claim: Banco de Moçambique admitted 11 participants, chosen from 19 applicants, to the sixth edition of its regulatory sandbox in March 2025, and at the same ceremony gave participation certificates to the five fintechs that had completed the fifth edition.

metric.name: Participants admitted to the sixth edition of the regulatory sandbox

secondMetric.name: Fintechs completing the fifth edition and receiving participation certificates

source.publisher: Banco de Moçambique, highlight 'Governor Rogério Zandamela launches the sixth edition of the regulatory sandbox'

records.limits: The regulator reports on its own sandbox in a news item, not in a statistical series, and the page gives one cohort only: it does not give cumulative admissions or exits across the six editions, nor how many of the 11 went on to complete testing. 'Participants' can include incumbents as well as start-ups (the five graduates named include Vodafone M-Pesa, a large mobile money operator), so the count is not a count of new firms. Completing the sandbox makes a firm eligible to apply for a licence; the page does not say how many were licensed. The 2018 start is the establishment date in the World Bank's Appendix 3 database (May 2018, five firms in the sandbox at the time), not stated on the cited page. The sandbox page (bancomoc.mz, BM Regulatory Sandbox) shows a call for an eighth edition dated September 2026 and a seventh-edition invitation dated 1 October 2025 for testing from February 2026, so the regime was running at retrieval, but neither document carries a participant count. Against a population of about 34 million, 11 admissions is about 0.3 per million people.

pattern.mechanism: The central bank runs its sandbox in annual editions: it opens a call, selects a cohort, runs roughly nine months of preparation, testing and reporting, and certifies the firms that finish so they can apply for a licence.
preconditions: A sandbox regulation issued by the central bank with fixed phases and exit rules
A financial inclusion office with staff to supervise each cohort
A licensing route for payment and credit services that a graduate can apply to
pattern.travelled: The cohort model with a public certificate ceremony is the format several southern African central banks adopted later; Mozambique is among the earliest in the region, with a first cohort in 2018.

records.title: Regulatory Sandbox Licence of the Economic Development Board
records.claim: Mauritius's Economic Development Board, operating a regulatory sandbox licence regime for innovative financial projects since September 2018 by the World Bank's dating, had nine firms in its sandbox when the World Bank compiled its global database of sandboxes in 2020.

metric.name: Firms in the sandbox (EDB Regulatory Sandbox Licence)

source.publisher: World Bank, Global Experiences from Regulatory Sandboxes (Fintech Note No. 8, November 2020), Appendix 3 Database of Global Sandboxes, row 'Mauritius, EDB'

records.limits: The figure is a stock of firms in the sandbox at an unstated date in 2020, compiled by the World Bank from EDB sources, not an annual count of admissions and exits, and it sits in a wide table in the plain-text version of the report (the row lists 'Operational', 9, 'Regulatory Sandbox license', established Sep-18). EDB's own annual reports do not give admissions: the 2020/21 report says only that the EDB 'registered 8 new applications for fintech RSL' and that licences were issued when positively determined, and the 2021/22, 2022/23 and 2023/24 reports read today do not mention the licence at all. A licence under the EDB regime could cover activities with no legal framework at all, so some licensees used it as a market-entry route rather than a time-limited test. Since 2021 the sandbox function has also sat with the sector regulators: the Financial Services Commission issued its first Regulatory Sandbox Authorisation under section 14B of the Financial Services Act on 30 March 2022 and reported that entity exiting after successful testing in its 2022/23 annual report, and the Bank of Mauritius issued a Guideline for Regulatory Sandbox Authorisation in May 2024 with no participant count in its 2024 annual report or December 2024 Financial Stability Report. Status operating rests on those successor regimes, not on evidence that the EDB licence itself still admits firms.

pattern.mechanism: The investment promotion board issued time-bound sandbox licences to firms proposing financial activities for which Mauritian law had no framework, on the recommendation of a national committee, before the sector regulators took on their own sandbox authorisations.
preconditions: A statute letting a non-regulator body license activities outside existing financial law
A cross-agency committee to vet applications on behalf of several regulators
Regulators willing later to absorb the function under their own statutes

records.title: Bank of Uganda regulatory sandbox
records.claim: The Bank of Uganda reviewed five applications to its regulatory sandbox in the year to June 2025, issued deficiency letters to all of them, and reported one firm, Rexial Payment Systems Limited, exiting the sandbox after testing and applying for a payment systems operator licence.

metric.name: Firms exiting the regulatory sandbox in the financial year

secondMetric.name: Applications to the regulatory sandbox reviewed in the financial year

source.publisher: Bank of Uganda, Integrated Annual Report for the year ended 30 June 2025, 'FinTech innovation and emerging technology exploration'

records.limits: The bank reports on itself, in a 188-page PDF (PDF page 59). The report gives no count of firms admitted in the year: that none of the five applicants was admitted is our reading of 'Deficiency letters were issued to all applicants', so the year's admissions may be zero, and the count of firms still testing is not given. One exit is the whole completion figure, and the report does not say whether the licence was granted. The 2021 start is the year the sandbox framework launched, not stated in this report. The same report lists 'review the regulatory sandbox framework' among next-year priorities. The Capital Markets Authority launched separate Regulatory Sandbox Rules in October 2025 (cmauganda.co.ug news, 8 October 2025) with no participant count, so the record covers only the central bank's sandbox. Against about 48 million people, one completion is a rate near zero per million.

pattern.mechanism: The central bank screens sandbox applications against its framework, sends deficiency letters rather than admitting weak proposals, supervises the experiments it has admitted, and steers firms that finish testing into its licensing regime.
preconditions: A sandbox framework issued under the central bank's payment systems law
A licence category (payment systems operator) that a graduate can move into
Supervisory staff to monitor experiments for scalability and market suitability

records.title: Regulatory Sandbox Framework for Capital Markets, first cohort
records.claim: Zambia's Securities and Exchange Commission admitted four innovations to the first cohort of its capital markets sandbox, with testing starting on 19 November 2021, and announced on 15 July 2024 that live testing had been completed and directed all four to suspend operations inside the sandbox pending evaluation and exit.

metric.name: Innovations admitted to the first sandbox cohort and completing live testing

source.publisher: Securities and Exchange Commission of Zambia, Press Release 'Regulatory Sandbox Framework for Capital Markets' (15 July 2024)

records.limits: The regulator reports on itself in a one-page press release (PDF). The four are named innovations from four firms (Kukula Capital, Lupiya Circle, Lusaka Securities Exchange and Premier Credit Zambia), one of them the national stock exchange. The release says the framework was issued on 18 December 2022 but that testing began on 'Wednesday, 19th November 2021', which cannot both be right, and neither date matches its weekday (19 November 2021 was a Friday, 18 December 2022 a Sunday); the start year 2021 is the earliest date the release gives and is not confirmed by any other source read. Completion of testing is not a successful exit: the release says each innovator will or will not be permitted to deploy commercially after review, and no outcome statement was found on the SEC site; its list of sandbox participants page is empty. If the 2021 date is right, testing ran over two and a half years for one cohort of four, and no second cohort was found. The Bank of Zambia runs a separate sandbox and reports that 'one financial innovation exited the Sandbox after a successful test' in 2024 (Annual Report 2024, printed page 69, PDF page 86, https://www.boz.zm/sites/default/files/2026-01/Bank_of_Zambia_2024_Annual_Report.pdf); summed, the two regulators show about five firms through a sandbox over three years for 21 million people.

pattern.mechanism: The securities regulator admitted a single cohort of capital markets innovations, let them take real investors under parameters and caps, then froze onboarding at the end of testing so it could evaluate each before deciding on commercial deployment.
preconditions: A sandbox guideline issued under the Securities Act
Firms, including the national exchange, willing to test under caps
A licensing decision process after testing, which here had not been published

records.title: Securities and Exchange Commission of Zimbabwe regulatory sandbox
records.claim: The Securities and Exchange Commission of Zimbabwe published a list of seven innovative financial technology solutions approved for testing in its regulatory sandbox in July 2026, among them asset, securities and infrastructure tokenisation platforms, a crowdfunding platform and a blockchain capital raising platform.

metric.name: Solutions approved for participation in Regulatory Sandbox testing

source.publisher: Securities and Exchange Commission of Zimbabwe, Public Notice SCZ24072026 'Update on approved regulatory sandbox participants'

records.limits: The notice is a one-page PDF listing approvals; it calls itself an update but gives no earlier list, no admission date per firm, no testing period and no exits, so the figure is a stock of approved participants at July 2026, not an annual admissions count, and started is set to the notice year because no earlier admission was read at a source. Approval for testing is not testing: the notice warns that representations beyond testing are misleading, and some entries (Financial Securities Exchange, a licensed exchange) are incumbents. The Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe has run a separate fintech regulatory sandbox since March 2021, whose admissions are not counted here because no current count was read at an official source today. Seven approvals against about 16 million people is about 0.4 per million.

pattern.mechanism: The securities regulator approves named solutions into a timed, supervised sandbox under its own guidelines and publishes the list as a public notice so investors can tell a sandbox participant from a licensed firm.
preconditions: Sandbox guidelines issued by the securities regulator
A fintech unit to monitor and evaluate the tests
Demand from tokenisation and crowdfunding firms with no licence category to apply under

records.title: National Planning Commission foresight work for Malawi 2063
records.claim: Malawi's National Planning Commission, which signed a UNDP initiation plan in November 2020 to create a foresight unit and horizon scanning capability, reported for 2022/23 that it produced a foresight modelling report with modelled scenarios for the Malawi 2063 vision, policy briefs on three of the vision's pillars with UNDP and the finance ministry, and foresight modelling training for planners from ministries and academia.

metric.name: Foresight modelling reports produced (assessing Malawi's trajectory towards MIP-1 milestones and MW2063 aspirations)

source.publisher: National Planning Commission of Malawi, 2023 Annual Report (financial year 2022/2023), section 3.3.3 Enhanced Foresight Initiatives

records.limits: The commission reports on itself, in a PDF (section 3.3, printed pages 38 to 39, PDF page 42). The metric is a single report, and the text does not say how many policy briefs were written, only that they covered the urbanisation, industrialisation and agricultural productivity pillars, so the delivery figure is thin. The foresight work leans on UNDP: the unit was set up under a six-month UNDP initiation plan (NPC news item, 26 November 2020, https://npc.mw/2020/12/npc-undp-sign-agreement-to-initiate-implementation-of-foresight-project/) and the 2022/23 briefs were produced with UNDP, so the record cannot separate national capacity from donor support. The commission is primarily a development planning body that monitors the Malawi 2063 vision and its first ten-year implementation plan, which sits closer to planning than to open-ended scenario foresight; its modelled scenarios are tied to vision targets. No later annual report was read, so status rests on 2022/23, and the report gives no staff count or budget for the foresight function.

pattern.mechanism: The statutory planning commission that owns the national long-term vision built a small foresight and modelling capability with UNDP support and used it to test the vision's targets against scenarios and to train planners in ministries.
preconditions: A statutory planning commission with a mandate over a long-term vision
Donor funding and technical partners to seed the capability
Ministry planners and academics willing to adopt the methods
pattern.travelled: The commission organised a learning visit on foresight planning to South Africa in the same year, so the method was borrowed from a regional neighbour as well as from UNDP.

records.title: Collaborative Research and Innovation Grant Scheme (CRIGS)
records.claim: The Mauritius Research and Innovation Council's Collaborative Research and Innovation Grant Scheme, which co-funds projects led by a local company with a local academic or research institution, had completed 17 projects and had 14 more under way as at 30 June 2020, with 61.5 million rupees of private contribution to the completed ones.

metric.name: CRIGS projects completed (project value Rs 115.9 M, private sector contribution Rs 61.5 M, MRIC amount Rs 53.4 M)

secondMetric.name: CRIGS projects ongoing (project value Rs 102.18 M, private sector contribution Rs 57.22 M)

source.publisher: Mauritius Research and Innovation Council, Annual Report September 2019 to June 2020, Portfolio section

records.limits: The council reports on its own scheme. The figures sit in a PDF on page 23 of 66 (printed page 22); the portfolio table on the same page gives a different split for the reporting year alone (10 ongoing and 3 completed CRIGS initiatives), so the cumulative and annual counts must not be mixed. 2019-20 is the latest annual report the council has published: its publications page lists the 2020-21 to 2023-24 reports as awaiting audit or in process, so nothing after June 2020 can be checked against an annual report. The scheme page (mric.mu/collaborative-research-and-innovation-grant-scheme) still describes the scheme and lists 18 funded projects, all marked completed, with no ongoing project and no call dates, so the scheme may have funded little or nothing since 2020; 'operating' rests on the page still offering it and is the weakest part of the record. Thirty-one projects over six years is small even for a country of 1.3 million people, the counts are projects rather than distinct firms, and project value includes the firm's in-kind contribution. The start year is the first call for proposals, June 2014, stated in the council's Annual Report 2014, not at the cited URL. Nothing here shows the research results or commercial outcomes.

pattern.mechanism: The national research council pays roughly half the cost of an R&D project only when a registered company applies with a local university or research institute as partner, so public money follows a firm's own commitment.
preconditions: A national research and innovation council with a competitive grant budget
A university and research institute base able to take on contract work for local firms
Firms large enough to co-fund half of a multi-million rupee project

records.title: Mauritius Institute of Training and Development part-time training
records.claim: The Mauritius Institute of Training and Development, the state technical and vocational training body, enrolled 3,352 trainees on part-time courses across its training centres between July 2022 and June 2023, out of 8,668 people it trained that year in full-time, part-time and apprenticeship modes.

metric.name: Part-time enrolment, all MITD training centres

secondMetric.name: People trained by MITD in full-time, part-time or apprenticeship mode

source.publisher: Mauritius Institute of Training and Development, Annual Report 2022/2023, table 'Part time enrolment by training centres and gender for the period July 2022 to June 2023'

records.limits: MITD reports on itself. The part-time table is on page 54 of the PDF (printed page 52) and the 8,668 total is in the opening statement on page 6. The counts are enrolments, not unique adults, and the report gives no ages: part-time courses are the mode most likely to serve working adults, but the full-time courses (2,993 trainees on page 50) mainly take school leavers and are not adult learning in the sense of the indicator, which is why the part-time figure is the metric. Professional drivers training (526) and hotel school short courses (787) make up close to two fifths of the part-time count. MITD is one provider: the Human Resource Development Council's training schemes, private providers and the universities are not in it, so it is not a national participation rate. 2022/23 is the latest annual report on the MITD site. The start year is the 2009 Act that created MITD from the former Industrial and Vocational Training Board, as commonly reported; it was not read at the cited source.

pattern.mechanism: A statutory training institute under the education ministry runs a national network of training centres that sell evening and part-time courses to workers alongside its full-time and apprenticeship programmes, and publishes centre-by-centre enrolment each year.
preconditions: A network of public training centres spread across the island
A national qualifications framework that part-time courses lead into
Employers and a training levy that make part-time study affordable

records.title: NAMCOL secondary education programme for out-of-school learners
records.claim: The Namibian College of Open Learning, a state-owned distance education college, registered 27,242 learners in its Grade 11 and 12 secondary programme in 2025, against a peak of 30,999 in 2017 and a low of 23,258 in 2022.

metric.name: Learners enrolled in NAMCOL secondary education programmes (NSSCO and NSSCAS)

secondMetric.name: Same count at its peak year

source.publisher: Namibian College of Open Learning (NAMCOL), Statistical Digest 2024/25, section 2 Learner enrolment, Figures 1 to 3

records.limits: NAMCOL reports on itself. The numbers are read off charts in a PDF laid out as two-page spreads: the 2025 total and the 2010 to 2025 trend (Figure 3) are on PDF page 15 (printed pages 28 to 29). The digest publishes no age profile, so the record cannot show how many learners are adults rather than young people repeating Grade 11 or 12 after leaving school; NAMCOL's secondary programme is a second-chance route and many of its learners are in their late teens and early twenties, so this is the weak point of the record for an adult learning indicator. Learners take an average of about two subjects, part-time, so a registration is not full-time study. The digest attributes the 2018 to 2022 fall, sharpest in 2022 at 17.7 percent, to curriculum changes, and enrolment has risen each year since; 2025 is still 12 percent below the 2017 peak, which is why the peak is carried but the status is operating, not eroded. TVET enrolment at NAMCOL is small (327 in 2025) and is not included. The 1998 start is the year the digest's foreword dates the publication series from; NAMCOL was created by an Act of 1997.

pattern.mechanism: The state set up a distance-learning college that lets anyone who left school without the senior secondary certificate register for individual subjects, study from printed and online materials and attend weekend tutorials at centres across the regions, then sit the national examinations.
preconditions: A national examination that any registered candidate can sit regardless of age
A network of tutorial centres in schools used after hours
Public subsidy keeping per-subject fees low

records.title: Alfabetização e Educação de Adultos (public adult literacy and adult primary education), and its decline
records.claim: Mozambique's education ministry counted 243,655 learners in its public adult literacy and adult primary education classes in the April 2025 school survey (169,341 in literacy and 74,314 in primary education for young people and adults), against 302,207 in 2024 and 529,314 in the March 2014 survey.

metric.name: Learners in public Literacy and Adult Education (Alfabetizacao e Educacao de Adultos), Annual School Survey 30 April

secondMetric.name: Learners in adult education (Educacao de Adultos), Annual School Survey 15 March

source.publisher: Ministério da Educação e Cultura, Direcção de Planificação, Estatística e Cooperação, Levantamento Estatístico do Sector 2025 (Statistical Survey of the Sector 2025), summary enrolment table, as archived by the Internet Archive on 7 November 2025

records.limits: The cited URL is an Internet Archive copy: mined.gov.mz timed out on 2026-10-02. Both numbers sit in PDFs: the 2025 total is in the summary table on page 14 of 73 and broken down by province on later pages; the 2014 figure is in the same summary table of the 2014 edition (levantamento_estatistico_do_sector_2014.pdf, page 13, archived copy of 19 August 2026). The comparison is computed by the record (a fall of about 54 percent) and crosses a change in the survey: 2014 was taken on 15 March and labelled 'Educacao de Adultos', 2025 on 30 April and split into literacy and primary education for young people and adults after the 2018 education system law, so part of the gap may be definitional. The intermediate editions read on the same day (290,478 in 2016, 251,887 in 2018, 262,641 in 2019, 229,329 in 2020, 302,207 in 2024) show most of the fall happened between 2014 and 2016 and that the level has moved between about 230,000 and 300,000 since, so 'eroded' rests mainly on one early drop; the 2014 and 2016 editions report the same 2,647 centres, which suggests some figures were carried forward. 2014 is the earliest edition read, not a demonstrated all-time peak. Counts are learners attending at survey date, not completers, and about two thirds are women; nothing here shows literacy gained. Private centres (a few hundred learners) are excluded. The 1975 start is the national literacy campaigns after independence, as commonly dated; it was not read at the cited source.

pattern.mechanism: The education ministry runs literacy and adult primary classes in community centres staffed by paid or volunteer literacy teachers, counts the learners in its annual school census alongside children, and publishes the totals by province.
preconditions: A national adult education directorate with provincial and district officers
Literacy teachers paid a stipend or volunteering in each community
An annual school census that also reaches non-formal centres
pattern.travelled: The same census shows the programme concentrated in Nampula, Tete and Sofala in 2025; a programme that depends on stipended community teachers is the first to shrink when the education budget is squeezed.

records.title: Tosika Fameno, the COVID-19 urban emergency cash transfer
records.claim: Madagascar's social protection agency FID designed the Tosika Fameno emergency cash transfer after the March 2020 urban lockdown, registered almost 200,000 households in about 12 days, made the first payment four weeks after the lockdown began, and reached more than 368,000 urban households in ten cities with 100,000 ariary payments.

metric.name: Time from the start of the urban lockdown to the first Tosika Fameno payment

secondMetric.name: Vulnerable urban households reached (more than)

source.publisher: UNICEF, Being Prepared and Acting Fast: Madagascar case study on UNICEF's role in the social protection response to COVID-19 (2021)

records.limits: The figures are in an eight-page UNICEF case study PDF (PDF page 4: first payment four weeks after the start of the urban lockdown, registration of almost 200,000 households in about 12 days, more than 368,000 households; PDF page 6: registration completed two weeks after the declaration of the state of health emergency, first payments within one month; the 368,000 by the end of 2020 also on PDF page 2). UNICEF co-led the cash working group and directly supported 8,500 of the households, so it is grading a response it helped build, and the case study gives no exact dates for the lockdown or the first payment. The 368,000 mixes government payments financed by the World Bank with humanitarian top-ups by UNICEF, WFP, the EU and NGOs using the same parameters; the World Bank's Social Safety Net Project ICR (2025, P149323, paragraph 43 and annex note 2) counts 215,093 households paid under its own financing, a smaller number on a different scope. The benefit was 100,000 ariary (about US$26), small against lost urban income, and coverage was limited to ten cities. The speed came from an agency that already ran rural safety nets, not from a standing urban programme.

pattern.mechanism: The President asked the national social protection fund FID to extend its rural cash transfer machinery to the locked-down cities; FID and WFP built a rapid registration process, paid by mobile money and post, and partners aligned their transfers on the same amount and targeting.
preconditions: A national social fund already running cash transfers and a payment chain
Donor finance that could be redirected within weeks
Mobile money and postal networks able to pay urban households
pattern.travelled: Madagascar later turned the urban response into a longer urban safety net under the World Bank project; similar lockdown transfers in Malawi (mwi-cuci) took ten months to pay, which shows how much the existing agency mattered.

records.title: Wage Assistance Scheme and Self-Employed Assistance Scheme, paid by the MRA
records.claim: Mauritius made its revenue authority, the MRA, a payer of COVID-19 income support in March 2020, and by end June 2020 the MRA had disbursed Rs 9,985 million under the Wage Assistance Scheme (Rs 7,603 million) and the Self-Employed Assistance Scheme (Rs 2,382 million) to some 500,000 workers and self-employed people, after receiving 176,000 online SEAS applications within 10 days of the lockdown.

metric.name: Wage Assistance Scheme and Self-Employed Assistance Scheme disbursements, March to June 2020

secondMetric.name: Online SEAS applications received within 10 days during the lockdown

source.publisher: Mauritius Revenue Authority, Annual Report 2019/20

records.limits: The MRA reports on its own delivery. The 9,985 is the sum we computed from Table 3 of the annual report (Rs 7,603 million WAS plus Rs 2,382 million SEAS, March to June 2020; the text rounds it to Rs 10 billion); the 500,000 recipients is the Director General's 'some 500,000 workers and self-employed individuals', paid 'directly or indirectly', so wage subsidies reached employees through their employers and the count is approximate. The 176,000 applications in 10 days is a pull quote, not a table, and the report gives no time to first payment. The scheme rules date the speed: the MRA communique announcing the Wage Assistance Scheme is dated 23 March 2020 (mra.mu communique list, WageAssistanceScheme230320.pdf), and the first SEAS payment covered the period from 16 March 2020, but the annual report itself gives no date for the first payment. Mauritius had a complete PAYE and pension contribution register to verify claims against, which most countries in this group did not. The report does not show fraud, errors or employees laid off despite the scheme, and the WAS was extended for tourism-linked firms into 2021, so this record covers only the first four months.

pattern.mechanism: The government handed income support to the tax authority, which built online application forms, verified wage claims against employers' PAYE and pension returns, and paid employers and self-employed people directly into bank accounts.
preconditions: A tax authority with near-universal electronic filing and employer payroll returns
Bank accounts for most workers, including informal ones
A fiscal buffer large enough to pay a month's wages for most of the private sector
pattern.travelled: The same tax-authority route was used by Australia's JobKeeper and Ireland's wage subsidy; in Mauritius it was extended to the informal self-employed, who had no prior payroll record.

records.title: Child Grants Programme drought top-ups, 2020
records.claim: After Lesotho declared a drought emergency in October 2019, the government and the World Bank restructured the Social Assistance Project in January 2020 to reallocate US$7.4 million, and between February and September 2020 the Ministry of Social Development paid more than 40,000 Child Grants Programme households a LSL 500 monthly top-up for six months and added about 10,000 new households, which it kept on the programme at its own cost.

metric.name: Child Grants Programme households receiving drought top-ups (more than)

secondMetric.name: New households added in the horizontal expansion and retained on the budget (around)

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Lesotho Social Assistance Project

records.limits: The figures are in a PDF (the restructuring in paragraph 39 on PDF page 22; the top-up figures in paragraph 62 on PDF page 31). The World Bank financed the top-ups and rates its own project. The elapsed time is about four months from the October 2019 declaration to the first top-ups in February 2020, which we computed from dates in the report; the report gives no date for the first payment, only the February to September window. The results framework counts 67,000 beneficiaries of emergency top-ups against a target raised to 50,000, a different unit from the 40,000 households in the text, and the extra reach is partly attributed to exchange rate movements during COVID-19. Fewer than 10 percent of payments were digital, so most top-ups went out at cash pay points. The government paid the base benefit and absorbed the 10,000 new households; the top-ups themselves were donor money.

pattern.mechanism: The social development ministry used its national household registry (NISSA) and the Child Grants Programme to add a temporary top-up for existing recipients and enrol new poor households in drought districts, financed by restructuring an existing World Bank credit instead of waiting for new money.
preconditions: A household registry covering every rural council before the shock
A standing cash transfer with pay points in the affected districts
A lender willing to reallocate an existing loan within three months
pattern.travelled: Lesotho used the same route after the 2016 drought (27,000 recipients topped up in 2017, per the same ICR); NGOs also used NISSA to target their own responses.

records.title: COVID-19 Urban Cash Intervention, and its slow payment
records.claim: Malawi declared a State of Disaster over COVID-19 on 20 March 2020 and enrolled 194,762 eligible urban households in a three-month cash transfer in four cities, but first payments came only after January 2021, and by 30 June 2021 just 32,000 households, 16 percent, had received all three payments while 29 percent had received none.

metric.name: Eligible households that had received all three CUCI payments by 30 June 2021

secondMetric.name: Eligible households enrolled

source.publisher: World Bank, Malawi COVID-19 Urban Cash Intervention Process Evaluation Report (2021)

records.limits: The figures are in a PDF (State of Disaster date on PDF page 19, printed page 18; Table 8 and the January 2021 payment plan on PDF page 41). The World Bank co-financed the intervention with KfW, the EU and others, and commissioned the evaluation, but its own report documents the delay rather than hiding it. The record is evidence of slow responsiveness: about ten months from the State of Disaster to the first planned payment, a span we computed from the report's dates, and 15 months later only one in six households was fully paid. The report attributes the lag to know-your-customer failures between registration data and mobile network operator records and to agent liquidity, not to political choice. The 199,000 households cited elsewhere in the report is the enrolment target; the 194,762 is the eligible count in Table 8. Payments continued after June 2021 and the final completion figure is not in this report.

pattern.mechanism: The social welfare ministry designed a new urban transfer from scratch, registering households door to door in hotspots and paying by mobile money, with no prior urban registry to draw on.
preconditions: An urban beneficiary registry, which Malawi did not have, so registration took most of 2020
Mobile money accounts already verified in the recipients' names
Agent networks with enough cash for a sudden mass withdrawal
pattern.travelled: Madagascar's Tosika Fameno (mdg-tosika-fameno) paid in four weeks through an agency that already ran transfers; the contrast is the evaluation's own lesson about building delivery systems before the shock.

records.title: Bank of Uganda COVID-19 credit relief and loan restructuring
records.claim: The Bank of Uganda gave supervised financial institutions exceptional permission to restructure the loans of borrowers hit by COVID-19 from 1 April 2020, and banks restructured UGX 2.3 trillion of loans in April 2020 alone and UGX 5.9 trillion by July 2020, approving 893,018 of 895,241 applications.

metric.name: Loans restructured under BOU credit relief, April to July 2020

secondMetric.name: Credit relief applications approved, April to July 2020

source.publisher: Bank of Uganda, Financial Stability Report June 2020 (archived copy)

records.limits: The live Bank of Uganda site is now a JavaScript application and the original PDF path returns a web page, so the source is the Internet Archive copy of the central bank's own report, fetched today. The figures are in Box A on PDF pages 27 to 29 (printed pages 19 to 20) and in the policy summary. The central bank is the rule-maker and the reporter. Restructuring is forbearance, not new money: it postponed repayments and recognition of bad loans, and the same report warns that NPLs could materialise when the relief matured; the 5.9 trillion is a flow of restructurings, while the stock under relief at end June was UGX 4.9 trillion, 31.2 percent of loans. Granting relief was at each bank's discretion, so the approval rate reflects applications banks chose to process. The report dates the relief window from 1 April 2020 but not the decision itself, so the time from shock to rule is not shown here.

pattern.mechanism: The central bank suspended the usual classification and provisioning rules for restructured loans for 12 months, so banks could reschedule borrowers' repayments without eating their capital, and paired it with a liquidity facility for distressed lenders.
preconditions: A banking system well capitalised enough to carry deferred repayments
A supervisor with power to waive its own prudential rules by circular
Credit reference and reporting systems to track restructured loans
pattern.travelled: The same forbearance was used across East Africa in 2020: the report itself notes that Rwanda had the highest restructured-loan ratio in the region at 39.0 percent at end June 2020.

records.title: MauCAS Instant Payment System, run by the Bank of Mauritius with banks and non-banks
records.claim: The Bank of Mauritius launched the Mauritius Central Automated Switch in August 2019 as a central hub through which banks and non-bank payment providers route instant payments, and its Instant Payment System grew from 126,000 transactions in FY2019-20 to 19.4 million transactions worth Rs63.0 billion in FY2024-25, with 11 banks and 4 non-banks participating.

metric.name: MauCAS Instant Payment System transactions in the financial year

secondMetric.name: MauCAS Instant Payment System transactions in its first financial year

source.publisher: Bank of Mauritius, Annual Report for the year ended 30 June 2025

records.limits: The central bank owns and operates the switch, sets the fees and reports the volumes, so this is the system's owner grading its own system. The FY2024-25 figures are in the text on PDF page 88 of the 2025 annual report; the FY2019-20 baseline and the August 2019 launch are in the Annual Report for the year ended 30 June 2020 (https://www.bom.mu/AnnualReport/2020/BOM_June_2020.pdf, PDF pages 129 to 130), where only seven banks and one non-bank were connected. The 95.4 percent growth in FY2024-25 followed the Bank's own 2024 rule changes (interchange revisions, removal of person-to-person charges, a higher limit), so it measures a policy push as much as adoption. Nineteen million transactions a year in a country of about 1.3 million people is still modest beside card and cash use; the report gives no per-capita or merchant figure. The collaboration is a public switch with private participants, not a contractual PPP.

pattern.mechanism: The central bank built and ran a national switch that every bank and licensed non-bank could connect to, making transfers between any two accounts settle in seconds, then cut fees and raised limits to push use.
preconditions: A central bank with licensing power over banks and non-bank payment providers
A Real Time Gross Settlement system the switch could settle into
A banking population already using mobile apps
pattern.travelled: The same model as Bolivia's QR interoperability (bol-qr-bcb) and India's UPI, run on a small island economy where the central bank, not a bank consortium, owns the switch.

records.title: Private electricity distribution concessions, and the 2022 decision to end them
