records.claim: Uganda ran most of its electricity distribution through private concessions, with Umeme selling about 96 percent of grid energy to end users in 2024, but a Cabinet directive of October 2022 approved the non-renewal of all expiring concessions, and in 2024 the state utility UEDCL took over the assets of two private distributors whose licences were not renewed.

metric.name: Private distribution licences not renewed and taken over by UEDCL in 2024 (KIL and KRECS)

secondMetric.name: Umeme's share of grid energy sold to end users, the private concession at its peak (about)

source.publisher: Electricity Regulatory Authority (Uganda), Electricity Supply Industry Performance Report for the Year 2024

records.limits: The figures are in a PDF (the 96 percent and Table 6 on PDF page 21; the Cabinet directive and the KIL and KRECS takeover on PDF page 24). The report covers 2024, when Umeme still operated; it does not record the end of Umeme's own concession, which ran to 2025. That the state utility took over Umeme's area is documented by UEDCL itself: its '100 Days in the Driving Seat' report (https://www.uedcl.co.ug/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/100DaysInTheDriving-Seat-.pdf, page 1) says that on 1 April 2025 UEDCL began its national mandate of electricity distribution; ERA's tariff schedules for Umeme on its site also stop after January to March 2025. The started year is the start of the Umeme concession as commonly dated, not stated in this report. The concession's record is contested: ERA reports Umeme's losses at 16.0 percent in 2024 against a 13.24 percent target, and the decision to end private distribution was a policy choice by the Cabinet, so 'dismantled' records a decision, not a collapse. The report gives no buyout amount; an ERA annual report on the same site (wpdmdl=7485) lists 'no clear asset registers to determine buyout amount for UMEME' as a risk of the concession's expiry.

pattern.mechanism: The government concessioned the national distribution network to a private operator for 20 years under ERA regulation, then the Cabinet decided not to renew any expiring concession and folded each private distributor back into the state company as its licence ran out.
preconditions: A regulator able to set tariffs and verify investment over a long concession
A state utility able to absorb staff, customers and assets at handover
A settled buyout value for the operator's unrecovered investment, which was disputed
pattern.travelled: Uganda also took back Eskom Uganda's 20-year generation concession at its end in 2023 (per an ERA annual report, era.go.ug download wpdmdl=7485); Lesotho's hospital PPP and other African utility concessions show the same pattern of a long PPP ended at expiry rather than renewed.

records.title: Transport Infrastructure Investment Project (national roads, ports and the Northern Railway)
records.claim: Madagascar's road authority and transport agencies delivered road, port, airport and Northern Railway works under the Transport Infrastructure Investment Project from 2004, cutting travel time on the RN44 from 24 to 6 hours, with the closing date extended four years from 30 June 2008 to 30 June 2012 and IDA-financed costs of US$169.39 million against US$150.00 million at appraisal plus US$15.60 million of additional financing added in 2007.

metric.name: Total project costs, actual or latest estimate

secondMetric.name: Total project costs, appraisal estimate

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Madagascar Transport Infrastructure Investment Project (P082800), 2013

records.limits: The costs are in Annex 1 of the World Bank's own completion report, which rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory. They are IDA disbursements only (the borrower's own contribution is shown as US$1.11 million against 17.42 appraised), and the 112.9 percent of appraisal is almost entirely the US$15.60 million additional financing of 2007 for the Northern Railway component, which was not in the appraisal; against the revised estimate including that financing, the outturn is 102.3 percent, so the record shows no meaningful cost overrun and should not be read as one. Port and airport components spent a fraction of their estimates and the RN5a upgrade was dropped at the January 2006 restructuring, so scope shrank in some places while it grew in others. The RN44 travel-time result is the report's own indicator comment. The closing date moved through five restructurings, and the 2009 political crisis froze disbursements during implementation. The project is a portfolio of works, not one build, so no single project's baseline and outturn are shown. Plain-text file, no PDF page numbers.

pattern.mechanism: Madagascar's road authority and port and rail agencies ran a multi-modal investment programme on a lender credit, re-scoping it repeatedly as priorities and the political situation changed, and finished four years late.
preconditions: A road authority and transport agencies able to procure civil works
Lender flexibility to restructure and add financing
Political continuity through implementation, which Madagascar did not have

records.title: Energy Sector Support Project (substations and distribution lines)
records.claim: Malawi's electricity utility ESCOM completed and energised all 10 substations and seven of nine planned distribution lines under the Energy Sector Support Project approved in 2011, closing on 15 October 2018 against an original closing date of 30 October 2016, having disbursed US$72.1 million of US$84.7 million.

metric.name: Substations completed, energised and loaded

secondMetric.name: Distribution lines completed out of nine planned

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Malawi Energy Sector Support Project (P099626), 2019

records.limits: The World Bank's completion report, which rated the outcome Satisfactory, is the source; the substation and line counts are in paras. 103 and around 583 of the text file and the dates and amounts in the data sheet. The report gives no appraisal cost per work package, so cost performance cannot be read beyond the undisbursed balance, which reflects delay and cancellation rather than savings. The two-year extension followed procurement delays the report attributes to the political situation and inexperience with Bank procedures, and the implementation consultant stopped work in December 2017 when its budget ran out, leaving ESCOM to finish alone. At US$85 million this is a modest programme of grid reinforcement, not a single major build, so it is weak evidence on major project delivery. Plain-text file, no PDF page numbers.

pattern.mechanism: Malawi's state utility reinforced the grid in its load centres with a package of substations and lines on concessional credit, and finished the works itself after its supervising consultant ran out of budget.
preconditions: A utility with in-house engineers able to finish works without a consultant
Concessional finance with room to extend closing dates
Demand growth that kept the works a priority

records.title: Morupule B coal power station, and its underperformance
records.claim: Botswana Power Corporation built the 600 MW Morupule B coal power station under an EPC contract appraised in 2009, taking the plant over with known defects on 4 May 2014 against a target of 31 December 2013, after which it ran at a capacity factor of 52 percent from April 2015 to January 2016 against the 80 percent projected at appraisal.

metric.name: Plant gross capacity factor, measured (Table 2)

secondMetric.name: Capacity factor projected at appraisal

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Botswana Morupule B Generation and Transmission Project (P112516; P116784), Report No. ICR3301, revised January 2017

records.limits: The World Bank's completion report rated outcome, Bank and borrower performance all Unsatisfactory. The 52 percent is the measured gross capacity factor for the whole plant in Table 2 for April 2015 to January 2016 (54 percent for April 2014 to March 2015); Table 1 gives about 38 percent from grid connection to March 2014, and paras. 91 and 96 describe availability 'hovering around 50 percent'. On cost the project did not overrun: the power-station, transmission and water component came to US$1,188.6 million against an appraisal estimate of US$1,539.6 million (Annex 1), so the failure is in schedule and performance, not budget. The report attributes the defects mainly to the Chinese EPC contractor's design and construction quality, with some operation and maintenance issues, and records three site fatalities; the plant was financed largely by an ICBC loan with a World Bank guarantee. The report does not cover the plant after 2016, so whether it later reached its design output is not shown. 'Operating' is used because the plant generates; the record documents a delivery that never reached its design performance rather than one that eroded from a peak.

pattern.mechanism: The state utility bought a large coal plant on a turnkey contract from a lowest-cost bidder, accepted it with a punch list of defects to meet a power shortfall, and then imported power and ran diesel units while the defects were chased.
preconditions: Owner's engineering capacity to verify design and construction quality under an EPC contract
Contract terms that let the owner refuse takeover of a defective plant
A grid with enough backup supply to wait for a plant to be fixed

records.title: Metolong Dam and Water Supply Programme
records.claim: Lesotho's Metolong Authority built the Metolong Dam and raw water pump station near Maseru, starting impoundment on 15 February 2014 against a contract date of 31 October 2012 and delivering 93 megalitres a day on 8 October 2014 against a contract date of 1 July 2013, with every component of the programme overrunning its cost.

metric.name: Delay in reaching water delivery of 93 Ml/day (contract date 1 July 2013, achieved 8 October 2014)

secondMetric.name: Delay in starting impoundment (contract date 31 October 2012, achieved 15 February 2014)

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Lesotho Water Sector Improvement APL Phase II: Metolong Dam and Water Supply (P108143), 2019

records.limits: The contract and revised dates are in Table 9.1 (Annex 9, page 53 of 59) of the World Bank's completion report, which rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory; both delays in months (15.2 and 15.5) are computed here from the dates in that table. The report states that all components overran their cost, attributing it partly to construction-price inflation from South Africa's 2010 World Cup works (para. 72), but gives no programme-wide baseline and outturn cost, and the World Bank financed only part of a programme co-financed by the Kuwait Fund, Arab and other lenders, the EIB and the government. The project closing date was extended three times for a cumulative 42 months, to 31 December 2018. Impoundment coincided with the 2015 to 2016 drought. Plain-text file of a PDF.

pattern.mechanism: Lesotho created a dedicated authority to deliver a dam, treatment works and bulk pipelines for the lowlands with many co-financiers, and delivered water about 15 months behind contract after price escalation and procurement delays.
preconditions: A ring-fenced delivery authority for one programme
Several co-financiers able to cover cost gaps
Experience from the Lesotho Highlands Water Project to draw on

records.title: B6 Belle Rive to Quartier Militaire road upgrade
records.claim: Mauritius's Ministry of Public Infrastructure upgraded the 12.1 km B6 Belle Rive to Quartier Militaire road under the World Bank Infrastructure Project approved in 2009, at a cost of US$33.88 million against an appraisal estimate of US$21.60 million, 157 percent of the estimate.

metric.name: Cost of upgrading works on the Belle Rive to Quartier Militaire road, actual

secondMetric.name: Cost of upgrading works, appraisal estimate

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Mauritius Infrastructure Project (P091828), Report No. ICR3303, 2015

records.limits: The costs are in Annex 1 of the World Bank's own completion report, which rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and the borrower Moderately Unsatisfactory. Para. 41 explains most of the increase as poor checking of the estimate at appraisal and added scope requested by stakeholders (junctions, a bridge, village works), with further increases from weather and flooding, and gives slightly different totals (about US$32 million, then about US$35 million for the contract), so the 157 percent is the annex figure and the narrative does not match it exactly. A 12 km road is a small project for the construct, chosen because it is the one Mauritian build with an official baseline and outturn found; Mauritius's larger Metro Express light rail was not assessed. The project closed on its original date, 31 December 2014. Plain-text file, no PDF page numbers.

pattern.mechanism: The infrastructure ministry procured a rural road upgrade on an estimate that was never checked against designs, then added scope under local pressure, and paid half as much again as appraised.
preconditions: Detailed engineering designs before the cost estimate is fixed
A scope-change control that resists late stakeholder additions
A lender willing to reallocate funds from cancelled technical assistance

records.title: Response to the 2022 Sudan ebolavirus outbreak
records.claim: Uganda's Ministry of Health contained the Sudan ebolavirus outbreak declared on 20 September 2022, for which no licensed vaccine existed, through national and district emergency committees, listing 4,793 contacts, and declared it over on 11 January 2023 after 142 confirmed and 22 probable cases and 77 deaths.

metric.name: Days from outbreak declaration (20 September 2022) to declared end (11 January 2023)

secondMetric.name: Contacts listed during the outbreak

source.publisher: World Health Organization, Disease Outbreak News, Ebola disease caused by Sudan ebolavirus, Uganda, 2023-DON433

records.limits: The 113 days are computed here from the two dates in the WHO notice; the case, death and contact counts are WHO's summary of Ministry of Health data. Containment within four months with no vaccine is the claim, but the outbreak reached nine districts including Kampala, the case fatality was 47 percent, and the record cannot separate the government's response from luck in transmission chains or from the over US$27 million of international support WHO mentions. An epidemic is a different shock from the climate hazards the construct names first, filed on the same terms as the COVID-19 vaccination precedents, and a single 2022 outbreak says little about cyclone or flood preparedness. Uganda's earlier Ebola and Marburg experience is part of why the system existed.

pattern.mechanism: The health ministry activated standing national and district emergency committees, traced and followed contacts, and isolated and treated cases in dedicated treatment centres.
preconditions: Standing outbreak response structures from earlier Ebola and Marburg outbreaks
A national reference laboratory able to confirm cases fast
District health teams able to trace thousands of contacts

records.title: COVID-19 vaccination campaign
records.claim: Botswana's health authorities reported to WHO that 1,951,054 people, 83 per 100 population, had received at least one COVID-19 vaccine dose by 31 December 2023, from a first dose given on 26 March 2021, with 1,663,490 (71 per 100) completing the primary series.

metric.name: People vaccinated with at least one COVID-19 vaccine dose

secondMetric.name: People who completed the primary series (last dose)

source.publisher: World Health Organization, COVID-19 dashboard vaccination data (vaccination-data.csv)

records.limits: The figures are Botswana's own reports to WHO (DATA_SOURCE 'REPORTING'), with no independent coverage survey behind them, read from one row of a CSV with no prose. First-dose reach was 83 per 100 and completion 71 per 100, among the highest in sub-Saharan Africa, which partly reflects a small population and a strong primary health system rather than a crisis-specific capability. Booster or additional doses reached 510,809 people, 22 per 100. The VACCINES_USED field is empty, so the record cannot show which products were used or where the doses came from, and it evidences distribution only. The per-100 rates divide by WHO's population estimate. Vaccination is a response to one shock, not proof of preparedness for cyclones, floods or droughts, and the brief for this column prefers a hazard-specific delivery; this is filed because none with an official figure was found in the time available. The cited URL is the blob the WHO dashboard serves, as in bol-covid-vaccination.

pattern.mechanism: Botswana's health ministry ran a national COVID-19 campaign through its clinics and mass vaccination sites and reached over four in five residents with a first dose.
preconditions: A routine immunisation programme with a cold chain beyond the capital
A supply of doses large enough for a national campaign, however obtained
Registers good enough to count who received a second dose
pattern.travelled: Bolivia (bol-covid-vaccination) and Venezuela (ven-covid-vaccination) are filed on the same terms.

records.title: COVID-19 vaccination campaign
records.claim: Mauritius's health authorities reported to WHO that 1,123,773 people, 88 per 100 population, had received at least one COVID-19 vaccine dose by 31 December 2023, from a first dose given on 26 January 2021, with 1,088,142 (86 per 100) completing the primary series.

metric.name: People vaccinated with at least one COVID-19 vaccine dose

secondMetric.name: People who completed the primary series (last dose)

source.publisher: World Health Organization, COVID-19 dashboard vaccination data (vaccination-data.csv)

records.limits: The figures are Mauritius's own reports to WHO (DATA_SOURCE 'REPORTING'), with no independent coverage survey behind them, read from one row of a CSV with no prose. Completion of 86 per 100 is near-universal, but Mauritius is a small island of about 1.3 million people with a dense public health network, so the scale says little about logistics capacity. Booster or additional doses reached 654,507 people, 51 per 100. The VACCINES_USED field is empty, so the record cannot show which products were used or where the doses came from, and it evidences distribution only. The per-100 rates divide by WHO's population estimate. Vaccination is a response to one shock, not proof of preparedness for cyclones, floods or droughts, and the brief for this column prefers a hazard-specific delivery; this is filed because none with an official figure was found in the time available. The cited URL is the blob the WHO dashboard serves, as in bol-covid-vaccination.

pattern.mechanism: Mauritius's health ministry vaccinated almost the whole adult population through its public hospital and health centre network, aided by a small island population and early dose supply.
preconditions: A routine immunisation programme with a cold chain beyond the capital
A supply of doses large enough for a national campaign, however obtained
Registers good enough to count who received a second dose
pattern.travelled: Bolivia (bol-covid-vaccination) and Venezuela (ven-covid-vaccination) are filed on the same terms.

records.title: Bureau National de la Prospective et de la Veille Stratégique and the national prospective studies
records.claim: Côte d'Ivoire's Ministry of Planning and Development completed its fourth national prospective study, Côte d'Ivoire 2040, under the technical responsibility of the Bureau National de la Prospective et de la Veille Stratégique, after earlier national studies in 1973 to 1974, 1983 to 1984 and 1993 to 1995, and built eighteen thematic and three global scenarios to the 2040 horizon.

metric.name: National prospective studies completed (Côte d'Ivoire 2000, 2010, 2025 and 2040)

secondMetric.name: Thematic scenarios built in the Côte d'Ivoire 2040 study

source.publisher: Ministère du Plan et du Développement, Bureau National de la Prospective et de la Veille Stratégique, Etude Nationale Prospective Côte d'Ivoire 2040: Résumé

records.limits: Both figures are in a 12-page PDF (page 5 for the four studies, page 6 for the scenarios); the date comes from the file name (final version, 13 March 2017), not from the document. The ministry reports on itself, and the figures count studies and scenarios, not influence: the same summary says the 2025 study did not lead to a plan and that the 1999, 2002 and 2010 to 2011 crises followed scenarios the government had not used. The four studies span four decades with a gap the summary attributes to structural adjustment, so continuity is episodic, and the bureau's own creation date is not given; started records the first national study. The ministry's own site (plan.gouv.ci/structure/5, read 2 October 2026) still lists the BNPVS among its attached directorates and keeps a prospective and strategic watch section, which supports the operating status, but no dated output after 2017 was read at an official source; a national prospective day in May 2024 and a sectoral foresight manual in September 2025 were seen only in press. The study claims a strategic watch mechanism was to follow; no figure for it was read.

pattern.mechanism: The planning ministry keeps a standing foresight bureau with the rank of a directorate general that runs a national prospective study about once a decade, using an expert group drawn from universities and ministries and national and local commissions to debate the results.
preconditions: A planning ministry with a mandate for long-term perspective, not only five-year plans
University and ministry staff available for a multi-year expert group
Political sponsors willing to adopt the study's vision, which the 2025 study lacked
pattern.travelled: National prospective studies of the same method ran in several West African states, including Mali, whose 1997 to 1999 Mali 2025 study its government evaluated at national prospective days in January 2014.

records.title: Sistema Nacional de Formação Profissional under INEFOP
records.claim: Angola's national vocational training system, the INEFOP-supervised centres together with the accelerated 'plano intercalar' courses, FUNEA and licensed private centres, enrolled 204,026 trainees in 2024, against 112,478 in 2023, with 152,625 passing, across 1,914 training centres.

metric.name: Matriculados no Sistema Nacional de Formação Profissional (Tabela 3)

secondMetric.name: Same count for the previous year (Tabela 3)

source.publisher: Instituto Nacional de Estatística (INE) Angola with the Ministério da Administração Pública, Trabalho e Segurança Social, Anuário de Estatística do Trabalho Estruturado e Segurança Social 2024, section 4.2 Formação profissional, Tabela 3

records.limits: The numbers sit in a 43-page PDF: the breakdown by channel is on printed page 12 and Tabela 3 on printed page 19. The figures are the labour ministry's administrative returns from its own training institute and from centres it licenses, republished by INE. The text calls the trainees 'jovens' throughout, gives no age split, and the system includes initial vocational training for school leavers, so this is a count of vocational trainees rather than of adults returning to learning. The 81 percent jump from 2023 rests largely on the 'plano intercalar', an acceleration programme that enrolled 56,329, and on 57,127 enrolments reported by private centres, whose returns the ministry does not audit in this document. Counts are enrolments, not unique people. Only two years are compared, so the series cannot show whether 2024 is a lasting scale or a one-year push. The started year is the first year in the cited table, not the start of INEFOP, which is older.

pattern.mechanism: The labour ministry's training institute runs its own centres and mobile units, licenses private providers into one national system, and adds an accelerated short-course programme, then counts enrolment, passes and dropouts across all of them in an annual yearbook.
preconditions: A licensing regime that brings private training centres into the national count
Mobile and rural units that reach trainees outside the main cities
A ministry statistics office that publishes the returns with the national statistics institute

records.title: Institut National de Préparation Professionnelle (INPP)
records.claim: The Democratic Republic of the Congo's Institut National de Préparation Professionnelle recorded 34,376 learners in initial and continuing vocational training in the first half of 2026, against a semester forecast of 42,850, according to the mid-term review of its 2026 performance contract.

metric.name: Apprenants en formation initiale et continue, premier semestre

secondMetric.name: Semester forecast of people to train under the 2026 performance contract

source.publisher: Institut National de Préparation Professionnelle (INPP), news release 'Contrats de performance 2026 : l'INPP évalué à mi-parcours', 21 September 2026

records.limits: The source is the institute's own news release reporting a mid-term review by a joint commission under the employment ministry; it is self-reporting, not a statistical series, and no annual INPP report with a time series was found at an openable official page. The figure covers one semester and mixes initial training for job seekers with continuing training for employees, without a split. 34,376 learners in six months in a country of over 100 million people is a small reach, and the release gives no completion or placement figures. The execution rate of about 80 percent is the release's own arithmetic. The started year is the creation of INPP by Ordonnance-loi n°206 of 29 June 1964, as stated on the institute's history page, not on the cited release.

pattern.mechanism: A tripartite public training institute financed by an employer payroll levy runs training centres in the provinces for employees and job seekers, and the employment ministry holds it to an annual performance contract with a numeric training target reviewed mid-year.
preconditions: An employer training levy collected from formal firms
A network of provincial training centres with workshops
A ministry performance-contract regime that sets and reviews numeric targets

records.title: Burkin-Naong-Sa Ya adaptive cash transfers for COVID-19 and the lean season
records.claim: Burkina Faso's national safety net programme (Burkin-Naong-Sa Ya) paid three rounds of FCFA 20,000 adaptive cash transfers to over 42,800 people between May and September 2020 in response to COVID-19, including 21,160 vendors from temporarily closed markets, and later raised the lean-season transfer from FCFA 20,000 to FCFA 45,000 in 2022 to align it with the food security response, paying three extra monthly payments to over 763,700 people in IPC3+ areas over the 2021 to 2023 lean seasons.

metric.name: People who received three rounds of COVID-19 adaptive cash transfers, May to September 2020

secondMetric.name: Lean-season adaptive transfer per household after the 2022 increase (from FCFA 20,000)

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Burkina Faso Social Safety Net Project (P124015), January 2024

records.limits: The World Bank financed the programme and reports on its own project; paragraphs 34 and 35 are on page 10 of the plain-text ICR. The COVID-19 response was small: over 42,800 people, against a regular programme the ICR targeted at 948,100 people and says reached close to 1.05 million, and the ICR mixes units (21,000 of the beneficiaries are described as households in Ouagadougou and Bobo Dioulasso). The ICR gives the payment window, May to September 2020, not the date of the first payment, so the most that can be read is that cash started within about two months of the first COVID-19 measures. The 2020 audit was qualified, finding FCFA 27 million of overpayments to COVID-19 beneficiaries by payment agencies and discrepancies in payment lists (page 24). The ICR says the 2022 increase was made to align with the food security response under the Sahel Adaptive Social Protection Program, not as an indexation rule, and it converts both the 2022 and 2023 amounts to about US$85, so the change kept pace with prices rather than raising real support. All the money is IDA and trust fund money, not the national budget, and the ICR records that the two military coups of 2022 (January and September) led to pauses in disbursements, so the responsiveness shown in 2020 did not hold steady through the period.

pattern.mechanism: The safety net unit kept an 'adaptive' transfer window inside its regular programme and pointed it at whichever shock arrived: market closures and urban poverty in 2020, then IPC3+ lean-season food crises from 2021, raising the transfer amount when food prices rose.
preconditions: A regular cash transfer programme with payment agencies and beneficiary lists already in place
A food security classification (Cadre Harmonise) to decide where adaptive payments go
Donor financing that allowed components to be reoriented without new approvals for each shock
pattern.travelled: The same adaptive safety net design runs through the Sahel Adaptive Social Protection Programme countries (Mali, Niger, Senegal, Chad, Mauritania); compare mli-pgtmu, where the government funded the response itself.

records.title: Programme de transferts monetaires productifs (PTMP), government-funded COVID-19 expansion
records.claim: In response to COVID-19, the government of Cote d'Ivoire used its own budget to enrol a fourth cohort of 100,000 households (80,000 urban, 20,000 rural) in December 2020 into the World Bank supported productive cash transfer programme, through the programme's existing targeting, enrolment and digital payment systems, taking it to 227,000 households and over 1.3 million people.

metric.name: Households enrolled in cohort 4 with government funding (Table 2)

secondMetric.name: Beneficiary households of the cash transfer programme, all cohorts

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Cote d'Ivoire Productive Social Safety Net Project (P143332), 25 June 2024

records.limits: The World Bank financed the programme, rates its own project Highly Satisfactory, and reports results jointly for its project and the government-funded cohort, so the 100,000 is the financier's account of a government action it supported technically. Table 2 and paragraphs 32 to 34 are on page 13 of 48 in the plain-text version; paragraph 85 (page 21) says the pandemic triggered the expansion with government funding. The speed is modest: the first COVID-19 measures were in March 2020 and the cohort enrolled in December 2020, about nine months later, and the ICR gives no date of first payment to the new cohort. The separate emergency transfer the government announced in April 2020 through the Fonds special de solidarite (reported in the press at about 177,000 households) is not covered by this source and is not counted here. The ICR also says the project was never formally restructured to take in the government money and that the social registry (RSU) was underdeveloped, so the expansion rode on one programme's lists rather than a national registry. Households are counted at enrolment; the source reports payment receipt only through sample surveys.

pattern.mechanism: Faced with the pandemic, the government put its own money into an existing donor-built cash transfer instead of creating a new scheme, so the new cohort used the programme's community targeting, enrolment and mobile payment machinery and was enrolled within the year.
preconditions: A cash transfer programme already running with digital payments before the shock
Budget room to fund a cohort from domestic resources
A delivery unit able to extend targeting from rural to urban households, which the 2019 urban pilot had prepared
pattern.travelled: The same piggybacking on a standing programme as Honduras's 2020 top-ups (hnd-cct-shock-response) and Togo's Novissi, though slower than Novissi, which built a new digital transfer within weeks.

records.title: Lisungi emergency cash transfers for COVID-19
records.claim: The Republic of Congo's Ministry of Social Affairs and the Lisungi programme unit paid one-off emergency cash transfers of about US$82 to more than 206,800 mostly urban households hit by COVID-19 by April 2022, above a target of 200,000, while the social registry used to target them grew to more than 830,000 households and 95 percent of the transfers were paid digitally.

metric.name: Households that received emergency cash transfers (ECTs) under the Lisungi Emergency COVID-19 Response Project

secondMetric.name: Households registered in the social registry (RSU) after the ECT targeting

source.publisher: World Bank, Project Paper, First Additional Financing for the Lisungi Emergency COVID-19 Response Project (P177453, parent P174178), April 2022

records.limits: The World Bank financed the transfers (an IDA credit of US$50 million, US$20 million for the ECTs) and reports on its own project; the figures are in paragraphs 23 to 25 of the plain-text project paper, pages 12 to 13 of 59. The project's later Implementation Status Report (June 2026, P174178) gives 231,562 households benefiting from emergency cash transfers, so the count moved after this paper; the record uses the earlier dated figure. The response was slow for an emergency: the project was approved on 24 June 2020 and became effective on 9 October 2020, and the paper gives no date for the first or last ECT payment, so the time from shock to cash cannot be stated, only that 206,800 households had been paid by April 2022. Each household got one payment of about US$82, small against lost income. The same paper says the focus on the crisis delayed the government's plan to scale Lisungi to national coverage, and that procurement delays and a change of ministry leadership in May 2021 held up the registry and digital payment work. The government asked for the emergency money; the money and the design were the World Bank's.

pattern.mechanism: The social affairs ministry used the existing Lisungi conditional cash transfer unit and its social registry to register urban households hit by COVID-19 and pay each a one-off digital transfer, growing the registry in the process so that later programmes could target from it.
preconditions: A standing cash transfer programme unit (Lisungi) with a registry to build on
Emergency IDA financing approved within three months of the shock
Digital payment providers able to reach urban households
pattern.travelled: The same piggybacking on a standing programme as civ-ptmp-covid and cod-step-kin, but with a single small payment per household rather than a recurring transfer.

records.title: Domestic Debt Exchange Programme, December 2022 to February 2023
records.claim: After losing market access and requesting IMF support in July 2022, Ghana's government launched a domestic debt exchange on 5 December 2022 covering all medium- and long-term local-currency government, Daakye and ESLA bonds, and settled it on 21 February 2023 with 85 percent of the face value of bonds held by investors other than pension funds exchanged, giving almost GHS 50 billion of cash debt relief in 2023.

metric.name: Share of the face value of eligible bonds held by investors other than pension funds exchanged in the DDE

secondMetric.name: Days from launch of the exchange (5 December 2022) to settlement (21 February 2023), computed

source.publisher: International Monetary Fund, Country Report No. 23/168, Ghana: Request for an Arrangement Under the Extended Credit Facility, staff report, Box 2 (copy hosted by the Ministry of Finance of Ghana)

records.limits: The figures are in Box 2 of the staff report (PDF page 22, printed page 18) and the July 2022 request for IMF support is in the debt sustainability annex (PDF page 95); the URL is the Ministry of Finance's copy of the IMF report, because imf.org returned an HTML bot page to a script. The 78 days is computed by us from the two dates in Box 2. The IMF is a party to the programme the exchange was a prior condition for, so this is not an independent evaluation. The speed is of the rule change once decided: the fiscal and debt pressures that forced it built up over years and Ghana lost market access in 2022, so a responsive state would arguably have acted earlier and with less damage. The 85 percent covers only the eligible perimeter: pension funds, about 20 percent of eligible debt, were excluded after bondholder protests, and 85 percent equals only 28 percent of all domestic debt; dollar bonds and Cocobills needed later exchanges. The exchange imposed an average NPV loss of about 30 percent on bondholders, weakened bank balance sheets and was contested in court and on the street; the number shows the operation closed fast, not that its costs were well distributed.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Finance offered domestic bondholders a menu of new longer, lower-coupon bonds at fixed ratios with a deadline, renegotiated the perimeter (exempting pension funds and adjusting terms for individuals) during the offer, and closed within eleven weeks so the IMF programme could be approved.
preconditions: A domestic bond market concentrated in a few banks and institutions that could be negotiated with directly
A central depository able to swap instruments on a fixed settlement date
An external anchor (the IMF arrangement) that made the exchange a precondition for financing
pattern.travelled: Jamaica's 2010 and 2013 domestic exchanges are the template Ghana's design follows; Sri Lanka's 2023 domestic optimisation used a similar perimeter carve-out for pension funds.

records.title: Nafa Quick, the COVID-19 cash transfer carved out of the Nafa programme
records.claim: The Gambia's government had its new social safety net project restructured within three months of the pandemic (restructuring dated 9 June 2020) to create Nafa Quick, which between July and October 2020 paid two transfers of GMD 3,000 to 78,359 rural households in 30 districts, against a target of 60,000, with all payments made before the end of the lean season.

metric.name: Households benefiting from the temporary Nafa Quick intervention (OI 2.1)

secondMetric.name: Share of Nafa Quick payments made before the end of the lean season (IR 2.1)

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, The Gambia Social Safety Net Project (P167260), June 2024

records.limits: The World Bank financed the project and rates its own efficacy High; the figures are in the plain-text ICR: the June 2020 restructuring on page 9 (paragraph 17), the 78,359 households and the 100 percent lean-season indicator in Table 2 on page 14 (paragraph 34), and 'restructured in three months' with the July to October 2020 payment window on page 24 (paragraph 70). The ICR says Nafa Quick ran before the delivery system existed, so no socio-economic data were collected on its beneficiaries and its targeting of the poor cannot be assessed. The speed was bought by cutting the longer-term programme: the extreme-poor Nafa transfer was halved from 36 to 18 months to pay for Nafa Quick, and the additional financing meant to restore it was not approved because a COVID-19 waiver expired first, so the remaining 18 months were deferred until a new project, The Gambia RISE (approved February 2024), began paying them from July 2024 (page 24, paragraph 69). Two payments of GMD 3,000 is a small, temporary transfer. The money came from an existing IDA project, not from the national budget.

pattern.mechanism: The government asked the World Bank to repurpose its freshly started safety net project, and the project unit ran a separate, simple rural cash transfer, two payments timed to the lean season, through community targeting in 30 districts while the social registry and the regular programme were still being built.
preconditions: An externally financed safety net project already effective, with money that could be reallocated
A project unit and community structures able to list households without a registry
Willingness to sacrifice the duration of the long-term programme to pay for the emergency one
pattern.travelled: Like hnd-cct-shock-response and cog-lisungi-covid, a donor project became the shock-response channel; The Gambia's case shows the cost explicitly, because the regular programme was cut to fund it.

records.title: Programme Gouvernemental de Transferts Monetaires d'Urgence COVID-19 (PGTMU)
records.claim: Mali's government launched its own emergency COVID-19 cash transfer programme in 2021, paying one-off transfers to 400,000 poor households across the country through the targeting and payment systems built by the Jigisemejiri safety net project, and kept it running in 2022, but only FCFA 42 billion of the FCFA 100 billion budgeted was disbursed because of the political crisis.

metric.name: Households covered by the PGTMU one-off emergency transfers

secondMetric.name: PGTMU funds disbursed against FCFA 100 billion budgeted

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Mali Emergency Safety Nets Project (Jigisemejiri, P127328), March 2024

records.limits: The numbers are reported by the World Bank about a programme it did not finance, in paragraph 42 of the ICR of its own project (page 18 of 67 in the plain-text version), with no government source cited and no date of first payment; the 400,000 is a round figure and the ICR does not say whether it counts households paid or households planned. Elsewhere the ICR says 'approximately 400,000 households'. The response was slow: the programme was launched in 2021, a year or more after the first COVID-19 measures, and only 42 percent of its budget was disbursed (computed by us from FCFA 42 billion of 100 billion) because of the political crisis that followed the coups of August 2020 and May 2021. The same paragraph records that the government's regular safety net budget line (PGFS) disbursed FCFA 6.2 billion of 12.5 billion over 2017 to 2022. The ICR also records World Bank disbursement suspensions to Mali in August 2020, May 2021 and January 2022 for a cumulative 18 months (page 27), which slowed the systems the transfer relied on. A one-off transfer does not show a lasting change in the rules.

pattern.mechanism: The government funded an emergency transfer from its own budget and ran it through the social registry, targeting procedures and payment contracts that a donor project had built over a decade, so it could reach 400,000 households without building new machinery.
preconditions: A social registry (RSU, over 1.1 million household records) and a government safety net unit (UTGFS) already in place
Budget room for a FCFA 100 billion programme, which in the event only partly materialised
Political stability to sustain disbursement, which the 2020 to 2022 crisis undercut
pattern.travelled: The same reuse of donor-built delivery systems as civ-ptmp-covid; Mali's case shows a government paying with its own money, and the budget gap shows the limit of that.

records.title: Transrail concession of the Dakar to Bamako railway, and its collapse
records.claim: Mali and Senegal concessioned the 1,288 km Dakar to Bamako railway to Transrail in 2003 for 25 years, terminated the concession on 5 December 2015 after it failed, and rail traffic, which at its peak had carried about 1.5 million tons of freight a year, stopped completely in 2018.

metric.name: Freight and passenger rail traffic on the Dakar to Bamako line after the concession's termination

secondMetric.name: Freight carried by the Dakar to Bamako railway at its peak (about)

source.publisher: World Bank, Concept Project Information Document, Dakar-Bamako Intermodal Corridor Project (P171122), September 2019

records.limits: The facts are in paragraphs 7, 9 and 16 of a concept-stage document (pages 4 to 6 of 14 in the plain-text version); the zero is the document's statement that traffic 'stopped completely in 2018', not a published tonnage, and the 1.5 million ton peak has no year, so it may predate the concession. The World Bank supported the wave of African rail concessions this one belonged to and is preparing the follow-on corridor project, so the publisher is not neutral about why it failed; the PID also says both governments ignored the Bank's advice to restructure the concession as a lease. The concession was binational: Senegal is an equal party and the record is filed under Mali, where Transrail was headquartered, but it describes both states' collaboration. The PID's diagnosis is shared blame: a 'full concession' design that made the operator pay for track and trains from revenue that could not cover both, decades of underinvestment by both governments before 2003, and road competition after the 2002 Cote d'Ivoire crisis sent Mali's trade through Dakar. After termination both governments paid staff salaries through an interim company (Dakar Bamako Ferroviaire) with a heavy fiscal cost.

pattern.mechanism: Two governments handed a run-down binational railway to a private consortium in a single full concession covering track and operations, keeping minority stakes; the operator could not fund maintenance from traffic revenue, service degraded, the states terminated the contract and the line stopped.
preconditions: A track and rolling stock base good enough for operating revenue to fund maintenance, which was missing
A concession design that separated infrastructure funding from train operations, which was missing
Two governments able to coordinate oversight of one operator across a border
pattern.travelled: The PID places it in a wave of full rail concessions in Sub-Saharan Africa and draws the lesson that infrastructure funding should be separated from train operations, which is the model the follow-on corridor project proposes.

records.title: Sudan Family Support Programme (Thamarat), and its halt after the October 2021 coup
records.claim: After Sudan cut fuel subsidies and unified its exchange rate in February 2021, the transitional government's Sudan Family Support Programme began paying cash in March 2021 and by 25 October 2021 had registered about 2.7 million families and paid about 30.6 billion Sudanese pounds to 1.4 million families, about 4.7 million people, before all activities, including cash delivery, were halted after the military takeover of that day.

metric.name: Families paid by the SFSP/Thamarat before the halt (Table E4 total, paid families)

secondMetric.name: Families registered against a planned 6.5 million

source.publisher: World Bank, Sudan Transition and Recovery Support Trust Fund (STARS) Annual Report 2021

records.limits: The World Bank and the STARS donors financed the programme, decided its pause and wrote this report, so the publisher is grading its own operation and also chose to end it. The numbers are in a PDF: the subsidy and exchange-rate reforms of February 2021 on PDF page 10, the halt of all activities 'including delivery of cash to beneficiaries' on PDF page 16, the 2.7 million families registered and 1.4 million families (about 4.7 million people) paid on PDF page 23, and the per-state table (Table E4, 2,637,632 enrolled and 1,395,295 paid) on PDF page 85, which notes that the first 80,000 families were paid in March 2021 (PDF page 77). The 1.39 million families paid include families in two states where the World Food Programme, not the ministry, implemented payments (PDF page 75), so not every paid family was reached by the government's own delivery. Table E4 has visible inconsistencies (East Darfur shows 391,900 families paid against 4,291 enrolled), so the state rows should not be quoted. The speed claim is about seven months from first payment to 1.4 million families, against a target of 6.5 million; the report says the programme started late because of exchange-rate problems, and paid families reached only 22 percent of the target population. What responded was a transitional government acting inside an IMF and World Bank reform package that conditioned arrears clearance, not on its own timetable. The halt was a decision by the financier after a coup, so the dismantling reflects a political break and donor policy (OP 7.30) as much as institutional capacity; later safety-net payments in Sudan were routed through the World Food Programme rather than the ministry.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of Labour and Social Development built a near-universal cash transfer to offset fuel subsidy removal and exchange-rate unification, registering families through 352 centres linked to the national civil registry and paying through banks, mobile money and cash cards, with donor money held in a designated account; the coup stopped the money and the programme with it.
preconditions: Donor financing large enough to compensate most households for a subsidy cut
A national ID registry to validate enrolment against duplicates
A government that the financiers continue to recognise, which is the precondition that failed in October 2021
pattern.travelled: The same compensation logic as Iran's 2010 subsidy reform cash transfer and Egypt's Takaful and Karama, but financed almost entirely from outside, which made it end the day the financiers paused.

records.title: Response to the 2018 to 2020 North Kivu and Ituri Ebola outbreak
records.claim: The Democratic Republic of the Congo's Ministry of Health, supported by WHO and partners, ran the response to the North Kivu and Ituri Ebola outbreak from August 2018 until it was declared over on 25 June 2020, vaccinating more than 303,000 people, registering 250,000 contacts and testing 220,000 samples, in an outbreak that counted 3,481 cases and 2,299 deaths.

metric.name: People vaccinated with the rVSV-ZEBOV-GP Ebola vaccine during the response

secondMetric.name: Total Ebola cases (3,323 confirmed and 158 probable), of whom 2,299 died

source.publisher: World Health Organization, Ebola outbreak 2018 to 2020, North Kivu and Ituri, situation page (case counts sourced to the Ministry of Health of the Democratic Republic of the Congo)

records.limits: This is the second largest Ebola outbreak on record, and the vaccination count measures the size of the response, not its success: it ran for almost two years and killed 2,299 people, about two thirds of the cases, so the record evidences a delivery under extreme conditions rather than early containment. WHO and many partners carried much of the operation, the vaccine was used under a ring vaccination protocol, investigational for most of the outbreak until its licensure in late 2019, which the page does not discuss, and the page does not split national from international effort. The figures are WHO's summary of Ministry of Health reports, and the vaccination count is a rounded 'over 303 000'. The outbreak ran in an active conflict zone, which the page names but does not describe or quantify. A resurgence in North Kivu followed in February 2021, listed on the same page, so the declared end did not mean the virus was gone from the region.

pattern.mechanism: The health ministry ran an incident management structure with WHO, traced contacts across three provinces and used ring vaccination with a new vaccine to cut chains of transmission, while working through community leaders in a conflict zone.
preconditions: A health ministry with prior Ebola outbreak experience and field teams
A licensed or investigational vaccine and the cold chain to deliver it at minus 60 degrees or colder
International surge capacity and money for a response lasting years, not weeks
pattern.travelled: The same ring vaccination approach was used in Guinea in 2021 (gin-ebola-2021), where the outbreak was far smaller and ended in four months.

records.title: Rahad Irrigation Project, and its cost and time overrun
records.claim: Sudan's government and the Rahad Corporation (RAHCO) built the Rahad irrigation scheme, 300,000 feddans east of the Rahad River, a tributary of the Blue Nile, with a main pumping station, a siphon under the Dinder River and a barrage on the Rahad River, under credits approved in March 1973; the physical works were completed in December 1982 against a planned June 1978, at a final cost of US$395.6 million against an appraisal estimate of US$125.0 million.

metric.name: Final estimated total project cost at completion

secondMetric.name: Total project cost estimated at appraisal

source.publisher: World Bank Operations Evaluation Department, Project Performance Audit Report, Sudan: Rahad Irrigation Project (Credits 364 and 364-1-SU), Report No. 5130, 13 June 1984, with the Project Completion Report attached

records.limits: The report is the World Bank auditing a project it financed alongside the Kuwait Fund, the Arab Fund, the Saudi Fund and others, so the delivery was Sudanese but the money and the judgement were largely external. Much of the threefold overrun came before construction: the project was reappraised in 1975 at US$320.7 million, 156 percent above 1973, because detailed designs had not been done at appraisal and the 1973 oil shock drove inflation, so only a 23 percent overrun is measured against a design-based estimate. The final cost is itself an estimate: the report says local costs such as administration and settlement are approximate and that better information had been requested. Figures are nominal dollars at the exchange rates of the time. The schedule comparison uses the dates for completing physical components in the report's data table (June 1978 appraised, December 1982 actual); the text says the project finished more than four years late. The scheme did develop the full planned area, and the auditors re-estimated its economic return at 20 percent against 14 percent at appraisal, so a cost overrun did not mean a failed asset. The text file is an OCR of a 1984 typescript and some table cells are garbled.

pattern.mechanism: The government let a large pump irrigation scheme go to tender before detailed design was finished, then refinanced a doubling of cost through a second round of Arab and IDA credits and absorbed the remainder in the national budget.
preconditions: Appraisal based on a feasibility study rather than detailed design
Several co-financiers willing to raise commitments mid-project
A construction market where contractors had better-paying bids elsewhere in the region

records.title: Routine immunization through the 2023 war, and its erosion
records.claim: WHO and UNICEF estimated that Sudan's national DTP3 coverage among one-year-olds fell from 95 percent in 2017 and 84 percent in 2022 to 51 percent in 2023 and 39 percent in 2024, after war broke out in April 2023, before recovering to 71 percent in 2025.

metric.name: Estimated DTP3 coverage among one-year-olds (WUENIC)

secondMetric.name: Estimated DTP3 coverage at its recent peak

source.publisher: World Health Organization, Global Health Observatory OData API, indicator WHS4_100 (DTP3 immunization coverage among 1-year-olds, WHO and UNICEF estimates of national immunization coverage)

records.limits: Routine immunization is a standing health service, not a hazard-specific preparedness delivery, and this record is filed on the precedent of hti-immunization-erosion: it reads the war as the shock and coverage as the capacity to keep a basic service running through it and restore it. The figures are WHO and UNICEF estimates built from administrative reports and surveys, not a census, and estimates for a country at war with displaced populations and collapsed reporting are especially uncertain. The API rows mix revisions: 2000 to 2024 carry a July 2025 timestamp and 2025 a July 2026 one, so the latest revision may have restated earlier years that the API does not show. 95 percent in 2017 is the highest value in the published series, which starts in 2000. The fall is caused mainly by war and displacement, outside the health system's control, and the 2025 recovery may owe much to UNICEF, WHO and Gavi supported catch-up campaigns rather than the national programme alone; the data cannot separate them. The started year is the start of the comparison, following hti-immunization-erosion, not the founding of the national programme.

pattern.mechanism: Sudan's Expanded Programme on Immunization kept national DTP3 coverage above 90 percent for most of the 2010s through fixed clinics and outreach, then lost more than half of it when war closed facilities, displaced millions and broke the supply chain from Khartoum, and partly rebuilt it with catch-up campaigns.
preconditions: A cold chain and clinic network that depends on the capital for supply and pay
Population registers and reporting that survive displacement
External partners able to fund and run catch-up campaigns in contested areas
pattern.travelled: Haiti (hti-immunization-erosion) shows a slower erosion under insecurity; Sudan's fall was faster and deeper, and its partial recovery came within two years.

records.title: Response to the 2025 cholera outbreak, with a high fatality rate
records.claim: Angola's Ministry of Health, with WHO, UNICEF, the World Bank and the ICRC, vaccinated over 900,000 people with oral cholera vaccine in a five-day reactive campaign in January 2025, with 99.5 percent administrative coverage, in an outbreak that had reached 8,543 cases and 329 deaths, a case fatality rate of 3.9 percent, in 16 of 21 provinces by 23 March 2025.

metric.name: People vaccinated in the January 2025 reactive oral cholera vaccination campaign

secondMetric.name: Case fatality rate of the outbreak (329 deaths in 8,543 cases)

source.publisher: World Health Organization, Disease Outbreak News, Cholera - Angola (2025-DON562), 28 March 2025

records.limits: The record shows a fast vaccination campaign inside a response that failed on its main outcome: WHO says a case fatality rate can be kept below 1 percent with timely care, and Angola's was 3.9 percent, with a third of deaths in the community, which WHO attributes to late presentation, gaps in surveillance and early response, and weak access to treatment. The 99.5 percent is administrative coverage of a target population the DON does not define, not a survey, and the 900,000 is rounded. The campaign was run with WHO, UNICEF, the World Bank and the ICRC, so the national share cannot be separated, and the DON does not say where the doses came from. The DON is a snapshot at 23 March 2025 while the outbreak was still spreading; this record does not show when or how it ended. The status 'concluded' refers to the January campaign, not the outbreak. The underlying cause, poor water and sanitation in crowded areas, is a standing gap the vaccination does not address; WHO notes cholera re-emerged in 2006 after a decade-long absence and recurs periodically.

pattern.mechanism: The health ministry used the international oral cholera vaccine stockpile to mount a five-day mass campaign in the first affected areas, while case management and water and sanitation lagged behind the spread to 16 provinces.
preconditions: Access to the global oral cholera vaccine stockpile and partners to fund delivery
Vaccination teams able to reach crowded urban districts within days
Treatment centres and oral rehydration close enough to patients to keep deaths low, which here was missing

records.title: Accra bus rapid transit under the Ghana Urban Transport Project, and its cancellation
records.claim: Ghana's Department of Urban Roads, joined in 2012 by the Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development, set out in 2007 to build Sub-Saharan Africa's first bus rapid transit corridor in Accra for an estimated US$46 million of infrastructure, but after a design review raised that estimate to US$100.7 million and counterpart funds did not arrive, the BRT was dropped in the 2014 restructuring without its 9.1 km of dedicated lanes being built, and the project closed in December 2015, 35.5 months after its original December 2012 closing date.

metric.name: Revised cost estimate for the BRT infrastructure after the 2013 design review

secondMetric.name: Original cost estimate for the BRT infrastructure (Component 3)

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Ghana Urban Transport Project (P100619, P092509), January 2017

records.limits: The source is the World Bank's own completion report on a project it financed with AFD and GEF money, and it rates the outcome Unsatisfactory, so it judges the Bank's design as well as Ghana's delivery: the report says the BRT design was not fully developed at appraisal and that bid documents were prepared during implementation. The US$100.7 million is a revised estimate, not money spent, because the BRT was cancelled before Lots 2 and 3 were contracted; what was built under Lot 1 (the Odaw Bridge expansion and a railway flyover) cost US$14.7 million against US$9.2 million estimated, a 60 percent overrun. The 35.5 months is computed from the original and actual closing dates in the report's key dates table (31 December 2012 and 15 December 2015); the text gives the extensions as 29.5 months for two of them. The remaining funds went to quality bus services on two other corridors, which were not operating at closure. What happened to bus services in Accra after 2015 is not covered here.

pattern.mechanism: Two government agencies split responsibility for the roads and the buses of a first-of-its-kind BRT, tendered it before the design was complete, and when bids came in at double the estimate and the treasury could not pay its share, cut the corridor and spent the remaining credit on cheaper bus lanes elsewhere.
preconditions: A new transit mode with no domestic design or operating precedent
An appraisal without an up-to-date land use plan or transport master plan for the city
Counterpart funding that depended on the annual budget rather than a ring-fenced allocation

records.title: Ghana's 2022 Marburg virus disease response
records.claim: Ghana's Ministry of Health declared the country's first Marburg virus disease outbreak on 7 July 2022, identified and monitored 198 contacts through 42 days, and declared the outbreak over on 16 September 2022 after three confirmed cases, all from one household, and two deaths.

metric.name: Contacts identified, monitored and completed observation

secondMetric.name: Confirmed Marburg cases (two deaths, CFR 67 percent)

source.publisher: World Health Organization, Disease Outbreak News, Marburg virus disease - Ghana (2022-DON409), 26 September 2022

records.limits: Three cases in one household is a very small event, and containing it shows that surveillance and contact tracing worked once, not a standing national capacity; a small outbreak can end quickly by luck of the transmission chain. Detection was late for the first case: the index patient was admitted on 26 June and died the next day, and a second household member, a child, was infected and died before isolation, so two of three cases were fatal. The figures are WHO's restatement of Ministry of Health reports, so the government is reporting on its own response, with WHO and partners in support. The national laboratory (Noguchi Memorial Institute) confirmed the virus, but Institut Pasteur Dakar's confirmation was part of the timeline, as the DON describes. The record says nothing about Ghana's response to other shocks such as the 2023 Akosombo dam spillage floods.

pattern.mechanism: The Ghana Health Service ran its integrated disease surveillance and response system: a suspected viral haemorrhagic fever was tested at the national reference laboratory, the ministry declared the outbreak, traced and followed every contact for 42 days and isolated the remaining case in a designated centre.
preconditions: An integrated disease surveillance and response system reporting from district level
A national laboratory able to test for filoviruses
Designated isolation facilities and contact tracing teams ready before the event
pattern.travelled: Rwanda's 2024 Marburg response (rwa-marburg-2024) ran the same playbook at twenty times the case count.

records.title: Yabayo-Gagnoa road under the Fourth Highway Project, and its cost and time overrun
records.claim: Côte d'Ivoire's Ministry of Public Works built the 70 km Yabayo-Gagnoa road and rebuilt the bridge over the N'Zi River under the Fourth Highway Project (Credit 406-IVC, approved June 1973), completing it in September 1978 against a planned June 1976, at a cost of US$24.7 million against an appraisal estimate of US$12.3 million, an overrun of 101 percent.

metric.name: Actual total project cost (Fourth Highway Project)

secondMetric.name: Appraisal estimate of total project cost

source.publisher: World Bank Operations Evaluation Department, Project Performance Audit Report, Ivory Coast Second Highway Project (Loan 761-IVC), Third Highway Project (Loan 837-IVC) and Fourth Highway Project (Credit 406-IVC), Report No. 3665, 28 October 1981

records.limits: This is a modest project by today's standards: a 70 km road and one bridge, US$24.7 million in 1970s dollars, of which the IDA credit was US$7.5 million and the rest the government's, so it is a mid-sized public works delivery rather than a national megaproject; no larger Ivorian project with a published baseline and outturn was found. The source is the World Bank auditing its own lending. The audit attributes the overrun to the road construction and the 27-month delay mainly to the decision, accepted by the Bank, to split the works by function: a government-owned enterprise lacking managers and trained operators did the earthworks late, holding up the French-Ivorian joint venture that was to lay the base and surface. The schedule figures come from the audit's basic data sheet (June 1976 planned, September 1978 actual, a 175 percent time overrun); the text gives completion as 27 months after the project completion date. Despite the overrun, the auditors re-estimated the economic return at 24 percent against 14 percent at appraisal. The text is an OCR of a 1981 typescript.

pattern.mechanism: The public works ministry split a new road into separate contracts for earthworks, paving and aggregate, gave the first to an inexperienced state enterprise, and the later contracts stalled waiting for it, doubling cost and tripling the construction time.
preconditions: A government push to upgrade main roads to high standards in the 1970s boom
State-owned construction enterprises given work without proven capacity
A lender that accepted the borrower's contract split against internal warnings

records.title: COVID-19 vaccination campaign
records.claim: Côte d'Ivoire's health authorities reported to WHO that 13,568,372 people, 51 per 100 population, had received at least one COVID-19 vaccine dose by 31 December 2023, from a first dose given on 1 March 2021, with 12,164,304 (46 per 100) completing the primary series.

metric.name: People vaccinated with at least one COVID-19 vaccine dose

secondMetric.name: People who completed the primary series (last dose)

source.publisher: World Health Organization, COVID-19 dashboard vaccination data (vaccination-data.csv)

records.limits: COVID-19 vaccination is a response to one shock and a judgement call for this column, which prefers a hazard-specific delivery; no hazard-specific Ivorian case with an official figure was found. The figures are Côte d'Ivoire's own reports to WHO (DATA_SOURCE 'REPORTING') with no independent coverage survey. First-dose reach was barely a majority (51 per 100) and fewer than half completed the primary series (46 per 100), with boosters at 12 per 100, so this is a partial delivery on the same terms as ven-covid-vaccination; it is filed because it reached about half the population nationally, which most of its West African neighbours did not. The VACCINES_USED field is empty, so the record cannot show which products were used or where the doses came from, and evidences distribution only. The per-100 rates divide by WHO's population estimate. The file was last updated for this country on 31 December 2023. The WHO dashboard address covid19.who.int/who-data/vaccination-data.csv now returns an HTML page, so the cited URL is the blob the dashboard serves, the same one bol-covid-vaccination cites.

pattern.mechanism: The health ministry ran a national COVID-19 campaign through its immunisation programme and vaccination sites, and reached about half the population with a first dose within three years.
preconditions: A routine immunisation programme with a cold chain reaching districts
Donated or COVAX doses arriving in large enough volume for a national campaign
Registers able to count completion of the primary series
pattern.travelled: Bolivia (bol-covid-vaccination) and Venezuela (ven-covid-vaccination) reached similar partial coverage; among this batch's West African countries only Guinea (66 per 100 first dose) reported more.

records.title: Mali's 2014 Ebola containment
records.claim: After Mali confirmed an imported Ebola case on 23 October 2014 and a second, unrecognised imported case started a chain of seven further cases in a Bamako clinic, the government with WHO and partners identified and followed 433 contacts for 21 days, set up a hotline receiving about 6,000 calls a day, built isolation and treatment facilities, and ended monitoring of the last contacts on 15 December 2014.

metric.name: Contacts identified and followed up for the 21-day incubation period

secondMetric.name: Calls per day to the Ebola telephone hotline (approximate)

source.publisher: World Health Organization, One year into the Ebola epidemic: Successful Ebola responses in Nigeria, Senegal and Mali (January 2015)

records.limits: The page is a WHO narrative written to present the response as a success, not a dataset, and it was written before Mali was declared free of transmission (WHO says that would happen on 18 January 2015 if no further cases arose). The second chain shows a detection failure: a patient from Guinea was admitted to a private clinic in Bamako with a diagnosis of kidney failure and died, and seven further cases followed, five of them fatal, including a doctor and a nurse who treated him; the page does not give a single total for cases and deaths. WHO and partner staff already in the country for preparedness shifted to the response, and the Bamako laboratory used was built with US National Institutes of Health support, so the national share cannot be separated. This is one small event seeded by two imported cases, and it says nothing about Mali's capacity for other hazards, including the conflict that has displaced people in the north and centre since 2012.

pattern.mechanism: Mali's government, on alert since a false alarm in April 2014, traced every contact of two imported cases with medical students trained in epidemiology as extra tracers, isolated them, and used a hotline to find rumours and suspected cases.
preconditions: A biosafety laboratory in the capital able to confirm the virus within days
Months of preparedness work and a rehearsal before the first case
A pool of trainable people, here medical students, to scale contact tracing quickly
pattern.travelled: Nigeria (nga-ebola-response) ran the same playbook three months earlier, and the WHO page groups the two as models.

records.title: Fourth Highway Project: paving of the Mamou-Kankan and Dubreka-Kolaboui roads
records.claim: Guinea's Ministry of Transport and Public Works paved the Dubreka-Kolaboui (196.5 km) and Mamou-Kankan (401 km) national roads under the Fourth Highway Project, approved in June 1988, at a latest estimated cost of US$207 million against an appraisal estimate of US$200 million, with the IDA credit closing on 31 December 1996, three years late, and the last 94 km of Mamou-Kankan still under construction in 1997.

metric.name: Latest project cost estimate at completion

secondMetric.name: Project cost estimated in the staff appraisal report

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion Report, Republic of Guinea Fourth Highway Project (Credit 1915-GUI), Report No. 16646, 5 June 1997

records.limits: The report is the World Bank's own completion report on a credit it made, and the IDA credit was only US$55 million of the US$207 million: parallel finance of US$143 million came from the AfDB, the French CFD, USAID, Japan's OECF, BADEA and the European Community, so the cost figure covers a multi-donor programme run through the ministry. The cost is a 'latest estimate', not an audited outturn, and the 3.5 percent overrun is small partly because the scope changed: about 500 km of cement-stabilised base and asphalt concrete on 310 km were added, so the money bought a higher standard than appraised. The three-year delay is on the credit's closing date, not on road completion dates; the report says the last 94 km of Mamou-Kankan, financed by the EC, was to be finished by the end of 1999. The government paid about US$8 million of its planned US$19.2 million contribution. The report blames delays on a slow restructuring of the ministry, poor technical studies, cumbersome procurement and late payments to contractors.

pattern.mechanism: The public works ministry packaged two long trunk-road upgrades with spot repairs and labour-based maintenance into one programme, and paid for it by assembling seven donors in parallel, each financing particular sections.
preconditions: Donors willing to finance road sections in parallel under one sector programme
A ministry able to procure and supervise several international civil works contracts at once
Counterpart funds for local costs, which here arrived at less than half the planned level

records.title: Realignment of the Congo-Ocean Railway through the Mayombe, and its overruns
records.claim: The Republic of the Congo's transport agency ATC rebuilt an 88 km section of the Brazzaville to Pointe-Noire railway through the Mayombe range, with 19 bridges, three tunnels including one of 4.6 km and 17 million m3 of earthworks, completing it in mid-1985 against an expected end of 1979 at a cost of US$399 million against an estimate of US$149 million, an overrun of 168 percent.

metric.name: Total cost of the CFCO realignment at completion

secondMetric.name: Cost of the CFCO realignment estimated at appraisal

source.publisher: World Bank Operations Evaluation Department, Project Performance Audit Report, People's Republic of the Congo Second Railway Project (Loan 1228-COB, Credit 1047-COB), Report No. 8898, 29 June 1990

records.limits: The audit is the World Bank's evaluators on a project the Bank appraised and part financed: the realignment had ten financiers, including France, the European Community and the Bank's US$38 million loan and US$30 million supplementary credit, so the money was largely external and the audit judges the Bank's appraisal as much as ATC's execution; it says the Bank accepted detailed engineering based on inadequate soil, topographic and geological study and allowed physical contingencies of only 10 percent for earthworks and 15 percent for tunnels. Figures are nominal dollars over a decade of high inflation, so part of the overrun is price escalation. The 168 percent and five and a half year delay (a 157 percent time overrun) are the audit's own computations. Traffic, expected to double, stayed flat, and the audit puts the economic return at zero or negative and calls the project unsustainable, so the record is a delivery that was finished but did not pay off. The text is an OCR of a 1990 typescript and some words are garbled.

pattern.mechanism: The state transport agency, running the railway at the same time, managed a mountain realignment with tunnels on engineering that underestimated the ground, and when bids came in high and the works slipped, ten lenders refinanced the doubling of cost rather than stop.
preconditions: A single national rail corridor whose collapse was feared, which made stopping politically impossible
Lenders willing to add supplementary credits to a half-built line
Traffic forecasts tied to timber and manganese exports that did not materialise

records.title: Banjul Rehabilitation Project (roads, drainage and sewage), and its delay
records.claim: The Gambia's Ministry of Transport, Works and Infrastructure contracted the US$35.7 million (D1.8 billion) Banjul roads, drainage and sewage rehabilitation in May 2019 without tender, for completion by November 2021; by August 2021 12,953 m of the 15,216 m of roads, 85 percent, were built and 63 percent of the contract price paid, the pumping and lifting stations were outstanding, and the completion date had been extended to November 2022.

metric.name: Road length completed as at August 2021 (85 percent of 15,216 m)

secondMetric.name: Contract sum of the EPC contract

source.publisher: National Audit Office of The Gambia, Banjul Rehabilitation Project, Final Management Letter for the period 1 January 2019 to 31 August 2021, April 2022

records.limits: The audit is a compliance management letter, not a completion audit: it stops at 31 August 2021, three months before the original deadline, so it shows progress and a one-year extension of the deadline to November 2022, not an outturn. Whether the project was finished, at what final cost and on what date is not shown here, and the status 'operating' rests only on the audit's finding that most roads were built and in use. The 85 percent is of a road length that an addendum had raised from 14,614 m to 15,216 m, and the audit does not report a cost increase from that addendum. The figures are in a 24-page PDF (site verification on page 23). The audit's main findings are about process, not schedule: the contract was single sourced and gazetted only in February 2021, works began on 18 March 2019 before the contract was signed on 11 May 2019, no performance security was provided, withholding tax was not deducted, and 63 percent had been paid while critical components worth US$2.47 million, 6.9 percent of the sum, were outstanding. A contractor-initiated, pre-financed offer is how the project began, so the institutional delivery is partly the contractor's proposal.

pattern.mechanism: The works ministry accepted a contractor's unsolicited offer to pre-finance the reconstruction of the capital's roads and drains, signed a single-source design-and-build contract, then switched to paying it from the budget in interim instalments ahead of the hardest components.
preconditions: A procurement authority that can be bypassed by single sourcing for a presidential priority
A contractor willing to start work before a signed contract
Budget room to pay interim certificates once the pre-financing was dropped

records.title: COVID-19 emergency food support distributed by the National Disaster Management Agency
records.claim: The Gambia's government bought 264,500 bags of rice, 279,500 bags of sugar and 185,200 drums of oil for vulnerable households with about GMD909.9 million redirected in 2020, and the National Disaster Management Agency distributed them between May and 28 September 2020, with 228,367 bags of rice recorded as delivered to households, 36,133 fewer than procured.

metric.name: Bags of rice (50 kg) delivered to households as recorded in the Kobo-Collect system

secondMetric.name: Bags of rice (50 kg) procured for distribution
