source.publisher: National Audit Office of The Gambia, Audit Report on the Government COVID-19 Response: Procurement and Distribution of Medical and Food Items (Phase 1), September 2021

records.limits: The audit office judged the distribution untimely, unequal and poorly recorded, so this is a record of a national relief delivery with large leaks, not a model. Procurement deliveries ran from 1 to 12 May 2020 but the last household distribution was on 28 September 2020, nearly five months later. The delivered counts come from the Kobo-Collect tool, which the audit says recorded what a household should receive rather than what it received, some households recorded as served could not be reached, and coordinators' reports disagree with it, so 228,367 is an upper bound on what reached people. The same delivered figure appears for rice and sugar in the audit table. Households were selected without a needs assessment, some vulnerable households in two Kanifing wards were never registered, and food stored in the open was damaged without records. The audit examined Banjul, Kanifing and West Coast Region in detail and left the other regions to a later audit. The number of households reached is not reported. The figures are in a 156-page PDF (executive summary, pages 18 to 24).

pattern.mechanism: The government redirected debt-relief money to buy staple food in bulk and used the disaster management agency and local authorities to hand it out through distribution points with coupons to households identified as vulnerable.
preconditions: A disaster agency with a field network able to run distribution points nationwide
Household lists from local authorities, here incomplete and drawn up without criteria
Stock records and storage that let food be tracked from purchase to household, which here were missing

records.title: Bissau Port Project, delivered two and a half years late
records.claim: Guinea-Bissau's port authority (JAPG) rehabilitated the old commercial wharf of Bissau Port, built river ports and ferry ramps and, with a new deepwater wharf financed in parallel by four Arab funds, completed the IDA-financed Bissau Port Project on 30 June 1990 against a planned 31 December 1987, at a final cost of US$20.0 million against an appraisal estimate of US$17.36 million.

metric.name: Final cost of the IDA-financed Bissau Port Project

secondMetric.name: Cost of the project estimated at appraisal

source.publisher: World Bank, Project Completion Report, Guinea-Bissau Bissau Port Project (Credit 1392-GUB), Report No. 9901, 16 September 1991

records.limits: The report is the World Bank on its own credit, and it notes that the government sent no comments for Part II, the borrower's review, despite repeated requests; consultants acting for the borrower prepared a final report the PCR drew on, so the borrower's own view is largely missing. The cost figures cover only the IDA-financed part (wharf repair, river ports, technical assistance and supervision of the new berth); the new deepwater wharf itself was financed separately by the Kuwait Fund, the Saudi Fund, BADEA and the OPEC Fund, and its cost and schedule are not reported here, though the report blames repeated suspensions of Arab Fund disbursements, triggered by the government's late repayment of earlier loans, for most of the delay. The 14.9 percent overrun is in dollars; the report says the credit, made in SDRs, covered the work without an overrun, and scope grew with four extra ferry ramps, container storage and more technical assistance. The project is small in absolute terms, about US$20 million, but Bissau is the country's main port and the report credits the project with a modern deepwater facility where only a badly damaged wharf had existed. The text is an OCR of a 1991 typescript.

pattern.mechanism: The government split its port programme into an IDA part and an Arab-funded new berth awarded to the same contractor, so when the Arab funds suspended payments over the country's arrears the contractor slowed work on both, and IDA supervision kept the project going to completion.
preconditions: A port authority set up as a separate agency able to borrow and contract
Several lenders financing separate parts through one contractor
A government able to keep current on earlier loans, which here it was not

records.title: FMA Regulatory Sandbox
records.claim: Austria's Financial Market Authority admitted eight FinTechs to its Regulatory Sandbox between its launch on 1 September 2020 and January 2023, five seeking authorisation as European crowdfunding service providers and three offering crypto-asset or securities services, and one participant had obtained a licence for a digital trading platform by the start of 2022.

metric.name: FinTechs admitted to the Regulatory Sandbox since launch

secondMetric.name: Participants per year the federal funding was designed for, in the 2019 impact assessment of the FMABG amendment

source.publisher: Finanzmarktaufsicht (FMA), press release 'FMA's Regulatory Sandbox presents positive results', 2 January 2023

records.limits: The count is the regulator's own and dates from January 2023; no later total was found, and an FMA notice on a later admission returned 403 to a script and was not read. Eight admissions in 28 months is below the five a year the federal contribution of EUR 500,000 a year was sized for (impact assessment, Vorblatt, https://www.ris.bka.gv.at/Dokumente/Begut/BEGUT_COO_2026_100_2_1632524/COO_2026_100_2_1632539.pdf, page 1), so the regime ran under its design volume. The sandbox grants no relief from regulatory requirements: the impact assessment says a core principle is that requirements are not lowered, so it is supervised testing with guidance rather than derogation. Five of the eight were crowdfunding platforms preparing for one EU regulation, which inflates the count with a one-off wave. Admission is not completion: the release names one licence obtained. The page was read through WebFetch because the FMA site returns 403 to curl.

pattern.mechanism: Parliament amended the Financial Market Authority Act to create a sandbox at the FMA, with a federal grant for running it and an advisory board at the finance ministry that comments on each application's economic interest and readiness before the FMA decides.
preconditions: A statutory basis and earmarked federal funding
An advisory board that can vet applications quickly
An EU rule change (here the Crowdfunding Regulation) that creates a cohort of firms needing supervised preparation

records.title: Regulatorisk sandkasse for AI (Datatilsynet and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen)
records.claim: Denmark's data protection authority and digitalisation agency selected two projects from 23 applications for the first round of their regulatory sandbox for AI in July 2024, two from 18 applications in June 2025 and three more in July 2026, seven projects in all.

metric.name: Projects selected across the first three rounds (2 + 2 + 3)

secondMetric.name: Applications received for the first round

source.publisher: Datatilsynet, news 'Tre nye AI-projekter udvalgt til den regulatoriske sandkasse' (9 July 2026), with the round one (8 July 2024) and round two (18 June 2025) announcements

records.limits: The total of seven is our sum of three announcements (https://www.datatilsynet.dk/presse-og-nyheder/nyhedsarkiv/2024/jul/to-ai-projekter-udvalgt-til-foerste-runde-af-den-regulatoriske-sandkasse and https://www.datatilsynet.dk/presse-og-nyheder/nyhedsarkiv/2025/jun/to-ai-projekter-udvalgt-til-anden-runde-af-den-regulatoriske-sandkasse); the third announcement gives no application count. Not every participant is a firm: round one included a project led by three municipalities with Systematic, round two the charity Boerns Vilkaar, and round three Region Hovedstaden with Kintella, so firms are fewer than seven. The sandbox offers guidance on data protection law, not derogations, and it is a GDPR sandbox rather than the AI Act sandbox the EU requires. Applications fell from 23 to 18 between the first two rounds. The Danish FSA's FT Lab, the financial sandbox since 2018, publishes admissions only as individual news items and no total, so it was not used; the national figure across regulators is therefore higher than seven by an unknown amount.

pattern.mechanism: Two agencies run annual application rounds, pick a handful of AI projects whose questions others share, give each months of guided dialogue on data protection, and publish final reports so the answers reach firms that never applied.
preconditions: A data protection authority willing to give advance guidance outside enforcement
A digitalisation agency to co-fund and co-select
Applicants willing to have their compliance questions published
pattern.travelled: The model follows Norway's Datatilsynet sandbox (nor-datatilsynet-sandkasse), running since 2020, with a smaller intake per round.

records.title: Datatilsynet's regulatory sandbox for privacy-friendly innovation
records.claim: Norway's data protection authority ran eight sandbox projects at the end of 2025, five of them jointly with the Financial Supervisory Authority on data sharing against financial crime, and completed two projects (Akershus University Hospital and Mobai's SALT biometric verification) during the year.

metric.name: Sandbox projects in progress at year end

secondMetric.name: Sandbox projects completed during the year

source.publisher: Datatilsynet, Aarsrapport for 2025, chapter 'Prioritert omraade II, Regulatorisk sandkasse'

records.limits: The authority reports on its own sandbox. It gives dialogue-based guidance and no exemption from law, so it is a controlled advisory regime rather than a derogation sandbox. Participants include public bodies (a hospital) and banks working as a group, so projects are not firms. The report is internally inconsistent on the joint financial sandbox: the chapter says five projects, the director's foreword in the PDF version (https://www.datatilsynet.no/contentassets/112abf21f900417f859c66c8f7d838de/datatilsynets-arsrapport-for-2025.pdf) says four were taken in; Finanstilsynet's own announcement of 2025 names five. The joint projects are counted here and are not added again from Finanstilsynet. Finanstilsynet's separate fintech sandbox admitted few firms (two of 12 applicants in the first pool in 2020, then single firms such as Abendum, R8Me and Qbig) and was not summed in. The sandbox is staffed by one full-time coordinator, per the same PDF, which limits its scale. The 2020 start is from the authority's earlier evaluation material, not read today.

pattern.mechanism: The data protection authority takes a few projects a year into a structured dialogue on how privacy law applies to a new use of data, then publishes a final report and podcast so the answer reaches the whole sector, and in 2025 opened a joint sandbox with the financial supervisor.
preconditions: A ministry mandate and allocation letter that name the sandbox as a priority area
Regulators willing to give advance interpretations in public
Applicants whose question is general enough that a published answer helps others
pattern.travelled: Denmark's data protection authority opened a similar AI sandbox in 2024 (dnk-ai-sandkasse).

records.title: Bank of Lithuania regulatory sandbox, with one test in seven years
records.claim: The Bank of Lithuania opened its regulatory sandbox to applications on 15 October 2018 and, by the page's last update on 27 June 2025, listed one innovation ever tested in it: UAB Workpower's peer-to-peer insurance platform, authorised on 13 June 2019 and tested from 24 October 2019 to 23 October 2020, which led the bank to draft proportionate rules for P2P insurance.

metric.name: Innovations listed as tested in the regulatory sandbox since applications opened

source.publisher: Lietuvos bankas, Regulatory sandbox page (archived copy of 20 August 2026)

records.limits: The live page (https://www.lb.lt/en/regulatory-sandbox) returned a bot challenge and 403 to scripts, so the archived copy was read; it carries the bank's own 'last update' date of 27 June 2025. The count is one firm in about seven years, so the regime exists but barely delivers; the page's heading 'Financial innovations currently tested' still shows a test that ended in 2020. The bank's better-known LBChain blockchain platform, which 11 fintechs from 8 countries used during development to May 2020 (https://www.lb.lt/en/lbchain, archived), was a technical test environment without regulatory relief and is not counted. The bank also runs a newer sustainability-report test under the GFIN initiative (news of 16 July 2021) that is not listed as a firm test on the page. Lithuania's high fintech licensing volume runs through ordinary licensing, not this sandbox.

pattern.mechanism: The central bank offered live testing under supervision for financial innovations new to the Lithuanian market and used its one completed test to write proportionate guidelines for peer-to-peer insurance.
preconditions: A regulator with authority to set test conditions under existing licences
Firms whose model does not fit existing licences, which in Lithuania were few because licensing was already fast
A route from test results to guidelines
pattern.travelled: The single test did travel into rules: the bank's 2021 news says it would issue P2P insurance guidelines, the sandbox-to-rule step that most sandboxes lack.

records.title: Narodna banka Slovenska regulatory sandbox
records.claim: Slovakia's central bank opened its regulatory sandbox on 1 January 2022 and lists one former participant, Crowdberry Investment Platform, which entered on 22 November 2023, tested an electronic bulletin board for secondary trading of crowdfunded securities with selected clients from 15 December 2024 to 18 April 2025, and exited on 15 May 2025.

metric.name: Firms listed as former participants (completed) of the regulatory sandbox

source.publisher: Narodna banka Slovenska, Regulatory sandbox page

records.limits: The page lists former participants only and gives no count of current participants or applications, so admissions in progress are unknown; one completion in nearly four years of operation is the figure the page supports. The sandbox waives no regulatory requirement: the page says requirements cannot be waived, so it is supervised testing with consultation. The bank states that its innovation hub handles far more interactions than the sandbox, which reflects the design rather than a measured failure. The regulator reports on its own programme.

pattern.mechanism: The central bank admits firms year-round into a preparation phase of up to six months of consultations and a testing phase of up to six months on real clients under a test plan, ending with a final report and meeting.
preconditions: A published methodology for entry criteria
Staff in a fintech department to run long consultations
Firms with a product that needs real-client testing, which in a small market are few

records.title: Teknologiraadet, the Norwegian Board of Technology
records.claim: Norway's Board of Technology, an independent public advisory body created in 1999 on the Storting's initiative that also serves as secretariat for the Storting's technology group, delivered eight publications and held eleven meetings, four of them for the Storting's technology group, in 2025 on operating income of NOK 13.8 million.

metric.name: Publications delivered

secondMetric.name: Operating income

source.publisher: Teknologiraadet, Aarsrapport for 2025 til Naerings- og fiskeridepartementet

records.limits: The board reports on itself to its parent ministry; the figures are in a 41-page PDF, publications and meetings on PDF page 5 and income on page 3. It is a technology assessment body more than a strategic foresight unit, though its 2025 work included a project on strategic foresight methods and an annual trend report for the Storting. Publication counts measure output, not influence on law or budgets. It is small: the secretariat had eight permanent staff in 2025. Its funding line moved in 2025 from the trade ministry's research council chapter to the research council's allocation letter from the education ministry, which the report describes as an administrative change; continuity since 1999 is stated on the board's own about page (https://teknologiradet.no/forsiden/om-oss/), not in an external evaluation.

pattern.mechanism: The government appoints a 15-member council for four-year terms with a small independent secretariat that chooses its own projects, convenes expert groups and lay panels, and briefs the Storting through a cross-party technology group it services.
preconditions: A parliament that wants an independent source of technology advice and a cross-party group to receive it
A stable budget line outside any single policy ministry
A council free to choose topics, set in its statutes
pattern.travelled: Denmark's equivalent body, also called Teknologiraadet, was defunded and abolished in 2012 (dnk-teknologiraadet); the Norwegian one survived on a similar design.

records.title: Teknologiraadet, the Danish Board of Technology, abolished in 2012
records.claim: Denmark's parliament abolished the statutory Board of Technology, set up by Act no. 375 of 14 June 1995 to assess technology and report to the Folketing, by Act no. 559 of 18 June 2012, after an all-party budget agreement of 15 November 2011 withdrew its annual grant, which had been DKK 10.5 million in 2011, to fund the research reserve.

metric.name: Annual grant to the Board of Technology in the Finance Act

source.publisher: Folketinget, L 79 (2011-12), Forslag til lov om ophaevelse af lov om Teknologiraadet, explanatory notes, via Retsinformation

records.limits: The figure was read in the bill's XML (https://www.retsinformation.dk/eli/ft/201112L00079/xml), because the eli page renders with JavaScript; the vote (104 for, none against) and the law number and date come from the Folketing's open data API (oda.ft.dk, case 9940). The board was a technology assessment body with participatory methods, which is adjacent to strategic foresight rather than the same thing. Its work did not stop: Aktstykke 65 of 20 March 2012 let it create a foundation, Fonden Teknologiraadet, which continues as a non-profit that sells projects, so what ended is the statutory public function and its guaranteed grant, not every activity. The bill puts the annual saving at about DKK 10 million and sets aside DKK 4.5 million for winding up in 2012. The 1995 act replaced an earlier Technology Board (Teknologinaevnet) under a 1989 consolidated law, so the public function predates the start year given.

pattern.mechanism: A statute gave a self-governing board its own Finance Act grant and a duty to report to parliament each year; an all-party budget deal then reallocated that grant to research funding, and parliament repealed the act unanimously.
preconditions: A separate, visible grant line that could be reallocated in one budget agreement
No parliamentary committee that owned the board and would defend it
A foundation route that let staff and methods continue privately, which removed resistance to closure
pattern.travelled: Poland's strategic studies centre (pol-rcss) was closed in 2006 by a similar budget-line logic; Norway's board of the same name (nor-teknologiradet) survived.

records.title: Bureau federal du Plan
records.claim: Belgium's Federal Planning Bureau, which produces the government's economic forecasts and long-term demographic, ageing, energy and transport outlooks, published 34 publications in 2025 and employed 91 full-time equivalents at the end of the year, down from 96 at the end of 2023, after it stopped replacing departing staff in 2024 to meet savings targets.

metric.name: Staff, full-time equivalents at 31 December

secondMetric.name: Staff, full-time equivalents at 31 December (earlier level, not shown to be a peak)

source.publisher: Bureau federal du Plan, Rapport d'activite 2025

records.limits: The bureau reports on itself; the 91 FTE (80 funded by the federal grant, 11 by contracts) and the hiring freeze are on PDF page 12, the 34 publications on page 19. The 96 FTE is from the 2023 activity report (https://www.plan.be/sites/default/files/documents/OTH_ACTIV_2023_FR.pdf) and the 2024 report gives 94 (https://www.plan.be/sites/default/files/documents/OTH_ACTIV_2024_FR.pdf). The record is filed as operating, not eroded: the fall is five FTE, about 5 percent, from a 2023 level that is not shown to be a peak (earlier reports were not found at the same address), and output held, with 37 publications in 2023, 45 in 2024 and 34 in 2025. The staff trend and the bureau's statement that it no longer replaces leavers to meet savings targets are a documented squeeze on capacity, and a later report showing a deeper loss would justify eroded. Most of the bureau's work is medium-term forecasting and policy costing, not scenario-based strategic foresight; its long-term population, ageing and sustainable development outlooks are the foresight part. The report says nearly 40 percent of staff will retire within ten years, which is a risk stated by the bureau, not a measured loss. The 1959 start is the Act of 23 December 1959 named on the bureau's legal basis page (https://www.plan.be/en/about-us/legal-basis).

pattern.mechanism: A statutory, de facto independent planning bureau receives mandates from government, parliament and social partners, and publishes forecasts and long-term outlooks that the federal budget and pension debates rely on; in a savings drive the government cut its grant and it stopped replacing leavers.
preconditions: A statute that makes its forecasts the official basis for the budget
Social partners and parliament as co-principals, which protects independence
A core grant large enough to keep long-term modelling teams, which savings measures are now eroding

records.title: Special Secretariat of Foresight (now of Long-term Planning)
records.claim: Greece's Special Secretariat of Foresight published its Megatrends 2040 report and seven megatrend notes in February and March 2022 and then six further foresight studies to September 2026, including Generative AI Greece 2030 (January 2024), The Future of Work and Skills in Greece (February 2025) and Mediterranean Foresight (September 2026).

metric.name: Foresight studies published on the Secretariat's studies pages, January 2023 to September 2026

secondMetric.name: Megatrends 2040 report and megatrend notes published in February and March 2022

source.publisher: Special Secretariat of Foresight (Eidiki Grammateia Makroprothesmou Schediasmou), Studies pages

records.limits: Both counts are ours: the two studies list pages show no dates, so each item's date is the datePublished stamp in the metadata of its own page (for example Mediterranean Foresight, 29 September 2026; The Future of Work and Skills, 24 February 2025), and the site states no total. Of the six later items, several were made with partners (the National Centre for Social Research on internet use, the UNESCO Chair on Futures Research on innovation to 2035, and the High Level Advisory Committee on AI for the AI blueprint), so the Secretariat's own output is smaller; reposted EU Strategic Foresight Reports are excluded. Output fell from a launch burst in 2022 to one or two studies a year. The site's footer and its July 2026 press release now name the body the Special Secretariat of Long-term Planning, a renaming whose date and legal basis were not read; the 2022 start is the date of the first study, not the founding act, which was not read. A count of studies says nothing about use in policy.

pattern.mechanism: A special secretariat at the centre of government runs foresight studies with universities and research centres, trains a network of public servants in foresight tools, and represents Greece in EU foresight networks.
preconditions: A secretariat placed close to the head of government
Research partners to co-produce studies, since the unit is small
EU foresight networks that supply method and a reporting rhythm

records.title: STRATA foresight for the Lietuva 2050 state progress strategy
records.claim: Lithuania's Government Strategic Analysis Center (STRATA) followed six thematic public discussions on the country's future in May and June 2022 with nine foresight studies on megatrends and scenarios by policy area, which fed the vision and strategic ambitions of the draft state progress strategy Lietuva 2050.

metric.name: Foresight studies prepared for Lietuva 2050

secondMetric.name: Thematic discussions on Lithuania's future

source.publisher: Vyriausybes strategines analizes centras (STRATA), Ateities izvalgos page (archived copy of 10 August 2025)

records.limits: The live site (https://strata.gov.lt/) returned 403 to scripts, so an archived copy was read. The counts are stated by the centre about its own work and measure output, not influence; the page does not date each study, and 2022 is the year of the discussions. The exercise was tied to one strategy, so it shows a foresight delivery and not, by itself, a standing foresight function; STRATA's wider role (research, impact assessment, training) continues but was not counted. Whether the final Lietuva 2050 strategy adopted the scenarios was not read.

pattern.mechanism: The government's strategic analysis centre ran public thematic discussions, commissioned studies that turned their megatrends into sector scenarios and SWOT analyses, and used them in workshops that drafted the long-term state strategy.
preconditions: A government-owned analysis centre with a mandate in strategic planning
A strategy cycle that asks for a long-term vision
Experts and citizens willing to take part in discussions

records.title: AMS training measures (Schulungen) for jobseekers
records.claim: Austria's Public Employment Service (AMS) had on average 76,496 people a day enrolled in its training measures in 2025, up 1.3 percent on 2024, against an annual average of 65,126 in 2015.

metric.name: Schulungsteilnehmer_innen gesamt, annual average stock

secondMetric.name: Same annual average ten years earlier (Übersicht Jahr 2015)

source.publisher: Arbeitsmarktservice Österreich (AMS), 'Übersicht über den Arbeitsmarkt, Jahr 2025' (Spezialthema Jahreswerte)

records.limits: The agency reports on its own measures, in a five-page PDF (the training table is on page 3). The figure is an annual average stock, the number enrolled on an average day, not the number of different people trained in the year, which is several times larger and is not in this file. It counts only registered jobseekers placed in AMS-funded courses, so employed adults, apprentices and adults in schools or universities are outside it, and it moves with unemployment and with the AMS budget: in 2021 it reached 70,337 after a 23.2 percent rise during the pandemic job programme. The 2015 comparison is from the 2015 edition of the same report (https://www.ams.at/content/dam/dokumente/berichte/001_uebersicht_jahr2015.pdf). The trainees are excluded from the registered unemployment count, which gives the agency an incentive to place people on courses. The 1994 start is the year the AMS was established as a separate agency, not stated in this file.

pattern.mechanism: The public employment service buys and runs courses for registered jobseekers, from basic skills to vocational qualifications, and pays an allowance while they attend.
preconditions: An unemployment insurance system that pays a training allowance
A purchasing budget and a market of adult education providers
Case workers who can assign jobseekers to courses
pattern.travelled: Most public employment services run this model; Austria keeps the training stock at about a fifth of everyone the AMS counts as unemployed or in training (76,496 of 394,036 in 2025, our division), a high share by European standards.

records.title: COMET, Competence Centers for Excellent Technologies
records.claim: Austria's COMET programme, run by the FFG for the federal ministries and co-funded by the Länder, had approved 81 competence centres and K-projects with eligible costs of 1,669.80 million euros by 30 March 2017, in which about 450 scientific partners and about 1,000 company partners cooperated, according to the Court of Audit.

metric.name: COMET centres and projects approved since programme start (21 K1 centres, 5 K2 centres, 55 K-projects), Table 2

secondMetric.name: Company partners cooperating within COMET (rounded)

source.publisher: Rechnungshof Österreich (Austrian Court of Audit), Bericht 'Forschungsförderungsprogramm COMET: Competence Centers for Excellent Technologies', Reihe BUND 2018/38

records.limits: The figures sit in an 86-page PDF: Table 2 on printed page 33 (PDF page 35) gives the 81 approved centres and projects and 1,669.80 million euros of eligible costs (federal funding 522.06 million, Länder 262.79 million), and the partner counts are on printed page 24 (PDF page 26), both rounded ('rd. 450' and 'rd. 1.000'). The counts are approvals since 2007, not centres running in a given year, and the partner figures count organisations once without saying over what period; the court notes elsewhere about 970 company participations including multiple participations, so 1,000 is not a count of distinct firms. Scientific partners include non-university research bodies, not only universities. The audit period ended in 2016 and the numbers are nine years old; the FFG programme page said on 2026-10-02 that the network currently comprises 23 COMET centres, 17 COMET modules and 15 COMET projects, with no reference date, which supports 'operating' but is not the metric. The court audits spending and compliance, not research output, and it criticised conflicts of interest in centre governance.

pattern.mechanism: Two federal ministries fund, through their research promotion agency, multi-year competence centres in which universities and firms run a joint research programme, with the Länder adding about half the federal share and companies paying roughly 40 to 60 percent of costs.
preconditions: A federal research promotion agency able to run multi-year centre funding and evaluations
Regional governments willing to co-fund centres located in their territory
Firms willing to commit cash to a shared pre-competitive programme for up to eight years
pattern.travelled: COMET succeeded Austria's 1990s Kplus and Kind/Knet competence centre programmes, and sits in the same family as Sweden's competence centres (swe-kompetenscentrum) and Norway's SFI scheme.

records.title: Human Resource Development Authority (HRDA) subsidised training programmes
records.claim: Cyprus's Human Resource Development Authority subsidised more than 106,000 participations in 11,064 single-company and multi-company training programmes in 2024, at a cost of 35.9 million euros, including 68,064 participations of employed persons in standard single-company programmes against 32,987 in 2023.

metric.name: Participations in single-company and multi-company training programmes ('more than 106.000')

secondMetric.name: Participations of employed persons subsidised in standard single-company training programmes

source.publisher: Αρχή Ανάπτυξης Ανθρώπινου Δυναμικού (Human Resource Development Authority of Cyprus), Ετήσια Έκθεση 2024 (Annual Report 2024), bilingual Greek and English

records.limits: The authority reports on its own schemes, in a 185-page PDF: the 106,000 headline is a rounded floor ('more than') in the summary of results on PDF page 16, and the scheme figures are on PDF page 22. The counts are participations, not people: one employee attending three subsidised courses counts three times, many courses last a day or less, and the report gives no count of distinct individuals. The bulk is employer training of people already in work, subsidised from a levy employers pay; the unemployed and adults outside employment are a small part. The doubling of single-company participations from 2023 to 2024 coincides with what the report calls a substantial increase in subsidy amounts and simplified approval, so part of the rise may be employers claiming for training they would have run anyway. The 1979 start is stated in the report's introduction as the year the authority began operating. The URL carries a cache identifier from the authority's portal and may change.

pattern.mechanism: A levy-funded public authority reimburses employers part of the cost of training their staff, in their own firm or through accredited training centres, against a list of priority themes agreed with the social partners.
preconditions: A payroll levy that gives the authority its own income
Accredited private training centres able to run courses across sectors
Social partners on the authority's board who agree the training priorities
pattern.travelled: Levy-grant systems of this kind run in Malaysia, South Africa (zaf-seta-wbl) and Latin America (gtm-intecap, dom-infotep); Cyprus's is among the oldest in Europe and shows the usual sensitivity of claims to the subsidy rate.

records.title: Centra kompetence, the Technology Agency's competence centres programme 2012 to 2019
records.claim: The Technology Agency of the Czech Republic funded 34 competence centres under its Centra kompetence programme from 2012, joining 334 participants, 115 research organisations, 118 SMEs and 101 large firms, against a planned 31 centres and 248 participants.

metric.name: Projects (centres) supported, realised against the programme's planned 31 (Table 2)

secondMetric.name: Supported participants in total (115 research organisations, 118 SMEs, 101 large enterprises), Table 2

source.publisher: Technologická agentura České republiky (TA ČR), Průběžné hodnocení programu Centra kompetence (interim evaluation of the Competence Centres programme)

records.limits: The agency evaluated its own programme, and the figures sit in a 101-page PDF: Tables 1 and 2 on printed pages 23 to 24 (PDF page 25), with parameters updated to 30 June and 15 September 2015 from the agency's IS Patriot and the national R&D information system. The counts are of supported centres and participants at contract signature, not of active collaboration in a given year, and a participant is an organisation, so one university can count several times across centres. The evaluation itself says the main objective of developing cooperation between research organisations and firms proved 'nepříliš dostatečné' (not sufficiently met), with results showing it only in part, and that the reported 25.9 billion koruna of product sales is dominated by one centre and was not verified. Funding received by the centres in 2012 to 2014 was 1.53 billion koruna. The programme ran to 2019 and was followed by Národní centra kompetence; this record does not cover the successor.

pattern.mechanism: The national technology agency funded long-term consortia of research organisations and firms, each at least one research organisation and several companies, to run shared applied research programmes with a minimum private share of costs.
preconditions: A national agency for applied research with its own programme budget
Universities and Academy of Sciences institutes able to lead multi-partner consortia
Industrial firms, including large manufacturers, willing to co-fund for up to eight years
pattern.travelled: The programme copied the competence-centre model used in Austria (aut-comet) and Sweden; its successor, the National Competence Centres, kept the consortium rule.

records.title: Arbejdsmarkedsuddannelser (AMU), adult vocational training courses, and their decline
records.claim: Statistics Denmark counted 386,879 participations in Denmark's state-funded adult vocational training courses (AMU) in 2024, about 7,056 full-time equivalents, down from 1,050,944 participations and 15,307 full-time equivalents in 2010.

metric.name: Participants in labour market educations (AMU), all Denmark, calendar year

secondMetric.name: Same series at its peak year

source.publisher: Danmarks Statistik (Statistics Denmark), StatBank table VEU20 'Participation in supplementary courses', field H39 'Labour market educations, AMU'

records.limits: A participant in this table is a course participation, not a person: AMU courses are typically one to a few days, so one worker taking several courses counts several times, and the full-time equivalent series (7,056 in 2024 against 15,307 in 2010 and 11,278 in 2005) is the better measure of volume. The 2009 and 2010 peak was inflated by the financial crisis, when laid-off and work-sharing workers were sent on courses; against the pre-crisis level of 621,037 participations in 2005 the 2024 count is still about 38 percent lower, so the erosion does not rest on the crisis peak alone, but it is smaller. The 2025 figure in the same table is 218,057, a fall we have not seen explained and which may reflect incomplete registration, so the record stops at 2024. The decline reflects several things the table cannot separate: user fees introduced and raised in the 2010s, cuts to adult education allowances, and changes in course supply. The 1960 start is the founding of the AMU system as commonly reported, not stated in the table.

pattern.mechanism: The state funds short, employer-relevant vocational courses for skilled and unskilled adults, designed by the social partners and delivered by vocational schools and AMU centres, with an allowance paid during the course.
preconditions: Social partners who agree on course content through sector committees
A national network of vocational schools and training centres
Wage compensation or allowances so workers can attend during working hours
pattern.travelled: AMU is the reference model of a social-partner adult training system; Denmark's own trajectory shows that participation follows the price set for users and the allowance, as in fin-adult-education-allowance.

records.title: Erhvervsforsker, the Industrial PhD and Industrial Postdoc programme
records.claim: Denmark's innovation fund (Danmarks Innovationsfond, formerly Innovationsfonden) awarded 138 Industrial Researcher grants in 2025, from 252 applications and for 147.4 million kroner, each funding a researcher employed by a company and enrolled at or supervised by a university.

metric.name: Grants awarded for Industrial Researcher (Industrial PhD and Industrial Postdoc)

secondMetric.name: Amount invested in the programme

source.publisher: Danmarks Innovationsfond (Innovation Fund Denmark), programme page 'Industrial Researcher'

records.limits: The fund reports on its own programme, and the page states only 'All figures are from 2025' with no earlier years, so no trend can be read from it. The page was read through a fetch service; the fund's web firewall refused direct script requests and the annual report PDFs, so the multi-year series could not be checked. A grant is an award at the start of a three-year project, not a completed doctorate, and the count mixes Industrial PhDs with Industrial Postdocs and does not say how many host organisations are public bodies rather than firms. The start year is the commonly cited 1970 founding of the Danish industrial PhD scheme and is not on the cited page. Applications fell to 252 in 2025, and a search snippet gave 140 grants and 149.6 million kroner for 2024, which we could not open at source.

pattern.mechanism: The state pays part of a company's salary cost for a researcher it employs and the university's supervision cost, so that a doctorate or postdoc is carried out on a company problem with joint supervision.
preconditions: Universities willing to supervise doctoral candidates who spend most of their time in a firm
Firms with research capacity able to co-fund a three-year salary
A national fund with an open, recurrent call and a mixed academic and business assessment panel
pattern.travelled: Industrial doctorate schemes elsewhere in the corpus include France's CIFRE (fra-cifre), Spain's Doctorados Industriales (esp-doctorados-industriales) and Poland's Doktorat wdrożeniowy (pol-doktorat-wdrozeniowy); the Danish one is the oldest.

records.title: Vaučeri za obrazovanje, training vouchers of the Croatian Employment Service
records.claim: The Croatian Employment Service enrolled 23,627 people in training paid for by its education vouchers in 2025, 9,786 of them in digital-skills programmes and 2,558 in green-skills programmes, and 53,106 people in total from the scheme's start on 1 April 2022 to the end of 2025.

metric.name: Persons included in the measure 'Obrazovanje za stjecanje kompetencija potrebnih za rad putem vaučera' during the year

secondMetric.name: Users included since the voucher system began (1 April 2022 to end of 2025)

source.publisher: Hrvatski zavod za zapošljavanje (Croatian Employment Service), Godišnjak 2025 (Yearbook 2025)

records.limits: The service reports on its own measure, in an 82-page PDF (printed page 43, PDF page 45). 'Included' means enrolled in a programme, not completed. The yearbook says 54, 13 and 33 percent of users 'completed' digital, green and other programmes; the three shares sum to 100, so they describe the mix of programmes and no completion or employment rate can be read from them. It also splits users into 70 percent 'tražitelji zaposlenja' (jobseekers) and 30 percent unemployed without defining the first group, which presumably holds employed people seeking training or a new job; the share of employed adults is therefore not stated. The vouchers are financed from Croatia's EU Recovery and Resilience Plan (reform C4.1 R3), so the scale depends on money that runs out in 2026, and the yearbook gives no budget beyond that. The 2025 intake is not compared with earlier years in this file.

pattern.mechanism: The public employment service gives unemployed and employed adults a voucher that pays for an accredited short programme chosen from a national catalogue of skills, booked through an online application.
preconditions: A catalogue of accredited providers and programmes tied to a national qualifications framework
A digital application through which adults apply and providers are paid
Temporary EU recovery funding large enough to open vouchers to employed people
pattern.travelled: Voucher and individual learning account schemes in the corpus include France's CPF (fra-cpf), Singapore's SkillsFuture (sgp-skillsfuture) and the Dutch STAP budget (nld-stap-budget), which was abolished; Croatia's is the newest and its continuation after the recovery plan is not yet funded.

records.title: Dottorati innovativi con le imprese (PNRR M4C2 investment 3.3), XXXVIII cycle
records.claim: Italy's Ministry of University and Research funded 1,708 company co-financed innovative doctoral scholarships in the 38th doctoral cycle (academic year 2022/2023), against the 5,000 that decree 352/2022 had allocated for that year, and cut the measure's target from 15,000 scholarships and 450 million euros to 6,000 scholarships and 360 million euros.

metric.name: Scholarships assigned ('Borse assegnate'), XXXVIII cycle, summed over Tabella A of D.D. 1424/2024

secondMetric.name: Scholarships planned for 2022/2023 by D.M. 352 of 9 April 2022 (allocation, not delivery)

source.publisher: Ministero dell'Università e della Ricerca, Decreto Direttoriale n. 1424 del 26 settembre 2024 (rideterminazione, XXXVIII ciclo, ex D.D. 2153/2022), as archived by the Internet Archive

records.limits: The 1,708 is our sum of the 'Borse assegnate' column over 533 rows of Tabella A (PDF pages 3 to 21), which prints no total; it agrees with the decree's Article 2 total of 85,400,000 euros at 50,000 euros a scholarship. mur.gov.it refused script requests, so the cited copy is the Internet Archive's. The 15,000 target, the 450 million euro original allocation and its redetermination to 360 million euros are in the decree's preamble; the 6,000 figure is on the ministry's measure page (archived 13 June 2026, https://web.archive.org/web/20260613095831/https://www.mur.gov.it/it/pnrr/misure-e-componenti/m4c2/investimento-33-introduzione-di-dott-innovativi-che), not in this decree. The 5,000 allocated by decree 352/2022 covered the 2022/2023 year across courses accredited under both the XXXVII and XXXVIII cycle rules; we read all of them as XXXVIII cycle scholarships, which the decree does not state in so many words. A scholarship counts as assigned when funded, not when the doctorate is completed, and firm co-financing is a condition of the measure rather than a separately counted payment. The shortfall against the 5,000 and the cut in the target are a plan that was not met, not a loss from a delivered peak, so the record is not classed as a reversal: it shows that far fewer firms co-funded than the ministry budgeted for, and the decree's response was to raise the ministry's unit contribution from 30,000 to up to 60,000 euros per scholarship (capped at 20,000 euros extra for this cycle), which shifts cost from firms to the state. Later cycles (decree 117/2023) are not counted here, and the measure ended with the recovery plan in 2026.

pattern.mechanism: The ministry offered universities EU recovery money for doctoral scholarships on condition that a company co-financed each one and hosted the candidate, then cut the target and raised the public share when firms took up far fewer places than planned.
preconditions: Universities accredited to run doctoral programmes with industrial partners
Firms with research functions willing to pay half a three-year scholarship
A temporary EU recovery budget large enough to fund thousands of scholarships at once
pattern.travelled: Industrial doctorate schemes funded from regular budgets (dnk-erhvervsforsker, fra-cifre) grew over decades; the Italian attempt to buy thousands in one year ran into the limit of firm demand.

records.title: Inočekiai LT, innovation vouchers for SMEs to buy research services from universities and institutes
records.claim: Lithuania's Agency for Science, Innovation and Technology (MITA) funded 815 innovation-voucher projects in three calls from 2012 to 2014, in which small firms bought applied research, experimental development or feasibility services from universities and research institutes, and 776 of them were completed successfully.

metric.name: Inočekiai LT projects funded across three calls, 2012 to 2014

secondMetric.name: Projects completed successfully

source.publisher: Lietuvos Respublikos ūkio ministerija (Ministry of Economy of Lithuania), final evaluation report 'Ūkio ministerijos priemonės Inočekiai LT poveikio verslo išlaidoms MTEP vertinimo paslaugos', prepared by UAB Visionary Analytics, 6 February 2017, as held in the SIPER evaluation repository

records.limits: The report was commissioned and paid for by the ministry and written by a consultancy, and the copy that opens is held by SIPER, an academic repository of innovation policy evaluations, not by the ministry; the counts themselves come from MITA's activity reports for 2012 to 2015, which the evaluation cites. The figures are on printed page 19 (PDF page 19) of a 112-page PDF, with the call-by-call table (Table 6: 185, 174 and 456 funded applications). Each voucher was small, up to 5,792.4 euros at up to 80 percent public funding, so a project is a short service purchase rather than joint research, and 104 firms were funded in two calls, so 815 projects are fewer distinct firms. The third call relaxed the private contribution and favoured firms with no prior research contact, which raised volume. The vouchers were EU structural fund money and the measure ended with the 2007 to 2013 period; a successor, 'Inovaciniai čekiai', was being prepared for 2014 to 2020 and is not covered here.

pattern.mechanism: The innovation agency gave small firms a fast, small grant that could only be spent on research services from accredited universities and research institutes, to make a first contact between the two cheap and quick.
preconditions: A list of research services that universities and institutes are able and allowed to sell
A simplified application procedure so very small firms can apply
Structural fund money willing to finance many small grants despite the administrative cost
pattern.travelled: Innovation vouchers began in the Netherlands (Limburg, 1998) and spread across Europe; the Lithuanian evaluation found the EU-funded version carried higher administrative costs than the earlier nationally funded pilot of 2010 to 2012.

records.title: Mācības pieaugušajiem, the ESF training programme for employed adults 2017 to 2023
records.claim: Latvia's State Education Development Agency (VIAA) trained almost 77,000 employed adults aged 25 and over through its ESF-funded 'Mācības pieaugušajiem' project between 2017 and 2023, in ten rounds and 2,309 programmes offered by 124 education institutions, with 90 to 100 percent of fees covered.

metric.name: Employed persons aged 25 and over who improved their competence in the project ('teju 77 000', almost 77,000)

secondMetric.name: Education programmes offered in the project

source.publisher: Valsts izglītības attīstības aģentūra (State Education Development Agency of Latvia), project page 'ESF projekts Nodarbināto personu profesionālās kompetences pilnveide', published 4 December 2024

records.limits: The agency reports on its own project, and the headline is a rounded 'almost 77,000' credited to 'project data' with no table behind it; whether it counts people or enrolments is not stated, and an adult who took part in two rounds may be counted twice. The figure covers seven years, roughly 11,000 a year against fewer than a million employed people, and only employed adults aged 25 and over, so the unemployed and young adults are outside it. 'Improved their competence' is the agency's wording; the page does not say how many completed a programme or gained a qualification, beyond 1,909 people compensated for a qualification exam. The project was financed by the European Social Fund and ended in 2023; the agency has since moved to individual learning accounts funded by the EU recovery plan, which this record does not cover.

pattern.mechanism: The national education agency bought places on formal and non-formal programmes from colleges, universities and vocational schools and offered them to employed adults in competitive rounds, with EU money paying almost the whole fee.
preconditions: European Social Fund money large enough to cover 90 to 100 percent of fees
Education institutions willing to adapt programmes for working adults, including distance formats
A national agency able to run open application rounds and pay providers
pattern.travelled: Portugal's Novas Oportunidades (prt-novas-oportunidades) and Croatia's vouchers (hrv-vauceri) are other EU-funded adult training pushes; Latvia's ended with its funding period and was replaced by a different instrument, individual learning accounts.

records.title: Kompetences centri, the industry competence centres programme
records.claim: Latvia's six industry competence centres, funded through the Investment and Development Agency with 53.2 million euros of ERDF money, had run 231 research projects involving 164 companies and 33 scientific partners by 31 December 2014, of which 78 were completed and 44 percent involved cooperation with scientific institutions.

metric.name: Research projects supported in the six competence centres (Table 3, total)

secondMetric.name: Industry partners in the six competence centres (Table 3, total)

source.publisher: Ekonomikas ministrija (Ministry of Economics of Latvia), ex-ante evaluation of SAM 1.2.1.1 'Atbalsts jaunu produktu un tehnoloģiju izstrādei kompetences centru ietvaros', Riga 2015, chapter 2 (evaluation of the 2007 to 2013 programme)

records.limits: The ministry evaluated a programme its own agency ran, and the figures are in a 43-page PDF: the 164 companies, 231 projects and 78 completed are on printed page 10 (PDF page 10) and Table 3 with 33 scientific partners on printed page 10 to 11 (PDF page 11). Most projects were firms' own research: the same evaluation says only 44 percent of projects involved cooperation with private or public scientific institutions, with 24 registered institutions, so the 231 overstates university-firm collaboration, and the 33 scientific partners count partners of the centres, not distinct universities. The programme was suspended from December 2011 to May 2012 and the centres only started full operation in 2013; by the end of 2014 they had drawn 56 percent of their funding and completed 34 percent of projects. Patents (3) and publications (25 against 107 planned) were few. The data are eleven years old. The evaluation states the 2007 to 2013 centre projects were to run until 31 December 2015, so this delivery is concluded; a successor competence centre programme for 2014 to 2020 under the same agency is what this ex-ante evaluation prepares, and this record does not show its scale.

pattern.mechanism: The economics ministry funded industry-led competence centres, companies grouped by sector, which commissioned or ran research projects for their members, partly with universities and institutes, from EU structural funds.
preconditions: EU structural funds large enough to finance a sector-by-sector research programme
Industry associations able to form a centre company and choose projects
A few large public universities able to supply contract research
pattern.travelled: Latvia borrowed the competence-centre label from Austria (aut-comet), which the evaluation cites, but put firms rather than universities at the centre, so most projects ended up as firm research with optional academic input.

records.title: Grunnskoleopplæring for voksne, municipal primary and lower secondary education for adults
records.claim: Norway's municipalities, delivering the statutory right of adults to primary and lower secondary education, taught 10,223 adult participants in 2025, 7,588 in ordinary basic education, 2,435 in special education and 200 in both, against a high of 13,946 in 2019.

metric.name: Number of participants in adult training (primary and lower secondary education and special education for adults), the whole country

secondMetric.name: Same count in the highest year of the series

source.publisher: Statistisk sentralbyrå (Statistics Norway), StatBank table 12237 'Participants in adult training, by region, contents and year' (KOSTRA municipal reporting)

records.limits: The URL is the table's API endpoint; the national row ('EAK The whole country') is returned by a POST query on it, or can be read in the StatBank interface for table 12237. The counts come from municipalities' own KOSTRA reports. They cover only compulsory-level schooling for adults (and special education), a small part of adult learning: upper secondary education for adults, vocational training, study associations and employer training are outside it, and it reaches about 10,000 people in a population of 5.6 million. Most ordinary participants are recent immigrants and refugees completing basic schooling, so the series follows arrivals: the rise to 2019 tracks the 2015 to 2016 refugee intake and the fall since then reflects fewer such learners as much as any change in provision, which is why the record is not classed as an erosion. The 2002 start is the year the adult right to primary and lower secondary education took effect, not stated in the table, and the series itself starts in 2015.

pattern.mechanism: National law gives every adult who lacks it a right to primary and lower secondary education, and the municipality must provide it free, reporting participants to the national municipal statistics system.
preconditions: A statutory individual right that municipalities must honour regardless of budget
Municipal adult education centres, often combined with Norwegian language teaching for immigrants
A common municipal reporting system (KOSTRA) that counts participants the same way everywhere
pattern.travelled: Sweden's Komvux and Estonia's adult gymnasiums (est-adult-gymnasiums) rest on the same idea of a legal right to second-chance schooling; Norway's version is small because few native-born adults lack compulsory schooling.

records.title: Senter for forskningsdrevet innovasjon (SFI), Centres for Research-based Innovation
records.claim: The Research Council of Norway allocated 354 million kroner in 2025 to its Centres for Research-based Innovation, eight-year consortia of research institutions, companies and public bodies whose business and public-sector partners must co-finance at least half the cost, and in December 2025 named eight new centres with 98 business partners and 22 public-sector partners.

metric.name: Funding allocated to the SFI centres

secondMetric.name: Business partners in the eight SFI centres announced in December 2025

source.publisher: Norges forskningsråd (Research Council of Norway), programme page 'Sentre for forskningsdrevet innovasjon (SFI)'

records.limits: The council reports on its own scheme. The 354 million kroner is a funding figure shown as a number block on the programme page, not a count of collaborations, and the page gives no partner count for the centres running in 2025; the same page lists 22 centres under SFI-IV (2020-2028) and 17 under SFI-III (2015-2023), counted by us from the lists. The partner figures come from a separate council news item of 15 December 2025 (https://www.forskningsradet.no/nyheter/2025/nye-forskningssentre-innovasjon/), describe centres that were only being contracted, and the centres also include 16 research institutions, 17 international research partners and 13 foreign companies. Host institutions include research institutes such as SINTEF, not only universities. The 2007 start is from the history of the scheme (first centres appointed 2006, operating 2007) and is not stated on the cited page. Nothing here measures the innovation the centres produced.

pattern.mechanism: The research council funds eight-year centres in which a university or institute and research-active firms run a shared programme, with the council paying up to half and the partners the rest, and renews the portfolio in generations through open competitions.
preconditions: Research-active firms in sectors such as energy, maritime and seafood that can co-fund long programmes
A research council with a stable budget line for long centre grants
Host institutions with the administration to manage multi-partner consortia
pattern.travelled: The SFI model mirrors competence centre schemes in Sweden and Austria (aut-comet); Norway pairs it with Centres of Excellence (SFF) for basic research, keeping the two instruments separate.

records.title: Zručnosti pre trh práce, retraining and training contributions of the labour offices
records.claim: Slovakia's Central Office of Labour, Social Affairs and Family enrolled 17,008 clients in its national project 'Zručnosti pre trh práce' in 2025 and paid training contributions for 16,853 of them, 14.56 million euros in all, with 9,714 registered jobseekers starting retraining courses against 5,904 in 2024.

metric.name: Clients enrolled in the national project Zručnosti pre trh práce

secondMetric.name: Registered jobseekers who started retraining under the project

source.publisher: Ústredie práce, sociálnych vecí a rodiny (Central Office of Labour, Social Affairs and Family), Vyhodnotenie aktívnych opatrení na trhu práce za rok 2025, section 6.4

records.limits: The office evaluates its own project, in a 76-page PDF (printed pages 36 to 37, PDF page 37). The 17,008 mixes three activities, retraining of registered jobseekers, skills for young people not in employment or training, and training of registered job applicants (záujemcovia o zamestnanie), who may be in work, and the client counts are enrolments and payments, not completions; the retraining contributions are paid after a course ends, so some 2025 payments relate to agreements from 2024. The client chooses the course and provider from the open market and the office only reimburses it, so course quality is not controlled by the office. The six-month placement rate the office reports (53.83 percent for retrained jobseekers) is not a measured effect, since there is no comparison group. The project began in April 2024, so the 2024 comparison covers only part of a year; earlier demand-led retraining schemes of the labour offices (known as REPAS+ and KOMPAS+) are not covered in this report and their scale was not checked.

pattern.mechanism: Labour offices let registered jobseekers pick an accredited course and provider themselves, approve a contract, and reimburse the fee and travel costs once the course is completed.
preconditions: A market of accredited adult training providers across regions
Labour offices with case workers able to assess applications individually
EU co-financing to pay course fees in full
pattern.travelled: The demand-led design resembles voucher systems such as hrv-vauceri, with the difference that the Slovak office pays after completion rather than issuing a voucher up front.

records.title: Upper secondary education for adults (srednješolsko izobraževanje odraslih)
records.claim: Slovenia's publicly accredited upper secondary programmes for adults, run by schools and adult education centres, enrolled 17,858 adults in the 2024/25 school year, up from a low of 13,851 in 2020/21 but below the 20,580 enrolled in 2015/16.

metric.name: Adults in upper secondary education, all types of education, both sexes, all ages

secondMetric.name: Same count, first year of the current series

source.publisher: Statistični urad Republike Slovenije (SURS), SiStat table 0953322S 'Adults in upper secondary education by type of education, age and sex, Slovenia, annually'

records.limits: The URL is the table's API endpoint; the national total is returned by a POST query selecting the totals for sex, age and type of education, or can be read in SiStat. The count is enrolment in formal upper secondary programmes leading to a state-recognised qualification, from short vocational to the matura course, so it leaves out the non-formal adult education that makes up most adult learning in Slovenia, and it reaches about 1.5 percent of the working-age population. Enrolment is not completion: SURS publishes adult graduates in a separate table that was not used here. The series restarts in 2015/16 under a new methodology; the old series (table 0953356S) gives 13,327 in 2014/15 and 15,963 in 2011/12, which cannot be joined to the new one without a break. The 2020/21 low coincides with the pandemic. Adult upper secondary education predates 1991; the start year is that of the independent state's school system and is not in the table.

pattern.mechanism: The state accredits upper secondary programmes adapted for adults, delivered part-time by secondary schools and folk high schools (ljudske univerze), so adults can earn the same vocational or general qualification as young people.
preconditions: A national qualification framework that lets adult programmes award the same certificates as youth schooling
A network of folk high schools and school adult units in every region
Public co-funding or employer payment of fees, which adults otherwise bear
pattern.travelled: Poland's licea dla dorosłych (pol-licea-dla-doroslych) and Estonia's adult gymnasiums (est-adult-gymnasiums) are the same instrument; the Slovenian series shows the usual dip in the pandemic and a partial recovery.

records.title: COVID-19-Kurzarbeit, 2020 to 2021
records.claim: Austria's social partners drafted a COVID-19 short-time work model on 13 and 14 March 2020, the AMS adopted its directive on 18 March and the ministers approved it on 19 March, three days after the first lockdown began, and in 2020 113,771 firms with 1.25 million employees used the scheme, against 508 firms in 2009.

metric.name: Employees in firms using COVID-19 short-time work in the year

secondMetric.name: Days from the start of the first lockdown (16 March 2020) to ministerial approval of the AMS directive (19 March 2020)

source.publisher: Rechnungshof Österreich, Bericht des Rechnungshofes: COVID-19-Kurzarbeit (Reihe Bund 2022/7)

records.limits: The figures are in a PDF: the 113,771 firms and 1.25 million employees, the EUR 7.849 billion paid from March 2020 to March 2021 and the EUR 500 million overpayment are in the summary (PDF page 10, repeated in TZ 18); the timeline (social partner talks on 13 and 14 March, the punctation handed to the AMS on 15 March, the AMS board decision on 18 March, ministerial approval on 19 March, retroactive to 1 March) is in TZ 2 (PDF page 21). The three days are our arithmetic from those dates. The audit office is critical, not celebratory: it found that speed came at a cost, with an unsuitable flat-rate method and over-compensation of municipal tax causing overpayments of about EUR 500 million in phase 1, a directive amended twelve times by March 2021, often retroactively, the AMS and the ministry's labour market experts left out of the design, and no concept for targeted detection of abuse. The 1.25 million counts employees in participating firms over the year, not workers on short time at one moment. Austria already had a short-time work instrument, so the move was a redesign of an existing rule, not a new one, and the number of jobs it saved is an estimate the office treats cautiously.

pattern.mechanism: The government let the social partners (the chambers of commerce and labour and the trade unions) write the crisis model over a weekend, the employment service turned their outline into a directive within three days, and parliament adapted the existing short-time work law by initiative motion on 15 and 20 March.
preconditions: A standing short-time work instrument and an employment service that already processed it
Social partners with the authority to agree terms for the whole economy in days
Fiscal room to pay out EUR 6.4 billion in a year
pattern.travelled: The same corporatist route as Germany's Kurzarbeit (deu-kurzarbeit), made faster and more generous; the audit office's verdict is the price of that speed: overpayment and repeated retroactive change.

records.title: Lønkompensation, the 2020 wage compensation scheme
records.claim: Denmark's government, employers and unions agreed a wage compensation scheme on 14 March 2020, the Danish Business Authority opened applications 11 days later on 25 March and decided about 90 percent of applications within 30 days, paying DKK 12.7 billion in the first phase (March to August 2020) on 66,631 applications from 34,042 firms.

metric.name: Days from the tripartite agreement to the opening of applications

secondMetric.name: Wage compensation paid in the first phase

source.publisher: Rigsrevisionen, Beretning 6/2021 om Erhvervsministeriets forvaltning af hjælpepakker under COVID-19

records.limits: The figures are in a PDF: the 14 March agreement and the 25 March opening on printed page 7 (PDF page 14), Table 1 with applications, firms and payments on PDF page 11, and the 90 percent decided within 30 days on page 4 (PDF page 10). The audit office states that the ministry normally needs several months to set up such a scheme; the comparison is the ministry's own claim. Speed was bought with deferred control: the office found that control relied mainly on an after-control that had not yet been carried out, had been postponed by about 11 months to as much as a year and a half after payment, and had no earlier check of the riskiest cases, so some firms may have received compensation they were not entitled to and that cannot be recovered (Statsrevisorernes bemaerkning, PDF pages 3 to 4). The scheme was later extended into four phases, with DKK 19.4 billion paid by October 2021; the claim covers the first phase only. The record counts firms and applications, not employees: the office's report gives no count of workers covered.

pattern.mechanism: The government agreed the scheme with the employers' and workers' organisations in one tripartite deal, and the Danish Business Authority built the application system on existing case systems and public register data, with automatic checks deciding low-risk cases at once and a later control for the rest.
preconditions: Tripartite bargaining that can reach a national deal in a weekend
Register data on firms and employees that can check applications automatically
Parliamentary approval of spending by account (aktstykke) instead of a new law
pattern.travelled: The Netherlands' NOW scheme and Austria's Kurzarbeit (aut-corona-kurzarbeit) took similar weeks; what Denmark adds is an audit of the trade-off, which shows the after-control lagging the payments by more than a year.

records.title: Chômage temporaire corona, 2020
records.claim: Belgium's National Employment Office treated every COVID-19 work stoppage as temporary unemployment for force majeure and paid allowances to 939,532 workers for March 2020 and 1,117,133 for April, when 1,221,412 workers, 35.3 percent of private and contractual employees, were declared temporarily unemployed; almost 1.4 million received at least one payment during 2020.

metric.name: Workers paid a temporary unemployment allowance for April 2020

secondMetric.name: Workers paid a temporary unemployment allowance for March 2020

source.publisher: Office national de l'emploi (ONEM), Chômage temporaire en chiffres (press page, May 2020); annual report figures in Rapport annuel ONEM 2020

records.limits: The monthly counts and the 35.3 percent share are on the ONEM press page; the 1.4 million for 2020 and the monthly average of 504,657 are on the annual report page (https://www.onem.be/espace-presse/rapport-annuel-onem-2020). The press page gives no date for the rule change itself, so the record shows speed only as payment for the first month of the crisis, not as days from shock to rule. ONEM does not pay most allowances itself: the payment bodies (the trade union funds CSC, FGTB and CGSLB, and the public fund CAPAC) do, and the press page splits the amounts between them. The 35.3 percent is computed on 3,458,136 salaried employees excluding civil servants. A worker counted in April was unemployed for 14 days on average, and only 20 percent for the whole month, so the head count overstates lost hours. The cost was large: ONEM's annual report records EUR 4.042 billion of extra temporary unemployment spending in 2020. ONEM later ran controls on corona temporary unemployment; their results are not reflected here.

pattern.mechanism: The employment office widened an existing rule, temporary unemployment for force majeure, to cover every corona stoppage and simplified the employer procedure, so firms could suspend contracts without proving economic grounds and existing payment bodies paid workers within the month.
preconditions: A standing temporary unemployment regime with electronic social risk declarations from employers
Payment bodies, including trade union funds, already paying unemployment benefits
A legal concept (force majeure) broad enough to be reinterpreted by the administration
pattern.travelled: France's activité partielle (fra-activite-partielle) followed the same route of stretching an industrial instrument to the whole economy; Belgium's version paid workers directly rather than reimbursing employers.

records.title: Cassa integrazione con causale Covid-19, 2020
records.claim: Italy's Cura Italia decree of 17 March 2020 created wage supplementation with a Covid-19 cause across ordinary CIG, the solidarity funds and CIG in deroga, and INPS recorded 5.27 million beneficiaries in April 2020 and 2.8 billion authorised hours from March to August, but about 83 percent of firms asked INPS to pay workers directly and the institute's own report records the resulting delay in payments for the first period.

metric.name: Beneficiaries of wage supplementation with Covid-19 cause in the month

secondMetric.name: Hours authorised with Covid-19 cause, March to August 2020

source.publisher: INPS, XIX Rapporto annuale (October 2020)

records.limits: The figures are in a 482-page PDF: the monthly beneficiary counts are Tavola 1.7 (PDF pages 43 to 44, in thousands: 4,240 in March, 5,274 in April across ordinary CIG, solidarity funds and CIG in deroga), the 2.8 billion hours on PDF page 16 and again on page 33, and the direct-payment share and the delay in footnote 12 (PDF page 40). The institute reports on its own delivery. Speed is mixed: the rule changed within days of the lockdown, but the decree let any firm request direct payment by INPS without proof of financial difficulty, about 83 percent did, and the report says this produced a delay in payments, especially for the first period requested; it gives no figure for the delay. Authorised hours are not hours used: the report estimates take-up at 63 percent for March and 60 percent for April. The report itself judges the solidarity funds that covered smaller firms evidently inadequate, and the CIG in deroga ran through the regions, which added a step before payment.

pattern.mechanism: The government extended the existing wage supplementation funds to a Covid-19 cause by decree, covered firms outside the ordinary funds through the solidarity funds and the regional CIG in deroga, and let firms shift payment to INPS, which then had to authorise and pay an unprecedented volume at once.
preconditions: Standing wage supplementation funds with an authorising and paying institute
Decree-law powers that take effect on publication
Payment capacity at the paying institute, which is the precondition that strained here
pattern.travelled: Belgium (bel-chomage-temporaire-corona) also paid workers directly through existing bodies and paid within the month; Italy's direct-payment option moved the cash-flow burden from firms to INPS and slowed the first payments.

records.title: MitID, the digital identity built by the state and the banks
records.claim: Denmark's Agency for Digital Government, representing the state, regions and municipalities, and the banks, through a Finance Denmark subsidiary, jointly own MitID, launched in May 2021 to replace NemID and migrated in 2021 and 2022; by July 2026, 97.2 percent of residents over 15 had an active MitID, and it averaged 94.4 million transactions a month in 2025.

metric.name: Share of the population over 15 with an active MitID

secondMetric.name: MitID transactions per month, average for 2025

source.publisher: Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, MitID statistik (mitid.dk); partnership terms on digst.dk, Om MitID

records.limits: The page is run by the partnership the record describes, so this is the owner grading its own system; it says the figures were updated in July 2026 and the 94.4 million is labelled an average for 2025, while the 97.2 percent and the 5.3 million registered users carry no separate date. The page refused WebFetch with HTTP 403 and was read with a browser user agent. The partnership terms (established in 2016 after a tender, the state represented by the agency, the banks by an FR I subsidiary of Finance Denmark, the partnership owning the rights to the solution, name and logo) and the timeline (go-live May 2021, migration through 2021 and 2022) are on https://digst.dk/it-loesninger/mitid/om-mitid/. The build and operation were contracted to one private supplier, Nets DANID, for DKK 939 million plus ten years of operation, so the private side is both the banks as co-owners and a vendor. Near-universal coverage follows from mandatory digital post and bank login in Denmark, not only from the partnership's design, and the share says nothing about people who cannot use the app; the minister sent parliament a project evaluation in September 2024 (ft.dk, DIU Alm.del bilag 3), which this record has not read.

pattern.mechanism: The state and the banks tendered and co-own one identity solution that works for both online banking and public services, contracted one supplier to build and run it, and moved about five million users off the previous shared solution, NemID.
preconditions: A previous shared public and bank identity (NemID) that had already made one login normal
A banking sector organised to act through one industry body
Mandatory digital communication with the state, which drives near-universal take-up
pattern.travelled: Sweden's BankID (swe-bankid) is bank-owned with state acceptance, the Netherlands' DigiD is state-only; MitID is the case where the two sides share ownership of the same credential.

records.title: SPID, the public digital identity issued by accredited private providers
records.claim: Italy's Agency for Digital Italy runs SPID, the public digital identity system in which accredited identity providers, private firms such as Aruba, InfoCert, Namirial and Register alongside state-controlled Poste Italiane and public companies such as Lepida and InfoCamere, issue the credentials under agreements with the agency, and by 8 October 2025 41 million SPID identities had been issued, when the agency extended the providers' agreements to 2027.

metric.name: SPID digital identities issued

secondMetric.name: Electronic identity cards (CIE) issued, the state-only alternative (of which 9 million CIE credentials activated)

source.publisher: Agenzia per l'Italia Digitale (AgID), SPID, rinnovate le convenzioni con gli Identity Provider fino al 2027 (news, 8 October 2025)

records.limits: The 41 million is a rounded figure in a news item, not a statistics series, and counts identities issued, not active users; one person can hold SPID from more than one provider, so the count overstates people. The mix of providers is read from the agency's list of accredited identity providers (https://www.agid.gov.it/it/piattaforme/spid/identity-provider-accreditati), which shows the first accreditations in December 2015, the first agreements in February 2016, an additional act signed with each active provider on 8 October 2025, and one provider (In.Te.S.A.) that ceased in April 2023; the agency publishes no split of identities by provider, so the private share of issuance is not known, and the largest provider, Poste Italiane, is state-controlled. The future of the partnership is uncertain: the news item frames the extension as accompanying a transition toward a single national identity built on the state-issued CIE and the IT Wallet. If the government moves logins to CIE the partnership will shrink; this record does not count that as erosion because the item reports no loss yet. The item gives no transaction figure, so the record shows reach, not use. The 55 million CIE in the second metric are cards issued; the same item says only 9 million CIE digital credentials had been activated, so the two counts in the item's 96 million total are not like for like.

pattern.mechanism: The digital agency set technical rules and signed agreements with accredited identity providers, who verify citizens and issue credentials that every public administration must accept, so private firms carried the cost of enrolment while the state set the standard.
preconditions: Firms and public companies with existing identity verification channels (post offices, trust service providers, chambers of commerce)
A legal mandate obliging public administrations to accept the credential
A fee model or public payment that keeps providers in the scheme, which is what the 2025 renewal negotiated
pattern.travelled: Sweden's BankID (swe-bankid) and Denmark's MitID (dnk-mitid) put banks at the centre; SPID spread issuance across many accredited providers, and Italy is now weighing a return to the state card.

records.title: D4 Příbram to Písek motorway, the first Czech transport PPP
