records.claim: The Czech Ministry of Transport procured the completion of the D4 motorway between Příbram and Písek as the country's first transport public-private partnership, and the concessionaire Via Salis opened 32 km of new motorway and 16 km of modernised sections on 17 December 2024 after 43 months of construction, as the ministry had announced in June 2021, with the state paying an availability payment until 2049.

metric.name: New motorway built and opened under the PPP

secondMetric.name: Availability payment approved by the Chamber of Deputies, against the audit office's inflation-adjusted estimate of about CZK 33.7 billion

source.publisher: Ministerstvo dopravy ČR, Dálnice D4 se otevřela řidičům, první dopravní PPP projekt zrychlí cestu na jih (press release, 17 December 2024)

records.limits: The opening, the kilometres and the 43 months are the ministry's own press release; the planned December 2024 opening is in the ministry's release of 9 June 2021 as listed on its D4 tag page, so on-time delivery is the ministry's claim checked against its own earlier announcement. The cost figures come from the Supreme Audit Office (NKÚ, audit 22/29, press release of 11 December 2023, https://www.nku.cz/cz/pro-media/tiskove-zpravy/nku-upozornuje:-vystavba-dalnice-d4-formou-projektu-ppp-mozna-pro-stat-nebude-tak-vyhodna--jak-se-predpoklada-id13640/), which warned that the value-for-money case rested mainly on the adviser's foreign experience because the ministry could not state its own maintenance costs for the 1,276 km of motorway it ran, and that with inflation the state's availability payment would be about CZK 4.2 billion above the CZK 29.5 billion approved. One project is not a programme: the record shows that the Czech state can close and deliver a PPP, not that it does so often. The concessionaire is French-owned (VINCI Highways and Meridiam), and the construction was done by VINCI's Czech subsidiary.

pattern.mechanism: The ministry tendered a design, build, finance, operate and maintain concession for one motorway corridor, the concessionaire took over the existing sections in 2021 and built the gap, and the state pays monthly only once the road is open, with deductions when availability or quality falls short.
preconditions: Parliamentary approval of a multi-decade availability payment as a quasi-mandatory expenditure
Advisers able to structure the first deal in a country with no PPP track record
A corridor already permitted by the roads directorate, which spent CZK 364 million preparing it
pattern.travelled: Latvia's Ķekava bypass (lva-kekava-ppp) and Slovakia's D4/R7 (svk-d4r7-ppp) used the same availability-payment model in the region; the Czech audit office's warning about missing domestic cost data is the lesson most likely to recur.

records.title: Ķekava bypass, the first major road PPP in the Baltic states
records.claim: Latvia's Ministry of Transport and the state roads company signed a design, build, finance and maintain contract for the Ķekava bypass on the A7 on 16 July 2021, the private partner Kekava ABT built the roughly 18 km road from 2021 to 2023 and it opened on 13 October 2023, with the state paying EUR 250.13 million in availability payments over 20 years.

metric.name: Total availability payments over the 20-year maintenance period

secondMetric.name: Months from contract signature (16 July 2021) to opening (13 October 2023)

source.publisher: Centrālā finanšu un līgumu aģentūra (CFLA), Atklāj vērienīgāko PPP ceļu projektu Baltijā: Ķekavas apvedceļu (news, October 2023)

records.limits: CFLA supervises PPP projects in Latvia and is part of the delivery it reports, so this is the supervisor's announcement on opening day, not an audit. The 27 months are our arithmetic from the two dates on the page; the page gives no planned opening date, so it does not show whether the road opened on schedule, and it gives no construction cost separate from the availability payments. The same page says the state roads company had to obtain several Eurostat opinions to keep the project off the government balance sheet, and that CFLA is working to remove that step: the procedure was slow before construction began. One project is not a programme; the page calls it the first large road PPP in the Baltic states, which also means Latvia has no record of repeating it. Representatives of the Nordic Investment Bank and the European Investment Bank took part in the opening; the page does not describe the financing.

pattern.mechanism: The transport ministry and the state roads company procured a bypass as one design, build, finance and maintain contract, the private partner built it in about two years, and the state pays quarterly for 20 years once the road is available.
preconditions: A PPP law and a supervising agency (CFLA) to run procurement
Eurostat clearance that the project sits off the public balance sheet
Lenders willing to finance a first-of-kind deal in a small market
pattern.travelled: The Czech D4 (cze-d4-ppp) followed the same availability model at larger scale; Lithuania's PPP portfolio (ltu-vpsp) shows the municipal route the Baltic states use more often.

records.title: Public-private partnership contracts monitored by CPVA
records.claim: Lithuania's state and municipal institutions had concluded 76 public-private partnership contracts by 31 December 2025, 49 of them in force at the end of 2025 across culture and sport, waste, energy, law enforcement, education, transport and defence, with only one new contract signed in 2025.

metric.name: PPP contracts concluded, cumulative

secondMetric.name: PPP contracts in force

source.publisher: Centrinė projektų valdymo agentūra (CPVA), PPP Lietuva, Viešojo ir privataus sektorių partnerystė Lietuvoje: 2025 m. rezultatai ir 2026 m. projektų planai

records.limits: CPVA compiled the figures from data submitted by state and municipal institutions; it is the national PPP centre, not an auditor, and the underlying annual report is linked from the page but was not opened. Most contracts are municipal (24 municipalities in 2025), so the count mixes national objectives such as defence and law enforcement, where the public sector made its largest payments in 2025 (EUR 32.5 million and EUR 10.3 million), with local sports halls and street lighting. A contract count says nothing about value for money; the National Audit Office has published a critical audit of PPP project management (valstybeskontrole.lt), which this record has not read. The gap between 76 concluded and 49 in force is not explained on the page (expiry, termination or both). The pace is slow: one contract in 2025, and 18 projects planned for 2026 that are still in preparation. The start year 2009 is the year of the finance minister's reporting rules (order 1K-489 of 24 December 2009) cited on CPVA's statistics page, not a documented first contract.

pattern.mechanism: A central agency advises and monitors, and individual ministries and municipalities procure PPP contracts for buildings, lighting, waste and defence facilities, reporting each year so the agency can publish a national portfolio.
preconditions: A PPP law with a central agency that collects data from every contracting authority
Municipal borrowing limits that make off-budget delivery attractive
Eurostat treatment of the contracts, which decides whether they count against the deficit
pattern.travelled: Latvia's single large road deal (lva-kekava-ppp) is the alternative model; Lithuania now plans larger transport PPPs (a regional road and bypasses worth EUR 20 to 250 million) on top of its many small municipal ones.

records.title: D4/R7 Bratislava bypass PPP
records.claim: Slovakia built the D4 motorway and R7 expressway around Bratislava, 59.0 km at EUR 1,670 million, as a public-private partnership between 2016 and 2021, the only PPP among the major road projects the Supreme Audit Office listed in its 2025 audit of road investment.

metric.name: Length of the D4/R7 PPP project

secondMetric.name: Cost of the D4/R7 PPP project as listed by the audit office

source.publisher: Najvyšší kontrolný úrad Slovenskej republiky (NKÚ SR), Správa o výsledku kontroly: Investičné projekty v cestnej doprave (2025)

records.limits: The figures are one row of a table on printed page 12 of the audit office's PDF, which lists the period 2016 to 2021, 59.0 km, EUR 1,670.00 million and 'PPP' as the funding source; the audit is about road investment generally and does not evaluate the PPP itself, its cost against a public alternative or its schedule against plan. The table gives no definition of the cost (construction cost, capital value or total availability payments), so the EUR 1,670 million cannot be compared with the other rows without that caveat. The opening dates of the sections are not on this page; 2021 is the end of the period the table gives. The same table shows every other major road project financed from EU or state funds, so the record documents one delivered PPP, not a programme, and this source says nothing about Slovakia's earlier PPP attempts.

pattern.mechanism: The transport ministry procured the Bratislava bypass as one availability-payment concession covering design, construction, financing and decades of operation, so a single private partner delivered 59 km at once rather than in budget-limited sections.
preconditions: A ministry able to procure and supervise a EUR 1.7 billion concession
International lenders and sponsors willing to finance it
Budget room for decades of availability payments
pattern.travelled: The Czech D4 (cze-d4-ppp) and Latvia's Ķekava bypass (lva-kekava-ppp) used the same model later and at smaller scale.

records.title: OPS road projects of the Norwegian Public Roads Administration
records.claim: The Norwegian Public Roads Administration has delivered four road sections as public-private partnerships (OPS) now in operation, opened in 2005, 2006, 2009 and July 2020, each run by a private company for 20 to 25 years, and had two more under planning or construction in 2026, Rv. 555 Sotrasambandet and E10/Rv. 85 Tjeldsund to Langvassbukt.

metric.name: OPS road projects completed and in operation

secondMetric.name: OPS road projects in planning or under construction

source.publisher: Statens vegvesen, Våre OPS-prosjekter

records.limits: The page is the roads administration's own list with no date of update, so the asOf is the retrieval date. It gives no cost, schedule or value-for-money figure, so the record shows frequency and duration, not performance. Six projects in two decades is a small programme for a country that builds many roads, and it moved in fits: three sections opened between 2005 and 2009, then nothing opened until 2020, after the transport ministry asked the agency in 2015 to use the model on three new projects (stated on the agency's OPS page, https://www.vegvesen.no/vegprosjekter/prosess/ops-ppp/); the list does not say what became of each of those three. The page says parliament decides which projects use OPS, so the count reflects political choices project by project. Projects by Nye Veier, the state road company, are not on this list.

pattern.mechanism: Parliament designates a road section for OPS, the roads administration tenders it, and a private company plans, builds, finances, operates and maintains the section for 20 to 25 years against state payments, after which it returns to the state.
preconditions: A parliament willing to commit payments decades ahead project by project
Domestic contractors and financiers able to take on whole-life road risk
A roads agency that can write performance requirements instead of designs
pattern.travelled: Sweden's Trafikverket is studying OPS projects for its 2026 to 2037 plan; Norway's experience shows a model that survives but stays a small share of road building.

records.title: Antivirus job retention programme, 2020 to 2022
records.claim: The Czech government approved the Antivirus employment support programme on 31 March 2020, with costs eligible from 12 March, and the Labour Office paid CZK 51.2 billion through it from 2020 to 2022 to almost 71,000 employers for 1.2 million employees.

metric.name: Antivirus contributions paid, 2020 to 2022

secondMetric.name: Days from the start of eligible costs (12 March 2020) to the government resolution approving the programme (31 March 2020)

source.publisher: Nejvyšší kontrolní úrad (NKÚ), Kontrolní závěr z kontrolní akce 22/28 and press release of 4 December 2023

records.limits: The figures are in the audit office's PDF (CZK 51.2 billion and 70,971 employers in the summary table on PDF page 2; the government resolution No. 353 of 31 March 2020 and the eligibility period from 12 March 2020 in Table 1 on PDF page 7) and in its press release of 4 December 2023 (https://www.nku.cz/cz/pro-media/tiskove-zpravy/miliardy-na-udrzeni-pracovnich-mist-v-dobe-covidu-19-dostaly-od-statu-i-firmy--kterym-rostl-zisk-a-pocet-zamestnancu-id13610/), which gives almost 71,000 firms and 1.2 million employees. The audit office's verdict is negative: part of the money was spent ineffectively, CZK 9.8 billion went to industries where output did not fall, the A Plus regime paid 100 percent of wage compensation against the principle of cost sharing used elsewhere in the EU (CZK 4.4 billion could have been saved), ten of 31 audited firms drew CZK 1.9 billion while paying dividends, and the ministry and Labour Office did not monitor or evaluate the programme's effects. The 19 days from the eligibility date to the government decision are our arithmetic and are the second metric; the 1.2 million employees covered are in the press release only; the record does not show when the first payments arrived. The rule change was speedy; whether it was well targeted is what the audit disputes.

pattern.mechanism: The government used an existing power in the Employment Act to declare a targeted programme by resolution, so the Labour Office could reimburse employers for wage compensation paid to workers in quarantine or kept idle, backdated to the start of the emergency.
preconditions: A statutory power to create targeted employment programmes by government resolution
A Labour Office able to sign agreements with tens of thousands of employers
Labour law that already obliged employers to pay wage compensation during obstacles to work
pattern.travelled: Slovakia's First Aid (svk-prva-pomoc) was approved the same day; the Czech audit shows the cost of a rule written for speed with no sharing of the burden and no impact monitoring.

records.title: Prvá pomoc (First Aid) job retention scheme, 2020 to 2022
records.claim: Slovakia's government approved the labour ministry's job retention scheme on 31 March 2020, labour offices began accepting applications on 6 April with support backdated to 13 March, and over two years the scheme paid almost EUR 2.5 billion to 176,000 employers and self-employed people, 5.7 million monthly payments covering more than 770,000 employees.

metric.name: Days from government approval to the first applications

secondMetric.name: First Aid support paid over the life of the scheme (almost)

source.publisher: Ministerstvo práce, sociálnych vecí a rodiny SR, Prvá pomoc (pomahameludom.sk), closing summary

records.limits: The page is the labour ministry's own scheme site and its closing summary is promotional: it quotes the minister calling the ministry the most successful state body at delivering aid, and cites a supportive analysis by the ministry's own Institute of Social Policy. The figures are rounded ('almost 2.5 billion', 'more than 770 thousand') and the page has no publication date; the eligible period it states runs from 13 March 2020 to 28 February 2022. The six days are our arithmetic from the two dates on the page; the record does not show how long the first payments took after applications opened, and this record has not read any audit of the scheme. Employees counted are those in supported firms, not jobs shown to have been saved, and nearly half of the money went to micro-enterprises, per the institute's director quoted on the page.

pattern.mechanism: The labour ministry designed a state aid scheme paid through the network of labour offices, with separate measures for closed businesses, firms with falling revenue and the self-employed, and the government approved it so offices could take applications within a week.
preconditions: Labour offices that already contracted with employers for active labour market measures
European Social Fund money that could be reallocated to the scheme
EU state aid temporary framework rules allowing wage subsidies
pattern.travelled: The Czech Antivirus (cze-antivirus) was approved the same day with a similar design; both were later criticised for poor targeting.

records.title: Potpore za očuvanje radnih mjesta (job preservation grants), 2020
records.claim: The governing board of the Croatian Employment Service decided on 20 March 2020 to introduce job preservation grants for employers hit by COVID-19, the service began implementing them on 23 March, taking applications online, and in 2020 it paid HRK 7.70 billion to 109,431 employers covering 697,126 workers on 225,390 applications.

metric.name: Workers covered by job preservation grants in the year

secondMetric.name: Days from the board decision (20 March 2020) to the start of implementation (23 March 2020)

source.publisher: Hrvatski zavod za zapošljavanje (HZZ), Godišnjak 2020

records.limits: The employment service reports on its own measure. The figures are in a PDF: the 20 March decision on PDF page 9 and again on page 41, the 109,431 employers, 697,126 workers and HRK 7,703,685,673 on PDF page 10 and page 41, the 23 March start and the 225,390 applications on page 41. The three days are our arithmetic. The yearbook counts workers covered at any point in 2020, and the same employer could apply repeatedly, so workers are not a monthly peak. To run the grants the service suspended part of its regular active labour market programmes from March to May 2020, which the yearbook states; the record does not show how many jobs the grants preserved or whether any money went to firms that would have kept their staff anyway.

pattern.mechanism: The employment service's governing board created a flat per-worker grant by decision, took applications online through a dedicated site, and paid employers monthly for March to May, then extended and adjusted the grant through the year as restrictions continued.
preconditions: An employment service whose board can create a measure without new legislation
An online application channel built in days
European Social Fund and state budget money that could be redirected
pattern.travelled: Croatia reused the same instrument for later shocks: in 2026 the service ran a job preservation grant for employers hit by wildfires in Omiš and Brač (mjere.hr).

records.title: Public-private partnership contracts in Croatia's PPP register, and their dwindling
records.claim: Croatia's register of public-private partnership contracts lists 17 contracts with an estimated capital value of EUR 338.3 million, 13 of them signed between 2006 and 2008, mostly Varaždin county schools, one in 2013 for Zagreb Airport, one in 2016 and two street lighting contracts in 2018, and none since October 2018.

metric.name: PPP contracts entered in the register with a signature date after October 2018

secondMetric.name: PPP contracts signed 2006 to 2008, the peak

source.publisher: Ministarstvo gospodarstva, Registar ugovora javno-privatnog partnerstva (Invest Croatia)

records.limits: The counts are ours: the register page lists 17 contracts and a total of EUR 338,260,027, and the signature dates are on each contract's own page under /jpp-project/ (for example Zagreb Airport, 2 December 2013; Novi Vinodolski street lighting, 25 October 2018, the latest), which we opened one by one and tallied. The register holds only contracts entered under the PPP framework; concessions under the separate concessions law, such as motorways, are not in it, so the record does not show that private participation in Croatian infrastructure stopped, only that the PPP model did. The ministry's project list (https://investcroatia.gov.hr/jpp/projekti/) also shows approved projects not yet contracted, such as Trg pravde in Zagreb (EUR 179.2 million) and county schools, so the pipeline is not empty. The peak itself was narrow: ten of the 13 early contracts are in Varazdin (eight school extensions, the county building and a sports hall). Zagreb Airport alone is EUR 188.6 million, more than half the register's value. The register page has no date of update, so the zero is as of retrieval.

pattern.mechanism: Counties and cities signed design, build, finance and maintain contracts for schools, halls and a bus station in a burst before the 2008 crisis, the state concessioned the Zagreb Airport terminal in 2013, and then PPP contracting all but stopped while responsibility for PPP passed to the economy ministry.
preconditions: A PPP law and a ministry able to approve projects quickly
Local governments with the capacity to prepare PPP tenders, which only a few had
Eurostat treatment that keeps contracts off the deficit, whose tightening after 2008 made the model less attractive
pattern.travelled: Lithuania (ltu-vpsp) kept a steady flow of small municipal PPPs with a central agency's support; Croatia's register shows what happens without that pipeline.

records.title: Greece's PPP programme under the 2005 PPP law
records.claim: Greece's Inter-Ministerial PPP Committee and the finance ministry's PPP Unit have taken 33 public-private partnerships to signed contracts since 2006, from Attica school buildings and fire stations to waste plants, the Kalamata to Rizomylos and Crete northern road sections and ultrafast broadband, with another 34 projects listed in procurement or preparation in 2026.

metric.name: PPP contracts signed since 2006

secondMetric.name: Projects in the PPP Unit's list still in preparation or procurement

source.publisher: Ministry of Economy and Finance, Public Private Partnerships Unit (pppunit.minfin.gov.gr), home page and project list

records.limits: The home page states 33 signed PPP contracts and 34 approved PPP projects since 2006, without a date of update. We read the 67 project pages in the unit's list (https://pppunit.minfin.gov.gr/en/sdit/erga, seven pages) and tallied their status fields ourselves: 33 'Contract signed', 13 in competitive dialogue, 13 at request for proposals, 6 at expression of interest and 2 approved and in preparation, so the 34 in the second metric is our count. The list counts the ultrafast broadband programme as seven lots, each showing the programme's EUR 868 million cost, so a sum of project costs would be wrong and the record gives none. 'Contract signed' is the unit's last populated status; no project is marked completed, so the list does not say how many assets are in operation or whether they came in on time and budget, and several roads and waste plants took three to ten years from committee approval to signature (for example the Peloponnese waste system, approved December 2011, signed June 2018, and the Nafplio marina, approved November 2013, signed April 2023). The unit is part of the ministry that runs the programme, and its home page cites a World Bank ranking as an endorsement; the ranking is not the evidence here. 2006 is the first committee approval in the list (Attica schools, April 2006).

pattern.mechanism: A 2005 law set up an inter-ministerial committee that approves which projects may be procured as PPPs and a central unit in the finance ministry that prepares and tenders them for ministries, regions and municipalities, mostly as availability-payment contracts.
preconditions: A central PPP unit with its own procurement expertise, co-financed by EU funds
Committee approval at ministerial level, which gives projects political cover
EU structural and recovery funds that can co-finance availability payments
pattern.travelled: The same centre-led model as Lithuania's CPVA (ltu-vpsp) at larger scale; Croatia (hrv-jpp-registar) had a similar law but no comparable pipeline after 2008.

records.title: De Kade prison in Antwerp, a federal DBFM contract
records.claim: Belgium's federal Buildings Agency had the new 440-place prison de Kade in Antwerp, part of the federal prisons masterplan, designed, built and financed by the consortium Hortus Conclusus under a DBFM contract, with works from 2023 to 2026 at a construction cost of EUR 195.5 million and an annual availability fee of EUR 23.1 million for 25 years of maintenance, after which the prison returns to the federal state free of charge.

metric.name: Construction cost of the DBFM prison, excluding VAT

secondMetric.name: Annual availability fee, including VAT, 2023 prices

source.publisher: Régie des Bâtiments / Regie der Gebouwen, Nouvelle prison « de Kade » (project page, updated September 2025)

records.limits: The page is the contracting agency's own project sheet. It says the prison 'a été réalisée' under a DBFM contract and that Antwerp 'now has two prisons', but it states the works period as 2023 to 2026 and gives no opening date or planned date, so the record cannot show whether the prison opened on time or on budget; status operating rests on the page's own past tense, updated September 2025. The construction cost and the availability fee are the agency's figures, not an audit; 25 years of fees at EUR 23.1 million in 2023 prices would be about EUR 578 million before indexation (our arithmetic), well above the construction cost, which is the normal shape of a DBFM but means the cost to the state is the fee stream, not the build cost. One project is not a programme: the page places the prison in the federal masterplan for detention and internment, but this record documents only this contract and says nothing about the masterplan's other projects. The consortium's members are named on the page (TINC, Jan De Nul, EEG, with ISS for services).

pattern.mechanism: The federal Buildings Agency tendered a design, build, finance and maintain contract for a new prison, a consortium of an infrastructure investor and contractors built and financed it, and the state pays an annual availability fee for 25 years while the Justice ministry runs the prison.
preconditions: A federal prisons masterplan with a pipeline of projects to justify the procurement effort
Legal and financial advisers for the agency (here a consortium led by Stibbe)
Domestic contractors and investors able to carry construction and 25-year maintenance risk
pattern.travelled: The same availability-payment structure as the Czech D4 (cze-d4-ppp), applied to social infrastructure instead of a road.

records.title: Šoštanj thermal power plant unit 6 (TEŠ 6), and its cost overrun
records.claim: Slovenia's state-owned power holding HSE and its subsidiary TEŠ raised the estimated cost of the 600 MW Šoštanj unit 6 from 1,302,747 thousand euros in the August 2011 investment programme, the ceiling written into the 2012 law guaranteeing its 440 million euro EIB loan, to 1,428,457 thousand euros in the February 2014 programme, breaching the condition on which the state guarantee was given, according to the Court of Audit.

metric.name: Estimated investment value of unit 6, revised investment programme no. 6 (NIP 6)

secondMetric.name: Estimated investment value in revised investment programme no. 4 (NIP 4), the ceiling set as a condition of the state guarantee

source.publisher: Računsko sodišče Republike Slovenije (Court of Audit of the Republic of Slovenia), post-audit report 'Popravljalni ukrepi pri reviziji obvladovanja denarnih tokov skupine HSE zaradi investicije v blok 6', no. 321-1/2014/70, 7 January 2016

records.limits: Both figures are in a PDF, on PDF page 9 of the post-audit report, which restates finding 2.1.2 of the main audit report of 19 August 2015 (no. 321-1/2014/49). The main report itself is published with the investment values redacted as business secrets (marked (P)) in its OCR copy, so the post-audit report is the readable source. The comparison is between two revisions of the investment programme, not between the first approved estimate and the final outturn: the record does not show the earlier, much lower estimates of the original 2006 to 2008 investment documents, which this protocol did not read at an official source, and so understates the full growth. NIP 6 is an estimate made while the unit was being built, not a final account. The court's main finding concerns HSE's management of the group's cash flows, and it also found the assumed coal cost (2.25 euros per GJ) and electricity prices unachievable, so the unit's financial case failed on more than construction cost. The unit was built under contract by an Alstom consortium; the delivering institutions are the state-owned HSE and TEŠ, and the state as guarantor and owner (through AUKN, SOD and SDH), whose oversight the court also faulted. The started year is the main construction contract with Alstom, as commonly reported; it was not read at the cited source. Status is concluded because the unit was built and operates; the record says nothing about its economics after 2016 or Slovenia's coal exit plans.

pattern.mechanism: A state-owned utility group committed to a single large lignite unit, financed it with a state-guaranteed EIB loan conditioned on a cost ceiling, and then revised the investment programme upward several times while construction ran, leaving the state as guarantor to accept the breach.
preconditions: A state holding with a captive coal mine and a political mandate to keep the lignite region working
A state guarantee law that set a cost ceiling but no mechanism to stop the project when it was crossed
Shareholder oversight bodies that did not ask for cash-flow reports until after the overrun

records.title: Rail Baltica in Latvia, and its cost and schedule overrun
records.claim: The Latvian State Audit Office found in June 2024 that the estimated construction cost of Rail Baltica's main line in Latvia had risen sevenfold since 2017 to about 8.7 billion euros, that design work due by the end of 2021 was only 54 percent complete and now planned to finish by the end of 2027, and that the Riga Central Station works contracted in 2019 at 430 million euros had risen to 565 million euros.

metric.name: Estimated construction cost of the Rail Baltica main line, Latvian section

secondMetric.name: Share of main line design work completed, against an original deadline of end 2021

source.publisher: Valsts kontrole (State Audit Office of the Republic of Latvia), news release 'Rail Baltica tvērums Latvijā mainījies bez vienotas pieejas un lēmumi ir grūti izsekojami', 12 June 2024, with the attached infographic of the national situation review

records.limits: The source is a situation review (situācijas izpēte), which the audit office itself describes as a short compilation of facts with no conclusions or recommendations, not a full audit. The 8.7 billion is stated as 'aptuveni' (about) and as a sevenfold rise since 2017, so the 2017 baseline (roughly 1.2 billion) is implied, not printed; it is not used as a metric here. Much of the rise is scope and specification change (the design guidelines were revised more than 100 times after 2018, and the station node went from two tracks to four), so the multiple measures how far the 2017 estimate was from a buildable project as much as delivery performance. The project is not finished: the release says only 4.5 percent of the needed main line financing was available, and the joint Baltic review it summarises puts the whole three-country project at 23.8 billion euros in 2023 against 5.8 billion in 2017, with the first phase now due in 2030. Rail Baltica is a joint Estonian, Latvian and Lithuanian project funded about 85 percent by the EU; this record covers only the Latvian section and the Latvian ministry's management. Status is operating because the project is under construction; a decision to phase or cut the Latvian scope after June 2024 was not checked at an official source. The started year is the 2016 Cabinet approval of the project scope named in the release. The 565 million euro station figure is computed here: the release says the 2019 contract cost of 430 million euros rose by a further 135 million in 2024, and does not print 565.

pattern.mechanism: The transport ministry approved scope changes and cost increases for stations, the Riga node and the main line itself, often without bringing a full cost picture to the Cabinet, while design guidelines kept changing and EU co-financing deadlines kept slipping.
preconditions: A first cost estimate made before any design guidelines existed
A ministry able to approve scope changes without a single Cabinet-level change process
Financing that depends on successive EU funding calls rather than a committed national budget
pattern.travelled: The joint Baltic review found the same pattern in Estonia and Lithuania, so the overrun is a property of the joint project's governance as well as of Latvian administration.

records.title: Koralmbahn Graz to Klagenfurt, opened seven years after its contracted completion date
records.claim: Austria's federal rail infrastructure company ÖBB-Infrastruktur AG forecast the Koralmbahn's total cost at 6.139 billion euros at the end of 2023, 282.4 million euros or 5 percent above the 2012 baseline, but missed both the 2018 completion date in the 2004 Koralmbahn contract and the 2023 opening date in the 2012 to 2017 framework plan, according to the Court of Audit, and the line entered passenger service on 14 December 2025.

metric.name: Forecast total cost of the Koralmbahn project

secondMetric.name: Cost increase against the 2012 baseline, including the later addition of the airport branch

source.publisher: Rechnungshof Österreich (Austrian Court of Audit), news release 'Rechnungshof veröffentlichte Bericht Projekt Koralmbahn', 4 April 2025, on report Bund 2025/14

records.limits: The cost figure is ÖBB-Infrastruktur's own forecast, which the court reports; it is a forecast at the end of 2023, not a final account, and the 5 percent increase is measured from 2012, when the project was already well advanced, so it says nothing about growth from the first estimates of the 1990s and 2000s, which the release does not give. The court's audit covered 2012 to 2023. The release says the tunnel lot KAT 2 alone rose 297.75 million euros and took about 31 months longer, with contractor claims above a third of the original contract sum, and that the company paid tunnel stoppages contrary to the contract. The opening date of 14 December 2025 is taken from ÖBB's own project page (https://www.unsereoebb.at/de/suedstrecke, 'Am 14. Dezember 2025 geht die Koralmbahn in den Fahrgastbetrieb'), not from the court. The full report PDF (https://www.rechnungshof.gv.at/rh/home/home/2025_14_Koralmbahn.pdf) was not opened; the figures come from the release. The started year is approximate and was not read at either source: preparatory works on the line began in the late 1990s and the Koralm tunnel drives later. ÖBB-Infrastruktur is a state-owned company, so the delivery is institutional, but the record reports cost and time only, not ridership.

pattern.mechanism: The federal government funded a new high-speed line through the federal rail framework plan and its state-owned infrastructure company managed the build, holding total cost close to the 2012 estimate while a hard-rock tunnel lot overran in cost and time and pushed the opening back twice.
preconditions: A rolling multi-year federal rail framework plan that funds the project year by year
A state infrastructure company with project controlling strong enough to absorb a lot overrun inside the total
A supreme audit institution that audits individual construction lots, not only totals

records.title: Fehmarn Belt fixed link, and its cost and schedule overrun
records.claim: The European Court of Auditors found in 2020 that the Fehmarn Belt fixed link, the 18 km rail and road tunnel that Denmark finances, designs and builds through its state company Femern A/S, had an initial cost estimate of 4.4 billion euros at 2008 prices (5.0 billion at 2019 values) against a latest estimate of 7.7 billion, a 54 percent increase, and that construction planned to start in 2012 for opening in 2018 had started in 2020 with opening expected in 2028.

metric.name: Latest cost estimate of the Fehmarn Belt fixed link transport flagship infrastructure, 2019 values

secondMetric.name: Initial cost estimate re-indexed to 2019 values (4.4 billion euros at 2008 values)

source.publisher: European Court of Auditors, Special Report 10/2020 'EU transport infrastructures: more speed needed in megaproject implementation to deliver network effects on time', Annexes II and III and Table 3

records.limits: The figures are in a PDF: the timeline table is Annex II (PDF page 66) and the cost table Annex III (PDF page 67), with the 5,016 to 7,711 million euro comparison and 54 percent in the table on PDF page 36. The ECA compares the latest estimate with the first political estimate on purpose, so part of the increase reflects scope settled after 2008, and the re-indexation uses the GDP deflator, not construction prices. The ECA's 'transport flagship infrastructure' includes the Danish and German rail access lines, and Germany finances and builds its own access lines, so the 7.7 billion is not a purely Danish cost; the report states that the tunnel itself is financed, designed and built by Denmark (paragraph 23, PDF page 21) and that the fixed link is therefore a Danish project. The figures are from 2019 and 2020; the tunnel is still under construction, and later Danish estimates and the current opening date were not checked at a Danish source, so the 2028 opening is the ECA's estimate at the time. The ECA reports that the construction start slipped largely because of the German planning approval process and litigation, which is outside Danish institutions' control. The EU co-finances the project, and the ECA audits EU spending, not Femern A/S's management.

pattern.mechanism: Denmark took on the whole financing and construction risk of a cross-border tunnel through a state-owned company repaid from future tolls, under a state treaty that limits the neighbouring country to its own access lines.
preconditions: A state company model already used for the Great Belt and Øresund links, financed by state-guaranteed loans repaid from tolls
A bilateral treaty dividing responsibilities, which also left the timetable exposed to the other country's planning law
EU co-financing under the trans-European transport network
pattern.travelled: The same state-guaranteed company model built the Great Belt and Øresund fixed links, so this is the third use of the Danish model; the delay this time came from the planning process on the other side of the border.

records.title: Reconstruction after the 2016 and 2017 Central Italy earthquakes
records.claim: Italy's Extraordinary Commissioner for reconstruction after the 2016 Central Italy earthquakes reported that by 31 May 2026 private reconstruction had received 36,149 grant applications for 17.82 billion euros, approved 24,650, granted 12.59 billion and paid 7.99 billion, and that 14,968 of 23,361 authorised building sites had been completed across the 138 municipalities of the crater.

metric.name: Private reconstruction building sites completed (cantieri conclusi)

secondMetric.name: Private reconstruction building sites authorised (cantieri autorizzati)

source.publisher: Commissario Straordinario Ricostruzione Sisma 2016 (Presidency of the Council of Ministers), Rapporto sulla ricostruzione Centro Italia post sisma 2016, Anno 2026, Executive Summary

records.limits: The commissioner reports on its own programme, and the executive summary is written as advocacy ('La cura funziona'). The figures are in a PDF, on PDF pages 3 to 5. The host sisma2016data.it rate-limited scripted requests (HTTP 429), so the PDF was read through a fetch tool, not curl. Ten years after the August 2016 shock, about 64 percent of authorised private sites were complete and less than half of the 17.82 billion requested had been paid; the report itself says 69 percent of the payments were made from 2023 onwards, so most of the recovery happened six to ten years after the earthquake, which is evidence of slow recovery as much as of capacity. Applications and sites are counts of files and works, not households rehoused; the report gives one household figure, over 1,300 families (about 2,800 people) returning home in the last year, without a cumulative total. Public reconstruction, 3,667 programmed works for over 4.85 billion euros, is reported as reaching 40 percent of sites under way or finished. The record shows recovery after a shock, not preparation before one: Italy's seismic prevention and the emergency response in 2016 are outside it.

pattern.mechanism: Parliament created a dedicated extraordinary commissioner with ordinance powers, regional special reconstruction offices and a single digital platform for grant files, and the commissioner pays reconstruction grants for private homes and runs a programme of public works across four regions.
preconditions: A national grant scheme that pays the full cost of rebuilding damaged primary homes
Regional reconstruction offices able to process tens of thousands of technical files
A legislative decree (D.L. 189/2016) that keeps the commissioner in place across changes of government
pattern.travelled: The same model was applied in 2025 to the Ancona and Umbertide earthquakes, according to the commissioner's own site; the Emilia 2012 and L'Aquila 2009 reconstructions used regional and municipal structures instead.

records.title: Zagreb earthquake recovery under the World Bank loan, and its delays
records.claim: Croatia's Ministry of Construction, Physical Planning and State Assets and Ministry of Health had disbursed 16 percent of the 200 million US dollar World Bank earthquake recovery loan approved in June 2020 by November 2024, when the closing date was extended for the second time to 30 June 2027, and by May 2026 had restored 40 percent of the targeted health and education buildings.

metric.name: Health and education buildings with restored operational capacity and higher seismic performance, share of target

secondMetric.name: Share of the IBRD loan disbursed at the second restructuring

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Status and Results Report, Earthquake Recovery and Public Health Preparedness Project (P173998), sequence 12, archived 19 June 2026

records.limits: The World Bank finances the project and rates it (moderately satisfactory on both counts in June 2026), so this is a lender reporting on its own loan. The 40 percent is an intermediate indicator in the ISR's results table; the 16.32 percent disbursed and the extension from 31 December 2024 to 30 June 2027 (after an earlier extension from 30 June 2024) are in the Second Restructuring Paper of November 2024 (https://documents.worldbank.org/curated/en/099110624203564259/text/P173998-7d9a1555-e106-4a16-b043-2253208f955b.txt, paragraphs 1, 4 and 5). The loan is a small part of Croatia's recovery: the restructuring paper itself says about 1 billion euros of EU Solidarity Fund grants had to be spent within 18 months and became the government's priority, which is one reason the loan lagged, so this record shows the slow track, not the whole national response, and Croatia's own reconstruction fund figures for private homes were not read at an official source. The paper also cites a government change, four changes of ministry leadership in four years, the December 2020 Petrinja earthquake and construction labour shortages. The project builds hospital and school buildings that are not finished, so the record documents recovery in progress, not completed. Status is operating, not eroded, because no part of a delivered peak has been lost; the delay is the finding.

pattern.mechanism: After the March 2020 Zagreb earthquake the government borrowed from the World Bank to rebuild damaged hospitals and schools and to fund public health preparedness, while spending EU Solidarity Fund grants first; the loan's complex hospital works then took years to tender and its closing date was extended twice.
preconditions: A rapid damage and needs assessment that sized the loan within three months
Implementing units inside the construction and health ministries that survive changes of minister
A construction market with capacity to absorb recovery works, which was lacking after the second earthquake

records.title: Motorway construction by the Road and Motorway Directorate, and its unit cost
records.claim: The Czech Supreme Audit Office reported in June 2026 that 41 motorway sections totalling more than 300 km were opened to traffic between 2020 and 2024, after years with almost none (no kilometre in 2014, four in 2018), but that the average cost the state paid per kilometre of motorway opened rose from nearly CZK 275 million in 2020 to CZK 505 million in 2024, an increase of nearly 84 percent.

metric.name: Average cost to the state per kilometre of motorway opened

secondMetric.name: Average cost to the state per kilometre of motorway opened (nearly)

source.publisher: Nejvyšší kontrolní úřad (Supreme Audit Office of the Czech Republic), press release on the comprehensive report on the state's investment policy 2020 to 2025 from the perspective of audits of transport infrastructure, 8 June 2026

records.limits: The source is the audit office's English press release; the comprehensive report it summarises, based on 13 audits completed from 2020 to 2025, was not opened. Cost per kilometre opened is an average over whatever sections happened to open in each year, so it mixes simple and complex sections (tunnels, bridges, terrain) and nominal prices across a period of high construction inflation; the office says the rise 'cannot be attributed solely' to inflation or complexity, which is a judgement, not a decomposition, and no baseline against outturn is given for any single section. The 2020 figure is stated as 'nearly' 275 million. The same release gives project-level findings that support the schedule side: preparation of the D4 section took the Ministry of Transport and the Road and Motorway Directorate 21 years and was delivered as a PPP whose payments run to 2049, and the directorate had not completed the modernisation of 20 sections of the D1 for CZK 28 billion after 10 years. The record shows delivery volume rising and unit cost rising together; it does not show whether the 2020 to 2024 output was on its planned schedule. The started year is the first year of the audit office's comparison, not the start of the motorway programme.

pattern.mechanism: The transport ministry and its Road and Motorway Directorate prepare motorway sections through long zoning and permitting processes and then build many of them in a short window financed by the State Fund for Transport Infrastructure and EU funds, paying whatever the market price is when the sections finally reach construction.
preconditions: A state road directorate with a pipeline of permitted sections ready to tender
A transport fund able to raise annual spending sharply
Permitting reform that releases sections held up for years, which is also what bunches them into a high-price period

records.title: Civil defence public warning sirens (tyfoner) and their twice-yearly test
records.claim: The Norwegian Civil Defence tested 1,130 public warning sirens in its national warning test on 14 January 2026 and reported an uptime of 89 percent, which it called a clear improvement on the January 2025 test and a slight fall from the June 2025 test.

metric.name: Uptime of public warning sirens in the national warning test

secondMetric.name: Public warning siren installations tested

source.publisher: Sivilforsvaret (Norwegian Civil Defence, under the Directorate for Civil Protection), news item 'Resultater etter varslingsprøven'

records.limits: The civil defence reports on its own system, in a short news item that does not print the publication date; the test date is given as Wednesday 14 January and the comparison with 'January 2025' places it in 2026. A test is not a shock: the record shows that the warning hardware works on a set day, not that people were warned, sheltered or evacuated in a real event. Uptime of 89 percent means roughly one installation in nine failed, mostly from frost and cold according to the item, and installations disconnected for maintenance or relocation were not tested and are not in the denominator, which flatters the figure. The item does not give the earlier test percentages it compares with, nor the share of the population within siren range. Norway has had a cell broadcast system (nødvarsel) since 2024, which this figure does not cover. The started year is an approximation for the post-war civil defence siren network and was not read at the cited page.

pattern.mechanism: The national civil defence keeps a network of public warning sirens in populated areas and sounds every one of them in a national test twice a year, publishing the share that worked and following up each failure.
preconditions: A state civil defence organisation that owns and maintains the sirens rather than leaving them to municipalities
A central control system able to trigger and log every installation at once
Regular public tests, which double as a reminder of the signals
pattern.travelled: Germany dismantled its federal siren network after the Cold War (deu-siren-network) and is rebuilding it; Norway kept its network under the civil defence and tests it on a fixed calendar.

records.title: Pelješac Bridge, the first stage of the road connection to South Dalmatia
records.claim: Croatia's road authority awarded the 2,440-metre Pelješac Bridge to China Road and Bridge Corporation in 2018 for HRK 2.081 billion excluding VAT with a 36-month completion deadline, works started on 31 July 2018, the last steel segment was installed by 28 July 2021, and the government expected the bridge and access roads to open in June 2022, in a project whose eligible costs of 420 million euros were 85 percent financed by an EU grant of 357 million euros.

metric.name: Contract price for the bridge, excluding VAT

secondMetric.name: Contracted completion period from the start of works on 31 July 2018

source.publisher: Government of the Republic of Croatia (vlada.gov.hr), news item 'Pelješac Bridge joined together', 28 July 2021

records.limits: The source is a government news item written by the national news agency Hina at the moment the span was closed, so it carries the government's framing and gives a contract price and a deadline, not a final cost: no final account or audit of the bridge's outturn cost was read. The page puts the total project value at '€526 billion', an evident typing error for 526 million, and the EU grant figure appears as '€357' without a unit; the record uses the 420 million euro eligible cost and 357 million euro grant stated elsewhere on the same page, and the European Commission's release of 7 June 2017 (read through the Internet Archive, https://web.archive.org/web/20190715235249/https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/en/newsroom/news/2017/06/06-07-2017-commission-approves-eu-financing-of-the-peljesac-bridge-in-croatia) confirms 357 million euros and 85 percent. The 36-month deadline from 31 July 2018 fell at the end of July 2021, when the span was joined; the expected June 2022 opening was a forecast on the page, and the actual opening date (reported as 26 July 2022) was not read at an official source, so the record can say only that the structure was joined on its contract deadline and opened about a year later with its access roads. The project had an earlier history the page omits: a first construction contract from 2007 was cancelled by a later government, according to press reports not used as a source. The bridge was built by a Chinese state-owned contractor, so the delivery attributable to Croatia is the procurement, financing and project management.

pattern.mechanism: The government revived a cancelled bridge as an EU cohesion-funded major project, tendered it on price with a fixed deadline, and let it to the lowest bidder, a Chinese state contractor, while EU money covered 85 percent of eligible costs.
preconditions: An EU cohesion allocation large enough to cover most of a single national megaproject
A feasibility study commissioned by the European Commission that settled the choice of route
A road authority able to run an open international tender and enforce a fixed deadline

records.title: Recovery after the August 2023 floods
records.claim: Slovenia's Ministry of Natural Resources and Spatial Planning reported in July 2025 that after the floods of 4 August 2023 it had completed all intervention and emergency works on 850 km of watercourses by June 2024, paid 35.7 million euros in advance payments for home repairs to more than 7,350 individuals, transferred 218 million euros in advances to municipalities and completed more than 430 watercourse repair sites, within a five-year recovery programme funded at 2.3 billion euros.

metric.name: Individuals paid advance payments for urgent repair of damaged homes

secondMetric.name: Length of watercourses on which all intervention and emergency works were completed by June 2024

source.publisher: Ministrstvo za naravne vire in prostor (Ministry of Natural Resources and Spatial Planning) and Direkcija RS za vode, news release 'Dve leti po poplavah: krepimo odpornost na podnebne spremembe', 25 July 2025, gov.si

records.limits: The ministry reports on its own response at a press conference marking two years since the floods, and calls its results 'an excellent result', so the framing is the government's. The figures are stated as 'more than' and are not broken down by date, apart from the June 2024 completion of emergency works. Advance payments to 7,350 people are not completed repairs: the same page says more than 5,000 applications from individuals and firms for building repair were still being processed and that 'more than half' of beneficiaries had received all the funds they needed, so the household recovery was incomplete two years on. The 2.3 billion euro programme is money allocated, not spent; the ministry says watercourse works rose more than tenfold after the floods, with 240 million realised in 2024 and 332 million forecast for 2025. A separate release of the cohesion ministry (12 June 2025) says Slovenia had used 88 percent (376.6 million euros) of the 428 million euro EU Solidarity Fund grant, so part of the recovery was EU money. The record shows recovery after the shock, not the warning or evacuation before it; the August 2023 floods killed several people and damaged a large share of municipalities, which this record does not measure.

pattern.mechanism: The government passed an intervention law, paid flood-hit households and municipalities in advance instead of after damage assessment, mobilised more than a thousand machines on rivers at once, and then adopted a five-year recovery programme with dedicated funding through a new reconstruction office.
preconditions: A water directorate and concession contractors able to scale works more than tenfold in a year
Fiscal room and a law allowing advance payments before final damage assessment
EU Solidarity Fund support to cover part of the eligible public costs

records.title: First state aid payments after Storm Daniel (Kratiki Arogi)
records.claim: Greece's Ministry of Climate Crisis and Civil Protection paid almost 65 million euros of first state aid (proti arogi) to about 14,000 people affected by the September 2023 Thessaly floods within the first month after the storm, and by 15 February 2024 had paid 154.94 million euros to 45,292 households, firms, farms and livestock units in the first round.

metric.name: Recipients of first state aid (households, businesses, farms and livestock units), first round, cumulative

secondMetric.name: Recipients paid within about the first month after the floods

source.publisher: Ministry of Climate Crisis and Civil Protection, General Secretariat for Natural Disaster Recovery and State Aid, press release '29th payment of First Aid', 15 February 2024, arogi.gov.gr

records.limits: The ministry reports on its own payments in press releases, and the one-month figure comes from the deputy minister's statement in a separate release of 13 October 2023 (https://arogi.gov.gr/deltia-typou/hr-triantopoylos-8i-katavoli-protis-arogis-65-ekat-eyro-se-14000-polites-mesa-se-peripoy-ena-mina/), worded as 'almost 65 million' to 'about 14,000'. Recipients mix households, businesses, farms and livestock units, so the count is not people or homes; first aid is an advance against later compensation and covers basic needs and household contents, not rebuilding. The release gives no figure for the number of eligible victims, so coverage cannot be computed. Speed of payment is a recovery measure, not preparedness: the record says nothing about warning, evacuation or the flood defences of Thessaly, where Storm Daniel caused deaths and flooded large areas. The 15 February 2024 cumulative covers households and firms hit by the flood 'in Thessaly, but also other areas', so it is not strictly limited to Thessaly.

pattern.mechanism: A general secretariat for disaster recovery runs a single online platform where victims apply, cross-checks applications against tax and property data held by the revenue authority, and pays first aid in weekly batches within weeks of the event, before full damage assessment.
preconditions: A tax administration with property and bank account data that can be matched to applicants
A standing legal framework for state aid after disasters, so no new law is needed per event
A ministry unit dedicated to recovery that survives between disasters
pattern.travelled: The same platform paid the Evros fire, Samos earthquake and Chios fire victims; the release pattern is identical across events.

records.title: Decommissioning of the Bohunice V1 nuclear power plant, and its four-year slip
records.claim: Slovakia's state decommissioning company JAVYS, which the European Court of Auditors reported in 2016 as holding the Bohunice V1 decommissioning end date at 2025 with a cost estimate of 1,239 million euros, reported in its 2025 annual report that the final decontamination and demolition contract signed on 18 December 2024 runs 60 months, putting the end of decommissioning at the end of 2029, at a total estimated cost of 1,220 million euros, with 66 decommissioning projects completed by 31 December 2025.

metric.name: Total estimated cost of decommissioning Bohunice V1

secondMetric.name: Expected year of completion of the whole V1 decommissioning process, against 2025 in the plan the ECA reviewed in 2016

source.publisher: JAVYS, a.s. (Jadrová a vyraďovacia spoločnosť, state-owned), Výročná správa 2025 (annual report 2025), section on V1 decommissioning

records.limits: JAVYS reports on its own programme; the figures are in a PDF, the 2029 end date and the 60-month contract of 18 December 2024 on PDF page 17, the 1,220 million euro estimate and the 735 million EU share on PDF page 19, and the 66 completed projects on PDF page 20. The baseline comes from a different publisher: the European Court of Auditors' Special Report 22/2016 (https://www.eca.europa.eu/Lists/ECADocuments/SR16_22/SR_NUCLEAR_DECOMMISSIONING_EN.pdf) says the Slovak end date 'has remained at 2025' (paragraph 64, PDF page 40) and gives estimated costs of 1,146 million euros in 2011 and 1,239 million in 2015 (Table 8, PDF page 46). The two cost figures are not on the same basis, so the record does not claim the cost fell; it claims cost was held roughly flat while completion slipped about four years. Decommissioning is a stretch for 'major public infrastructure projects': it is a large state engineering programme that builds waste facilities and demolishes a plant rather than a new asset, and it is mostly paid for by the EU (735 million euros of the 1,220 million, through the EBRD-managed BIDSF fund and the Slovak Innovation and Energy Agency). The started year is 2015, the start of the second decommissioning stage under the nuclear regulator's licence of 23 December 2014; the first stage began earlier. Whether the 2029 date holds is not known.

pattern.mechanism: A state company created to decommission shut-down reactors runs dozens of EU-funded projects under a detailed decommissioning plan monitored by the European Commission and the EBRD, and reschedules the end date when the final demolition contract is procured.
preconditions: A dedicated state decommissioning company with its own nuclear licences
EU accession commitments that fund most of the cost through a ring-fenced programme
A regulator able to license each decommissioning stage separately
pattern.travelled: Lithuania's Ignalina decommissioning, funded under the same EU arrangement, slipped much further (ltu-ignalina-decommissioning).

records.title: Decommissioning of the Ignalina nuclear power plant, and its delays
records.claim: The European Court of Auditors found in 2016 that Lithuania's Ignalina nuclear power plant decommissioning had pushed its end date back by a further nine years since 2011 to 2038, that the interim spent fuel storage facility was ten years behind the 2005 decommissioning plan, and that the estimated decommissioning cost had risen 15 percent from 2,930 million euros in 2011 to 3,376 million in 2015, and 67 percent since the 2010 estimate.

metric.name: Estimated total cost of decommissioning Ignalina

secondMetric.name: Estimated total cost of decommissioning Ignalina

source.publisher: European Court of Auditors, Special Report 22/2016 'EU nuclear decommissioning assistance programmes in Lithuania, Bulgaria and Slovakia: some progress made since 2011, but critical challenges ahead'

records.limits: The figures are in a PDF: the 2038 end date and the nine-year postponement in paragraph 60 (PDF page 38), the ten-year delay of the interim spent fuel storage facility in Table 6, the 67 percent rise in paragraph 73 (PDF page 44) and the 2011 and 2015 estimates in Table 8 (PDF page 46). The report is ten years old and the current end date and cost estimate were not checked at a Lithuanian source; the Lithuanian audit office's site (valstybeskontrole.lt) returned a Cloudflare challenge. The ECA audits EU spending, and the EU funds most of the programme, so the figures describe a jointly financed delivery carried out by the state enterprise Ignalina NPP. Decommissioning is a stretch for 'major public infrastructure projects': it builds waste and fuel storage facilities and dismantles a plant, and the report says delays came partly from contractual disputes with a foreign contractor and from poor information on how the Soviet-built plant was constructed. The started year is approximate: 2010 is the base year of the ECA's cost comparison, and the report does not give a start date for decommissioning itself.

pattern.mechanism: A state enterprise decommissions a large Soviet-designed plant under EU accession commitments, building fuel and waste storage through international contracts paid by an EU fund, and its end date moves each time a key facility is delayed.
preconditions: EU accession-linked funding that covers most of the cost
Reliable design records of the plant being dismantled, which were missing here
Contract management capacity strong enough to resolve disputes with foreign suppliers quickly
pattern.travelled: Slovakia's Bohunice V1, funded under the same arrangement, held its end date until 2025 and then slipped to 2029 (svk-bohunice-v1).

records.title: Civil defence shelters and protective trenches, and their erosion
records.claim: Denmark's Emergency Management Agency counted about 4,693,000 places in public shelters, protective concrete trenches and building shelters at the end of 2001, and the municipal count it collected in 2022, the first since then, recorded about 3.54 million, with places in concrete trenches down from 152,335 to 107,658 and in building shelters (sikringsrum) from 3,743,822 to 3,307,400, after municipalities had stopped requiring shelters in new buildings.

metric.name: Places in concrete trenches, other public shelters, building shelters and supplementary rooms, sum of the four national totals in the 2022 count

secondMetric.name: Places in shelters (concrete trenches, combined public shelters, supplementary public shelters and building shelters)

source.publisher: Beredskabsstyrelsen (Danish Emergency Management Agency), 'Opgørelse over antal pladser i beskyttelses- og sikringsrum 2022', table updated 27 June 2022

records.limits: The 2022 total is computed here by adding the four national totals printed at the foot of the two-page table (107,658 trench places, 60,432 other public shelter places, 3,307,400 building shelter places and 63,105 supplementary places); the agency itself prints no grand total. Its release (https://www.brs.dk/da/nyheder-og-publikationer/publikationer2/alle-publikationer/2022/beskyttelsesrum-2022/) says the data were not yet validated, that building shelters are under-registered in the building register, and that it expects the consolidated count of building shelter places to be 'somewhat higher' than the table but lower than in 2002, so the size of the fall is uncertain. The 2001 figure is from the agency's August 2002 report on shelter preparedness (https://www.brs.dk/globalassets/brs---beredskabsstyrelsen/dokumenter/ovrige-emner/2020/-rapport_om_beskyttelsesrumsberedskabet-.pdf, PDF page 23), which also gives the categories; the supplementary category fell most (720,000 to 63,105) and may not be defined the same way in both counts. The same 2002 report says the need under the old target of one place per resident was estimated at 6.5 million places in 1991, so the stock never met the target. The erosion follows a policy choice: shelters have been a municipal responsibility since 1993 and municipalities stopped imposing shelters in new buildings. The record measures places on paper, not whether the rooms could be readied in time. The started year is approximate for the post-war shelter programme and was not read at either source.

pattern.mechanism: The state built public shelters and protective trenches and required shelters in new buildings during the Cold War, then devolved shelters to municipalities in 1993, which stopped requiring new ones and let some be closed, until the 2022 security shock prompted the first national count in twenty years.
preconditions: A building rule requiring shelters in new construction, which is what kept the stock growing and what lapsed
A national register of shelter places kept up to date, which Denmark did not keep after 2002
Municipal budgets for maintaining rooms that have no peacetime function
pattern.travelled: Germany (deu-public-shelters) and Norway (nor-tilfluktsrom) ran their shelter stock down after the Cold War in the same way; Finland (fin-civil-defence-shelters) kept the building requirement and its stock.

records.title: National warning siren network and its twice-yearly test
records.claim: Latvia's State Fire and Rescue Service tested the national early warning siren network on 23 May 2025 and reported that 160 of the 162 sirens tested worked without faults, out of 164 installed, against 119 of 155 in the test of 20 May 2024.

metric.name: Sirens that worked without faults in the national test

secondMetric.name: Sirens that worked without faults in the national test a year earlier

source.publisher: Valsts ugunsdzēsības un glābšanas dienests (State Fire and Rescue Service of Latvia), news item 'Pārbaudot 162 trauksmes sirēnas, bez traucējumiem nostrādāja 160 sirēnas', 23 May 2025

records.limits: The fire service reports on its own system. A test is not a shock: the record shows that sirens sounded on a set day, not that people were warned or acted in a real event, and the item does not say what share of the population lives within hearing range of 164 sirens. Sirens not tested because they were being moved, repaired or renewed (two in May 2025, nine in May 2024) are outside the denominator. The 2024 figure is from the service's item of 20 May 2024 (https://www.vugd.gov.lv/lv/jaunums/parbaudot-155-trauksmes-sirenas-bez-traucejumiem-nostradaja-119-sirenas); other items in the series give 152 of 158 (May 2023), 138 of 159 (November 2023) and 151 of 158 (November 2024), and in June 2022 the remote activation software failed and the sirens had to be started by hand, so performance has swung between tests rather than improved steadily. No test result after May 2025 was found in the service's sitemap. The started year is the first test in the series read (June 2022), not the founding of the network; Latvia also sends cell broadcast and app alerts, which this figure does not cover.

pattern.mechanism: The fire and rescue service sounds every national warning siren twice a year, publishes how many worked by region, and repairs or relocates the failures before the next test.
preconditions: A remotely triggered siren network owned by a national service
A published test result after every test, which makes failures visible
Maintenance funding, which rose after 2022 with the security situation
pattern.travelled: Norway's civil defence publishes the same kind of test result for a network seven times larger (nor-tyfonvarsling).

records.title: Sandbox for AI and blockchain products, Ministry of Digital Transformation and Ukrainian Startup Fund
records.claim: Ukraine's Ministry of Digital Transformation and the Ukrainian Startup Fund opened a sandbox for AI and blockchain products in 2025 and, in its first year, received more than 80 applications and admitted 15 companies to a first cohort that completed testing.

metric.name: Companies admitted to the first cohort that completed testing

secondMetric.name: Applications received in the first year (more than)

source.publisher: Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine, AI portal, news item 'One year of the AI and blockchain Sandbox' (4 June 2026)

records.limits: The ministry reports on its own programme in a news item, not a statistics page, and 80 is a floor ('more than 80'). The sandbox grants no statutory derogation that this check found: what participants receive is a free legal, technical and business audit by outside experts with recommendations, and the ministry's statement that firms test 'without fines or legal risks' is not backed by a legal instrument read today, so this is closer to an advisory sandbox than to a regime that relaxes rules, and it sits at the weak edge of the D152 construct. 'Completed testing' means completed the audit cycle; the ministry's page of 21 October 2025 names Artellence as the first company to finish it. Higher figures in the press (over 100 applications, 25 companies under review) were not found at an official publisher and are not used. The National Bank of Ukraine runs a statutory regulatory platform under the payment services and financial services laws, open only to firms it already licenses, but its page (promo.bank.gov.ua/sandbox) publishes no participant count, so the figure covers one programme and not every regulator.

pattern.mechanism: The digital ministry, with a state startup fund, invites AI and blockchain firms to submit products for an expert audit across law, technology and business, and feeds what it learns into drafting AI legislation aligned with the EU AI Act.
preconditions: A ministry with a standing AI policy unit and a lawmaking agenda to feed
A state startup fund able to recruit and pay outside experts under NDA
A pipeline of domestic AI and blockchain firms seeking EU market access

records.title: Public vocational training centres of the National Agency for Employment and Skills
records.claim: Albania's National Agency for Employment and Skills (AKPA) registered 11,250 trainees in 2021 in vocational courses at its ten regional public vocational training directorates, 7,052 of them on free places for registered jobseekers and other priority groups by the bulletin's text, after 15,143 in 2019 and 7,427 in the pandemic year 2020.

metric.name: Trainees registered in public vocational training centres (DROFPP) during the year

secondMetric.name: Of whom on free places (registered unemployed jobseekers and priority groups)

source.publisher: Agjencia Kombetare e Punesimit dhe Aftesive (AKPA), Buletini Statistikor 2021, section III.4 (participants in vocational training programmes)

records.limits: The agency reports on itself, on page 60 of an 83-page PDF in Albanian. The bulletin contradicts itself on the free places: the text on page 60 says 7,052 (about 63 percent), while Table 27 on page 61 and Table 29 on page 65 give 7,811 trainees on free places, 6,631 of them registered unemployed, so the free-place figure is uncertain by about 750 and the record carries the text figure. 2021 is the latest annual bulletin found at an open URL: the agency's publications page renders by script and no 2022 to 2025 bulletin was found, so the record cannot show the current scale, and 'operating' rests on the agency's site still listing course offers and centre notices on 2026-10-02, not on a count. The 2019 (15,143) and 2020 (7,427) figures are in the agency's 2019 and 2020 bulletins on the same host, not at the cited URL; the 2021 bulletin itself says 2021 was 50 percent above 2020, which fits the 2020 figure, and the 2019 figure was not re-checked. 2021 sits below 2019, but with pandemic disruption in both 2020 and 2021 the record does not call that an erosion. Counts are course registrations, not completions or unique people: Table 29 gives 6,180 certified of the 11,250. Most courses are short provider-level courses, but national-level courses can run up to two years. The started year is the earliest labour market bulletin the agency still hosts (2014); the public vocational training centres are older, and their founding year was not read at any source, so delivery began no later than 2014.

pattern.mechanism: The national employment and skills agency runs regional public training centres that offer short national and provider-level vocational courses, free for registered jobseekers and paid for others.
preconditions: A network of regional public training centres under the employment agency
A national catalogue of short qualifications that centres can certify
Referral from employment offices so jobseekers reach free places

records.title: Employment Agency adult training, including the DI-GI digital skills vouchers
records.claim: Bulgaria's Employment Agency (Agentsia po zaetostta) included more than 155,450 unemployed and employed adults in training in 2025, against just over 87,540 in 2024, with 97,911 people certified through digital skills vouchers financed under the national Recovery and Resilience Plan.

metric.name: Unemployed and employed people included in adult training by the Employment Agency ('over 155 450')

secondMetric.name: Same count for the previous year ('just over 87 540')

source.publisher: Agentsia po zaetostta (Employment Agency), Otchet na Plana za deystvie na Agentsiyata po zaetostta za 2025 g. (report on the 2025 action plan), text volume

records.limits: The agency reports on itself, and the cited URL is a zip archive from the agency's 'Otchet za deynostta na AZ' page holding two PDFs; the headline counts are on page 81 of the 84-page text volume (Otchet_Plan za deistvie_2025_text.pdf), and both are stated as 'over' and 'just over', so they are rounded. The 2025 jump is mostly vouchers: 97,911 people certified in basic and advanced digital skills under component 2 of investment C1.I3 of the Recovery and Resilience Plan (page 34), and 22,140 employed people trained under the ESF+ project for employed workers; much of the money is EU, though the agency delivers it. Digital skills courses can be short and online, the counts mix enrolment and certification, and one person may appear in more than one scheme. Training for the registered unemployed is far smaller: 6,705 unemployed people were included in training under the programmes and measures of the national employment action plan (page 17). The RRF component ends with the facility in 2026, so 2025 is unlikely to be a stable level. The 2002 start is the year of the Employment Promotion Act under which the agency trains adults, not read at the source.

pattern.mechanism: The national employment agency issues training vouchers to unemployed, inactive and employed adults, who choose a licensed provider, and pays the provider on completion, with EU recovery and social funds paying for most of the volume.
preconditions: A register of licensed vocational training providers under the national VET agency
An online voucher application system run through the labour offices
EU funding lines (RRF, ESF+) large enough to pay for courses at national scale

records.title: ANCD innovation vouchers (Vouchere Inovationale) for SME research services
records.claim: Moldova's National Agency for Research and Development (ANCD) financed 13 innovation voucher projects in 2025, in which small and medium firms buy research and development services from research organisations, after 28 applications to the 2025-2026 call yielded 10 funded projects and four funded projects were stopped when the firms declined to sign contracts.

metric.name: Innovation voucher projects financed in the year (10 from the 2025-2026 call plus continuing 2024-2025 projects, less those stopped)

secondMetric.name: Proposals submitted to the 2025-2026 innovation voucher call

source.publisher: Agentia Nationala pentru Cercetare si Dezvoltare (ANCD), Raport anual ANCD pentru anul 2025, section 1.4 Proiecte de Inovare si Transfer Tehnologic

records.limits: The agency reports on itself, on pages 28 and 29 of a 137-page PDF. The arithmetic in the report does not close on its face: 10 new projects plus 7 continuing ones is 17, and the report also says four projects were stopped when three firms refused to sign financing contracts, and states the total of 13 without showing the subtraction. The volume is very small: 1,073.0 thousand lei of state money and 153.4 thousand lei of firm co-financing in 2025, roughly 60,000 euros, and the same report counts five technology transfer projects approved in 2025 under a separate call, not added here. The 2024 report gives seven voucher projects funded in 2024, so the instrument is two years old and its scale is pilot-like even if national in reach. Counts are projects financed, not completed or commercialised. The started year is the first funded call read in the 2024 report, not a programme launch date.

pattern.mechanism: The national research agency gives small firms a voucher that pays a public research organisation to do a defined R&D or testing job for them, with the firm co-financing a share.
preconditions: A research funding agency able to contract firms as well as research institutes
Research organisations with services firms are willing to buy
Firms willing to sign a state contract and co-finance, which four 2025 winners were not

records.title: ANOFM voucher-based vocational training for the unemployed
