records.claim: Moldova's National Employment Agency (ANOFM) enrolled 1,751 registered unemployed people, 1,223 of them women, in voucher-based vocational training courses between January and August 2026, and 952 unemployed people graduated from voucher courses in the same months, some of them enrolled in 2025.

metric.name: Unemployed people enrolled in voucher-based vocational training courses since the start of the year (row 16, art. 32)

secondMetric.name: Unemployed people who graduated from voucher-based courses since the start of the year, including those enrolled in 2025 (row 17)

source.publisher: Agentia Nationala pentru Ocuparea Fortei de Munca (ANOFM), Raport statistic august 2026 (monthly statistical report)

records.limits: The agency reports on itself, in a monthly statistical PDF (rows 15 to 18); the figures are year-to-date for eight months, not a full year, and no December 2025 report was found at an open URL, so no full-year or prior-year comparison is made. The agency's 2025 activity report is a one-page scan with no text. Separately, 95 unemployed people enrolled in workplace training (art. 33) over the same months, not added. The scale is small: about 1,750 enrolments in eight months in a country of about 2.4 million, limited to the registered unemployed (6,010 at the start of August), so it says nothing about adults in work. The 2025 start is the date of the agency's launch event for its voucher platform for training the unemployed (17 April 2025, on the agency site); training of the unemployed under the employment law existed before vouchers, and that earlier delivery is not counted.

pattern.mechanism: The employment agency gives registered unemployed people a training voucher redeemable with an approved provider through an online platform, and reports enrolments and graduates monthly.
preconditions: A register of approved vocational training providers in the regions
An online voucher platform linked to the unemployment register
A state budget line for active measures under the employment law

records.title: Proiect de transfer la operatorul economic (PTE) research-to-firm transfer grants
records.claim: Romania's research funding agency UEFISCDI accepted 35 firm-led projects with research organisation partners for funding in the 2024 PTE (transfer to the economic operator) competition, plus one more on a second list, after 47 in the 2021 competition.

metric.name: PTE 2024 projects on the list accepted for funding

secondMetric.name: PTE 2021 projects on the list accepted for funding

source.publisher: Unitatea Executiva pentru Finantarea Invatamantului Superior, a Cercetarii, Dezvoltarii si Inovarii (UEFISCDI), Lista proiectelor PTE 2024 acceptate la finantare (PNCDI IV, Programul Parteneriate pentru Inovare)

records.limits: The count is ours: the four-page PDF numbers its rows 1 to 35 and is a list of projects accepted for funding, not contracts signed or completed; a separate 'Lista nr. 2' adds one more project (PN-IV-P7-7.1-PTE-2024-0336), and a reserve list exists, so the contracted number may differ. The 2021 figure is the row count of a different file on the same agency site (resource-862977, 'Lista proiectelor PTE 2021 acceptate la finantare'), not at the cited URL. Each project is coordinated by a company with one or more universities or national R&D institutes as partners, and the maximum grant was about 1.5 million lei, so this is a few dozen projects a competition in a country of 19 million. PTE competitions are not annual (2019, 2021, 2024, and a 2026 call that closed on 16 September 2026 with 378 proposals submitted and none funded yet), so the gaps between rounds are part of the record. The started year is approximate: PTE ran under PNCDI III from about 2014 to 2016, which is not stated in the cited file. The figures say nothing about technology actually transferred or sold.

pattern.mechanism: The national research funding agency runs a periodic competition in which a company leads a project to take a research organisation's result to market, with the state grant paying both sides under state aid rules.
preconditions: A national R&D plan with a partnerships programme and a budget line for it
Public universities and national R&D institutes with results ready for transfer
An agency with an online submission and peer evaluation platform

records.title: ANOFM national vocational training plan, and its fall after 2023
records.claim: Romania's National Employment Agency (ANOFM) enrolled 15,634 people in vocational training courses, skills assessment and apprenticeships under its national training plan in 2025, down from 27,843 in 2023, with unemployed trainees falling from 25,420 to 11,082 while the registered unemployment rate rose.

metric.name: People included in vocational training, skills assessment or apprenticeship programmes organised by ANOFM

secondMetric.name: Same count two years earlier (ANOFM activity report for 2023)

source.publisher: Agentia Nationala pentru Ocuparea Fortei de Munca (ANOFM), Raport de activitate al ANOFM pentru anul 2025, section III.1 Formarea profesionala

records.limits: The agency reports on itself; the figure is on page 17 of a 59-page PDF, and the plan target (24,440) is on the same page. The 2023 peak is from the agency's 2023 activity report (https://www.anofm.ro/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Raport_activitate_ANOFM_2023.pdf, 27,843 people, 25,420 unemployed), and the 2024 report gives 18,859, so the fall is over two years; earlier years were not read because the 2021 and 2022 report files are not text-searchable, so 2023 is the highest year checked, not a demonstrated all-time peak. The count mixes short courses, competence assessments and workplace apprenticeships (2,257 apprentices in 2025 against 591 in 2024, so the classroom fall is steeper than the total), and counts enrolments, not completions. The registered unemployment rate is from the same reports (2.89 percent average in 2023, 3.24 percent in 2025), so the fall is not explained by fewer unemployed. Against roughly 12 million Romanians aged 25 to 64 the programme reaches about one adult in 800, so it is a delivery record, not a participation rate. The 2002 start is the year the agency's training remit was set in law (Law 76/2002), not read at the source.

pattern.mechanism: The national employment agency sets an annual national training plan and delivers it mainly through its own regional adult training centres, free for the registered unemployed and paid for others.
preconditions: An unemployment insurance budget that can pay course costs
A network of regional adult training centres run by the agency
County agencies that refer registered jobseekers into courses
pattern.travelled: Romania's plan targets fell with delivery (28,877 places planned for 2023, 24,440 for 2025), so the agency planned the decline as well as reporting it.

records.title: Innovation Fund Collaborative Grant Scheme (Program saradnje nauke i privrede)
records.claim: Serbia's Innovation Fund financed 79 joint research and development projects of private small and medium firms with public research organisations across eight calls of its Collaborative Grant Scheme, the eighth call, decided in 2024, funding eight.

metric.name: Collaborative Grant Scheme projects listed as funded, all eight cycles (counted from the Fund's per-cycle lists)

secondMetric.name: Projects funded in the eighth cycle

source.publisher: Innovation Fund of the Republic of Serbia (Fond za inovacionu delatnost), Collaborative Grant Scheme, funded projects, all cycles

records.limits: The Fund reports on its own programme and publishes no total: 79 is our count of the project entries on its per-cycle pages (14, 9, 13, 12, 11, 6, 6 and 8 projects in cycles one to eight; each page renders every project twice, and the count is of distinct titles). The pages carry no dates, so the year of each cycle is not read there; that the eighth call funded eight projects in 2024 is from the Ministry of Finance CFCU release of 15 August 2024 ('8 under the Collaborative Grant Scheme Program'), and a Fund release of 20 March 2024 reports six joint projects in the call before. The counts are grants awarded, not completed projects or commercial results. The scheme is co-financed by the European Union through IPA and began under World Bank financing, so the delivery is the Fund's but the money is partly external. Annual volume has fallen from 11 to 14 projects a call in the early cycles to six to eight, and the programme page shows the call as closed with no ninth cycle listed on 2026-10-02, so 'operating' rests on the absence of any announced end. The started year is approximate: the first cycle is not dated on the cited page. Each consortium needs only one firm and one public research organisation, and requires firms to co-finance 30 to 40 percent, so 79 projects is a small national volume.

pattern.mechanism: The national innovation fund runs competitive calls in which a private SME leads a consortium with a public research organisation, pays part of the budget, and must route at least 15 percent of the grant to the research partner.
preconditions: An arm's length innovation agency with grant management capacity built under donor projects
Accredited public research institutes and faculties able to contract with firms
SMEs able to co-finance a third or more of an R&D budget
pattern.travelled: Montenegro's Innovation Fund runs a Collaborative Grants programme on the same template.

records.title: National Employment Service labour market training, and its 2025 non-delivery
records.claim: Serbia's National Employment Service put 1,613 unemployed people into labour market training (obuke za trziste rada) in 2024, but in 2025 it delivered none of the 1,100 places planned for that year for lack of accredited providers, and only 626 people trained under contracts carried over from the 2023 and 2024 plans.

metric.name: Unemployed people included in labour market training in the year (Table 6, 5.4), all from earlier years' plans

secondMetric.name: Unemployed people included in labour market training, previous year (Table 6, 5.4, report for 2024)

source.publisher: Nacionalna sluzba za zaposljavanje (National Employment Service), Izvestaj o radu Nacionalne sluzbe za 2025. godinu, Table 6 and section 5.4

records.limits: The agency reports on itself, in a 127-page PDF in Serbian Cyrillic: Table 6 is on page 23 and the statement that the measure was not realised in 2025 ('dovelo do nerealizacije ove mere u 2025. godini') is on pages 28 to 29, where the agency attributes it to too few training programmes with publicly recognised adult education provider (JPOA) status at the locations needed. The 2024 figure is in the 2024 report (Izvestaj o radu NSZ za 2024. godinu, Table 6, on the same agency page), not at the cited URL. 2024 is the previous year, not a demonstrated peak: the 2019 report gives 1,257. The scale is very small for a country of about 6.6 million: other NSZ measures in the same table (internships, functional basic adult education with 1,157 participants in 2025, employer-requested training with 601) are separate counts and were not added in. The counts are people included, not completions or job outcomes, and cover only the registered unemployed. A one-year procurement and accreditation failure may reverse; the record documents a dated loss, not a permanent end. The started year is approximate: the measure appears in the agency's reports from at least 2010 and the 2009 start is the year the current employment law took effect, not read at the source.

pattern.mechanism: The public employment service buys short vocational courses for registered unemployed people from a catalogue it procures each year, and since the adult education law only from providers accredited as publicly recognised adult education organisers.
preconditions: A national catalogue of training matched to local vacancies
Enough accredited private and public training providers in each district
A procurement cycle that closes early enough in the year for courses to run
pattern.travelled: Tying public training money to an accreditation register raises quality on paper; Serbia's 2025 report shows the cost when the register is thinner than the demand.

records.title: eSupport one-off 6,500 hryvnia payment to workers in combat regions, March 2022
records.claim: After Russia's full-scale invasion on 24 February 2022, Ukraine's Cabinet allocated UAH 21,450 million for a one-off eSupport payment by Resolution 199 of 4 March 2022, opened applications in the Diia app on 8 March to insured employees and sole proprietors in regions with active fighting, paid the first 6,500 hryvnia transfers on 21 March, and by 27 March had paid 2.7 million people UAH 17.9 billion against 4 million applications.

metric.name: People paid the 6,500 hryvnia eSupport payment, cumulative

secondMetric.name: Days from the invasion to the first eSupport payments (24 February to 21 March 2022)

source.publisher: Government of Ukraine portal (kmu.gov.ua), Ministry of Digital Transformation release 'Mintsyfry: maiemo 4 mln zaiavok na yePidtrymku', 27 March 2022 (Internet Archive copy of 31 March 2022)

records.limits: The 2.7 million and the UAH 17.9 billion are the Ministry of Digital Transformation's own running count on the Government portal, not an audited outturn; the final number of recipients is not on this page. The live page at kmu.gov.ua answered a captcha to a script on the day of retrieval, so the record cites the Internet Archive copy of 31 March 2022, which carries the same text. The release says the service opened on 8 March and was open to employees for whom the single social contribution was paid and to sole proprietors of all groups in 14 listed regions and Kyiv, so eligibility was by region, not by a test that the person's work had stopped. The 25 days is our count: the start date of payments comes from a second Government portal release of 22 March 2022 ('Pochalysia pershi vyplaty 6500 hrn yePidtrymky', kmu.gov.ua), which says payments began the day before and had reached almost 500,000 people, and the allocation and its date come from Cabinet Resolution 199 of 4 March 2022 on kmu.gov.ua. Speed was bought with eligibility checks that were later found loose: press reports from August 2022 cite tens of thousands of payments to ineligible people, a figure this record does not carry because no official page with it was opened. A one-off flat transfer to workers in listed regions is a fast payment, not a durable programme change, and it relied on a payment rail (the Diia app and the existing eSupport scheme) that already existed before the shock.

pattern.mechanism: The Cabinet reused the existing eSupport payment rail, let insured workers in combat regions apply in the Diia app, checked them against social insurance records and paid a flat sum to their bank cards within four weeks of the invasion.
preconditions: A national digital identity app with millions of users and verified bank cards
A social insurance register that could confirm employment and location quickly
A reserve fund the Cabinet could reallocate by resolution
pattern.travelled: The same rail paid later wartime transfers, and it is the Ukrainian version of what Togo (Novissi) and Brazil (Auxilio Emergencial) did in 2020: pay by phone first and check later.

records.title: State-paid technical unemployment indemnity in the 2020 state of emergency
records.claim: Two days after the state of emergency was declared on 16 March 2020, Romania's Government made the unemployment insurance budget pay 75 percent of base salary to employees whose contracts were suspended (Emergency Ordinance 30 of 18 March 2020), and by mid-June 2020 the employment agency ANOFM had approved the indemnity for 2,067,970 employees and paid RON 2,937 million, with 241,453 employer requests approved within the legal deadline and 61 late.

metric.name: Employees for whom the technical unemployment indemnity was approved

secondMetric.name: Indemnities paid for suspended contracts during the state of emergency

source.publisher: Curtea de Conturi a Romaniei (Court of Accounts), special report 'Gestionarea resurselor publice in perioada starii de urgenta', August 2020

records.limits: The live PDF at curteadeconturi.ro returned a Cloudflare challenge to a script on the day of retrieval, so the record cites the Internet Archive copy of the same file. The figures are in a 162-page PDF: Table 9 (payments at 15 June 2020) and Table 10 (requests, beneficiaries and on-time approvals by region) on printed page 59, the 2,067,970 and the 2,483,890 employees requested on printed page 60, and the ordinance date (OUG nr. 30/18.03.2020) in the annex on PDF page 132. The audit is independent but the counts are 'date furnizate de ANOFM'. The legal deadline was the agency's own procedural one, and Table 10 counts requests, not days, so the record shows that the agency kept its deadline, not the median time to payment. 409,876 employees' requests were still pending at the cut-off. The indemnity was paid to employers, who passed it to staff; the report finds overpayments and payments to ineligible people among its RON 38.3 million of damages across all emergency spending. The scheme suspended contracts rather than shortening hours, so it is a wage replacement for idle workers, and its speed owes much to an existing Labour Code mechanism that the ordinance financed from the state budget.

pattern.mechanism: The Government took the Labour Code's existing technical unemployment, which employers paid themselves, and by emergency ordinance moved its cost to the unemployment insurance budget for the emergency, with electronic filing and a statutory payment deadline for the county employment agencies.
preconditions: An existing statutory form of temporary contract suspension that employers already used
County employment agencies able to process employer lists against the employment register
An unemployment insurance budget with a surplus the Government could redirect by ordinance
pattern.travelled: Most EU members ran a short-time work or suspension scheme in 2020, financed in part by EU SURE loans; Romania's was a suspension scheme rather than Kurzarbeit and reached about two million employees in three months.

records.title: Prima Casa / Noua Casa state-guaranteed mortgages through banks, and their wind-down
records.claim: Romania's Prima Casa programme, renamed Noua Casa in 2020, had the National Credit Guarantee Fund for SMEs (FNGCIMM) issue 334,048 state guarantees and guarantee promises worth RON 31.68 billion on mortgages made by participating banks between 2009 and December 2024, but only 811 guarantees in 2024, and the ratio of guaranteed lending to banks' unguaranteed housing loans fell from about 70 percent in 2017 to about 10 percent in 2023.

metric.name: Ratio of Prima Casa / Noua Casa guaranteed lending to banks' unguaranteed housing loans to individuals

secondMetric.name: Same ratio in 2017, the first year of the 2017-2021 strategy and the earliest year the source gives

source.publisher: Ministry of Finance of Romania, Nota de fundamentare for the draft Government Decision on the Noua Casa guarantee ceiling for 2025, 4 March 2025

records.limits: The live file at mfinante.gov.ro did not answer a script on the day of retrieval, so the record cites the Internet Archive copy; the figures are on pages 1 and 2 of a nine-page PDF, prepared with FNGCIMM, which runs the programme, so the ministry is grading its own scheme. The decline was largely chosen: the note says the 2017-2021 medium-term strategy set falling guarantee ceilings to decelerate state intervention and that its objectives were met, while private mortgage lending without a state guarantee grew, so the erosion is a planned withdrawal as much as a loss of capacity. The 70 and 10 percent are approximate ('aprox.', 'circa') and describe a ratio of guaranteed to unguaranteed lending as the note words it, which is not the same as a market share. 2017 is the first year of the strategy, not a demonstrated peak: the note gives no earlier year, and the programme's share was probably at least as high in its first years after 2009. 811 guarantees in 2024 is a calendar-year count against a cumulative total, and the note does not give the annual peak; the 1,449 guarantees the Ministry of Finance paid out to banks since launch show the state carried real credit risk. Whether the programme raised home ownership or mainly house prices is not shown.

pattern.mechanism: The finance ministry, through a state guarantee fund acting as its agent, guaranteed half or more of each first-home mortgage that participating banks underwrote, set a lower interest cap and annual guarantee ceilings, and then cut the ceilings year by year so private lending took over.
preconditions: A guarantee fund with a mandate from the state and contracts with every major bank
Annual guarantee ceilings set in the budget law, which is the lever that also wound the programme down
A housing market where banks were willing to lend once the state took part of the risk
pattern.travelled: First-home guarantee schemes run through banks exist across Europe; Romania's is one where a crisis measure from 2009 grew to dominate the mortgage market and was then deliberately tapered.

records.title: Automatic loan repayment moratorium, March 2020
records.claim: On 18 March 2020 Hungary's Government introduced a repayment moratorium until the end of 2020 that applied automatically to household and corporate loans disbursed before that date, and by June 2020 about 1.6 million of the roughly 2.7 million household borrowers used it on at least one loan, while 44 percent of corporate loans outstanding were in moratorium at the end of the second quarter.

metric.name: Household customers using the moratorium on at least one loan (around 60 percent of about 2.7 million)

secondMetric.name: Share of corporate loans outstanding in moratorium

source.publisher: Magyar Nemzeti Bank, Financial Stability Report, November 2020

records.limits: The numbers are in a PDF: the 1.6 million household customers on PDF page 38 (Box 3), the 44 percent of corporate loans on page 39, and the 18 March 2020 start and its automatic application on page 48 (Box 5). The 1.6 million is the MNB's own calculation from bank-reported data. Because the moratorium was opt-out, participation measures inertia as well as need, and the report says the moratorium does not prevent credit risk rising. The speed figure is the date of a rule, not of a payment: a moratorium costs the budget nothing up front and shifts the cost to banks and to borrowers who keep accruing interest. The report records that the Government would extend it from January 2021 for vulnerable debtors; the record does not cover the later extensions or the losses when it ended. The MNB proposed the measure, so it is reporting on its own advice.

pattern.mechanism: The Government, on the central bank's proposal, suspended principal and interest repayments by decree for every existing loan unless the borrower opted out, which needed no application and no new administrative channel.
preconditions: Emergency decree powers that let the Government change private loan contracts overnight
A banking supervisor that could tell banks how to book the suspended instalments
Banks capitalised enough to absorb nine months of deferred cash flow
pattern.travelled: Most EU members ran payment moratoria in 2020, usually opt-in and bank-led under EBA guidelines; Hungary's blanket opt-out design reached more borrowers faster and was harder to unwind.

records.title: Funding for Growth Scheme (Novekedesi Hitelprogram), central bank refinancing lent by commercial banks
records.claim: Hungary's central bank refinanced commercial banks at zero interest on condition that they lent to small and medium firms at a capped margin under the Funding for Growth Scheme, and across its phases from June 2013 to 2022 some 75 thousand enterprises received about HUF 6,400 billion of loans, more than half of them investment loans.

metric.name: Enterprises that gained access to FGS loans across all phases

secondMetric.name: Loans granted under all FGS phases

source.publisher: Magyar Nemzeti Bank, From the turnaround in lending to the green transition: collection of studies on the nine years of the Funding for Growth Scheme to date, 2013-2022

records.limits: The central bank designed, financed and here evaluates its own scheme; both headline numbers are rounded ('some', 'approximately') and appear in a PDF on page 7 and again on pages 9 and 20; the MNB also publishes a Power BI dashboard of the loans that a script cannot read. The MNB carried the funding cost and banks the credit risk, so the partnership was a public subsidy delivered by private lenders, with the policy cost sitting off budget on the central bank's balance sheet. The book's estimate that the scheme added more than 5 percentage points to GDP between 2013 and 2021 is the MNB's own model result and is not used here. Enterprises are counted across phases (FGS 1 to 3, FGS fix, FGS Go!, Green Home), so the 75 thousand cannot be compared with the stock of firms in any one year, and the volumes include refinanced foreign currency loans in the first phase. Some lending would have happened without the subsidy; the record does not measure additionality.

pattern.mechanism: The central bank offered banks zero-cost refinancing for loans to small and medium firms on condition that they cap the client rate, so banks did the origination, credit assessment and servicing while the central bank bore the funding cost.
preconditions: A central bank willing to run a targeted quasi-fiscal programme on its own balance sheet
A banking sector with branch networks reaching small firms nationwide
Low inflation at launch, so zero-rate refinancing did not fight monetary policy, which ceased to hold by 2022
pattern.travelled: The design follows the Bank of England's Funding for Lending Scheme (2012); Hungary ran it longer and steered it to fixed-rate investment loans, and the end of low inflation closed it.

records.title: Three minimum wages paid to private employers in the 2020 state of emergency
records.claim: After the state of emergency of 15 March 2020, Serbia's Government presented a EUR 5.1 billion economic package on 31 March that included paying micro, small and medium firms one minimum wage per employee for three months if they cut staff by no more than 10 percent, and on 7 May 2020 the Ministry of Finance paid about RSD 32 billion as the first minimum wage for 1.055 million employees of 232,000 businesses.

metric.name: Employees covered by the first state-paid minimum wage

secondMetric.name: Days from the 31 March 2020 package to the first payment on 7 May 2020

source.publisher: Government of the Republic of Serbia portal (srbija.gov.rs), 'Sutra isplata prvog minimalca za vise od milion radnika', 6 May 2020

records.limits: The page reports the Finance Minister announcing on 6 May that the payment would be made 'tomorrow', so the record rests on a ministerial statement of a payment due the next day, not on a Treasury outturn, and the figures are approximate ('priblizno 32 milijarde dinara'). The package date and the eligibility condition come from a second Government portal release of 31 March 2020 ('Za ublazavanje posledica epidemije na privredu 5,1 milijarda evra', srbija.gov.rs/vest/456168), which also names 15 March as the cut-off for firms that stopped trading; the 37 days are our count between the two releases. The subsidy was nearly universal for private small firms that applied, so it paid many employers who would have kept staff anyway, and the same release says firms also deferred RSD 29.5 billion of taxes and contributions. The page does not give the second and third payments or a final total. The 'condition' that firms not cut staff by more than 10 percent is a rule, and this record does not show whether it was enforced.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Finance paid a flat minimum wage per employee straight into the accounts of every small private employer that opted in through the tax administration's portal, using payroll tax filings as the register, with a staff-retention condition.
preconditions: Monthly individual payroll tax returns that already listed every employee by employer
A tax administration portal through which firms could opt in without a separate application
Fiscal space from a prior surplus, which the minister cited as what made the payment possible
pattern.travelled: A cruder, faster cousin of short-time work schemes; North Macedonia's 14,500 denar per employee measure of 2020 used the same flat design.

records.title: Moja prva plata, state-paid first-job training placed with employers, and its 2025 halt
records.claim: Serbia's Government paid a monthly allowance to young people without work experience while employers trained them for nine months under the Moja prva plata programme run by the National Employment Service, which placed 9,237 young people with 5,471 employers in the 2021 cycle and 7,214 with 4,520 employers from the 2023 call in January 2024, but ran no call for 2024 and started no activity under the measure in 2025 against a plan of 10,000 places.

metric.name: Young people included in Moja prva plata in the year (Table 6, measure 5.8), against 10,000 planned

secondMetric.name: Young people selected by participating employers in the 2021 cycle, the highest dated count read

source.publisher: Nacionalna sluzba za zaposljavanje (National Employment Service), Izvestaj o radu Nacionalne sluzbe za 2025. godinu, Table 6 and section 5.8

records.limits: The agency reports on its own programme. The zero is in Table 6 (PDF page 23), measure 5.8, planned 10,000 and realised 0, and section 5.8 (PDF page 41) states that no activities to implement the measure were started in 2025; the report gives no reason. The 2021 figure is from a Government portal release (srbija.gov.rs/vest/595588, 3 December 2021), not at the cited URL, and counts young people employers selected at the start of a cycle, not completions; the 2022 cycle was not read, so 2021 is the highest dated count found, not a demonstrated peak. The 2024 report (Izvestaj o radu NSZ za 2024. godinu, Table 6 and page 45, nsz.gov.rs) gives 7,214 young people at 4,520 employers from the 2023 call, contracted between 1 and 19 January 2024, of whom 4,950 were with 3,892 private employers and 2,264 with 628 public employers, and says no public call for 2024 was carried out; the first cycle in 2020 also reserved 2,648 places for public-sector employers, so the programme was never wholly public-private. The 35 percent of first-cycle participants who signed an employment contract is stated in the 2021 release without a denominator or follow-up period. In 2025 municipalities co-financed 36 placements under a local variant (Table 18 of the 2025 report), which this record does not count. The programme portal (mojaprvaplata.gov.rs) still announces a new cycle of up to 10,000 places with no date, so the halt may be a gap between calls rather than an end; the record documents two years without a national call, not abolition. The state paid the allowance and the employer supplied the training and the workplace, so it is a wage subsidy for trainees as much as a training programme, and some employers may have used it in place of hires they would have made anyway.

pattern.mechanism: The Government let firms post training positions on a national portal, let young people apply, had employers pick candidates, and paid the trainees directly through a tripartite contract with the National Employment Service, so firms trained at no wage cost.
preconditions: A national employment service able to sign and monitor thousands of tripartite contracts
Employers short of staff and willing to train, which the programme was designed around
A budget line of about RSD 2 billion per cycle that the Ministry of Finance would renew
pattern.travelled: Close to the youth traineeships run under the EU Youth Guarantee; Serbia's version selects through a single online portal and leaves the choice of candidate to the employer.

records.title: The 60/40 employment retention measure, 2020 to 2021
records.claim: Bulgaria's National Social Security Institute paid employers 60 percent of the wages and contributions of staff kept on during the COVID-19 emergency under Council of Ministers Decree No. 55 of 2020, starting with 68 employers and 1,065 employees on 15 April 2020, and by 4 March 2021 the Ministry of Labour and Social Policy reported BGN 884 million paid under the measure and 300,000 jobs kept.

metric.name: Paid under the 60/40 measure, cumulative

secondMetric.name: Employees in the first published payment list (68 employers)

source.publisher: Ministry of Labour and Social Policy of Bulgaria, news release 'Ministar Sacheva: 884 mln. lv. sa plateni po myarkata 60/40, kato sa zapazeni 300 000 rabotni mesta', 4 March 2021

records.limits: The BGN 884 million and the 300,000 jobs are a minister's statement on the ministry's own site, with no breakdown; 'jobs kept' is the number of supported positions, not a counterfactual estimate of jobs saved. The start figures are our sums from the National Social Security Institute's first payment list (nssi.bg, 'Izplateni kompensatsii po PMS No. 55 ot 2020 g.', file pms55_15042020.xls: 68 employers, 1,065 persons, BGN 274,274), one of 45 lists the Institute published to December 2021; one of them (14 May 2020) is truncated at the source and cannot be read, so we do not give a total from the lists. Speed was modest: the ministry reported only 643 employer applications covering 7,231 employees in late April 2020 (mlsp.government.bg, '643 zayavleniya ot rabotodateli sa postapili po skhemata 60/40'), and uptake grew through May and June. The decree date and the date of the emergency declaration are not on the pages opened, so the record times the response from the first payment, not from the shock.

pattern.mechanism: The Council of Ministers decreed that the social security fund would pay 60 percent of wages and contributions for workers whose employers kept them on, with the employer paying the other 40 percent, and the Employment Agency approved applications that the social security institute then paid and published employer by employer.
preconditions: Monthly employer declarations to the social security institute that identified each insured worker
An Employment Agency able to process employer applications in county offices
A social security fund with the liquidity to pay employers before the budget was revised
pattern.travelled: A short-time work design of the German type with a fixed state share; Bulgaria's distinctive move was publishing every paid employer by name, which made the scheme auditable by the public.

records.title: Chisinau International Airport concession, and its rescission in 2020
records.claim: Moldova's Public Property Agency concessioned the assets of Chisinau International Airport and its land to Avia Invest under contract 4/03 of 30 August 2013, with investment obligations of EUR 244 million over the life of the concession, and in 2020 notified the concessionaire that the contract was rescinded for failing to post the performance guarantee, while Avia Invest claimed EUR 900 million from the state at arbitration in Stockholm.

metric.name: Total investment the concessionaire was to make over the life of the concession

secondMetric.name: Damages Avia Invest claimed from the state at arbitration in Stockholm

source.publisher: Agentia Proprietatii Publice (Public Property Agency of Moldova), 'Comunicat: unele detalieri privind rezolutiunea Contractului de concesiune a activelor aflate in gestiunea I.S. Aeroportul International Chisinau si a terenului aferent, nr. 4/03 din 30 august 2013', 22 July 2020 (Internet Archive copy of 21 September 2021)

records.limits: The source is one party to a dispute stating its case: the agency wrote the communique to answer press coverage, and the EUR 900 million is the concessionaire's claim as the agency reports it, not an award. The live page now returns 404 on app.gov.md and the record cites the Internet Archive copy. The EUR 244 million is a contractual obligation over the whole concession, not an amount invested; the communique gives no figure for what Avia Invest actually invested in 2013 to 2020, so the record shows the partnership's scale on paper and its end, not its delivery. The communique shows a rescission notice that the concessionaire contested, not the end of its operation: no official page opened shows when the airport returned to the state, and secondary sources (not used as evidence) date the final annulment to a Chisinau Court of Appeal ruling of November 2022. The state enterprise I.S. Aeroportul International Chisinau that appears in the agency's procurement notices held the conceded assets throughout the concession, so its presence does not by itself show a return of operations. The outcome of the arbitration is not covered. The concession was the country's flagship infrastructure PPP: the agency's own list of PPP contracts it signed (archived April 2021) showed a single other contract, for bus stations, signed on 19 December 2018, so Moldova's national PPP portfolio was thin before and after this rescission.

pattern.mechanism: The state property agency handed the airport's assets and land to a private concessionaire for investment and operation in exchange for fees and investment obligations, then used the contract's performance-guarantee clause to terminate it once a new government contested the deal.
preconditions: A concession law and a state property agency with authority to award and terminate concessions
A contract with enforceable performance-guarantee clauses, which is what made the rescission possible
Political continuity, which failed here: the concession did not survive a change of government
pattern.travelled: An airport is often a small state's first large concession; Moldova's shows how a concession awarded without broad political cover can be unwound by the next government and end in arbitration.

records.title: Corridor X motorway sections (E-75 and E-80)
records.claim: Serbia's state road company Koridori Srbije built 45.5 km of Corridor X motorway on the E-75 towards North Macedonia and the E-80 Dimitrovgrad bypass towards Bulgaria under a loan approved in July 2009, finishing at a total project cost of EUR316.2 million against an appraisal estimate of EUR318.2 million, but taking about 10 years from approval to full completion against a planned 6.5, with the loan closing in September 2019 instead of December 2015.

metric.name: Final project cost including government counterpart funds

secondMetric.name: Project cost estimated at appraisal, including contingencies

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Serbia Corridor X Highway Project (P108005), March 2020

records.limits: The figures are the World Bank's, in a completion report on a project it financed and rated, written with data from the implementing agency. The two costs are in para. 11 and Table 2 (printed page 8) and para. 54 (page 19); the 10 years against 6.5 and the closing dates are in para. 32 (page 13) and the datasheet (page 2). Staying on budget was helped by a 2016 additional loan of EUR35 million that covered overruns (datasheet and para. 58), and the construction cost alone rose 21 percent over the initial contract prices, so 'on budget' means within an appraisal estimate that carried contingencies, not within contract prices. The Dimitrovgrad bypass contractors were terminated twice and its works finished in November 2019 against an April 2012 contract date (Table 6). The record covers only the World Bank financed sections of a longer corridor co-financed by EIB, EBRD and others, whose cost and schedule are not reported here. Traffic in 2018 was 46 percent of the appraisal forecast on the E-80. The start year is the first works contract (April 2010, Table 6).

pattern.mechanism: A dedicated state motorway company procured large lots under development bank rules, held the cost line by re-bidding failed contracts and drawing an additional loan, and accepted years of delay rather than scope cuts.
preconditions: A single implementing company for the corridor with procurement and supervision staff
Contingencies in the appraisal estimate large enough to absorb variation orders
Government budget for expropriation, whose absence caused the early delays

records.title: Road Sector Development Project on the M-03 and M-12, and its cut scope
records.claim: Ukraine's road agency Ukravtodor rehabilitated or upgraded 156.3 km of the M-03 Kyiv to Kharkiv and M-12 corridors under a US$560 million loan approved in November 2015, after slow progress led the government in 2017 to cancel US$222.2 million of the loan, dropping three M-03 bypasses and two long-term maintenance contracts, so the loan closed at US$337.8 million in September 2022, nine months after its original date.

metric.name: Loan amount after cancellation, fully disbursed

secondMetric.name: Original loan amount at approval

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Ukraine Road Sector Development Project (P149322), November 2023

records.limits: The figures are the World Bank's, in a completion report on its own loan, and the loan amount is not the full cost of the works; no figure for the cost of the delivered roads against an appraisal estimate per km was used. The cancellation and its reasons (land acquisition not started at Poltava, community objections at Kopyly, a realignment at Chutove) are in paras. 23 and 26 to 27 (printed pages 10 to 12); the 156.3 km is in para. 41 (page 16); amounts and dates are on the datasheet (page 2). In 2019 disbursement was about 11 percent with over 60 percent of the period elapsed, and some lots were moved in from a parallel World Bank road project, so the delivered kilometres mix two programmes. Russia's invasion in February 2022 stopped the civil works under force majeure seven months before closing, so the final delay is not all the agency's. The record shows a scope cut, not a cost overrun, and says nothing about the separate Great Construction programme.

pattern.mechanism: The national road agency delivered the widening of a corridor it had already been rebuilding with the same lender, and when bypasses stalled on land acquisition the government cancelled them rather than extend the loan.
preconditions: An experienced implementation unit from earlier corridor loans
Land acquisition and resettlement procedures that can be completed before works are tendered
A lender willing to cancel and reallocate rather than hold undisbursed funds

records.title: M6 Minsk to Grodno transit corridor upgrade
records.claim: Belarus's Ministry of Transport and Communications widened 154 km of the M6 Minsk to Grodno highway to dual carriageway under a loan approved in December 2014, against 86 km planned, after civil works for the planned sections were awarded for less than half the estimate; the corridor component cost US$242.15 million against US$259.28 million at entry, and the loan closed in June 2022 against an original June 2020.

metric.name: Length of single carriageway reconstructed and widened to dual carriageway

secondMetric.name: Length planned at entry

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Belarus Transit Corridor Improvement Project (P149697), December 2022

records.limits: The figures are the World Bank's, from a completion report on its own loan, with costs reported by the borrower. The component costs are in Table 2 (printed page 9), the 154 against 86 km in para. 32 (page 14), the savings in para. 52 (page 21) and the dates on the datasheet (page 2). The low cost was helped by a government decision to exempt the works from VAT, so part of the saving is a transfer within the state, not efficiency. The actual cost excludes design, supervision and land acquisition, which the government paid separately. Works were not contracted until July 2016, more than a year after effectiveness, because of a dispute over whether state-owned Belarusian contractors were eligible, and the road safety centre was incomplete at closing. The report was written in 2022, after which World Bank engagement with Belarus stopped, so later maintenance of the road is unknown.

pattern.mechanism: The transport ministry tendered the corridor in lots to joint ventures of local state-owned contractors, and when bids came in far below estimate it used the savings to add 67 km of the same corridor without new financing.
preconditions: Complete designs before effectiveness, so works could start as soon as procurement closed
A domestic road construction industry with capacity and equipment
A cost estimate high enough that competitive bids produced savings rather than claims

records.title: Federation Road Sector Modernization Project, and its shrunken rehabilitation scope
records.claim: The Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina's public road company PC Roads FBH delivered 76.9 km of road works, including a 35 km upgrade of the Neum to Stolac road, under a project approved in August 2016, but rehabilitated only 41.75 km of main roads against an appraisal target of 178 km, which was cut to 42.23 km in 2021, and the closing date moved from December 2021 to September 2023.

metric.name: Roads rehabilitated, non-rural, achieved at closing

secondMetric.name: Target for roads rehabilitated, non-rural, at appraisal

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Bosnia and Herzegovina Federation Road Sector Modernization Project, April 2024

records.limits: The figures are the World Bank's, from a completion report on a project it co-financed with the EIB. The 178 and 42.23 km targets are in para. 55 (printed page 19), and the 41.75 km achieved against the revised 42.23 km target is in the outcome table (Table 4, page 13), the 76.9 km and the Neum to Stolac upgrade in paras. 30 to 31 (page 11), the cost per km in para. 45 (page 17) and the dates on the datasheet (page 2). The Bank attributes the cut to designs that were only 1.0 km complete at entry, so the 178 km target may have been an error of preparation rather than a delivery that shrank; the report says rehabilitation cost per km came out more than five times the plan for the same reason. Total project cost rose from US$101.3 million to about US$105.5 million, mostly as an EIB increase. Land acquisition and COVID-19 delayed the Crnaja tunnel and led to sections being cancelled. The project covers one of the country's two entities, not Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole.

pattern.mechanism: The entity road company took a multilateral loan for a list of sections whose designs did not yet exist, then cut the list to what designs, land and budget allowed and concentrated on one strategic coastal link.
preconditions: Detailed designs and land acquisition finished before the results framework is fixed
An entity-level road agency able to borrow with state guarantee
Co-financing that can be raised when costs move

records.title: Local Roads Improvement Project, and its halved scope
records.claim: Moldova's State Roads Administration upgraded 149.3 km of unpaved local roads to paved standard under a project approved in October 2015, after unit costs doubled from US$230,000 to about US$415,000 per km and contracts on 42.3 km were terminated, so a 2019 restructuring cut the target from 300 km to 150 km and the project closed in July 2023 instead of March 2021.

metric.name: Rural roads rehabilitated

secondMetric.name: Rural roads to be rehabilitated, target at appraisal

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Moldova Local Roads Improvement Project (P150357), January 2024

records.limits: The figures are the World Bank's, from a completion report on its own credit, which rated it. The 300 to 150 km cut and the unit cost doubling are in para. 54 (printed page 26), the terminated contracts on 42.3 km in para. 39 (page 21), the 149.3 km in the results table (page 16) and the dates on the datasheet. The doubling followed a switch from a cheap surface treatment that local contractors could not build to conventional asphalt, so part of the cost rise bought a more durable road. These are local roads, a programme of many small contracts rather than one major build, and the US$102.5 million project is small against Moldova's national road spending.

pattern.mechanism: The road administration designed for a low-cost paving technique, failed to attract bidders able to build it, then redesigned for asphalt at twice the unit cost and halved the length.
preconditions: A contractor market able to bid on the chosen technique
Bid and performance security terms small firms can meet
Maintenance budgets matched to the pavement type chosen

records.title: Regional and Local Roads Connectivity Project
records.claim: Albania's Albanian Development Fund rehabilitated about 70 km of regional and local roads under a US$50 million loan approved in April 2018, against 55 km planned, after civil works were awarded at up to 48 percent below estimate, with the closing date extended by 18 months to June 2024.

metric.name: Regional and local roads rehabilitated

secondMetric.name: Regional and local roads to be rehabilitated, original target

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Albania Regional and Local Roads Connectivity Project (P163239), December 2024

records.limits: This is a small programme of regional road contracts, not a major national build, and it is filed because no official cost or schedule outturn for a larger Albanian project (the Arbri road concession, the Durres to Kukes motorway) was found; it is weak evidence for the construct. The figures are the World Bank's, from a completion report on its own loan. The 55 and 70 km are in para. 12 and para. 58 (printed page 16); the report attributes the savings partly to the Albanian Development Fund's own cost estimation method, which it says overestimated costs, so 'under budget' partly measures a padded estimate. The 18-month extension is on the datasheet and in para. 21; the report cites COVID-19, the 2019 earthquake and land acquisition at Pogradec. 'About 70 km' is approximate in the source, and the source is inconsistent: the summary results table reports 62 km rehabilitated against the 55 km target, while the annex results table and the text give 70 km as of October 2024. The start year is the approval and signing year (2018); the first works date is not stated on the pages read.

pattern.mechanism: A development fund that has implemented donor-financed roads since 1993 ran competitive bids among local firms, and used the savings to extend the list of roads.
preconditions: An implementing agency with long donor procurement experience
Enough local contractors to make bidding competitive
A lender willing to let savings extend scope

records.title: Kicevo to Ohrid motorway, and its cost and time overrun
records.claim: North Macedonia's Public Enterprise for State Roads contracted Sinohydro in November 2013 to build the 56.7 km Kicevo to Ohrid section of motorway A2 for EUR411 million by January 2018; by December 2021 five annexes had moved completion to December 2023 and raised the contract value by EUR187 million (45 percent) to EUR598 million, and the State Audit Office found works 72 percent complete by value in August 2023.

metric.name: Contract value after annexes

secondMetric.name: Contract value at signing (contracted completion January 2018)

source.publisher: State Audit Office of North Macedonia, Final report on the financial and compliance audit of the Public Enterprise for State Roads for 2022, February 2024

records.limits: The figures are in a PDF in Macedonian, in the key audit matter section 5.1 (printed pages 25 to 27); the 45 percent increase is also stated in the summary (printed page 4). The road was still under construction when the audit was written, so the record shows an overrun in progress, not an outturn; later annexes and deadlines reported in the press (a further increase and a 2027 deadline) were not checked against an official document. The EUR598 million is the contract value; the audit puts total investment, including expropriation, interest and exchange differences, at about EUR575 million spent by November 2023, and financing at US$685 million in two Chinese loans. The audit attributes the overrun to a basic design drawn up between 2002 and 2010 that did not match the terrain, giving 42 variations, which is the auditor's reading. The contractor was named by a 2013 law rather than chosen by open tender, so the record also reflects a procurement choice. 'Operating' means the build is still running, not that the road is open.

pattern.mechanism: The government named a Chinese contractor by statute under a bilateral loan agreement and started construction on an old design, then absorbed the redesign of tunnels, cuttings and landslide sections through successive annexes that raised the price and moved the deadline.
preconditions: A loan-tied contractor selection that skips competitive tendering
A basic design old enough to be out of step with ground conditions
Parliamentary approval of annexes rather than a fixed-price baseline

records.title: Budapest metro line 4, first section, and its cost and time overrun
records.claim: Hungary's State Audit Office reported in September 2010 that the first section of Budapest metro line 4, approved by the capital in September 2004 at a cost of HUF236.5 billion with a deadline of end 2009, was forecast to cost HUF370 billion, 56.4 percent more, and to open in the second half of 2013.

metric.name: Forecast investment cost of the first section, current prices

secondMetric.name: Investment cost in the 2004 permit document, current prices

source.publisher: State Audit Office of Hungary (Allami Szamvevoszek), Report 1023 on the audit of the investment process of metro line 4, September 2010

records.limits: The figures are in a PDF in Hungarian (summary findings, printed pages 12 to 13, with a chart of planned dates and costs); they are a mid-construction forecast, not the final outturn, and the line's opening in March 2014 and its final cost are not in this source. The auditor attributes part of the increase to scope added after the permit: EU-supported municipal works around stations (HUF39.5 billion), a single-vault station redesign (HUF44.8 billion) and reserves of about 14 percent, so not all of the 56.4 percent is overrun on the same scope. The report's chart puts the opening date in the 1996 feasibility study at 2005, so the delay looks larger against that baseline. The investor was the City of Budapest through its project directorate, with central government paying a large share under a 2004 agreement, so the delivery is a joint municipal and national one. Later OLAF findings on irregularities were not used.

pattern.mechanism: The capital set a deadline in its 2004 permit before permits and land were secured, signed works contracts in 2006 with penalty deadlines it then had to relax, and redesigned stations after an architectural competition while construction was under way.
preconditions: A financing agreement between city and state that fixed the budget before design was complete
A permit deadline set without reference to the state of technical preparation
Contracts whose penalty dates were linked, so one slip moved all of them

records.title: Road Infrastructure Rehabilitation Project, and its cut after the 2009 budget squeeze
records.claim: Bulgaria's Road Infrastructure Agency rehabilitated national roads under a EUR144 million project approved in June 2007, but after budget cuts in 2010 cancelled three lots on about 87 km where works had not started, reducing the length from 450 km to 307 km, and closed in June 2013, two years late, at EUR97.1 million, 67 percent of the appraisal estimate.

metric.name: Total project cost, actual

secondMetric.name: Total project cost, appraisal estimate

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Bulgaria Road Infrastructure Rehabilitation Project, December 2013

records.limits: The figures are the World Bank's, from a completion report on its own loan, which reproduces the agency's own implementation report as an annex. The 450 to 307 km reduction and the cancelled lots are in section 1.6 (printed page 4); the costs in Annex 1 (page 19); the original and revised closing dates on the datasheet. Spending fell because scope was cut, not because works came in cheap, so the 67 percent is a measure of a shrunken programme, not of savings. The cause the report names is the government's fiscal restraint after the 2008 to 2009 crisis, with 2010 budget funds spent on 2009 obligations, and only 8 to 9 percent of the loan disbursed by mid-2009. These are rehabilitation lots on existing class I to III roads, not a new motorway, and the record says nothing about the EU-funded motorways built in the same years.

pattern.mechanism: The road agency contracted nine regional rehabilitation lots on a loan, then, when the national budget could not cover its co-financing and payments, cancelled the lots not yet started and stretched the rest over two more years.
preconditions: Co-financing from a national budget exposed to a fiscal shock
Contracts signed before the budget for their full duration was secured
A lender willing to restructure and extend rather than close

records.title: Recovery from the May 2014 floods: power supply and flood defences
records.claim: After the May 2014 floods evacuated about 32,000 people and flooded the Kolubara open-pit mines that fuel 40 percent of Serbia's generating capacity, the state utility EPS dewatered the Tamnava West mine by the first quarter of 2015 and kept supply at pre-flood levels with no recorded shortages, and the Directorate of Water Management rebuilt or upgraded 71 km of flood protection that by October 2019 covered 24,944 households against a target of 9,000.

metric.name: Households receiving improved flood protection

secondMetric.name: Length of flood protection works reconstructed or rehabilitated

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Serbia Floods Emergency Recovery Project (P152018), April 2020

records.limits: The figures are the World Bank's, in a completion report on an emergency loan it financed and rated; the event figures are in para. 1 (printed page 6), the power and mine results in para. 45 (pages 16 to 17), and the flood protection figures in para. 51 (page 19). Most of the loan bought electricity imports for the 2014 to 2015 winter, so 'no shortages' partly measures money, not preparedness, and the original power target was cut when demand proved lower. The 24,944 households exceeds its target mainly because funds were moved into flood works at restructuring, with a 22-month extension; the target itself was set low. Five substations were procured but never installed for lack of permits, and two meteorological radars were lost to mis-procurement, both before closing. The record is recovery from one event and does not show that warnings or evacuation worked in 2014, when 51 people died.

pattern.mechanism: The government used an emergency loan to buy power while the state utility pumped out its flooded lignite mines, then redirected the savings into rebuilding river defences to a higher standard.
preconditions: A vertically integrated state utility able to import power at short notice
An emergency lending window that disburses within months
A water directorate with designs ready for embankment works

records.title: Floods Emergency Recovery Project after the May 2014 floods
records.claim: After the May 2014 floods displaced about 90,000 people and directly affected about a million in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the two entities' agriculture and water ministries and Brcko District distributed US$27 million of emergency goods and restored 446 public service facilities to pre-flood condition against a target of 200, including more than 260 km of rural roads and 53,460 m of flood defences, by the project's June 2019 closing.

metric.name: Public service infrastructure facilities recovered to pre-flood condition

secondMetric.name: Target for facilities recovered

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Bosnia and Herzegovina Floods Emergency Recovery Project, December 2019

records.limits: The figures are the World Bank's, from a completion report on its own US$100 million emergency loan; the event figures are in the context section (printed page 5), the outcome table on page 13, and the road and flood defence figures on page 18. The 446 facilities exceeds its target partly because unused emergency-goods funds were moved into infrastructure in January 2016, so the target was not a fixed plan. 'Facilities' counts very different things, from a culvert to a bridge, and the report does not say how many were fully rebuilt. Emergency goods reached beneficiaries according to third-party audits in 2017, but some agricultural goods arrived late. The project closed six months after its December 2018 original date, five years after the floods, so this is slow recovery, not rapid response, and it covers one loan, not the whole post-flood programme financed by the EU and others.

pattern.mechanism: The state treasury on-lent an emergency loan to the two entities and Brcko District, whose ministries bought relief goods through strategic reserves and then rebuilt municipal and regional infrastructure from a list drawn from the joint needs assessment.
preconditions: A joint recovery needs assessment agreed by all levels of government within weeks
Entity-level strategic reserves able to procure and distribute goods
Municipalities with project lists ready for rebuilding

records.title: Hazard Risk Mitigation and Emergency Preparedness Project: seismic retrofitting and the emergency information system
records.claim: Romania's Ministry of Administration and Interior and Ministry of Regional Development completed seismic retrofitting of 44 high-risk public buildings, where about 23,350 people worked, and rolled out a modernised emergency communication system to 48 sites under a project approved in May 2004, after cutting the retrofit target from 84 buildings to 40 in 2010 and closing in June 2012 instead of December 2009.

metric.name: Public buildings with seismic retrofitting completed

secondMetric.name: High-risk public buildings selected for retrofitting at appraisal

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Romania Hazard Risk Mitigation and Emergency Preparedness Project (P075163), December 2012

records.limits: The figures are the World Bank's, from a completion report on its own loan, in the PDO indicator table near the front of the document and the restructuring section. The report itself says there was no opportunity to test the retrofitted buildings in the absence of a major earthquake, so the record shows preparation, not demonstrated performance in a shock. The 44 exceeds a target already cut from 84 to 40 because of construction cost increases and currency depreciation, and three buildings were left unfinished when the 2010 to 2011 budgets did not cover ongoing works. The 2007 EU accession forced redesigns, and the government changed seven times in eight years. More than 350 public facilities were assessed at risk at baseline, so 44 is a small share, and the separate Bucharest programme for residential buildings at seismic risk is not covered.

pattern.mechanism: The government used a development loan to strengthen the most dangerous public buildings in the Vrancea seismic zone and to give the emergency inspectorate a shared voice and data network, then trimmed the list as costs rose.
preconditions: A seismic risk inventory that ranks public buildings
Counterpart budget that survives a fiscal crisis
Building codes aligned with the EU norms the designs must meet

records.title: State Hydrometeorological Service severe weather warning upgrade
records.claim: Moldova's State Hydrometeorological Service, with the emergency situations department, installed a Doppler radar by June 2014 and extended the lead time of severe weather warnings from 10 minutes to 1 hour at baseline to 3 to 6 hours by 2016, against an original target of 12 hours, under a project approved in August 2010 that closed in September 2016, two years late.

metric.name: Lead time for severe weather warnings, upper bound achieved

secondMetric.name: Lead time for severe weather warnings, original target

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Moldova Disaster and Climate Risk Management Project (P115634), March 2017

records.limits: The figures are the World Bank's, from a completion report on its own credit, in the PDO indicator table near the front of the document; the achieved lead time is a range (3 to 6 hours) and the record's metric takes its upper bound. The 12-hour target was formally revised down, so 'achieved' is against the lowered target. No named severe weather event is shown in which the warnings were issued and acted on, so the record documents capacity built, not capacity used; it is filed on the same terms as other warning-infrastructure records in this corpus. The report notes repeated management changes at the hydromet service, which threaten sustainability, and gives no later figure for radar uptime.

pattern.mechanism: The environment ministry's weather service bought a Doppler radar and forecasting systems and wired its warnings into the emergency department's command centre, so warnings reach responders hours rather than minutes ahead.
preconditions: A national weather service with staff to run a radar and models
A link from the forecaster to the civil protection command centre
Budget to maintain the radar once the loan ends

records.title: Reconstruction programme after the 26 November 2019 earthquake
records.claim: Albania's government reported in November 2021, two years after the 26 November 2019 earthquake, that more than 33,400 families had received reconstruction and repair grants worth ALL12.7 billion, that 13,325 people were receiving rent bonuses while new homes were built, and that 27 schools had been completed, while promising 4,500 individual houses and 12,000 apartments by spring 2022.

metric.name: Families that received reconstruction and repair grants

secondMetric.name: Schools completed under the reconstruction programme

source.publisher: Office of the Prime Minister of Albania, newsroom page 'Rindertimi', 23 November 2021 (archived copy)

records.limits: The source is the government's own promotional page on its flagship programme, in Albanian; the live kryeministria.al page sits behind a bot wall, so the cited copy is the Internet Archive capture of July 2026. The figures are counts of grants, with no report of how many repaired homes were verified, and 'more than 33,400' is a floor. The completion promises for spring 2022 (4,500 houses, 12,000 apartments, no trace of the earthquake) are on the same page, and no official figure was found showing whether they were met, so status is left as operating. The page says EUR300 million of grants pledged at the donors' conference were active in more than 30 projects; the delivery is the government's, but the money is not all domestic. Nothing here measures preparedness before the earthquake.

pattern.mechanism: The government created a reconstruction ministry and programme within months of the earthquake, paid rent bonuses to displaced families and repair grants to owners through municipalities, and built new housing blocks and schools on cleared sites with state and donor funds.
preconditions: A damage assessment that classifies each building, so grants match damage
A state budget line and donor pledges large enough to fund rebuilding at once
Municipalities able to administer grants and clear sites

records.title: Bank of Russia regulatory sandbox (regulativnaya pesochnitsa)
records.claim: The Bank of Russia decided in 2025 to create the legal conditions for introducing 4 digital financial services piloted in its regulatory sandbox, out of 10 pilot applications it considered that year in identification, artificial intelligence, insurance, distributed ledgers and other areas.

metric.name: Sandbox applications for which the Bank decided to create legal conditions for introduction (the step its sandbox page says follows a successfully completed pilot)

secondMetric.name: Applications to pilot services considered in the regulatory sandbox

source.publisher: Bank of Russia, Annual Report for 2025 (Godovoy otchet za 2025 god), section 2.5.1 'Development of innovation on the financial market'

records.limits: The central bank reports on its own sandbox, in a 351-page PDF of 57 MB, on PDF page 213 (printed page 211). The unit is applications, not firms: the report does not say how many firms stand behind the 10 applications or the 4 decisions, and one firm can file several. The 4 are read as completions because the Bank's sandbox page (https://www.cbr.ru/fintech/regulatory_sandbox/) says it approves a roadmap for legal conditions when piloting is completed successfully; the annual report itself does not say the pilots ended in 2025, and the 10 considered are not admissions, since an application can be reviewed without a pilot running. The sandbox launched in April 2018 (the Bank's sandbox page) and the Bank said in August 2023 that 86 services had been submitted since launch, so 10 in 2025 is a modest flow, about 0.07 per million people, and 4 completions about 0.03. Experimental legal regimes under the 2020 federal law on digital innovation, which the Ministry of Economic Development registers for every sector, are a second channel the column should sum; the ministry's register did not open from here (connection refused) and its last archived copy is from 2022, so they are not counted. Participants are mostly large incumbent banks and infrastructure operators, so this is not a startup programme.

pattern.mechanism: The central bank runs an isolated environment in which any organisation can pilot a financial service that existing law would not allow, and when a pilot succeeds it approves a roadmap of legal changes so the service can be introduced.
preconditions: A central bank with rule-making power over most of the financial market
An expert review process for applications
A legislative route to turn a successful pilot into law, which the experimental legal regimes law of 2020 added

records.title: JoRegBox, the Central Bank of Jordan regulatory sandbox
records.claim: The Central Bank of Jordan approved three companies on 31 October 2024, out of nine applications to the first cohort of its JoRegBox regulatory sandbox launched in February 2024, to begin testing digital financial products with real customers, among them the escrow platforms E-Damana and Watheq.

metric.name: Companies approved to enter the sandbox for live testing

source.publisher: Central Bank of Jordan, news release 'CBJ approves three Entrepreneurial Companies to Enter the Regulatory Sandbox Environment (JoRegBox)', archived copy of 15 May 2025

records.limits: The live cbj.gov.jo page refused the connection, so the number was read on a Wayback Machine copy of the central bank's own release. Three is the admission decision for one cohort, the first under the JoRegBox name, and the release gives no count of firms completing the sandbox; the bank's annual report, which would carry later cohorts and exits, was not located today. The central bank had an earlier sandbox framework, which the World Bank's 2020 survey lists as operational from April 2018; the release treats JoRegBox as a new launch on 18 February 2024, and whether firms passed through the earlier framework is not shown here. The governor has been quoted in the press giving a cumulative count of tested products, which this record does not use because no official page carrying it was opened. Three admissions against about 11 million people is about 0.3 per million. The release frames the cohort as part of the government's economic modernisation programme, so the timing is partly political.

pattern.mechanism: The central bank admits fintech firms in cohorts to test mature products with real customers under its supervision, and links the sandbox to the national financial inclusion strategy and the economic modernisation vision.
preconditions: A central bank sandbox framework with published eligibility and exit rules
Partner banks willing to hold escrow and settlement accounts for test firms
A government programme that makes fintech a named priority

records.title: Special regulatory regimes (spetsialnye regulyativnye rezhimy) of the National Bank of the Kyrgyz Republic
records.claim: The National Bank of the Kyrgyz Republic approved six special regulatory regimes between October 2020 and August 2026, letting a microcredit company, three payment and e-money firms and two banks test operations outside its standing rules, judged testing successful and closed for four of them between April 2022 and February 2025, and ended one early with the licence revoked in March 2022.

metric.name: Special regulatory regimes approved and listed in the register

secondMetric.name: Regimes completed with testing judged successful

source.publisher: National Bank of the Kyrgyz Republic, Register of special regulatory regimes (Reestr spetsialnykh regulyativnykh rezhimov)

records.limits: Both counts are ours, made by reading the rows of the register page (dated 2 September 2026): it lists six regimes with approval, start and end dates, the words 'testing judged successful (regime completed)' against four, 'ended early, licence revoked' against the Bakai Bank regime (September 2021 to March 2022), and a sixth, Eldik Bank, approved on 7 August 2026 and testing until August 2027; the page itself states no total. Some regimes list partner institutions (the Interbank Processing Centre) as co-participants, so the count is of regimes, not of every firm involved. Six regimes in six years, about one a year in a country of about seven million people, is a thin flow, and the regime appears only once a firm asks for it rather than through open cohorts. The register says the national bank amended its regulations in May 2024 after the Regional Payment Systems regime, but it does not show whether the other completions led to rule changes. The register is a central bank page only; other Kyrgyz regulators were not checked.

pattern.mechanism: The central bank grants a firm a time-limited special regime, licensed and entered in a public register with start and end dates, to test a named banking or payment operation, then records whether testing succeeded and amends its rules where it did.
preconditions: A banking law provision allowing the national bank to set special regulatory regimes
A public register kept up to date row by row
Payment and e-money firms with products that standing rules did not allow
pattern.travelled: After the regime run by Regional Payment Systems, the board amended its regulations in May 2024 to remove obstacles to card acquiring by payment system operators, which is the route from test to rule.

records.title: Institut Royal des Etudes Stratégiques (IRES)
records.claim: Morocco's Royal Institute for Strategic Studies, announced in the 2003 Throne Speech to strengthen the country's capacities for analysis, adaptation and anticipation and created by Dahir No 1-07-183 of 30 November 2007, published the twelfth edition of its strategic dashboard on Morocco's international positioning on 28 November 2024 and was still issuing general reports in 2025.

metric.name: Editions of the strategic dashboard 'Tableau de bord stratégique: évolution du positionnement international du Maroc'

source.publisher: Institut Royal des Etudes Stratégiques, Publications: Rapports généraux (list page) and Présentation de l'IRES

records.limits: The institute reports on itself, and the figure is an edition number in the title of a listed report, not a count of output the institute publishes. The dashboard tracks Morocco's position in international indicators, which is strategic monitoring (veille) rather than scenario-based foresight, and the institute describes itself as a think tank, a watch function and a forum, working on questions referred by the King; the mandate and the Dahir are on the presentation page (https://www.ires.ma/fr/ires/presentation), where the 2003 Throne Speech that announced it names anticipation as its purpose. It sits outside the elected government, attached to the monarchy, so it is a centre-of-state body rather than a cabinet unit, and nothing read today shows its work entering a government decision. The page gives no budget, staff count or total of reports. Started is 2007, the year of the founding Dahir; the publication list begins in 2009.

pattern.mechanism: The head of state created by decree a strategic studies institute with a small project-based staff and associated researchers, which runs recurring monitoring products, national surveys and studies on questions he refers to it.
preconditions: A head of state who commissions long-range studies directly
A decree giving the institute a standing mandate and a guidance committee appointed from the top
Associated academics to staff time-limited study projects

records.title: Programme national d'enseignement des adultes (national adult education programme)
records.claim: Tunisia's Ministry of Social Affairs, through its national adult education centre and regional coordinations, taught 16,560 adult learners in the 2021-2022 school year, 10,320 in the basic cycle and 6,240 in the completion and intensive cycles, 9,799 of them women, against a forecast of 22,710.

metric.name: Adult learners in the national adult education programme, all governorates and cycles (Annex 5)

secondMetric.name: Forecast number of learners for 2022 in the same report

source.publisher: Ministere des Affaires sociales, Rapport annuel de performance 2022 (mission Affaires sociales), programme Promotion sociale, indicator 1.3.3 and Annex 5 'Distribution of learners by governorate and cycle, school year 2021/2022'

records.limits: The ministry reports on its own programme in its annual performance report, in Arabic. The numbers sit in a PDF: the narrative on page 43 and the governorate table on page 78; the text layer of this PDF maps digits wrongly (it extracts 16.362 and 22.912), so the figures were read from the rendered pages. The count is learners enrolled in literacy (basic) and post-literacy (completion and intensive) classes, not completions, and literacy classes are only part of adult learning. Against roughly eight million Tunisian adults it is a small reach, about two learners per thousand adults, in a country whose own report puts adult illiteracy at 16.8 percent in 2022. The report attributes the shortfall against forecast to the loss of contract teachers (954 at end 2021 to 943 at end 2022) and to difficulty attracting learners, and the 2024 report still speaks of 'targeting 22 thousand beneficiaries' with 885 contract and 113 tenured teachers, so the programme has not regained its forecast scale; no earlier enrolment peak was verified, so the record is not filed as an erosion.
