The 2000 start is the commonly reported launch year of the national programme and was not read at the cited source.

pattern.mechanism: The social affairs ministry runs a national adult education centre that hires contract teachers to give literacy and post-literacy classes in every governorate, and reports learners by governorate and cycle in its performance budget.
preconditions: A performance-budgeting system that makes ministries report indicators and enrolment annually
A pool of contract teachers paid from the ministry budget
Local venues and regional coordinators close to rural learners, especially women

records.title: Agence Nationale de Lutte contre l'Analphabetisme literacy and post-literacy programmes
records.claim: Morocco's national literacy agency (ANLCA) and its partners registered 763,744 adults in literacy programmes in 2023-2024, 570,507 at level 1 literacy and 193,237 in post-literacy, with about 81 percent of level 1 registrants women and 62 percent rural.

metric.name: Registrants in literacy programmes (level 1 literacy plus level 2 post-literacy)

secondMetric.name: Registrants in level 1 literacy programme (ALPHA) only

source.publisher: Agence Nationale de Lutte contre l'Analphabetisme (ANLCA), Alphabetisation, Indicateurs page

records.limits: The agency reports on its own programmes and the page carries no publication date. The counts are registrations, not completions or people who became literate: the Cour des comptes (annual report 2023-2024, principal axes, pages 49 to 52) found an average attendance index of about 40 percent and an assiduity index of 43 percent in 14,263 inspected classes over 2019 to 2022, so attendance is far below registration. Delivery runs mostly through civil-society associations under agency contracts (385,442 of the 570,710 level 1 registrants in the page's partner table) and through the Ministry of Habous mosque programme (165,290), so the agency finances and certifies rather than teaches; the partner table total (570,710) differs by 203 from the headline level 1 figure (570,507), and the page does not explain the gap. Literacy courses are basic education, which is only part of the adult learning construct. Press reports, citing the agency and the Cour des comptes, put registrations at over one million in 2023; that figure was not found at an official URL this protocol could open, so no peak is claimed, but if it holds for 2022-2023 the 2023-2024 count is about a quarter lower. The 2015 start is the year the Cour des comptes gives for the launch of the agency's programmes, not a date on the cited page.

pattern.mechanism: A national agency funds and certifies literacy classes that associations, the religious affairs ministry and other departments run in villages, mosques and neighbourhoods, and counts registrants each programme year.
preconditions: A dense civil-society network able to host classes close to where adults live
State subsidy that pays associations per class, with EU budget support at the margin
A registration system that collects counts by programme, region, sex and residence

records.title: Innovation Consortia Matching Grant Program (Fostering Productive Innovation Project)
records.claim: Kazakhstan's innovation ministry (MDDIAI), through the Innovation Consortia Matching Grant Program of the World Bank financed Fostering Productive Innovation Project, had supported 33 technology consortia of research teams and firms, including 12 competence centres, by September 2024, whose first sales and signed contracts totalled about 17 billion tenge.

metric.name: Technology consortia supported under the Innovation Consortia Matching Grant Program

secondMetric.name: First sales and signed contracts of Productive Sector Consortia subprojects

source.publisher: World Bank, Kazakhstan: Fostering Productive Innovation Project (P150402), Implementation Support Mission Aide Memoire, September 16 to 24, 2024

records.limits: The figure is the World Bank's mission account of a programme it financed, not a ministry statistic, and the number is in a PDF (paragraph 6 of the aide memoire). The sentence 'supported 33 technology consortia, including 12 competence centers, and 9 IICs' does not make clear whether the nine inclusive innovation consortia are inside or beside the 33. The aide memoire does not define a consortium's membership; the 2020 restructuring paper describes the window as a tool 'for fostering industry-science linkages' with an average 40 percent private co-financing in the first six grants, and the annex shows competence centres hosted by universities (Astana IT University, the ENU-Lab centre), but not every consortium is shown to include a university. The 17 billion tenge is first sales and contracts as reported by beneficiaries, rounded ('around'), and is not audited. The programme ran on loan money: the 2020 restructuring cut the consortia component from US$35 million to US$25.1 million, and in 2024 the ministry asked to cancel a further US$5.4 million of unused consortia grants because no new round could be run before closing (extended to June 30, 2025), so the status is concluded and a follow-on (FPIP-2) was only in preparation. The 2019 start is the year the first consortia grant agreements were signed according to the 2020 restructuring paper.

pattern.mechanism: The ministry ran a competitive matching-grant window that paid consortia of research teams and firms to take a technology to first sales, with firms co-financing and a project unit monitoring sales and contracts.
preconditions: Loan financing from a development bank with a project management unit able to run calls
Research teams with near-market technologies and firms willing to co-finance
A follow-on budget to keep calls running once the loan closes, which was not yet in place
pattern.travelled: The consortia window scaled up the earlier Technology Commercialization Project; its continuation depends on a second loan rather than the state budget.

records.title: Federal project Sodeystvie zanyatosti (Employment Promotion) vocational training of adults
records.claim: Under the federal project Sodeystvie zanyatosti of the national project Demography, which paid for vocational training and further professional education of selected groups of adults, more than 80,000 citizens had started training and 21,125 had completed it by the end of the third quarter of 2024.

metric.name: Citizens who completed training under the federal project

secondMetric.name: Citizens who had started training under the federal project

source.publisher: Government of the Russian Federation, news release 'Tatyana Golikova discussed with all regions the implementation of the national project Demography', 12 November 2024

records.limits: The source is a government press release reporting a meeting, not a statistical table, and the counts cover only nine months of 2024, the project's final year, so they are a partial year and understate annual scale. An earlier release (government.ru/news/50674, 22 January 2024) says more than 190,000 people had completed short courses under the Demography retraining programme, without stating a period, so the two figures cannot be compared as an erosion. The training is for eligible groups (jobseekers, people aged 50 and over, women on parental leave and others defined by government resolution), not all adults. The national project Demography ended in 2024 and the release says its lines move into new national projects from 2025, so the status is concluded; the successor was not verified. The 2019 start is the first year of the national project Demography; the federal project took its current training form in 2021.

pattern.mechanism: The labour ministry paid regional employment centres and accredited providers to train target groups of adults in short courses tied to regional demand, under a national project with quarterly reporting to the deputy prime minister.
preconditions: A national project budget line with targets reported quarterly to the centre of government
Regional employment centres able to enrol and refer trainees
A pool of accredited training providers, including universities and colleges

records.title: Short-term vocational training of the unemployed in monocentres and district vocational training centres
records.claim: Uzbekistan's Ministry of Poverty Reduction and Employment expanded short-term vocational skill training of unemployed people from 20,000 in 2018 to 110,000 in 2022, counting graduates of the regional monocentres and district vocational training centres, according to ministry data reported by the World Bank.

metric.name: Unemployed people covered by short-term vocational skill training (graduates of regional monocentres and district vocational training centres)

secondMetric.name: Same coverage in the base year

source.publisher: World Bank, Uzbekistan: Innovative Social Protection System for Inclusion of Vulnerable People Project, Project Appraisal Document, Annex 2 paragraph 1 and footnote 51 (data from the Ministry of Poverty Reduction and Employment), May 2024

records.limits: The numbers are the ministry's, passed on in a World Bank appraisal document as background, rounded to thousands and without a table; the ministry's own release was not found at an open URL. The footnote says the numbers include graduates of both the regional monocentres and district centres, so the figures are graduates rather than enrolments, and the text calls them 'coverage'. Only two years are given, so the path between 2018 and 2022 and anything after 2022 are unknown; 'operating' rests on the appraisal describing the system as current in 2024 and planning further support to it. The training is for registered unemployed people, not all adults, and courses are short (weeks to a few months). The 2018 start is the base year of the series, not a programme launch date read at the source.

pattern.mechanism: The employment ministry built a network of regional training monocentres and district vocational centres that give registered unemployed people short, free skill courses, and counts graduates centrally.
preconditions: A labour ministry with a district-level presence and registration of the unemployed
Budget for free short courses and for equipping training centres
Donor co-financing for equipment and curricula in the early years

records.title: Self-Employment Program business training
records.claim: Azerbaijan's State Employment Agency trained 24,399 successful applicants to the national Self-Employment Program in business skills and business planning between May 2021 and November 2024, 2,155 of them in the third quarter of 2024, as a condition of receiving start-up assets.

metric.name: Successful SEP applicants who completed business training (cumulative)

secondMetric.name: Applicants who completed training and prepared business plans in one quarter

source.publisher: World Bank, Azerbaijan Employment Support Project (P171250), Implementation Status and Results Report, sequence 9, archived 23 January 2025

records.limits: The count is from the World Bank's monitoring of a loan it finances, reported by the implementing agency, and covers only programme participants financed under the project from May 2021, not the Self-Employment Program's earlier cohorts, which the state budget financed from 2017. The training is short business training that gates an asset transfer, not vocational or general education, so it is a narrow slice of adult learning. The same report gives 27,452 SEP beneficiaries 'in training or have completed trainings' and 'over 27,000' participating in business training, so the denominator varies by indicator; the completed count is used. About 3,000 people a year passed through the ministry's two vocational training centres, by the 2020 appraisal document's account, and the vocational certification and on-the-job training windows of the restructured project had not started by December 2024.

pattern.mechanism: The employment agency selects vulnerable jobseekers into a self-employment programme, trains them to write a business plan, and transfers start-up assets to those whose plans pass, with mentoring visits afterwards.
preconditions: A registry of vulnerable jobseekers and a selection process for applicants
Contracted business trainers able to run batches across regions
Budget for in-kind asset transfers, here partly loan-financed

records.title: Water management contracts and leases, and the national lease from 2017
records.claim: Armenia ran a sequence of water public-private partnerships from 2000, a Yerevan management contract, a 2006 to 2016 Yerevan lease and management contracts for the national and three regional utilities, which raised daily supply from about 6 hours in 1998 to 24 hours in most of Yerevan by 2015, and from January 2017 consolidated them into a single 15-year national lease covering about 2.2 million people.

metric.name: People in the area covered by the 15-year national water lease from January 2017

secondMetric.name: Average daily water supply in most parts of the country, including Yerevan, before the PPPs
secondMetric.unit: hours per day (24 in most of Yerevan by 2015)

source.publisher: World Bank and PPIAF, Review of Armenia's Experience with Water Public-Private Partnerships (Marin, Muzenda and Andreasyan), 2017

records.limits: All figures are in the executive summary of a PDF (printed pages ix to xi). The review was written by World Bank staff with support from PPIAF, a facility that promotes infrastructure PPPs, and credits the operators generously, and the 24-hour figure is 'most of Yerevan', not the country. The same review says non-revenue water barely improved, that tariffs outside Yerevan stayed below cost recovery when the management contracts ended in 2016, and that capital investment was financed by the government, so the private operators ran networks without financing them. The record's newest verified fact is the start of the national lease in January 2017; we did not find an official account of its performance since then at an open URL, so 'operating' rests on its 15-year term, and any later dispute, renegotiation or early termination is not covered. The national lease introduced a single national tariff, a cross-subsidy from Yerevan to the rest of the country, whose effect on supply hours outside Yerevan is not shown here.

pattern.mechanism: The government contracted private operators in stages, first to manage the Yerevan utility for a fee with performance incentives, then to lease it, then to manage the national and regional utilities, and finally to lease all of them as one national concession paying a lease fee to the state, while the state kept financing capital works.
preconditions: Donor and state finance for network rehabilitation, which the operators did not provide
Government willingness to raise tariffs in steps matched to visible service gains
Successive contracts long enough to build a local record that justified the next, larger one

records.title: AZN 190 monthly allowance to people who lost work, April to June 2020
records.claim: After Azerbaijan's first COVID-19 case on 28 February 2020 and the first lockdown in March, the government paid a monthly allowance of AZN 190 to 600,000 unemployed citizens, formal and informal, from April to June 2020, and in 2020 also granted targeted social assistance to 9,000 newly poor families without the usual household assessment and extended expired assistance for 9,408 households.

metric.name: Unemployed citizens paid the AZN 190 monthly allowance, April to June 2020

secondMetric.name: Newly poor families granted targeted social assistance without a full household assessment

source.publisher: World Bank, Project Information Document, Azerbaijan COVID-19 Emergency Response Project (P176503), 11 May 2021

records.limits: The figures are in paragraph 14 and footnote 4 on page 6 of 9 of a World Bank project information document, written a year later to prepare a loan that would retroactively finance the payment for 170,000 of the 600,000 recipients; it relays the government's figures and is not an evaluation. The document says 'from April to June 2020' but not whether all 600,000 were paid in April or how many months each received, so the speed shown is the month, not days; registration was online, with a phone route through district employment centres. 600,000 is a round number. The first case date and 'three lockdowns between March 2020 and January 2021' are in paragraph 4 (page 4). The document calls AZN 190 commensurate to the cost of living, and the payment stopped after three months; the 9,000 families added to targeted social assistance were few next to 600,000 allowance recipients, which suggests the standing safety net expanded little.

pattern.mechanism: The government created a temporary flat allowance for anyone who registered as having lost work, including informal workers, through an online registration with the State Employment Service, and relaxed the targeted social assistance rules so newly poor families could be added without a home assessment.
preconditions: An online registration route with a telephone fallback through district employment centres
Budget resources to pay first and refinance part of the cost later from a donor loan
A targeted social assistance programme whose eligibility checks could be relaxed by decision

records.title: Private solar and wind plants under government investment agreements
records.claim: Azerbaijan's government brought its first utility-scale private solar plant, Masdar's 230 MW Garadagh plant built with US$262 million of foreign investment, into operation on 26 October 2023, followed on 16 September 2026 by the 100 MW Gobustan plant won at a 2024 auction, with further private wind and solar plants under investment agreements and power purchase contracts.

metric.name: Capacity of the Garadagh Solar Power Plant, the first private utility-scale plant, in operation

secondMetric.name: Foreign investment in the Garadagh plant

source.publisher: Ministry of Energy of the Republic of Azerbaijan, 'Use of renewable energy sources in Azerbaijan'

records.limits: The ministry describes its own programme on an undated web page that has been updated at least to September 2026; the investment figure and capacities are the ministry's, with no audited cost and no published tariff. Two private plants are operating, 330 MW together by our sum, against 2,170 MW of renewable capacity the same page reports in operation, most of it state hydropower; the rest of the private pipeline (ACWA Power's 240 MW Khizi-Absheron wind farm, bp's 240 MW Shafag plant, Masdar's 1 GW 'mega project', two 50 MW plants in Jabrayil) is under construction or planned, and the page gives no completion dates. 'Implemented jointly with local and international partners' covers different structures: Garadagh and Gobustan are built and owned by foreign developers, though the page does not name their buyer or contract terms, Shafag serves bp's own terminal through a 'virtual' transmission swap, and the page does not say which plants were competitively tendered beyond Gobustan. The collaboration is recent, so the record shows a start, not a sustained programme. The ministry's page describes Garadagh as 'put into operation as a pilot project'; it is a 230 MW grid-connected plant, so we read the word as first-of-kind rather than as a trial, but the source uses it.

pattern.mechanism: The government signed investment agreements, land leases, power purchase, grid connection and balancing agreements with foreign developers, first bilaterally with Masdar and then through an auction, for private plants connected to the national grid.
preconditions: A state counterparty able to sign long-term power purchase and grid agreements
Gas exports valuable enough that each kilowatt-hour from renewables frees gas for sale, which is how the ministry frames each plant
Gulf developers willing to invest on bilaterally negotiated terms before an auction was held
pattern.travelled: Uzbekistan's tendered solar IPPs (uzb-renewable-ipp) used the same Gulf developers in the same years.

records.title: Temporary unemployment benefit and one-off support for the self-employed, 2020
records.claim: Georgia, which had no unemployment benefit, announced a temporary GEL 200 monthly benefit for laid-off formal workers and a one-off payment for self-employed and informal workers on 24 April 2020, a month after declaring a state of emergency, and by September 2021 had paid 231,487 unemployed people and 307,236 self-employed people.

metric.name: Unemployed people paid the temporary unemployment benefit

secondMetric.name: Self-employed people whose activity was affected and who received support

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Status and Results Report, Georgia Emergency COVID-19 Response Project (P173911), sequence 3, 10 September 2021

records.limits: Both counts are in one sentence on page 1 of the status report, with no table behind them and no date of first payment; the timing comes from the project appraisal document (http://documents.worldbank.org/curated/en/949581588712278110/pdf/Georgia-Emergency-COVID-19-Response-Project.pdf: state of emergency on 21 March 2020 in paragraph 9, printed page 12; the Prime Minister's 24 April announcement in paragraph 26, printed page 18; the GEL 200 benefit for up to six months and the GEL 300 one-off benefit in paragraphs 45 and 46). The speed shown is therefore 34 days from emergency to announced rule, not to money paid. The World Bank and AIIB co-financed the programme, the report notes that its indicator values cover only the IBRD share of some outputs, and the counts are cumulative people paid at least once, not people covered for six months. The benefit was temporary by design and Georgia still has no permanent unemployment insurance, so the rule change did not outlast the shock. The self-employed figure is described as people 'whose activity was affected', a looser category than the one-off benefit's eligibility rule.

pattern.mechanism: The government used the Revenue Service's payroll tax records to identify laid-off formal workers and pay them a flat monthly benefit through the State Employment Support Agency, and opened an online portal for a one-off payment to self-employed and informal workers with no declared income.
preconditions: Monthly payroll tax declarations linking workers to employers and bank accounts
An employment agency able to verify eligibility against social assistance lists
External emergency finance (World Bank and AIIB) committed within weeks

records.title: National Aid Fund temporary cash transfers to informal workers, 2020
records.claim: Jordan's National Aid Fund reused the Takaful cash-transfer platform after the March 2020 curfew, opened online registration for ten days in mid-April and had paid about 150,000 newly identified households by 10 May 2020, and 237,000 households had received three months of temporary cash support by March 2021.

metric.name: Households identified and paid by the temporary cash transfer as of 10 May 2020

secondMetric.name: Households that had received temporary cash transfers (three months of support)

source.publisher: World Bank, Project Appraisal Document, Jordan Emergency Cash Transfer COVID-19 Response Project (P173974), June 2020

records.limits: The 150,000 figure is in paragraph 60 of the appraisal document (printed page 28 of 60), and the curfew dates are in paragraphs 2 and 3 (printed page 9). The 237,000 figure is in a second World Bank document, the Implementation Status and Results Report of 26 April 2021, sequence 2 (http://documents.worldbank.org/curated/en/429691619464662394/pdf/Disclosable-Version-of-the-ISR-Jordan-Emergency-Cash-Transfer-COVID-19-Response-Project-P173974-Sequence-No-02.pdf, page 1), which also says the transfers cost about US$114 million, of which the government paid about US$103 million through national charity accounts and the project financed US$11 million retroactively. Both documents come from the lender to the programme, and the PAD figure is an 'about'. The speed is the delivery system's, not a new law's: the Takaful platform, its registry of almost one million households and digital payments were built from 2019 with World Bank, UNICEF, WFP and other donor support, so the response mostly reused prior investment. The emergency transfer lasted three months per household and the project's own PDO indicator for cash support through the project still read zero in that report because the loan became effective only on 11 November 2020: the fast part was financed domestically. Refugees, about 655,000 registered, were outside this programme and were served by UN agencies.

pattern.mechanism: The National Aid Fund opened the Takaful online registration platform to informal workers who had lost income, selected households with the Takaful targeting formula against linked administrative data, and paid them into e-wallets and bank accounts authorised by the central bank.
preconditions: A cash-transfer registry and online enrolment platform built the year before
Central bank rules allowing the Fund to open e-wallets for beneficiaries remotely
Domestic charity accounts able to fund the first months before external finance arrived
pattern.travelled: The same reuse of a Takaful-style platform appears in Morocco (mar-tadamon-covid), where a health-assistance register played the role of the cash-transfer registry.

records.title: Utility-scale renewable power through direct proposals and IPP rounds, and the stop after 2021
records.claim: Jordan's Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources added utility-scale solar and wind plants selling to the grid every year from 2015 to 2021, mostly private projects under direct proposals and competitive rounds, peaking at 345 MWac commissioned in 2020, and then added none: its annual reports put grid-selling renewable capacity at 1,498 MW in 2022 and 2023 and 1,478 MW in 2024.

metric.name: Utility-scale renewable capacity selling to the grid added from 2022 to 2024 (computed from the reported stock)
metric.unit: MW (stock 1,498 MW in 2022 and 2023, 1,478 MW in 2024)

secondMetric.name: Utility-scale renewable capacity added in 2020, the peak year

source.publisher: Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources of Jordan, Annual Report 2024

records.limits: The 2024 annual report's year-by-year table, 'Renewable Energy Power Generation Projects: Direct Proposals and Grants', runs over PDF pages 13 to 15 with annual totals on page 15 (134.5, 270, 14, 339.1, 235.1, 345 and 135.5 MWac for 2015 to 2021, under a note that the 2015 to 2021 list 'remain[s] as stated'); the 2021 total is a misprint for 153.5, the sum of its three projects and the figure in the 2022 report. The zero is ours, not printed: it rests on the grid-selling capacity the ministry reports, 1,498 MW in the 2022 report (https://www.memr.gov.jo/ebv4.0/root_storage/en/eb_list_page/annual_report_2022.pdf) and the 2023 report (same path, annual_report_2023.pdf) and 1,478 MW on PDF page 12 of the 2024 report, and on the 2022 report's project table also stopping at 2021; the 20 MW fall in 2024 looks like reclassification (a new 10 MW biogas and hydro line) rather than a closure. The 345 MWac peak is a commissioning year for plants contracted in earlier rounds, so it overstates the pace at which new partnerships were being signed in 2020. The table mixes private independent power producers (Masdar's Baynounah 200 MW, ACWA's Mafraq plant, the Tafila wind farms) with plants financed by Gulf, EU and Spanish grants and loans, including an Air Force plant, so not every megawatt is a partnership; we did not separate them. The reports do not say why additions stopped. What kept growing was subscriber-owned capacity under net metering and wheeling, 1,079 MW in 2022 and 1,320.8 MW in 2024, which is private investment without a public counterpart contract. The erosion is in the frequency of new joint deliveries, not in the stock, which still operates. The ministry reports on its own programme, and the stop may be a pause rather than an end.

pattern.mechanism: The ministry offered sites and long-term power purchase agreements with the state-owned single buyer NEPCO to private developers through direct proposals and competitive rounds, alongside donor-financed public plants, and added no utility-scale plant after 2021.
preconditions: A single buyer, NEPCO, able to sign 20-year take-or-pay contracts with sovereign backing
A renewable energy law allowing direct proposals and a regulator able to license IPPs
Grid capacity and demand growth to absorb more contracted capacity, which the report does not discuss and which is the most likely limit
pattern.travelled: Egypt's feed-in tariff (egy-renewable-fit) and Uzbekistan's solar tenders (uzb-renewable-ipp) are the same move; Jordan is the case where the additions stopped.

records.title: KZT 42,500 income-loss payment during the 2020 state of emergency
records.claim: During the March to May 2020 state of emergency, Kazakhstan's government paid people who lost income because of business closures and lockdown KZT 42,500 per person per month, and about 4 million people received the payment.

metric.name: People who received the KZT 42,500 monthly income-loss payment

source.publisher: World Bank, Kazakhstan Economic Update, Summer 2020: Navigating the Crisis

records.limits: The figure is a rounded 'about 4 million people' in Box 1 on printed page 7 (PDF page 8) of a World Bank economic update; the Bank did not finance or evaluate the payment and relays the government's own figure. The government release with the exact count (gov.kz, Ministry of Labour and Social Protection) renders only through JavaScript and could not be opened for verification. The update gives the state of emergency's dates (quarantines from 19 March, lifted on 11 May 2020) but no date of first payment and no count of people paid in each month, so the speed claim rests on the payment having been made during an emergency that lasted under two months. The update publishes no targeting, error or rejection figures, so it cannot show how well the payment reached the people it was meant for. The update puts the whole anti-crisis package at 5.7 percent of GDP, of which this payment was one part. The payment was temporary and ended with the emergency.

pattern.mechanism: The government declared a state of emergency and attached to it a flat monthly payment for people who had lost income because of closures and lockdown, paid through the state benefit system for the duration of the emergency.
preconditions: Fiscal room for an anti-crisis package the World Bank put at 5.7 percent of GDP
Population and tax registers to check applicants against
A state benefit payment system already reaching most households

records.title: National and local PPP and concession contracts
records.claim: By the end of 2025 Kazakhstan's central and local governments had signed 1,257 PPP and concession contracts worth 3.6 trillion tenge, of which 697 were in implementation, 1,240 were local projects mostly in social services, health, education, energy and utilities, and 17 national projects accounted for more than 1.8 trillion tenge.

metric.name: PPP and concession contracts signed, cumulative

secondMetric.name: PPP and concession projects in implementation

source.publisher: Kazakhstan Public-Private Partnership Center (national operator for PPP), briefing on PPP results for 2025, 'From the number of contracts to the quality of projects'

records.limits: The figures come from the state-owned PPP Center reporting on the portfolio it promotes, at a briefing of the government's Central Communications Service; the page carries no date beyond 'results for 2025' and no table, and the Center's own homepage gives a different, later count (1,438 contracts and 3.8 trillion tenge as of 1 September 2026) that we could not reconcile with the briefing's 1,257. The gap between 1,257 signed and 697 in implementation is not explained: it mixes completed, not yet started and terminated contracts, so the share of contracts that failed is unknown. Most contracts are small local projects in social sectors, and the Center's PPP White Book describes availability payments from the budget as a standard repayment route, so many contracts may be deferred public procurement rather than shared risk; the briefing gives no split by payment mechanism. The briefing itself says the number of new contracts is falling while average project size rose from about 6 billion tenge before 2022 to 18 billion in 2022 to 2025, a policy shift away from the small local contracts that built the count. The start year is that of the Law on Public-Private Partnership of 31 October 2015, as cited in the Center's PPP White Book; the cumulative count also includes concessions signed under earlier law.

pattern.mechanism: The state set up a national PPP operator and let regional akimats sign PPP contracts for local social infrastructure, with the operator appraising projects, ranking regions each year and standardising contract documents.
preconditions: A PPP law that lets local governments commit future budget payments to private partners
A national operator to appraise projects and publish the portfolio
Budget room for long availability-payment obligations, which is what later pushed policy towards fewer, larger projects

records.title: Emergency Social Safety Net (AMAN), and its slow start
records.claim: Lebanon's emergency cash transfer for the economic collapse that began in 2019 was approved by the World Bank in January 2021, rewritten by Parliament in March 2021 and declared effective only in July 2021, so that in October 2021 the number of households receiving basic cash transfers still stood at its 15,153 baseline against a target of 147,000; the programme later reached 158,770 households by March 2025.

metric.name: Households receiving basic cash transfers, unchanged from the June 2020 baseline

secondMetric.name: Households that had received cash assistance under the programme (AMAN)

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Status and Results Report, Lebanon Emergency Crisis and COVID-19 Response Social Safety Net Project (P173367), sequence 2, 17 November 2021

records.limits: The 15,153 is the PDO indicator table on pages 2 and 3 of the status report, identical at baseline (30 June 2020), March 2021 and October 2021; the approval, ratification and effectiveness dates are on page 1, which says Parliament's changes cut budget allocations for fiduciary activities and that the Bank judged some of them would impede implementation, and that the government still had to meet disbursement conditions so that payments could begin before the end of 2021. The 158,770 is in paragraph 4 of the World Bank restructuring paper of 13 May 2025 (https://documents.worldbank.org/curated/en/099051325103513216/pdf/P173367-bed938d8-7d2a-4120-80a5-3da01c595ba8.pdf), which says about 94,000 households were enrolled in 2022 and 2023 and 65,000 were migrated in October 2024 from the National Poverty Targeting Program after it closed in June 2024 for lack of donor funding. The baseline households were beneficiaries of that older programme, not of this one. The record documents slowness, not failure: once paying, the programme reached roughly its target. The publisher is the lender, and part of the delay was the World Bank's own conditions and the process of agreeing them with Parliament across a change of government in September 2021; the record does not apportion blame. The start year is the year of approval, not the start of the crisis in late 2019.

pattern.mechanism: The government borrowed for a new cash transfer rather than extending an existing one, and the loan had to pass Parliament, which amended it, so the programme waited for a revised law, a new government and fiduciary conditions before it could pay.
preconditions: A cash-transfer instrument that requires parliamentary ratification of each external loan
No functioning domestic financing for safety nets during a banking and currency collapse
A donor-funded legacy programme whose end, in June 2024, showed how little was domestically owned
pattern.travelled: The contrast with Jordan (jor-naf-covid-cash), which paid 150,000 new households within two months by reusing a standing platform and domestic funds, is the point of the record.

records.title: Tadamon emergency cash transfers to informal workers, 2020
records.claim: Morocco created a Special Pandemic Fund in March 2020 and, through its Tadamon budget line, paid emergency cash transfers of MAD 800 to 1,200 to households of informal workers, reaching 4.2 million households in the first wave in April 2020 and 5.45 million across the first and second waves, for a total of MAD 16.15 billion by October 2020.

metric.name: Households reached by the first and second waves of Tadamon emergency cash transfers

secondMetric.name: Households reached by the first wave, paid in April 2020

source.publisher: World Bank, Project Appraisal Document, Morocco COVID-19 Social Protection Emergency Response Project (P172809), November 2020

records.limits: The figures are in paragraphs 13 and 14 of a PDF (printed pages 12 and 13 of 103, PDF page 18): 4.2 million households in the April 2020 first wave, 1.25 million added later through the grievance mechanism, 5.45 million across the first two waves (2.8 million RAMED and 2.65 million non-RAMED), a third wave in July 2020, and MAD 16.150 billion paid by October 2020. The World Bank wrote this appraisal to finance the programme retroactively (US$160 million for the Tadamon transfers), so it is a lender describing a programme it was about to fund, not an independent evaluation, and the document gives no exact payment dates beyond the month. Speed is shown only in months: the fund was set up in March 2020, enrolment for non-RAMED households was open on 10 to 16 April, and the first wave was paid in April. The 5.45 million counts households paid at least once, not households kept whole: transfers were flat amounts by household size and stopped after three waves. The 1.25 million added through grievances means the first list missed about a fifth of the households it finally paid, so targeting was fast but rough. The fund was financed in large part by contributions from public enterprises, banks, firms and individuals, not only the budget.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Economy and Finance opened a dedicated budget line in a pandemic fund, used the RAMED health-assistance register to pay listed informal-worker households by mobile phone without a new application, and opened a one-week web platform for informal households outside the register.
preconditions: A large existing register (RAMED, about 30 percent of the population) with household composition and phone contacts
A payment channel that could reach unbanked households through mobile cash withdrawal
A fund able to pool budget and private contributions within days
pattern.travelled: The emergency transfers fed directly into the 2020 royal social protection reform and the unified social register; RAMED was replaced by AMO-Tadamon in December 2022.

records.title: One-off COVID-19 payments to families with children, 2020
records.claim: Russia's government adopted rules on 11 May 2020, the day the President announced it, for a one-off payment of 10,000 rubles per child aged 3 to 16, applied for through the state services portal, and on the first day of payment, 1 June 2020, the Pension Fund paid it for 15.3 million children, more than 150 billion rubles.

metric.name: Children for whom the 10,000-ruble payment was made on the first payment day

secondMetric.name: Days from the decree (No. 652) to the first payment

source.publisher: Government of the Russian Federation (government.ru), briefing by the Minister of Labour and Social Protection, the Minister of Digital Development and the head of the Federal Tax Service on payments to families with children, 2 June 2020

records.limits: The 15.3 million children are the Minister of Labour Anton Kotyakov's spoken figure at a briefing on 2 June 2020, the day after payment began, given as the count 'as of this moment' and described as paid in one day; the 'more than 150 billion' rubles he added is that count times 10,000 rubles, not a separate payment total. It is not a statistical release. He said about 22 million citizens were expected to use the payment. The decree date (No. 652 of 11 May 2020), the President's announcement on the same day, the 5-day review and 3-day payment limits and the 1 June start are in the government's notice of 11 May 2020 (http://government.ru/news/39668/), and the 21 days is our count from 11 May to 1 June. The government and its ministers are reporting on their own measure. The payment was universal for the age group, not targeted at income loss, so speed was bought by not checking need: eligibility needed only the child's age and the parent's application, which the portal could match to civil registry records that, the head of the Federal Tax Service said at the same briefing, had been back-filled with more than 25 million records. A universal per-child cash payment is a broad response; it says nothing about how fast the state adjusted targeted programmes such as unemployment benefits.

pattern.mechanism: The government made the payment universal by age, took applications only through the state services portal and the Pension Fund, and checked them automatically against the digitised civil registry and tax data, with a legal limit of five days to decide and three to pay.
preconditions: A national e-government portal already used by tens of millions of people
A digitised civil registry of births linked to parents
Accumulated reserves, which the President cited when announcing the payment

records.title: Faster Payments System (SBP), run by the Bank of Russia with the banks
records.claim: The Bank of Russia's Faster Payments System, which commercial banks connect to so that customers can pay any account by phone number or QR code, processed more than 3 billion operations worth 14.4 trillion rubles in 2022 with 213 banks connected, and 18.3 billion operations worth 103 trillion rubles in 2025.

metric.name: Operations made through the Faster Payments System in the year

secondMetric.name: Operations made through the Faster Payments System in the year, with 213 banks connected

source.publisher: Bank of Russia, Faster Payments System key indicators, Q4 2025

records.limits: The 2025 figures (18.3 billion operations, 103 trillion rubles, 1.4 and 1.5 times 2024) are in the text of the Bank of Russia's quarterly indicator page; the 2022 figures, the 213 connected banks and the comparison with 2019 to 2021, which dates the start, are on the Q4 2022 page (https://www.cbr.ru/analytics/nps/sbp/4_2022/). The pages are HTML text over charts, with no downloadable series. The central bank owns the system, sets its tariffs and reports on it, so this is the operator grading itself. The collaboration is asymmetric: the Bank of Russia and its payment-card subsidiary NSPK built and run the infrastructure, and banks connect and offer it in their apps; the indicator pages do not say how far connection was voluntary, and the record does not claim it was. Growth after 2022 coincided with the exit of Visa and Mastercard and with sanctions on Russian banks, which pushed users towards domestic rails, so the count reflects a shock as much as the design. The values are nominal rubles in a period of high inflation. Russia's infrastructure PPP and concession programme is not covered by this record.

pattern.mechanism: The central bank built a national instant-payment switch addressed by phone number, capped what banks may charge individuals, and had commercial banks connect it to their own apps, so that a transfer or QR payment works across all connected banks.
preconditions: A central bank with its own retail payment operator (NSPK) able to build and run the switch
Regulatory power over every bank's fees and app offerings
Mobile banking already in near-universal use, so the system only had to be added to existing apps
pattern.travelled: The same move as Brazil's Pix and Bolivia's interoperable QR (bol-qr-bcb); in Russia, sanctions removed the foreign card schemes that compete with it elsewhere.

records.title: AMEN Social emergency transfers, 2020
records.claim: After the March 2020 lockdown, Tunisia's government announced in April 2020 a vertical and horizontal expansion of the AMEN Social programme: a TND 50 top-up for two months to all 260,000 poor households, two TND 200 transfers to 450,000 vulnerable households on the subsidised health card, and a one-off TND 200 transfer to 300,000 further vulnerable households enrolled through a new simplified platform.

metric.name: Vulnerable households outside the AMEN Social registry enrolled through a simplified platform and paid a one-off TND 200

secondMetric.name: Vulnerable households on the subsidised health card paid two TND 200 transfers

source.publisher: World Bank, Project Appraisal Document, Tunisia COVID-19 Social Protection Emergency Response Support Project (P176352), March 2021

records.limits: All three figures are in paragraph 23 of a PDF (printed page 15 of 86, PDF page 21), written a year after the event by the World Bank as it prepared a loan to finance the programme's next phase; it is a lender's description, not an audit, and the counts are round numbers. The document dates the announcement to April 2020 and says the households received the transfers, but it gives no payment dates, so the speed claim rests on the month of the announcement, not on the month money arrived. The 300,000 are households the Ministry of Social Affairs enrolled through a platform it built for the crisis, a horizontal expansion; the other two groups were already known to the state. The amounts were small (TND 200 is about US$73 at the document's rate), and the transfers were one-off or two-month measures. The responsiveness rested on the AMEN Social programme and registry built since 2019 with earlier World Bank support, which the same paragraph credits.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Social Affairs topped up existing cash-transfer beneficiaries, paid households already listed for subsidised health care, and opened a simplified enrolment platform to reach vulnerable households outside the registry.
preconditions: A social registry with accurate identification for most poor and vulnerable households
A legal framework for the AMEN Social programme adopted before the shock
Data cross-checks against other administrative registries to vet new applicants quickly

records.title: ONAS regional sanitation concessions, and their seven-year procurement
records.claim: Tunisia's national sanitation utility ONAS launched procurement of its first two ten-year regional concessions in September 2017; the south-east concession started in June 2024 and served 797,000 people by July 2026, and the North Tunis concession entered into force only on 9 July 2026 after the original consortium had to be reorganised.

metric.name: People receiving wastewater collection and treatment from the concessionaire (south-east lot only)

secondMetric.name: Concession agreements signed and effective at the June 2023 status report, against a target of two by December 2020

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Status and Results Report, Tunisia Sanitation PPP Support Project (P162957), sequence 7, 23 September 2026

records.limits: The 797,000 and the North Tunis entry into force are on pages 2 and 3 of the September 2026 status report, which says the count derives from the south-east lot only and is 92 percent of that lot's end target; the end target for both lots is 2,028,000 people by July 2030. The south-east concession with SCAST was 'scheduled to start on Jun 10, 2024' in the June 2024 status report, and the 783,000 beneficiaries the September 2026 report gives for February 2026 confirm it did. The zero signed agreements against a December 2020 target are in the June 2024 status report (https://documents.worldbank.org/curated/en/099061224041597450/pdf/P162957-61a112cc-f5f3-4ef2-ac1e-0e3c14a54b06.pdf, which also attributes the North Tunis delay to the reorganisation of the ADP-led consortium). The 2017 launch is in the project appraisal document of November 2022, paragraph 13. The World Bank finances the operators' payments through this loan (the status report lists the operation and maintenance component at a cost of 415.30, in US$ millions), so the concessions are public money paying private operators under performance contracts, not private finance, and the lender is reporting on its own project. 'People receiving services' counts the population in the concession area, not households newly connected: only 3,400 people had gained access to improved sanitation through the project by July 2026. The record shows a partnership delivered at national-utility scale but nine years after procurement began, which is as much evidence of slow delivery as of collaboration.

pattern.mechanism: The national sanitation utility bundled the operation, maintenance and rehabilitation of whole regional networks and treatment plants into ten-year performance-based concessions, procured with IFC transaction support and paid from a World Bank loan, replacing short task-based management contracts.
preconditions: An inter-ministerial decision (August 2016) approving a performance-based concession structure for a public utility
External finance to guarantee payments to operators while the utility's own tariffs covered only part of its costs
A concession unit inside the utility able to supervise operators, which the project had to build

records.title: COVID-19 low-income family allowances and unemployment benefits, 2020
records.claim: Uzbekistan's government expanded its COVID-19 unemployment support from a one-off to multiple benefits, which the World Bank followed by restructuring its emergency project on 12 August 2020, and with that financing had paid US$50.77 million in low-income family allowances to more than 1,000,000 families and US$0.65 million in unemployment benefits to 19,700 people by 1 January 2021.

metric.name: Families paid low-income family allowances under the emergency project

secondMetric.name: People paid unemployment benefits under the emergency project

source.publisher: World Bank, Disclosable Restructuring Paper, Uzbekistan Emergency COVID-19 Response Project (P173827), January 2021

records.limits: The figures are in paragraphs 2 and 6 of a World Bank restructuring paper, the lender's account of its own project. The record shows slowness as much as speed: the project was approved on 24 April 2020 but became effective only on 14 July 2020, the paper says it took the government three months to issue the Presidential Resolution enabling implementation, and payments under the component began only in November 2020, more than six months after the project was approved. The 1,000,000 families is 'more than', the families were recipients of an existing allowance financed partly from the project rather than new beneficiaries, and the paper does not say how many were added because of the pandemic. Unemployment benefit reached only 19,700 people, which says how narrow formal unemployment support was. Support the government paid from its own budget outside this project is not covered by this source.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Finance channelled an emergency donor credit into the existing low-income family allowance and a temporary unemployment benefit, changing the benefit from one payment to several when the shock outlasted the first plan.
preconditions: An existing means-tested family allowance with a beneficiary list
Emergency external finance, here an IDA credit approved within weeks
A presidential resolution to authorise spending, which was the slow step

records.title: Response and housing recovery after the spring 2024 floods
records.claim: Kazakhstan's government reported that during the spring 2024 floods, which it called the largest in 80 years, more than 120,000 people were rescued and placed in temporary accommodation centres, and that by December 2024 it had bought 5,767 homes, fully repaired 9,156 and built 2,680 new houses for owners of the 19,359 flooded homes inspected, while 36,455 families received one-off assistance.

metric.name: People rescued and placed in temporary accommodation during the flood period

secondMetric.name: New individual houses built for flood victims (64 billion tenge)

source.publisher: Office of the Prime Minister of the Republic of Kazakhstan (primeminister.kz), review '2024 zhylgy su tasqyny: azamattarga aleumettik komek, uyler men infraqurylymdar salu zhane qalpyna keltiru', 25 December 2024 (in Kazakh)

records.limits: The government reports on its own response in a press review, with no independent verification, and the page exists only in Kazakh (the English and Russian addresses redirect to the home page); figures were translated by me. 'Rescued and placed in temporary accommodation' counts evacuations, not people saved from death, and the page gives no count of deaths or of people who stayed. The housing figures answer only for homes that were the owner's sole dwelling (19,359 inspected), so second homes and renters are outside them, and the three remedies (purchase, repair, new build) add to 17,603 against 19,359 inspected by my sum, so about 1,750 cases are not accounted for on the page. The page itself says the scale could not have been forecast, which bears on preparation: the response was large but the warning system did not anticipate the event, and the President afterwards created a Committee for the Prevention of Emergencies inside the ministry. Spending figures are nominal tenge. Status 'concluded' rests on a December 2024 account; later complaints about the quality of new houses, if any, were not checked.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Emergency Situations coordinated a national and regional headquarters that evacuated whole settlements by land and air, and the government then used its reserve to buy housing on the market, repair, and build new houses within the same year.
preconditions: A civil protection system able to mobilise army, police and National Guard under one command
A government reserve fund large enough to pay for housing within months
A functioning housing market from which homes could be bought quickly in the affected regions

records.title: Earthquake Reconstruction Project in the Spitak earthquake zone
records.claim: Armenia's Ministry of Economy, through a project implementation unit, restarted reconstruction in the zone of the December 1988 Spitak earthquake that had stopped when Soviet work crews withdrew in 1991, and by April 1997 had provided 2,857 housing units against 2,069 planned, completed 10 factories against 7 and laid 41 km of water pipes against about 27 km, under an IDA credit closed in June 1997.

metric.name: Housing units provided (completed unfinished apartments and repaired or strengthened units)

secondMetric.name: Housing units planned at appraisal

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion Report, Armenia Earthquake Reconstruction Project (Credit 2562-AM), Report No. 17255, December 1997

records.limits: The World Bank wrote the report on a credit of about US$28 million. The unit counts are in Table 5 (Key Indicators for Project Implementation, printed page 17), which is OCR text with errors (the bathhouse row repeats the housing figure). The earthquake left about 530,000 people homeless (Part I, para. 1), so 2,857 units is a small fraction of the need, delivered five to eight years after the shock; the record shows recovery capacity in a newly independent state restarting a stalled Soviet programme, not a timely national recovery. The ICR says beneficiaries were slow to move out of temporary 'domiks', and that many families were still in temporary shelter in 1997. Units count apartments of different kinds (completion of unfinished blocks, repair and strengthening) and the project's single-family starter houses were scaled back. The ICR rates implementation satisfactory and credits an independent implementation unit, not a ministry line department.

pattern.mechanism: A small, politically insulated implementation unit under the economy ministry took over half-finished Soviet reconstruction sites and completed them through competitive local contracts, choosing nearly finished buildings to maximise habitable units per dollar.
preconditions: Sunk investment in partly built blocks that could be finished cheaply
Competitive local contractors willing to bid in dollar-equivalent contracts
An external credit when the state budget could not fund reconstruction

records.title: Flood Emergency Project after the 1998 southern floods
records.claim: After record floods in southern Kyrgyzstan in 1998 damaged about 1,000 houses, the Department of Water Resources rebuilt or built 27.4 km of river protection embankments against 8.8 km planned, directly protecting about 40,000 people, and in 2003 a flood greater than that of 1998 passed the new embankments without significant damage or overtopping.

metric.name: River protection embankments rehabilitated or constructed

secondMetric.name: People living in flood zones protected directly

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion Report, Kyrgyz Republic Flood Emergency Project, Report No. 29944, 2004

records.limits: The World Bank wrote the report on an IDA credit of about US$10 million and rated the outcome Satisfactory. The figures are in the outputs section and the summary of achievements; the 2003 test is described with a reference to Table 11.3 of the report, which is OCR text of a 2004 PDF. The 40,000 people protected is the report's estimate, not a count, and 'no significant damage' is the report's judgement; it also says sections downstream of the rebuilt embankments were weakened by the same 2003 floods and needed emergency repairs. The works took until March 2004 against a planned closing of September 2001, in part because floods in 2002 and 2003 swept away half-finished works and Uzbekistan closed its border to rock supplies. The record evidences preparation for the next flood at a few sites in three raions, not national flood preparedness, though the project set up a Flood and Mudflow Protection Agency responsible for some 460 km of embankments nationwide; whether that agency is still funded was not checked.

pattern.mechanism: After a record flood the water department rebuilt the failed river defences to a 1-in-200-year standard with more durable rock and gabion-mattress linings instead of patching them, and created a dedicated agency to maintain embankments.
preconditions: Emergency credit available within months of the flood
Hydrological records long enough (from 1927) to set a design flood
A maintenance budget for the new agency, which the report flags as limited

records.title: Sfax flood protection (belt canal) after the 1982 flood
records.claim: After the October 1982 flood in Sfax killed at least 70 people and destroyed about 700 houses, Tunisia's Urban Hydraulics Directorate built an eight-km belt canal and rehabilitated the city's wadi channels and dikes, completing the works in June 1988 as scheduled, and the January 1990 floods that damaged much of central and southern Tunisia did not damage the protected area.

metric.name: Belt canal built around Greater Sfax

secondMetric.name: Lives lost in the October 1982 Sfax flood (at least)

source.publisher: World Bank, Project Completion Report, Tunisia Sfax Flood Protection Project (Loan 2289-TUN), Report No. 9877, 30 August 1991

records.limits: The World Bank, which lent US$25 million (US$22.3 million disbursed), wrote the report. The belt canal length is in the project description and the completion date in the timetable table (Table 2, planned and actual June 1988); 'completed according to the original schedule' is para. 5.01. The evidence that the works protected the city is one sentence noting that the January 1990 floods did not damage the project area, which the report says was acknowledged by the press and local residents; no rainfall or discharge comparison is given, so the 1990 event may have been smaller in Sfax than 1982. The report warns that protection depends on maintenance funding without cost recovery, and recommends an impact evaluation within five years; none was read. This is a 1984 to 1988 build and says nothing about current Tunisian flood preparedness. The text is OCR of a scanned 1991 report.

pattern.mechanism: After a flood with an estimated 130-year return period, the urban hydraulics directorate built an intercepting canal around the city to divert runoff from the catchment above it, plus storm drains inside it, and set up a regional maintenance section.
preconditions: A 1978 master plan and long hydrological series that let a feasibility study finish within three months
Land expropriation for a canal corridor on the urban edge
A maintenance unit with a recurring budget, which the report doubted

records.title: Housing reconstruction after the February 2019 Shamakhi earthquake
records.claim: Azerbaijan's Minister of Emergency Situations reported on 5 December 2019, ten months after the February 2019 Shamakhi earthquake, that 580 houses had been built and 1,175 houses restored in Shamakhi district with state funds, while three apartment buildings with 174 flats were, by the President's account on the same page, still under construction.

metric.name: Houses restored in Shamakhi district

secondMetric.name: New houses built in Shamakhi district (three apartment buildings with 174 flats still under construction)

source.publisher: Official website of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, 'Ilham Aliyev viewed conditions created at newly constructed building for earthquake-affected families in Shamakhi', 5 December 2019 (statement by Minister of Emergency Situations Kamaladdin Heydarov)

records.limits: The figures are spoken by the emergency minister during a presidential visit and published on the President's website, in a text that is largely praise of the President; there is no independent verification, no count of houses damaged to set them against, and no cost. The President says on the same page that the three high-rise buildings with 174 flats were still under construction and that work was also done in Aghsu and Ismayilli districts, which the figures do not cover. The page says there were no fatalities, which reflects the earthquake's size as much as preparedness. The earlier May 2012 Zagatala and Gakh earthquake, where the ministry's commission found 3,336 private houses unusable in Gakh alone and construction had started on 266 by September 2012 (president.az articles 4823 and 5940), shows the same model at larger scale but with no completion figure read. The record shows rapid state-financed reconstruction, not risk reduction: nothing on the page concerns seismic codes or warning.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Emergency Situations acts as the builder after an earthquake, demolishing damaged houses and building replacements with state money within the year, under direct presidential instruction instead of through insurance.
preconditions: A ministry with its own construction capacity and direct budget access
Oil-revenue fiscal room to fund reconstruction without insurance
Political priority set from the top, which also makes the reporting promotional

records.title: Housing recovery after the Sardoba reservoir dam failure, 2020
records.claim: After the Sardoba reservoir dam broke on 1 May 2020 in Syrdarya region, Uzbekistan's government evacuated about 90,000 people from 24 mahallas of three districts, and by October 2020 had built 37 five-storey blocks with 1,480 flats in Sardoba district's Dustlik mahalla, given free to flood victims, and 86 five-storey buildings in Sardoba and Mirzaabad districts.

metric.name: People evacuated to safe areas from 24 mahallas of Sardoba, Akaltyn and Mirzaabad districts (about)

secondMetric.name: Flats in 37 five-storey blocks built in Dustlik mahalla, Sardoba district

source.publisher: Official website of the President of the Republic of Uzbekistan, 'Shavkat Mirziyoyev: the flood has proved a bitter lesson for us', 5 May 2020, and 'Modern enterprise, cozy housing breathe new life to Sardoba', 13 October 2020 (https://president.uz/en/lists/view/3891)

records.limits: The shock was itself a failure of preparedness: the president's own site calls it a 'man-made accident on the reservoir', a dam that failed within a few years of filling, so the record shows recovery after a failure the state caused, not readiness. The figures come from presidential news items (the 5 May address for the evacuation, the 13 October item for the flats, and 'Construction projects reported', 26 October 2020, https://president.uz/en/lists/view/3916, for the 86 buildings) with no independent check, and they mix counts of flats and of buildings. The plans of 15 May 2020 (lists/view/3572 to 3574) name about 4,500 affected homeowners and further blocks of 360 flats in Mirzaabad and 800 in Akaltyn plus repairs to hundreds of cottages; whether those were finished was not read, so the 1,480 flats show part of the programme. The evacuation figure is a round number in a presidential address, with no breakdown or timing beyond 'immediately', and the same address reports a separate storm in Bukhara region days earlier. Builders were mobilised from every region, so the speed reflects command mobilisation rather than a standing recovery system.

pattern.mechanism: The president set up a government commission, assigned each region of the country a mahalla to rebuild with its own construction teams, and the state built free apartment blocks for flood victims within five months.
preconditions: Central control over regional governments and state construction firms
Budget and donor money (including a private US$10 million donation) available within weeks
Land under destroyed houses left with owners, which eased acceptance of flats

records.title: Emergency Flood Assistance Project after the 1998 and 1999 floods
records.claim: After floods in 1998 caused damage estimated at US$40 million, about 2 percent of GDP, Tajikistan's Republican Project Coordination Unit for Liquidation of Consequences of Natural Disasters had repaired about 210 km of roads and fully completed seven bridges and structures by the credit's closing on 31 December 2001, with about 80 km of road repairs and three bridges unfinished, and the World Bank rated the outcome unsatisfactory.

metric.name: Road repairs completed at closing (about 80 km more unfinished)

secondMetric.name: Damage from the 1998 floods as estimated

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion Report, Tajikistan Emergency Flood Assistance Project (IDA-31230, IDA-31231), Report No. 24209, 2002

records.limits: The World Bank wrote the report and rated the outcome Unsatisfactory and sustainability Unlikely, mainly over poor works quality and financial management; it refused a further extension and closed the credit as planned. The record is filed as evidence of weak recovery capacity, not of success. The report says the roads actually damaged totalled about 105 km of the 210 km repaired, that works quality was poor because local firms lacked experience and supervision, and that only three of eight planned power substations were completed. The project came a year after the end of a five-year civil war, with a supplemental credit after further floods in 1999, so capacity was at a low point. The text is OCR of a scanned 2002 report, and the data sheet and narrative disagree on the original closing date (January 2000 against June 2001).

pattern.mechanism: A government emergency coordination unit repaired flood-damaged bridges, roads and embankments with an emergency IDA credit through local contractors, without the supervision capacity to hold them to quality.
preconditions: An emergency lending window that disburses within months
Local contractors with experience of the work, which were scarce after the civil war
A coordination unit with financial controls the lender trusts, which it lacked

records.title: Roshydromet modernization: accuracy of hazard warnings to emergency agencies
records.claim: Russia's federal hydrometeorological service Roshydromet raised the accuracy of its warnings on hazardous hydrometeorological events delivered to regional emergency agencies from 81 to 83 percent to 91 percent, and of its warnings on natural hazards from 88 to 95.8 percent, between 2014 and the end of 2022 under its second national modernization project.

metric.name: Accuracy of warnings on hazardous hydromet events delivered to regional emergency agencies (WMO standards)

secondMetric.name: Accuracy of warnings on natural hazards, perfect warnings as share of warnings issued (baseline 88 percent in 2014)

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Russia Second National Hydromet Modernization Project (P127676), 2024

records.limits: The World Bank wrote the report without site visits or formal interviews, because it suspended disbursements on 19 March 2022 (para. 1), so the indicator values are Roshydromet's own figures as reported to the Bank. The figures are in para. 49 and the results annex (ICR pages 18 and 37). Warning accuracy is a forecast-verification statistic, not a measure of whether warnings reached people or prompted action, and the record ties it to no single disaster; it is a preparedness capacity figure of the same kind as the South African radar availability record. The report says the improved reliability let Roshydromet sign, for the first time, binding agreements with the Ministry of Emergencies on hazard warnings. The final cost was US$174.89 million, 25 percent above appraisal, with the government financing what the Bank suspension left. Status 'operating' assumes the system still runs; nothing after 2022 was read.

pattern.mechanism: The national weather service modernised its observation network, computing and forecasting models over two successive World Bank projects, and measured itself on the verified accuracy of hazard warnings passed to emergency agencies.
preconditions: A national hydromet service with a single federal budget and network
Successive projects over a decade, the first (RHM-1) building the baseline
A verification method agreed with WMO so accuracy is measured the same way each year

records.title: COVID-19 vaccination campaign
records.claim: Egypt's health authorities reported to WHO that 56,907,319 people, 56 per 100 population, had received at least one COVID-19 vaccine dose by 31 December 2023, from a first dose given on 24 January 2021, with 42,337,175 (41 per 100) completing the primary series.

metric.name: People vaccinated with at least one COVID-19 vaccine dose

secondMetric.name: People who completed the primary series (last dose)

source.publisher: World Health Organization, COVID-19 dashboard vaccination data (vaccination-data.csv)

records.limits: The figures are Egypt's own reports to WHO (DATA_SOURCE 'REPORTING'), with no independent coverage survey behind them. Completion of the primary series reached 41 per 100 and boosters 15,217,352 people (15 per 100), so the record shows a partial delivery. The row reports 102,191,677 doses in total, 100 per 100 population. The VACCINES_USED field is empty, so the record cannot show which products were used or where the doses came from, and it evidences distribution only. The per-100 rates divide by WHO's population estimate. Vaccination is a response to one shock, not proof of general preparedness, and it is filed under the precedent of bol-covid-vaccination and ven-covid-vaccination as a judgement call because no hazard-specific delivery with an official figure was found for this country in this batch. The source is a CSV with no prose; the numbers are read from one row. The cited URL is the blob the WHO dashboard serves, the same one bol-covid-vaccination cites.

pattern.mechanism: Egypt's health ministry ran a national COVID-19 campaign through its primary care network and mass vaccination sites and reported progress to WHO.
preconditions: A routine immunisation programme and cold chain
A supply of doses large enough for a national campaign, however obtained
Registers good enough to count who received a second dose

records.title: COVID-19 vaccination campaign

metric.name: People vaccinated with at least one COVID-19 vaccine dose

secondMetric.name: People who completed the primary series (last dose)

source.publisher: World Health Organization, COVID-19 dashboard vaccination data (vaccination-data.csv)
