records.title: Ain Sokhna supercritical power plant
records.claim: The Egyptian Electricity Holding Company built the 1,300 MW Ain Sokhna supercritical thermal power plant, with its first unit entering commercial operation on 3 March 2015 and the second on 4 June 2015, at a final cost of US$1,159.4 million against a base cost of US$2,139.6 million estimated at appraisal in 2009.

metric.name: Final cost of the Ain Sokhna Power Plant component

secondMetric.name: Base cost of the power plant component at appraisal (PAD), excluding US$50.2 million contingencies

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Egypt Ain Sokhna Power Project (P100047), 26 June 2019

records.limits: The World Bank, which lent US$600 million of the cost, wrote the report. The costs are in Table 1 and para. 23 (ICR pages 8 to 9), the commercial operation dates in para. 20 of the annex on design and implementation; the report says construction was 'initially delayed' but finished 'about when expected' and gives no original target date for commercial operation, so schedule performance rests on that judgement and on the 2015 dates. The ICR does not explain why the plant cost 46 percent less than estimated; a 2013 restructuring had already cut the estimate to US$1,655.3 million, which suggests the 2009 estimate was high rather than that delivery was unusually efficient, and the savings went into a transmission component. That transmission component ran late: it was not finished at the extended loan closing of 31 December 2018 (original closing 31 December 2015), and its final cost was not known. The plant was designed to burn heavy fuel oil as well as gas, which the report says raised its cost and lowered its efficiency against a combined-cycle plant. The status rests on the report's account of operation in 2015 to 2018, not on a current source.

pattern.mechanism: The state power holding company procured a large thermal plant in a few big packages co-financed by four lenders, priced the appraisal estimate conservatively, and redeployed the savings into grid works.
preconditions: A state utility with an engineering department experienced in large thermal plants
Co-financing from several development lenders committed before bidding
A market for supercritical boilers and turbines competitive enough to bid below estimate

records.title: Hartha power station units 2 and 3 rehabilitation, and its halt
records.claim: Iraq's Ministry of Electricity set out in 2007 to restore 400 MW at Hartha power station units 2 and 3 by December 2010 under the Emergency Electricity Reconstruction Project, but when the project closed on 30 June 2015 no capacity had been restored, the works were about 70 percent complete, the cost estimate had risen from US$150 million to US$187.62 million with a US$98.97 million financing gap, and the contractor withdrew from the site.

metric.name: Generating capacity of Hartha units 2 and 3 restored at project close (target 400 MW)

secondMetric.name: Latest estimate of total project cost, against US$150 million at appraisal

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Iraq Emergency Electricity Reconstruction Project (P087734), report ICR3577, 2016

records.limits: The World Bank wrote the report and rated both itself and the borrower unsatisfactory or moderately unsatisfactory, and it says blame for the delays was shared between the ministry and the contractor (para. 53, PDF page 29). The 0 MW and 70 percent figures are in the results table (PDF page 7); the cost table and the US$98.97 million gap are in Annex 1 (PDF page 43); the halt is para. 46 (PDF page 25: 'works have practically stopped'). The cost estimate excludes about US$19 million the government paid for contractor security and an unsettled price adjustment. Much of the failure came from the design: the project had to reuse equipment bought in 1999 under the Oil for Food Programme, which narrowed bidding and bred disputes, and the security situation from 2014 raised costs. The status is 'concluded' because the financed project closed and its result, no capacity restored, stands; it is a delivery failure, not a reversal, since nothing delivered was later lost and the report does not say the rehabilitation was terminated. Whether the ministry later completed the units with its own money was not read at any Iraqi source. The units are part of one station, a modest project by value; the record evidences delivery failure on a rehabilitation, not on a new build.

pattern.mechanism: The ministry tried to finish a rehabilitation begun under sanctions by contracting one turnkey supplier to install equipment bought a decade earlier, and when disputes and budget shortfalls stalled the works, it could neither fund a variation nor terminate.
preconditions: Legacy equipment that tied the contract to bidders familiar with its design
A government budget able to fund variations and security costs, which was missing after the 2014 oil price fall
A contract with clear termination and dispute rules, which the report says were lacking

records.title: Greater Beirut Water Supply Project (Awali to Beirut conveyor), and its unfinished delivery
records.claim: Lebanon's Council for Development and Reconstruction and the Beirut Mount Lebanon Water Establishment built most of a system to bring 250,000 cubic metres a day from the Awali to 1.2 million people in Greater Beirut, but when the World Bank loan closed on 30 April 2025, 106 months after the original June 2016 closing date, no additional water had been delivered, the 24/7 supply reached in a 20,000-customer pilot zone in 2018 had not been maintained, and component costs had risen from US$370 million at approval to US$561.7 million.

metric.name: Customers in the Achrafieh pilot zone receiving 24/7 water supply at closing

secondMetric.name: Customers in the Achrafieh pilot zone receiving 24/7 water supply when the target was reached

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Lebanon Greater Beirut Water Supply Project (P103063, Loan 7967-LE), report ICR00441, 16 December 2025

records.limits: The World Bank wrote the report and rated the outcome Highly Unsatisfactory and its own performance Moderately Unsatisfactory. The 106 months are in para. 17; the zero water delivered, the 75, 84 and 89 percent completion of tunnels, pipelines and treatment plant and the 20,000-customer pilot are in Table 2 and paras. 29 to 31 (ICR pages 8 to 9). The US$561.7 million is the project budget at closing printed in Table 3 of the report against US$370 million at appraisal, and matches the sum of the three components in Annex 3 (US$434.0, 112.7 and 15.0 million; page 31) against 294.0, 61.0 and 15.0 at approval. Lebanon's 2019 financial collapse, COVID-19, the 2020 port explosion and a contractor's insolvency all fall inside the delay, so it is not a clean measure of institutional capacity in normal times, and a US$90 million additional financing approved in 2018 lapsed because Lebanon did not make it effective. The erosion is the pilot zone's 24/7 supply, reached in 2018 and lost; that is a small part of the project, and the main failure is non-completion, not loss. A follow-on Second Greater Beirut Water Supply Project was approved on 14 January 2025 to finish the works, so the delivery may still complete. The related Bisri dam, financed under a separate project, was partly cancelled before construction (footnote in para. 8) and is not counted here.

pattern.mechanism: The reconstruction council and the regional water utility split a gravity conveyance, treatment and distribution system between them, financed the start with a World Bank loan, and depended on utility surpluses and a second loan for the rest; when the utility's revenue and the state's finances collapsed, the scheme stopped short of delivering water.
preconditions: A utility with cash surpluses able to co-finance distribution, which disappeared with the 2019 crisis
Parliamentary ratification of loans in time, which failed for the 2018 additional financing
Contract terms that allocate contractor insolvency risk, which the report says were missing

records.title: Amman Development Corridor (Amman Ring Road phase 1), and its overrun
records.claim: Jordan's Ministry of Public Works and Housing built the 40 km first phase of the Amman Ring Road under the Amman Development Corridor Project, whose estimated total cost rose from US$160.6 million at appraisal in 2004 to US$455.97 million in March 2013, with the road works alone rising from US$106.92 million to US$279.87 million, while the loan closing date moved from June 2009 to December 2012 and one of three sections was 65 percent complete at closing.

metric.name: Actual or latest estimated total project cost (15 March 2013)

secondMetric.name: Total project cost estimated at appraisal

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Jordan Amman Development Corridor Project (P081505, Loan 7634), report ICR2661, 10 June 2013

records.limits: The World Bank, which financed one of three road sections (with the Arab Fund and the EIB financing the others), wrote the report and rated the outcome, its own performance and the borrower's Moderately Unsatisfactory. The costs are in Annex 1 (printed page 18): land acquisition rose from US$40.9 million to US$158.43 million and is a large part of the overrun, and the latest estimate includes US$42 million of payments due after closing to finish Section 1 and settle bills. Against the 2008 additional-financing estimate of US$343.18 million the overrun is 32 percent, so much of the growth was already recognised mid-project. The 65 percent figure for Section 1 is in the results table; the report says in para. 48 that the road remained uncertain of reaching operation 'when nearly twice the expected construction time has passed', and that the inland port and customs depot were 'gradually dropped'. The text is a scanned 2013 report with OCR errors in the data sheet. When the whole road opened was not read at an official source; 'concluded' means the financed project closed with the road mostly built.

pattern.mechanism: The public works ministry split a 40 km expressway around Amman into three sections financed by three lenders, acquired land late and at rising prices, and absorbed design changes during construction with additional financing rather than rescoping.
preconditions: A land acquisition budget fixed before prices rose along an announced alignment
Three lenders with separate procurement and supervision rules on one road
A ministry able to fund overruns from the budget, which ran short in the final section

records.title: East-West Highway Corridor Improvement Project (Rikoti Pass sections)
records.claim: Georgia's Roads Department completed most civil works on the Zemo Osiauri to Chumateleti and Chumateleti to Khevi sections of the East-West Highway across the Rikoti Pass by the project's closing on 30 June 2025, four and a half years after the original loan closing date of 31 December 2020, and the government's own financing rose to US$91.03 million against US$44 million planned for the enlarged project (US$24 million at approval plus US$20 million under the 2017 additional financing).

metric.name: Borrower co-financing actually disbursed

secondMetric.name: Borrower co-financing planned, parent project (US$24 million) plus 2017 additional financing (US$20 million), my sum of Table 2

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Georgia East-West Highway Corridor Improvement Project (P149952, Loans 8547-GE and 8788-GE), 2026

records.limits: The World Bank wrote the report and rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and efficiency Modest. The financing figures are in the data sheet and Table 2 (ICR page 4); the closing-date changes in the restructuring table (paras. 10 to 11) and para. 23. Much of the extra time and government money followed a 2017 decision to add the 11.6 km Chumateleti to Khevi link, co-financed by an EIB loan of EUR 67.47 million, so the plan the outturn is set against grew mid-project; Table 2's component 1 estimates (parent plus additional financing, US$273.48 million including EIB) against actuals (US$359.72 million) give a 32 percent overrun by my own sum, which the report does not state. The report attributes the 18-month extension of 2023 to re-tendering, COVID-19 and mountain construction, and the parallel Fourth East-West Highway project's ICR (2020) records that a Zemo Osiauri to Chumateleti lot was terminated in December 2018 and re-bid under this project. Most civil works were complete at closing, with residual works finished afterwards on government money; the date of full opening was not read at an official source.

pattern.mechanism: The Roads Department carried the national east-west highway over its hardest mountain pass in contracts financed by the World Bank and the EIB, and when contracts failed or were re-tendered the government covered the gap from its own budget instead of cutting scope.
preconditions: A sequence of earlier highway projects that built the Roads Department's contract management
Lenders willing to co-finance tunnels and bridges in seismic mountain terrain
Budget room to nearly quadruple counterpart funding

records.title: North-South Road Corridor Investment Program, Tranche 1
records.claim: Armenia's Ministry of Transport, Communication and Information Technologies reconstructed about 30 km of the M1 Yerevan to Ashtarak and M2 Yerevan to Artashat roads under the first tranche of the ADB-financed North-South Road Corridor programme for an implementation cost of US$68.70 million against US$68.0 million at appraisal, but completed the project on 16 June 2016 against a planned 31 December 2013, after one round of bids was rejected and the M1 section was cut from 18.4 km to about 10 km.

metric.name: Total implementation cost, actual

secondMetric.name: Total implementation cost at appraisal

source.publisher: Asian Development Bank, Completion Report, Armenia North-South Road Corridor Investment Program (Tranche 1), Project 42145-023, Loan 2561, January 2020

records.limits: ADB, the lender, wrote the report. The completion dates and costs are in the basic data table at the front of the PDF (pages 2 to 4); the scope changes are paras. 8 to 16. The 30-month slip from December 2013 to June 2016 is my subtraction from the two dates; the loan closed on 23 February 2018 against 30 June 2014 in the loan agreement. Cost held near appraisal only because the scope moved: the M1 section was cut to about 10 km because of land acquisition, 2 km was transferred to tranche 2 when Armenia hit fiscal limits, and 19.6 km of the M2 was added, so the outturn buys different roads; the combined tranche 1 and 2 works contract was US$10 million above the engineer's estimate and the government undertook to fund overruns (para. 14 and footnote 13). This is the first and smallest tranche of a programme to rebuild a 550 km corridor; later tranches, including the Talin to Gyumri works, were not read, and the programme's overall delivery is not evidenced here.

pattern.mechanism: The transport ministry used a multitranche ADB facility to rebuild the national north-south corridor section by section, adjusting each tranche's scope to land acquisition and fiscal limits instead of extending its budget.
preconditions: A multitranche facility that lets scope move between tranches
A project management unit that also prepares designs and tenders for later tranches
Government readiness to finance gaps when bids come in above estimate

records.title: Second National Water Supply and Sanitation Project (rayon centres), and its downsizing
records.claim: Azerbaijan's water agencies built water supply and sanitation systems in eight regional (rayon) centres under the Second National Water Supply and Sanitation Project, after a 2012 restructuring cut the scope from 21 rayons to 8 because of cost increases, while the total project cost rose from US$560 million to US$641.8 million and the loan closed on 30 June 2019 instead of 28 February 2013.

metric.name: Total project cost, actual disbursed (World Bank US$407.8 million plus Government US$234 million)

secondMetric.name: Total project cost at approval, for 21 rayons

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Azerbaijan Second National Water Supply and Sanitation Project (P109961), 18 December 2019

records.limits: The World Bank wrote the report and rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory. The financing and dates are in the data sheet (ICR pages 1 to 2); the cut from 21 to 8 rayons, the reasons and the closing extensions are in Box 1 (page 8), and footnote 7 attributes the reduction to cost increases and unanticipated investments. The approval cost and the final cost cover different scopes: the original estimates for 43 rayons across both national projects were 'not supported by thorough technical studies', so the 2008 figure was not a real baseline, and a US$150 million additional financing in 2014 paid for design changes required by new government policy (legalised dwellings, EU standards), not only for overruns. Implementation moved from AzerSu to the irrigation agency SAWMA in 2009 and then to its successor company after mis-procurement in Nakhchivan, so 'the country's institutions' here are several, and the record does not separate their performance. People served and service quality are in the report but are not the subject of this record.

pattern.mechanism: The government launched a national programme to rebuild water systems in all regional centres on rough cost estimates, financed slices of it with World Bank loans, and when real costs emerged, cut the number of towns and stretched the timetable instead of finding the money.
preconditions: Feasibility studies before approval, which were missing here
An implementing utility not already running a dozen donor projects at once
A lender willing to refuse additional financing and force a downsizing

records.title: National Road Rehabilitation (Osh-Batken-Isfana) Project
records.claim: The Kyrgyz Ministry of Transport and Communications rehabilitated 50 km of the Osh-Batken-Isfana road corridor, against about 30 km planned at approval in 2009, for a total project cost of US$52.46 million against US$30.72 million estimated, over four years and ten months instead of three, closing on 31 December 2014 instead of 30 June 2013.

metric.name: Total project cost, actual, with scope increased through two additional financings

secondMetric.name: Total project cost at appraisal, for about 30 km

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Kyrgyz Republic National Road Rehabilitation (Osh-Batken-Isfana) Project (P107608), report ICR3239, 2015

records.limits: The World Bank wrote the report and rated the outcome Satisfactory. The costs are in Annex 1 (PDF page 36), the 30 km plan in para. 1.5.2, the 50 km outturn in para. 3.2.2, and the schedule in para. 1.7.2. Most of the cost rise followed added scope: two additional financings added road length and the repair of about 350 km of Osh urban roads, both paid from the road component (US$27.29 million estimated, US$50.27 million actual), so no cost per kilometre of the corridor can be computed from the report and the record cannot separate overrun from added scope. The 18-month extension also followed the added scope. This is a 50 km rehabilitation, small against the country's network, and it says nothing about larger state-financed builds; no Kyrgyz audit was read.

pattern.mechanism: The transport ministry's implementation group rehabilitated a corridor section on a World Bank credit and, delivering on budget, was given two additional financings to extend the works along the same road.
preconditions: An implementation unit with a track record on other donors' road projects
A lender that rewards delivery with additional financing on the same corridor
A corridor whose remaining sections were already designed

records.title: Tehran Sewerage Project (first phase: interceptors, trunk main and southern treatment plant)
records.claim: The Tehran Sewerage Company built interceptors, trunk mains, tunnels and a wastewater treatment plant under the first phase of the Tehran Sewerage Project at a latest estimated cost of US$359.22 million against US$341.45 million at appraisal in 2000, with the treatment works costing 189 percent of their estimate and the loan closing on 30 June 2008, two years late, before the plant and the eastern trunk main were finished.

metric.name: Actual or latest estimated total project cost

secondMetric.name: Total project cost estimated at appraisal

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Iran Tehran Sewerage Project (P069941), report ICR1028, 29 June 2009

records.limits: The World Bank, which lent US$145 million, wrote the report and rated the outcome Satisfactory. The component costs are in Annex 1 (PDF page 36); the US$28.7 million funding shortfall, high inflation (12 to 24 percent a year) and a euro-denominated plant contract as the cause of the two-year extension are in para. 50 (PDF page 20). The total stayed near the estimate only because interceptors and laterals came in at 61 percent of estimate while the trunk main (178 percent) and treatment works (189 percent) overran, so the aggregate hides the overrun on the hardest parts. The plant and the eastern trunk main were unfinished at closing, and the report says only that the company had resources to finish them; completion was not read at a current source. The figures are 2000 to 2008 and say little about Iranian delivery under sanctions since.

pattern.mechanism: The capital's sewerage company built the network in parallel with a design-build-operate contract for the treatment plant, letting the network race ahead on cheap domestic pipe while the plant ran late and over budget under inflation and a foreign-currency contract.
preconditions: A domestic pipe industry able to supply at falling prices
Counterpart funds indexed for inflation, which were short here
A foreign-currency contract hedged against a weakening rial, which it was not

records.title: Central Ring Road around Moscow (TsKAD), audited by the Accounts Chamber
records.claim: Russia's Accounts Chamber found in June 2020 that the state company Avtodor's Central Ring Road project, whose first stage was originally to be built in 2014 to 2018 and was now scheduled for 2014 to 2021, had risen in cost by 2.6 billion roubles in 2019 to 315.9 billion roubles, and that launch complexes 1 and 5 were only 49 and 61 percent complete on 1 January 2020.

metric.name: Project cost after the 2019 increase

secondMetric.name: Technical readiness of launch complex no. 1

source.publisher: Accounts Chamber of the Russian Federation (Schetnaya palata), check report summary 'Stroitelstvo TsKAD dorozhaet, no ne zakanchivaetsya', 16 June 2020, archived copy

records.limits: The live ach.gov.ru did not answer a script today, so the cited copy is the Internet Archive's of 15 September 2020. The page is the audit office's summary of its check, not the full report, and it does not state the original cost, so the record shows cost growth in one year, not the full cost overrun against an approved baseline; the schedule baseline is in the page's footnote, which gives the construction period of the first stage as 2014 to 2021, originally 2014 to 2018; the Chamber's 5 August 2015 release on the same project (archived at https://web.archive.org/web/20210717054203/https://ach.gov.ru/news/sredstva-fonda-nacionalnogo-blagosostoyaniya-napravlennye-na-stroitelstvo-ckad-ne-ispolzuyutsya-v-po-22619) says construction of complexes 1 and 5 had not started a year after their agreements were signed and that National Wealth Fund money sat unused in a bank. The road is a concession-based project of a state company with private investors (33.8 billion roubles of 186.5 billion invested by end 2019), so delivery is partly private. The 2014 start is the year of the first concession agreements cited by the 2015 release. Status 'concluded' assumes the ring opened in the years after the audit; no official source for the final opening date or final cost was read, which is the record's main weakness.

pattern.mechanism: The federal road company procured a ring road around Moscow as long-term investment concessions, financed by the National Wealth Fund, budget subsidies and investors, and as works lagged the government extended deadlines and the Accounts Chamber audited the project year by year.
preconditions: A sovereign wealth fund able to buy the state road company's bonds
Concession contracts with enforceable milestones, which the audits found weakly policed
An audit office that publishes a check of the same project each year

records.title: SECP Regulatory Sandbox, four cohorts and an open window
records.claim: Pakistan's Securities and Exchange Commission approved 31 business models for testing in its Regulatory Sandbox across four annual cohorts from 2020 to 2023, out of 125 fintech applicants, with intake rising from six selected in the first cohort to 11 in the fourth.

metric.name: Business models approved for testing in the SECP Regulatory Sandbox, four cohorts, cumulative

secondMetric.name: Applicants selected in cohort IV

source.publisher: Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan, Annual Report 2024 (year ended 30 June 2024), section 'Promoting fintech and encouraging innovation', Regulatory Sandbox

records.limits: The regulator reports on its own sandbox. The figures are in a PDF on PDF page 82 (printed page 81), with a cohort chart giving applicants and selections per year (33 and 6, 38 and 6, 28 and 8, 26 and 11); the live secp.gov.pk site returns a Cloudflare challenge to scripts, so the report was read from a Wayback Machine copy of the SECP download link. 'Approved for testing' counts admissions, not completions: the report does not say how many business models finished testing or went to market. The cohort figures sum to 31, matching the stated total. After 2023 the SECP moved to an always-open format, and the same page says it had then received three applications with one testing, a much smaller intake than cohort IV, but over a shorter and unstated period, so it is not read as a decline. The State Bank of Pakistan runs a separate sandbox whose admissions are not counted here, so the figure understates the country total the construct asks for.

pattern.mechanism: The securities regulator issued sandbox guidelines under the Companies Act and ran annual cohorts in which fintech, insurtech and capital-market applicants were screened and the selected ones tested for six to nine months under agreed limits, then switched to year-round applications.
preconditions: A statutory power to issue sandbox guidelines, here section 458A of the Companies Act 2017 as cited in the reissued guidelines
A pipeline of fintech applicants large enough to select from
Regulator staff to evaluate applications and supervise tests

records.title: Bank of Jamaica FinTech Regulatory Sandbox
records.claim: The Bank of Jamaica's FinTech Regulatory Sandbox, effective from March 2020, had received 50 applications and approved 29 of them for testing by the end of 2025, including four new applications from three entities in 2025.

metric.name: Sandbox applications approved for testing since March 2020, cumulative

secondMetric.name: Sandbox applications received since March 2020, cumulative

source.publisher: Bank of Jamaica, Annual Report 2025, 'Fintech Regulatory Sandbox Development and CBDC (JAM-DEX)'

records.limits: The central bank reports on its own sandbox. The figures are in a 33 MB PDF served at that address, on PDF page 92 (printed page 66). They count applications, not firms: one entity can file several, as the three entities filing four applications in 2025 show, and 29 is approvals since 2020, not the number testing at year end or the number that completed and launched. The report gives 46 applications at end-2024, so only four arrived in 2025, but it gives no yearly approval figures. The approvals are described as mobile wallets, debit cards and prepaid card offerings; the same section of the report covers the bank's JAM-DEX digital currency roll-out, but it does not say whether any sandbox approval relates to it. The Financial Services Commission's activity is not included.

pattern.mechanism: The central bank opened a sandbox for deposit-takers, cambios, remittance providers, credit unions and locally incorporated fintechs partnered with a bank, admitting products to a controlled live test before authorisation.
preconditions: Guidelines and an application and fit-and-proper process run by the payments oversight function
Licensed deposit-takers willing to partner with fintechs
Fintech and payment firms with wallet and card products ready to test

records.title: Financial Regulatory Commission sandbox regulatory environment
records.claim: Mongolia's Financial Regulatory Commission admitted three products and services to its sandbox for one year in the fourth quarter of 2022 and released one, the MonPay digital bond, on 30 December 2022 after a year of testing, leaving four under test.

metric.name: Products and services admitted to the sandbox in 2022 Q4

secondMetric.name: Products and services released from the sandbox in 2022

source.publisher: Financial Regulatory Commission of Mongolia (Санхүүгийн зохицуулах хороо), Үйл ажиллагааны жилийн тайлан 2022 (annual activity report 2022), section 'Сэндбокс зохицуулалтын орчин'

records.limits: The regulator reports on itself, in Mongolian, in a PDF on PDF page 29 (printed page 30). It counts products and services, not firms. The same page breaks down requests submitted to the sandbox by type (6, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1), which sum to 15 by my addition, but it does not say over what period they were received or how many were refused. The admission figure covers one quarter, and the report gives no full-year admissions for 2021 or 2022, when MonPay's test began on 1 November 2021. Only one year was read: later FRC reports were not found today, so the record says nothing about whether the sandbox kept admitting products after 2022. The products under test were a repo platform, a peer-to-peer lender, an insurtech service and a crowdfunding platform, and virtual asset providers made up the largest group of requests. pattern.mechanism: The non-bank financial regulator adopted a sandbox regulation in 2021 and a sandbox council that admits fintech products for a one-year test and issues a recommendation to release each one.

A council to decide admission and exit
Domestic fintech and virtual asset firms seeking a route to licensing

records.title: Long-term Insights Briefings under the Public Service Act 2020
records.claim: New Zealand's Public Service Act 2020 required every departmental chief executive to publish a Long-term Insights Briefing on future trends, risks and opportunities at least once every three years, and nineteen were published in the first round, which concluded in mid-2023, four of them produced jointly by several agencies.

metric.name: Long-term Insights Briefings published in the first round

source.publisher: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, The Policy Project, Long-term Insights Briefings page (last updated 11 December 2025)

records.limits: The live dpmc.govt.nz page returns 403 to scripts, so it was read from a Wayback Machine copy of 18 June 2026; the page is the coordinating department reporting on a duty it guides. It is a statutory duty spread across departments, not a single foresight unit with its own budget and staff, and the count measures briefings published, not their quality or influence: DPMC's own review of the first round assessed the process only and said so. Started is 2020, the year of the Act that created the duty; the page does not give the year the first briefings were published. The briefings are think pieces independent of ministers and are not government policy. Whether the second round has kept the same number of briefings is not stated on the page.

pattern.mechanism: A public service statute obliges every department head to consult the public on a topic, write a briefing on medium and long-term trends with policy options, and table it at least once every three years, with the centre of government publishing guidance and reviewing the round.
preconditions: A statutory stewardship duty in public service law
A centre-of-government policy team to issue guidance and review rounds
Departments with analysts able to do futures work alongside daily business

records.title: HEART/NSTA Trust training enrolment
records.claim: Jamaica's HEART/NSTA Trust, the national training agency financed by a 3 percent payroll levy, enrolled 116,918 people in its own technical and vocational, work-based and second-chance programmes in the 2022-23 financial year, including 13,918 in the High School Diploma Equivalency programme, and 129,957 when Ministry of Education and private providers are counted.

metric.name: HEART total enrolment, own programmes and interventions (excludes MoEY CAP schools and private providers)

secondMetric.name: Enrolled in the High School Diploma Equivalency (HSDE) programme at end of financial year

source.publisher: HEART/NSTA Trust, Annual Report 2022-2023, performance summary, table 'HEART/NSTA enrolment by programmes/interventions' (page 39)

records.limits: The agency reports on itself in a 132-page PDF; the table is on page 39 and the HSDE figure on a later programme page. Counts are enrolments in programmes and interventions, not unique adults, and one person can enrol twice in a year. The total includes the HOPE National Service Corps and the School Leavers' Training Opportunities Programme, which serve school leavers and young people, and the agency gives no age breakdown, so the share of adults beyond initial education is unknown. The headline 129,957 also counts 11,104 enrolments in Ministry of Education CAP and other schools, a secondary-school programme, which is why the record uses the 116,918 HEART total instead. Enrolment is not completion: the same report gives 51,541 NVQ-J certificates for the year. The figure is one year against planned targets, not a series, so the record says nothing about trend. The 1982 start is the year the original HEART Act created the Trust as commonly reported; the report itself cites the HEART Act 2021 under which the merged HEART/NSTA Trust now operates.

pattern.mechanism: A statutory trust collects a payroll levy from employers and spends it on free institutional, community and workplace training and on a second-chance secondary diploma, setting enrolment targets every year.
preconditions: A payroll levy collected by the tax authority and ring-fenced for training
A network of training institutions and community sites across the island
A national qualifications framework (NVQ-J) so short courses lead to recognised certificates

records.title: Enhanced Vocational Education and Training (EVENT II) short-term training
records.claim: Nepal's Ministry of Education, Science and Technology, through the EVENT II project secretariat, put 111,062 people aged 16 to 40 through market-relevant short-term vocational training between 2018 and 2023, delivered by 142 private and public training providers in 68 of the 77 districts and paid partly on trainees' employment six months after completion.

metric.name: Youth (16 to 40) who enrolled in and completed project-supported short-term training

secondMetric.name: Of which trained with vouchers redeemed at a provider of their choice

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Nepal Second Enhanced Vocational Education and Training Project (EVENT II), 26 February 2024

records.limits: The figure is in a PDF completion report written by the World Bank about its own project, from data supplied by the ministry's project secretariat and checked by a joint monitoring team of local education officers, CTEVT, the ministry and SDC-Helvetas, which is not fully independent of the delivery; the Bank rated its own outcome. It counts trainees over a five-year project, not participation in the last 12 months, and amounts to roughly 22,000 a year against a labour force in the millions. The project defined youth as 16 to 40, so the count mixes recent school leavers with older adults and gives no age split. The total was 96.5 percent of a 115,000 target and training stopped for about 18 months during the pandemic. The training was financed by IDA credit, not the national budget, and the report does not say whether the government continued the results-based short-term training after the July 2023 closing, so 'concluded' describes the project window, not a measured end of the model. Employment rates of 70 to 83 percent six months after training are from the project's own tracer verification.

pattern.mechanism: The education ministry bought short courses from accredited private and public providers and paid them per trainee, with part of the payment withheld until the trainee was verified as employed six months later, and paid more for women, disadvantaged youth and the poorest districts.
preconditions: A pool of private training providers able to open courses in rural districts at short notice
A joint monitoring team to check enrolment, completion and employment before payment
A skills testing body (NSTB) to certify trades nationally
pattern.travelled: The model came from the Swiss-funded Employment Fund and ran through EVENT I before EVENT II; each version was a time-bound donor project, which is the weakness the pattern carries.

records.title: Adult and community education at tertiary providers, and its halving
records.claim: New Zealand's adult and community education (ACE) delivered by universities, polytechnics, wānanga and private training establishments enrolled 23,610 domestic students in 2021, down from 49,365 in 2012, according to the Ministry of Education's Education Counts tables.

metric.name: Domestic students in adult and community education, all tertiary sub-sectors (Table ACE.3)

secondMetric.name: Same count, first year of the published series

source.publisher: Ministry of Education (Te Tāhuhu o te Mātauranga), Education Counts, tertiary participation, Adult-and-Community-Education.xlsx, Table ACE.3, as archived by the Internet Archive on 25 March 2023

records.limits: The cited file is an Internet Archive copy: educationcounts.govt.nz answered 403 behind a bot check on 2026-10-02, and the archived September 2026 page that links a newer edition of the same spreadsheet returned 410 for the file, so the series stops at 2021 here although the ministry has published later years. The table counts only ACE delivered by tertiary providers; it leaves out ACE run by schools and community organisations, and 2012 is the first year of the table, not a demonstrated peak. Any funding change before 2012, including the reduction of ACE funding in schools commonly dated to 2009, is outside the series and was not read at a source for this record. Most of the fall is two steps: universities from 13,180 to 3,040 between 2012 and 2013, and polytechnics (now Te Pūkenga) from 35,235 in 2016 to 27,975 in 2017 and 20,890 in 2020; the 2020 and 2021 counts are also depressed by COVID-19 lockdowns. Equivalent full-time student units held near 3,200 to 4,100 throughout, so fewer people took longer courses, and the fall in headcount is not a fall in hours of learning. Counts are students enrolled at any time in the year, rounded to the nearest 5, and students in two sub-sectors count in each. The started year is the first year of the published table, not the start of ACE funding, which is decades older.

pattern.mechanism: The Tertiary Education Commission funds short, often non-credit community courses for adults through tertiary providers, and the education ministry counts enrolments each year from provider returns.
preconditions: A dedicated ACE funding pool inside the tertiary funding system
Providers with community reach willing to run low-margin courses
A single student enrolment return that captures non-credit learners
pattern.travelled: Headcount halved while study load held, so the remaining ACE places went to fewer people taking longer courses; whether that was a deliberate shift toward longer, credit-bearing courses is not shown by the table.

records.title: NCHD Adult Literacy Programme, and its collapse after 2013
records.claim: Pakistan's National Commission for Human Development opened 19,399 adult literacy centres enrolling 482,295 learners in 2009-10, but its literacy programme 'came to a halt since 2013 due to scarcity of funds', and in 2021 it ran a phase of 1,490 centres, financed by the Pakistan Human Development Fund, that enrolled 36,529 learners, mostly women aged 15 to 45.

metric.name: Learners enrolled in the 1,490 adult literacy centres of the project 'Promoting literacy in rural communities of Pakistan'

secondMetric.name: Peak: learners enrolled in 19,399 adult literacy centres, NCHD Annual Report 2012, year-wise table

source.publisher: National Commission for Human Development (NCHD), Ministry of Federal Education and Professional Training, Annual Report 2021

records.limits: The commission reports on itself. The 2021 figure is in the foreword of the 2021 annual report (PDF page 10, printed page 8, 'Around 36,529 learners, mostly women benefitted') and in its programme chapter (PDF page 38), which says 1,490 centres were established in 116 districts 'wherein, 36529 learners were enrolled' and 33,377 graduated; 1,500 centres were allocated and ten in North Waziristan could not be opened. The peak comes from a different document at the same host, NCHD Annual Report 2012 (https://www.nchd.org.pk/SiteImage/Misc/files/NCHD_Annual_Report_2012.pdf, PDF page 16), whose table gives 19,399 centres and 482,295 learners for 2009-10, 8,317 and 197,907 for 2010-11 and 8,270 and 202,349 for 2011-12; 2009-10 is the highest year in that table, not a demonstrated all-time peak, and the commission's cumulative claim of about 4.07 million people made literate since 2002 implies that earlier years were also large. The statement that the programme halted in 2013 for lack of funds is in NCHD Annual Report 2016 (https://www.nchd.org.pk/SiteImage/Misc/files/Annual%20Report-2016.pdf, PDF page 8), which also says the 2017 project approval cut the planned centres from 12,000 to 6,000. Enrolment is not completion or tested literacy. The 2021 centres were financed by the Pakistan Human Development Fund, a support fund set up under the commission's ordinance, rather than the commission's core development budget. Part of the fall may reflect the devolution of education to the provinces after the 2010 constitutional amendment, which moved literacy work to provincial departments that this record does not count. No annual figure after 2021 was found at the commission's site.

pattern.mechanism: A federal commission recruited local teachers to run six-month literacy centres in villages, mostly for women, funded from the federal development budget; when that budget line lapsed, delivery fell to small donor-funded rounds.
preconditions: A federal agency with district offices able to recruit and supervise thousands of local teachers
A recurring development-budget allocation, since each centre runs only one cohort
A political mandate for adult literacy that survives the devolution of education to provinces
pattern.travelled: Bangladesh's Bureau of Non-Formal Education ran the same project-by-project model (bgd-adult-literacy) and shows the same pattern of large reach followed by a gap when funding windows close.

records.title: Youth Training and Employment Partnership Programme (YTEPP), and its shrinking enrolment
records.claim: Trinidad and Tobago's YTEPP Limited, the state company that trains people aged 15 to 35 who are out of work or school, enrolled 1,601 persons in October 2024 to June 2025, 61 percent of its target, against 2,301 trainees in the Youth Training Programme over the same October to June window of 2019-20, according to the Ministry of Finance's Social Sector Investment Programme reviews.

metric.name: Persons enrolled in YTEPP youth training and employment programmes

secondMetric.name: Trainees enrolled in the YTEPP Youth Training Programme, same months five years earlier (SSIP 2021)

source.publisher: Ministry of Finance, Trinidad and Tobago, Social Sector Investment Programme 2026, chapter 3B Review of Social Programmes, Ministry of Tertiary Education and Skills Training

records.limits: Both counts are the ministry's own programme reporting, collected in budget documents. The earlier figure is in a different edition, Social Sector Investment Programme 2021 (https://www.finance.gov.tt/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Social-Sector-Investment-Programme-2021-1.pdf), and the two may not count the same thing: 2021 counts trainees in the Youth Training Programme, 2026 counts persons in 'youth training and employment programmes', and 2026 separately reports 1,323 youths in CVQ/TVET, NEC or YTEPP-certified programmes. 2019-20 is not a demonstrated peak; it is the earliest comparable count found, and its window already includes the first COVID-19 closures from March 2020, so the true fall is probably larger. The money moved the same way: the SSIP 2017 table gives an estimate of TT$111 million for YTEPP in 2016, SSIP 2019 gives TT$64.4 million actual spending in 2017, and SSIP 2026 lists TT$41.4 million, but transfers between ministries make those columns hard to align, so they are context, not the metric. The programme serves ages 15 to 35, so part of it is young people just out of school rather than adults returning to learning. Enrolment is not completion. The 1988 start is YTEPP's founding year as commonly reported; it was not read at the cited source.

pattern.mechanism: The state funds a training company that runs short vocational and life-skills courses in centres across both islands for young people outside work and school, and reports enrolment against a yearly target in the budget's social sector review.
preconditions: A recurrent transfer from the budget, which in a hydrocarbon economy moves with energy revenue
Training centres spread across districts, including Tobago
A national vocational qualification (CVQ/NEC) that short courses can certify against
pattern.travelled: Caribbean youth training agencies founded in the 1980s (HEART in Jamaica, YTEPP in Trinidad and Tobago) share the design. YTEPP depends on a yearly budget transfer that fell after 2016, while Jamaica's levy-financed HEART reported growing enrolment (jam-heart-nsta).

records.title: COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme
records.claim: Cabinet agreed a 12-week wage subsidy on 16 March 2020, the Government announced it on 17 March, and the Ministry of Social Development paid employers on average within three and a half days of an application, paying more than NZ$13 billion across three stages by the end of December 2020.

metric.name: Average time from application to payment

secondMetric.name: Wage subsidy paid, March to December 2020 (more than)

source.publisher: Office of the Auditor-General New Zealand, Management of the Wage Subsidy Scheme (performance audit, 2021), Part 3: Making subsidy payments

records.limits: The live OAG pages answer scripted requests with HTTP 403; the text was read on 2026-10-02 from the Internet Archive copy (https://web.archive.org/web/2026/https://oag.parliament.nz/2021/wage-subsidy/part3.htm), with the dates in Part 1 (paragraphs 1.12 to 1.13) and the 3.5 days in paragraph 3.3. The average is the Ministry of Social Development's figure as reported by the auditor, with no distribution: it does not say how long the slowest payments took. Speed was bought with a high-trust design in which applicants declared their own eligibility; by 5 March 2021 the Ministry had received 20,973 repayments worth NZ$726.2 million, about 5 percent of payments, and nearly NZ$300 million went to public organisations before decisions were made to return money. The NZ$13 billion is a spending figure, not a measure of jobs saved: the Government's estimate that the scheme indirectly supported about 1.8 million employees is not an outcome measure, and the auditor notes it could not determine with certainty how many recipients could have used other support. The audit covers the scheme to early 2021 and not the later 2021 stages.

pattern.mechanism: Cabinet approved a flat per-employee subsidy paid as a lump sum to employers, and the Ministry of Social Development ran it through its existing benefit payment systems on applicant self-declaration, with Inland Revenue data used for checks after payment.
preconditions: A payment agency with bank details and identity data for most employers and workers already on file
A fiscal position that allowed NZ$5.1 billion to be committed within a day and raised to NZ$9.3 billion within a week
Political acceptance of overpayment risk, recovered afterwards by audit and voluntary repayment
pattern.travelled: The same flat-rate, employer-paid design was used in Australia's JobKeeper (March 2020); New Zealand reused its own scheme for the August 2020 and 2021 resurgences.

records.title: Ultra-Fast Broadband programme
records.claim: The Crown's infrastructure investment company, now National Infrastructure Funding and Financing, co-funded a fibre network built and owned by Chorus, Northpower, Enable and Tuatahi First Fibre, which was completed in December 2022 covering 87 percent of the population in 412 towns and cities, with NZ$1.75 billion of government funding in a programme costing more than NZ$5.5 billion.

metric.name: Population covered by the UFB fibre network at completion

secondMetric.name: Government funding invested in UFB since 2010, of a total cost exceeding NZ$5.5 billion

source.publisher: National Infrastructure Funding and Financing (formerly Crown Infrastructure Partners), Fibre programme page

records.limits: The Crown company that ran the programme reports on itself, and the page is promotional ('world leading', 'on time and under budget'); no audit figure for cost against the original budget was checked. The 87 percent is coverage (premises passed), not use: the same page gives uptake as 73 percent of UFB premises passed at 30 June 2025. The total cost above NZ$5.5 billion includes partner co-funding, so the private share is inferred, not stated, and NZ$390 million of the Crown's investment was repaid and recycled into extensions, which the page treats as reinvested rather than spent twice. The page does not describe how partners were chosen or on what terms; the corporate history (Crown Fibre Holdings, then Crown Infrastructure Partners, then National Infrastructure Funding and Financing) and the role of the incumbent's structural separation are background not shown on this page. The page has no date stamp; the uptake figure dates it to after June 2025.

pattern.mechanism: A Crown-owned company invested in regional fibre companies on the condition that they build an open-access, wholesale-only network to a fixed rollout plan, and recovered its investment as the companies sold connections, recycling the repayments into further extensions.
preconditions: Structural separation of the incumbent telecoms firm, so that the main partner sold wholesale only
Local lines companies able to bid for regions alongside the incumbent
A Crown investment vehicle with commercial terms, not a grant ministry
pattern.travelled: Australia chose a fully public National Broadband Network for the same goal at the same time; Singapore's Next Gen NBN used a similar regulated open-access model.

records.title: COVID-19 Allocation of Resources for Employees (CARE) programme
records.claim: From March 2020 the Government of Jamaica built the CARE programme on its PATH cash transfer and tax registration systems, paying cash transfers to 458,295 beneficiaries (183,326 men and 274,969 women) for job and income losses and a COVID-19 PATH grant to about 266,100 PATH beneficiaries within the first year of the pandemic.

metric.name: Beneficiaries receiving CARE cash transfers (sum of the published male and female counts)

secondMetric.name: PATH beneficiaries receiving the CARE COVID-19 PATH grant (125,700 male, 140,400 female)

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Jamaica COVID-19 Response and Recovery Development Policy Financing (P174531)

records.limits: Both totals are published in the ICR's results framework (Annex 1, page 23: 458,295 and 266,100) and equal the sums of the male and female counts in Table 3 (page 18); the text on page 12 says 'more than 450,000 beneficiaries', 6.6 percent above target. The CARE measures were prior actions of a World Bank development policy loan approved in 2021, so the lender wrote the targets and rates its own operation (Moderately Satisfactory overall). The construct is speed, and the ICR gives no elapsed time from shock to first payment: it dates the measures to Cabinet decisions from March 2020 and says the PATH grant reached households 'within the first year of the pandemic', with beneficiaries determined in mid-2020. Eligibility for SET Cash covered job losses from 10 March 2020, so the rule was written to the shock, but the record cannot say whether money arrived in weeks or months. The ICR notes the government did not collect data on all indicators (for example, tourism jobs retained under BEST Cash). Beneficiary counts are not household counts and may overlap across grants.

pattern.mechanism: The Ministry of Finance created a family of temporary grants (SET Cash for those who lost jobs, general grants for registered self-employed workers, compassionate grants for others) and paid them by matching applications against tax registration numbers, while the Ministry of Labour and Social Security paid an extra PATH grant through the existing conditional cash transfer.
preconditions: A tax registration number held by most adults, which let the government verify applicants it had no benefit record for
An existing conditional cash transfer (PATH) with a beneficiary roll and payment channel
Fiscal buffers built during the 2013 to 2019 consolidation, which paid for the response before external finance arrived

records.title: COVID-19 frontloading of old age, widow and disability allowances
records.claim: Bangladesh's Department of Social Services paid old age, widow and disability allowance entitlements early from 25 March 2020 to 30 June 2020, reaching about 4.36 million beneficiaries through its digital government-to-person payment system, and the World Bank reimbursed US$165.84 million within 16 days of the government's July 2020 request.

metric.name: Beneficiaries receiving cash transfers financed under the COVID-19 contingent emergency component

secondMetric.name: Days from the government's request to full disbursement of the emergency financing

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Bangladesh Cash Transfer Modernization Project (P160819)

records.limits: The figures are in a PDF: the 4.36 million in paragraph 44 (page 10) and indicator I.11, and the dates in Annex 6 (page 31). The World Bank financed the project and the ICR praises its own instrument: the 16 days measure how fast the Bank reimbursed spending already made, not how fast the government acted, since the financing was retroactive for transfers paid from 25 March to 30 June 2020. The government's own change was modest: it paid existing beneficiaries of existing allowances early and through mobile money, and the source reports no new beneficiaries; other COVID-19 transfers paid outside these allowances are not covered by this record. The ICR also records the limits of shock response: Component 5, a cash transfer for people injured in the 2024 uprising, had policies and systems in place but was never paid, because the government's prefinancing did not arrive, and the allocation was cancelled. The poverty database meant to target new shocks (the National Household Database) never became usable.

pattern.mechanism: The social services department advanced payment of existing allowances through the government-to-person system that pays straight into beneficiaries' bank and mobile money accounts, and a contingent emergency component in an existing World Bank loan refinanced the outlay after the fact.
preconditions: A government-to-person payment platform already paying allowances into individual accounts
Mobile money accounts held by most beneficiaries
A contingent emergency clause in an active loan, so that refinancing did not need a new operation

records.title: Public Private Partnership Authority project portfolio
records.claim: Bangladesh's Public Private Partnership Authority listed 81 projects in its portfolio as last updated on 19 August 2026, of which four were in operation (including Patenga Container Terminal, the NIKDU and Chittagong haemodialysis centres and two Info-Sarkar 3 rural broadband components), three were partly operating while still under construction (among them the Dhaka Elevated Expressway), and 10 were under construction.

metric.name: PPP projects in operation, fully or partly
metric.unit: of 81 portfolio projects (4 operational, 3 partial operation and construction)

secondMetric.name: PPP projects under construction

source.publisher: Public Private Partnership Authority Bangladesh, PPP projects list

records.limits: The counts are ours, tallied from the stage column of the authority's project list, which the page says was last updated on 19 August 2026 and which was read on 2026-10-02; the page gives no totals, and it reports stages, not dates of financial close or of operation. Two of the four operating entries are components of one rural broadband project (Info-Sarkar 3), so the operating count overstates distinct partnerships by one. The authority promotes its own portfolio. The headline is how little has reached operation: 7 of 81 projects after some 16 years, with 24 still at feasibility study and 6 at conditions-precedent stage, so the record documents scale of activity more than delivery. Several listed projects are land leases for commercial development (shopping malls, textile mills on state land), not public services. The Dhaka Elevated Expressway opened in parts against long delays. A 2026 Invest Bangladesh Act appears on the same site and may reorganise the authority; its Bangla text could not be read in this session, so the record does not say whether the authority continues in its current form.

pattern.mechanism: A dedicated authority under the head of government screens line-ministry projects, runs procurement with technical assistance and viability gap funds, and takes them to the economic cabinet committee for approval and award.
preconditions: A PPP law (2015) and rules for viability gap funding and unsolicited proposals
Line ministries willing to give up projects they could fund from the development budget
Investors willing to take Bangladeshi currency and land risk, which is the precondition the low operating count suggests is scarce

records.title: COVID-19 Economic Relief Plan household transfers, and their halt after the 2021 coup
records.claim: Under its COVID-19 Economic Relief Plan, Myanmar's government distributed food to about 5.4 million households in April 2020 and cash transfers that had reached about 6 million vulnerable households by November 2020, and the World Bank reported in July 2021 that these transfers had come to a sudden halt after the military takeover of 1 February 2021.

metric.name: Vulnerable households reached by COVID-19 cash transfers by November 2020, before the transfers halted (about)

source.publisher: World Bank, Myanmar Economic Monitor, July 2021: Progress Threatened; Resilience Tested

records.limits: The 6 million and the halt are in one sentence on printed page 38 of the July 2021 Monitor ('reached about 6 million vulnerable households by November 2020 have come to a sudden halt'). The source does not say who stopped the transfers, by what decision, or whether every government transfer stopped: the line on printed page 43 that 'all government cash transfer programs and remittances stopped' is an assumption of the Bank's poverty simulation (method in Annex 1, page 51), not an observation, so the record does not claim that the maternal and child cash transfer or the social pensions ended. The food distribution to about 5.4 million households in April 2020 and repeated cash payments of 40,000 kyat to 5.4 million households in July and August 2020, rising to 5.6 million in September and 6.1 million in November, are the government's figures as relayed by the December 2020 Monitor (Coping with COVID-19, https://documents.worldbank.org/curated/en/906171608086222905/pdf/Myanmar-Economic-Monitor-Coping-with-COVID-19.pdf, printed pages 52 and 66), which notes its own survey found lower numbers. The figures are approximate and dated by month only, so the speed of the 2020 response is shown only by month. The COVID-19 transfers were emergency rounds of modest size (the December 2020 Monitor calls the support far from meeting needs), so part of what stopped was temporary by design; the reversal is that they stopped suddenly during a deeper crisis rather than being replaced. The halt followed a coup, not a policy judgement on the programme, and the source does not separate loss of finance, loss of donor support and loss of administrative capacity. A World Bank country monitor is an international source reporting on the government's programme, not the government's own accounts.

pattern.mechanism: The civilian government widened its maternal and child cash transfer and social pensions and set up emergency food and cash distributions through ward and village administrators, using community identification of the neediest households because no national poverty registry existed.
preconditions: A functioning civilian administration down to ward and village tract level
Donor and budget finance that could be reallocated within weeks
Political continuity, which is the precondition the 2021 takeover removed

records.title: Social insurance contribution exemption, April to September 2020
records.claim: Mongolia's parliament passed the Law on Exemptions for Social Insurance Contributions and Assistance from the Unemployment Insurance Fund on 9 April 2020, waiving contributions retroactively from 1 April to 30 September 2020 for voluntary contributors and affected employers and workers, and 152,475 workers had received relief under the World Bank-financed part of the measure by 31 December 2020.

metric.name: Workers under the mandatory scheme receiving at least one month of contribution relief under the World Bank-financed part

secondMetric.name: Days from the start of the relief period to the law's passage
secondMetric.unit: days (law passed 9 April 2020, relief from 1 April 2020)

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Status and Results Report No. 2, Mongolia Emergency Relief and Employment Support Project (P174116), May 2021

records.limits: The 152,475 (71,894 women) is an indicator in an implementation status report, not a completion report, and it covers only the part of the relief the World Bank refinanced (US$10 million); the Project Appraisal Document of June 2020 (https://documents.worldbank.org/curated/en/815051592878000582/pdf/Mongolia-Emergency-Relief-and-Employment-Support-Project.pdf, paragraph 22) gives the law's date and expected the whole measure to reach about 120,000 voluntary contributors and over 400,000 workers and 38,000 employers at about US$228 million, so the national total is larger and is not in this source. The 8 days is our arithmetic from those two dates and flatters the speed: the law was retroactive, so it says nothing about when employers actually stopped paying. The relief was part of a March 2020 stimulus package; waived contributions weaken the social insurance fund, a cost the indicator does not show. The ISR is the lender reporting on its own project.

pattern.mechanism: Parliament legislated a time-limited waiver of social insurance contributions for employers and workers hit by the pandemic, administered by the social insurance administration through its contribution records, with a development loan refinancing part of the foregone revenue.
preconditions: A contribution-based social insurance system with employer and worker records
A parliament able to pass emergency legislation within weeks
External finance to backfill the insurance fund

records.title: Emergency cash transfer top-ups after the 2022 default
records.claim: After Sri Lanka suspended external debt service on 12 April 2022, the government topped up Samurdhi and categorical cash transfers to Rs 5,000 to 7,500 per family per month from May to December 2022 for 2.5 million existing recipients and 0.8 million waitlisted recipients, raising spending on these programmes to Rs 142 billion in 2022.

metric.name: Recipients of crisis top-up or additional cash transfers, May to December 2022 (2.5 million existing plus 0.8 million waitlisted)

secondMetric.name: Spending on the four main social safety net programmes in 2022
secondMetric.unit: billion Sri Lankan rupees (0.6 percent of GDP)

source.publisher: International Monetary Fund, Country Report No. 23/116, Sri Lanka: Request for an Extended Arrangement Under the Extended Fund Facility (staff report and Memorandum of Economic and Financial Policies)

records.limits: The recipient counts and the Rs 142 billion are the government's own statement in its Memorandum of Economic and Financial Policies (attached to the Letter of Intent of 6 March 2023), published by the IMF, not an IMF measurement; the 3.3 million is our sum of the 2.5 and 0.8 million, which the staff report also gives as about 3.3 million beneficiaries at end-2022. The eLibrary HTML has no page numbers. The top-ups were financed by emergency assistance from the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank, so the speed reflects donor money as well as the government's decision. The source gives the months, not the date of first payment, so the elapsed time from the April 2022 debt standstill to payment is known only to within a month or two. The staff report itself says the real value of cash transfers eroded in 2022, with poorer households facing higher inflation, and that Samurdhi targeting was poor (38 percent of the poorest quintile covered in 2019, 12 percent of the richest receiving transfers), so the speed of the top-up does not show that the money reached the right households. The 2023 replacement of Samurdhi by the Aswesuma scheme is a separate, slower reform and is not covered here.

pattern.mechanism: The government used the existing Samurdhi and categorical allowance rolls, plus the waiting list of households already screened but not enrolled, to add a flat monthly top-up within weeks of the debt standstill, with multilateral emergency loans paying for it.
preconditions: Existing transfer rolls and a waiting list of pre-screened households
Emergency multilateral financing available within weeks of a default
Payment channels that kept working during the 2022 fuel shortages

records.title: Nam Theun 2 hydropower concession
records.claim: The Government of Lao PDR granted a build-operate-transfer concession for the 1,070 MW Nam Theun 2 plant to the Nam Theun Power Company, in which it held 25 percent through Lao Holding State Enterprise; the plant was completed in 2010 in 58.5 months, 4.5 months over plan, at US$1,308 million against a US$1,250 million base estimate (US$1,450 million with contingencies), and paid the government US$180 million in net revenues from 2010 to 2017.

metric.name: Net revenues from NT2 to the Government of Lao PDR, 2010 to 2017

secondMetric.name: Installed capacity delivered (995 MW for export to Thailand, 75 MW for the Lao grid)

source.publisher: World Bank Independent Evaluation Group, Implementation Completion Report Review, Lao PDR Nam Theun 2 Social and Environment Project (2019)

records.limits: The World Bank financed and guaranteed the project (an IDA grant and a US$50 million partial risk guarantee), so the review is the lender's evaluation unit grading a flagship; it rates the outcome Satisfactory. The figures are in a PDF (cost and financing in the project data section, completion time and capacity and the revenue figures in the efficacy section). The US$180 million is net of nothing the review can confirm: it notes that the US$30 million a year target should be reduced for the government's repayments of the ADB and EIB loans that bought its 25 percent stake, information the Bank team could not provide, so the true net figure is uncertain. Revenue was about US$25 million a year, below the appraisal's US$30 million for the early years, and the much larger US$110 million a year expected after 2020 is a projection, not a result. Equity came from EDF, Italian-Thai Development and EGCO, debt from 14 commercial banks and multilaterals; the delivery is a foreign-led consortium that the state contracted and part-owns, and most of the output is exported to Thailand rather than serving Lao consumers. The resettlement and environmental programme, which the project was also judged on, is not covered by these numbers. The start year, 2005, is our inference from completion in 2010 after 58.5 months. The review also records that by 2014 a significant portion of NT2 revenues were being deposited directly into the Treasury rather than through the agreed special account, which weakened the earmarking of revenue to poverty programmes.

pattern.mechanism: The government granted a concession running to 2034 to a special-purpose company, took a minority stake through a new state holding company financed by multilateral loans, and relied on a long-term export power purchase agreement with a Thai buyer that made the debt bankable, with royalties, taxes and dividends earmarked to poverty programmes under a revenue management agreement.
preconditions: A creditworthy foreign buyer for most of the power under a long-term contract
Multilateral guarantees covering political and regulatory risk that commercial lenders would not take
A government willing to accept an external revenue management and audit regime

records.title: Nepal Rastra Bank COVID-19 refinance and loan relief
records.claim: Nepal Rastra Bank's monetary policy of 17 July 2020 expanded its subsidised refinance facility to five times the available fund for COVID-19 affected businesses, and by mid-July 2021 Rs 148.75 billion had been approved to 48,890 borrowers, against Rs 7.49 billion of refinance outstanding a year earlier.

metric.name: COVID-19 refinance approved, cumulative

secondMetric.name: Refinance outstanding before the expansion

source.publisher: Nepal Rastra Bank, Monetary Policy for 2021/22 (unofficial English translation, August 2021), paragraph 54

records.limits: The URL serves a PDF, which NRB labels an unofficial translation; the 7.49 billion baseline is in the Monetary Policy for 2020/21 (https://www.nrb.org.np/ofg/monetary-policy-2020-21-full-text-english-version/, paragraph 48) and the expansion in paragraphs 100 to 103 of the same document. The central bank reports on its own scheme. 'Approved' is not disbursed, and the two figures are different measures (an annual stock against a cumulative approval), so the comparison shows scale, not a like-for-like increase. The rule changed about four months after the March 2020 lockdown, at the regular annual monetary policy rather than in an emergency statement, so the speed is moderate. Uptake was uneven: under the same document the business continuity loan for tourism and small firms to pay wages reached only Rs 956.7 million, and 30 percent of refinance could go through customer evaluation or microfinance lump sums that the source does not break down. Refinance at 1 to 3 percent with borrowers paying 3 to 5 percent went to borrowers banks chose, and the document gives no count of first-time or small borrowers. Other relief in the same section (repayment extensions for Rs 93.63 billion of loans, restructuring of Rs 129.21 billion) is not added here.

pattern.mechanism: The central bank turned an existing subsidised refinance window into a pandemic credit programme by multiplying its size, setting sector rates (1 percent special, 2 percent small business, 3 percent general) and letting commercial banks, development banks, finance companies and microfinance institutions on-lend it.
preconditions: A standing refinance facility with procedures banks already used
A banking system with liquidity and branch reach to on-lend quickly
A central bank willing to take credit-allocation decisions by sector

records.title: COVID-19 Salary Relief Grant and income support
records.claim: After restricting non-essential activity in March 2020, the Government of Trinidad and Tobago paid a Salary Relief Grant of TT$1,500 a month for three months through the National Insurance Board, spending TT$226.3 million on it in fiscal 2020 against a TT$490 million allocation, and the Ministry of Social Development and Family Services paid income support to 46,533 people outside the national insurance scheme.

metric.name: Persons receiving COVID-19 income support (Ministry of Social Development and Family Services)

secondMetric.name: Salary Relief Grants paid in fiscal 2020 (October 2019 to September 2020), of a TT$490 million allocation

source.publisher: Ministry of Finance, Trinidad and Tobago, Review of the Economy 2020

records.limits: The figures are in a PDF: the 46,533 is footnote 54 on printed page 85 (Labour Force and Employment), the TT$226.3 million is on printed page 98 (Transfers to Households) and the TT$490 million allocation is in Box 4 that follows. The ministry is reporting on its own government's programme in a pre-budget document, with no audit. The source gives no date of first payment and no count of Salary Relief Grant recipients, so speed is shown only by the fiscal year: money was paid within the six months to September 2020. Less than half of the Salary Relief Grant allocation was spent in fiscal 2020, which may mean fewer eligible claims, slow processing or payments falling into fiscal 2021; the source does not say which. Eligibility for the grant depended on national insurance registration, so informal workers relied on the smaller income support channel. Persons and grants may overlap across programmes.

pattern.mechanism: The government split its pandemic income support by registry: the National Insurance Board paid a flat grant to registered workers who were terminated, suspended or lost income, and the social development ministry paid income support and food cards to people outside the insurance scheme.
preconditions: A national insurance register with employer and contribution records
A social assistance ministry with an existing public assistance and food card system
Fiscal room from energy revenues and the Heritage and Stabilisation Fund

records.title: Flood and Landslide Emergency Recovery Project, and its slow delivery
records.claim: Myanmar's Ministry of Construction and rural roads department had used US$37.2 million of a US$200 million IDA credit approved in July 2016 for recovery from the 2015 floods and landslides, rehabilitating 60 km of rural roads, 10 percent of the target, and starting no national road works in Chin State, when disbursements stopped after the military takeover of February 2021, and the project closed on its original December 2021 date with an Unsatisfactory outcome rating.

metric.name: Actual disbursement at closing

secondMetric.name: Original IDA financing at approval

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Myanmar Flood and Landslide Emergency Recovery Project (P158194), 29 June 2023

records.limits: The disbursement figures are on the ICR datasheet (pages 1 to 2) and the 60 km rural road figure, 10 percent of target, is in the component review (page 12); all were read from the plain-text version. The shortfall was mostly in place before the coup: by September 2020, four years after approval, US$27.4 million had been disbursed (ISR table, page 3), the national roads in Chin State never started because donor and government-financed linked works broke safeguards, design work for the large roads was unfinished, and in July 2020 the government requested a 23-month extension that was never processed. The World Bank's pause of all disbursements in February 2021 under its policy on de facto governments then fixed the outturn, so part of the Unsatisfactory rating reflects the lender's stop rather than the ministries' work. The ICR had no contact with the authorities after the takeover and no borrower report, so later works financed by other sources are not counted. US$12.4 million of goods under component 3 were procured and distributed with UNOPS support, so that part was not delivered by national procurement. Recovery of one flood event says little about warning or evacuation capacity, which this project did not measure. The 2015 floods themselves, and any relief delivered in 2015, fall outside it. Nothing delivered was lost, so this is a slow delivery and not a reversal.

pattern.mechanism: After the 2015 floods the government took an emergency recovery credit for roads, bridges and community works, but slow procurement, safeguards breaches and then the 2021 coup left most of the money unspent.
preconditions: Agencies able to design and procure civil works quickly after a disaster
Safeguards compliance on politically sensitive roads
A government the lender could keep financing
pattern.travelled: Same stop date as mmr-nep; the contrast with Nepal's earthquake housing (npl-ehrp), delivered through cash grants rather than procured works, is the useful one.

records.title: Rural housing reconstruction after the 2005 Kashmir earthquake
records.claim: Pakistan's Earthquake Reconstruction and Rehabilitation Authority inspected all 463,243 houses due for reconstruction in Azad Jammu and Kashmir and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa after the October 2005 earthquake and certified 438,789 of them, 95 percent, as compliant with seismic-resistant standards by the time the World Bank credit closed in May 2011.

metric.name: Reconstructed houses certified compliant with ERRA's seismic standards

secondMetric.name: Houses to be reconstructed (AJK and KP)

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Pakistan Earthquake Emergency Recovery Credit Project (P099110), 31 December 2011

records.limits: The table is in Annex 2 (printed page 23) and was read from the plain-text version. The same annex's text gives a different base, 353,931 houses to be reconstructed of which 337,177 were completed, and says 3.8 percent of eligible houses saw no work at all; the record uses the table, and the two figures cannot be reconciled from the document. The data are ERRA's own, compiled from army monitoring teams and partner organisations. Compliance at certification is not occupancy or durability. The programme cost about US$1.5 billion, of which the World Bank credit financed part, and the credit was later enlarged to cover the 2010 floods, which are outside this figure. It is a 2006 to 2011 delivery and says nothing about Pakistan's response to the 2022 floods.
