pattern.mechanism: A federal authority with army support paid owner-driven housing grants in four tranches, each conditional on an inspection against a seismic-resistant design, and trained masons to build to it.
preconditions: A damage census done within weeks
Military logistics in mountainous terrain
Bank branches or mobile payment points reaching rural households
pattern.travelled: Nepal (npl-ehrp) copied the tranche and inspection design after 2015; it is Sri Lanka's tsunami ICR (lka-tsunami-housing), not this one, that names Pakistan's programme as having learned from Sri Lanka's homeowner-driven model.

records.title: Owner-driven housing reconstruction after the 2004 tsunami
records.claim: Sri Lanka's government paid owner-driven cash grants through two state banks, with IDA refinancing, to 47,864 Phase I beneficiaries after the December 2004 tsunami, of whom a 100 percent audit found 44,944 eligible, and the physical completion rate for Phase I houses was 94 percent when the programme closed in September 2008.

metric.name: Phase I homeowner-driven beneficiaries supported with IDA financing

secondMetric.name: Physical completion rate for Phase I houses

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Sri Lanka Tsunami Emergency Recovery Program, 30 June 2009

records.limits: Both figures are in paragraph 2.2.6 of the ICR (printed pages 6 to 7), read from the plain-text version. They cover Phase I houses outside the coastal buffer zone only, about 68 percent of the homeowner programme's Phase I, not the whole national reconstruction of more than 110,000 damaged houses, and the donor-driven programme is excluded. About 6 percent of those paid were found ineligible, section 2.4.6 reports that 93 percent of beneficiaries with unfinished houses in the north and east named insufficient funds as the obstacle, and Annex 2 reports further damage to reconstructed houses after hostilities resumed in 2006, especially in Vaharai in Batticaloa District. The completion rate is from the government's own monitoring, reported by the World Bank. The figures describe recovery from one event and not warning or evacuation.

pattern.mechanism: The government paid fixed cash grants in tranches through two state banks to households rebuilding on their own land, with divisional secretaries certifying eligibility and IDA refinancing the banks.
preconditions: State banks with branches in every affected division
A buffer-zone policy settled enough to know who rebuilds where
Local administrations able to certify eligibility and progress
pattern.travelled: The ICR names Pakistan's 2005 earthquake programme (pak-erra-housing) as built on this model.

records.title: Road Maintenance and Rehabilitation Project
records.claim: Papua New Guinea's Department of Works restored or maintained 600 km of national roads against a 640 km target under the Road Maintenance and Rehabilitation Project, closing in June 2012 five and a half years after the original December 2006 closing date, with national road works under the original loan costing US$35.62 million, 158 percent of their US$22.52 million appraisal estimate.

metric.name: Actual cost of maintenance and rehabilitation of national roads

secondMetric.name: Appraisal estimate for maintenance and rehabilitation of national roads

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Papua New Guinea Road Maintenance and Rehabilitation Project, 20 December 2012

records.limits: The component costs are in Annex 1 (project cost by component, original loan) and the dates and road lengths on the datasheet (sections B and F), read from the plain-text version. The appraisal figure excludes VAT and the actual includes it, so part of the 158 percent is a tax difference the table itself flags. Total project cost was on budget (US$58.21 million against US$58.78 million) because bridge components were cut, so the overrun on roads was paid for by building fewer bridges: provincial bridges spent 11 percent of their estimate. The ICR attributes the road cost rise to the construction boom from the PNG LNG project and to sealing more gravel roads than planned. The World Bank rated the outcome Satisfactory, and the programme is maintenance and rehabilitation rather than one new structure. The cost comparison covers the original IBRD loan only; a 2007 IDA additional financing scaled the programme to two more provinces and extended it, and its national road works also overran, at US$40.86 million against US$28.72 million (142 percent, Annex 1 table b), so the June 2012 closing reflects added scope as well as delay. The government paid US$2.28 million of the US$25.07 million counterpart planned at appraisal, with provinces and other donors covering part of the gap.

pattern.mechanism: The works department ran a lender-financed maintenance and restoration programme on national and provincial roads, absorbed a cost surge on roads by cutting bridges, and extended the programme twice.
preconditions: Local contractors able to bid for maintenance packages
Provincial governments with budgets to co-fund their share
A lender willing to restructure scope inside a fixed envelope

records.title: Road No. 13 South upgrading under the Third Highway Improvement Project
records.claim: Laos's Ministry of Communication, Transport, Post and Construction upgraded about 200 km of Road No. 13 between Banlak 35 and Pakse to a bituminous standard, completed in March 2002, at US$157,785 per km against an appraisal estimate of US$209,670 per km, and the project closed on its original June 2003 date at US$63.78 million against US$68.92 million appraised.

metric.name: Actual unit cost of upgrading Road No. 13 South (calendar 2002 dollars)

secondMetric.name: Appraisal unit cost estimate (SAR)

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion Report, Lao PDR Third Highway Improvement Project, 26 May 2004

records.limits: The unit costs are in section 4.3 of the ICR and the totals in Annex 2 (printed page 30), read from the plain-text version; the record states the two published unit costs and does not compute a percentage. The saving is on unit cost, not on the road works line: Annex 2 shows Roads No. 13 and A-1 at US$34.58 million against US$33.45 million appraised even though the A-1 bypass was removed and financed under another project, and the project total came in under appraisal only because physical and price contingencies of US$9.96 million were not needed (actual US$63.78 million against a US$58.96 million baseline before contingencies). The Annex 3 table labels both unit costs 'Calendar 2002 US$ per km' and puts the contract cost at US$153,785, so the actual came in at 103 percent of contract; the 25 percent saving is against the appraisal estimate, which was set before the 1997 Asian crisis and may have been pessimistic. Actual construction took 45 months against 42 contracted, 7 percent longer. Annex 2 prints 88 percent beside the road works line although its own figures give 103 percent, so the table is not internally consistent. JICA separately financed 44 bridges on the road, about six of whose approaches still showed unacceptable settlement. The World Bank wrote and rated the report, and it describes a delivery finished more than 20 years ago.

pattern.mechanism: The transport ministry upgraded a 200 km trunk road under two international contracts and ran a multi-year routine and periodic maintenance programme alongside it.
preconditions: International competitive bidding that attracted capable contractors
A maintenance fund to protect the upgraded road
Grant finance from a second donor for bridges

records.title: Typhoon Ketsana road recovery under the Road Sector Project
records.claim: Laos's Ministry of Public Works and Transport repaired about 1,100 km of roads, including small and wooden bridges, damaged by Typhoon Ketsana in September 2009 across five southern provinces, out of about 1,842 km the post-disaster assessment found damaged, through a recovery component budgeted at US$8.8 million, and in 2011 used the contingency fund the project created to spend US$3.63 million repairing 28.6 km of National Road 13 North after Typhoons Haima and Nock Ten.

metric.name: Ketsana-damaged roads repaired and improved as per specifications

secondMetric.name: Roads severely or partially damaged by Typhoon Ketsana (Post-Disaster Damage, Loss and Need Assessment)

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Lao PDR Road Sector Project (P102398), 27 March 2018

records.limits: The damaged length is in paragraph 3 (page 5), the component in paragraph 11, the contingency fund use in paragraph 33, and the 1,100 km result in the results annex, all read from the plain-text version. The results table dates the achievement to February 2017 against a revised target date of September 2012; paragraph 32 says 55 percent of the damaged roads, against a target of 60 percent, had been rehabilitated by the end of 2011, about two years after the storm, and that the remaining 45 percent was completed by the government with other funds, at a date the ICR does not give. The 1,100 km is a rounded target reported as met, not a measured count. The repair money came from the IDA Crisis Response Window, and the component spent US$10.6 million against US$8.8 million at approval (Annex 3), so the delivery is the ministry's but the financing was external. The World Bank rated the project Highly Satisfactory.

pattern.mechanism: The public works ministry folded post-typhoon road repairs into a running road project and created a standing contingency fund that it could draw on within weeks of the next storm.
preconditions: A damage assessment done soon after the event
A road project already under way with procurement in place
A contingency line the ministry can trigger without a new loan

records.title: Second Energy Sector Project, distribution rehabilitation and the 10 MWp western solar plant
records.claim: Mongolia's Ministry of Energy and its distribution companies rehabilitated the Baganuur and Erdenet-Bulgan distribution networks and built a 10 MWp solar plant in the Western Energy System under the Second Energy Sector Project, spending US$53.35 million against a US$55.40 million appraisal estimate but closing in August 2024, 25 months after the original September 2022 closing date.

metric.name: Actual disbursement at closure

secondMetric.name: Appraisal cost estimate

source.publisher: World Bank Independent Evaluation Group, ICR Review, Mongolia Second Energy Sector Project (P152343), ICRR0024731, 14 January 2026

records.limits: The cost and date figures are in section 2e of the IEG review (pages 2 to 3), read from the plain-text version; the full ICR was not opened. IEG attributes 18 of the 25 months to subprojects added in the western system at the 2022 restructuring and seven months to inefficiencies, with COVID-19 equipment delays, government changes after elections and procurement problems named as causes, so roughly seven months is slippage on the original scope. The planned US$1.0 million borrower contribution was cancelled, so the project was wholly grant financed. The project is mid-sized, about US$55 million, so it shows delivery on a modest programme rather than on Mongolia's flagship builds such as the new Ulaanbaatar airport, for which no completion figures were found. The solar plant was reported operational in 2022, ahead of the formal closing, so the schedule figure mostly concerns the distribution works. IEG rated the outcome Satisfactory.

pattern.mechanism: The energy ministry split a lender-financed programme into distribution upgrades run by regional companies and one turnkey solar plant, kept costs inside the envelope and took two extensions to finish.
preconditions: Regional distribution companies able to act as implementing units
Grant co-finance for the renewable component
A lender willing to extend rather than cancel

records.title: City Rail Link, Auckland, and its cost and time overrun
records.claim: City Rail Link Limited, owned by the Crown and Auckland Council, achieved practical completion of Auckland's 3.45 km underground City Rail Link on 30 June 2026 against a target delivery cost of NZ$5,493 million, up from a NZ$3.4 billion estimate made in 2014, and the line opened to the public on 13 September 2026, after its company had planned completion for late 2024.

metric.name: Target Delivery Cost in the Project Delivery Agreement

secondMetric.name: Project cost estimate made in 2014

source.publisher: City Rail Link Limited, Annual Report 2025/26 (accessible Word version)

records.limits: The NZ$5,493 million and the 30 June 2026 practical completion are in the 2025/26 annual report, a Word document; the 13 September 2026 opening is on the company's home page (https://www.cityraillink.co.nz/). The NZ$3.4 billion 2014 estimate and the 'late 2024' completion plan come from the company's cost page as archived on 26 January 2023 (https://web.archive.org/web/20230126164501/https://www.cityraillink.co.nz/city-rail-link-cost-timeline), which also gives the April 2019 revision to NZ$4.419 billion; the live page no longer carries them. The 62 percent increase over the 2014 estimate is our calculation and mixes price bases: the company attributes the 2019 rise to construction inflation, a larger contingency and a scope change for nine-car trains. Total spend to 30 June 2026 was NZ$5,283 million against approved funding of NZ$5,644 million, and the company reports itself within budget, which is true only against the 2019 and later baselines. The company is reporting on itself; no Auditor-General review of the outturn was opened. 'Started' is the year main works began, which the cited report does not state.

pattern.mechanism: The Crown and Auckland Council set up a jointly owned delivery company, let the main stations and tunnels to an alliance, and re-baselined the budget twice as costs rose rather than cutting scope.
preconditions: A sponsor agreement splitting cost 50:50 between national and local government
An alliance contract that shares cost risk with the builders
Political tolerance for re-baselining a flagship project

records.title: Earthquake Commission Canterbury Home Repair Programme
records.claim: New Zealand's Earthquake Commission had practically completed 66,252 home repairs under its Canterbury Home Repair Programme by 30 June 2015, after the 2010 and 2011 earthquakes damaged about 180,000 homes, missing the December 2014 completion target it had brought forward from December 2015, with about 8 to 10 percent of repairs needing additional work after completion.

metric.name: Repairs practically completed by the Canterbury Home Repair Programme

secondMetric.name: Homes repaired by June 2013

source.publisher: Office of the Auditor-General New Zealand, Earthquake Commission: Follow-up audit on the Canterbury Home Repair Programme (2015), Part 2

records.limits: The 66,252 figure, the missed December 2014 target and the 8 to 10 percent rework estimate are in Part 2 of the 2015 follow-up audit; the June 2013 figure is from the Auditor-General's 2013 overview (https://ao.parliament.nz/2013/eqc). The Auditor-General's site at oag.parliament.nz refused scripted requests and the same pages were read at ao.parliament.nz. The Auditor-General says it could not reach an overall conclusion on quality: an MBIE review reported in Part 3 of the same audit found 26 of 74 sampled EQC repairs non-compliant with the structural or durability provisions of the Building Code, and the rework rate is EQC's own estimate. Repair counts are Fletcher Construction's and EQC's figures. The programme covered homes with damage under the EQC cap; about 20,000 more expensive claims went to private insurers and are outside it. Later remedial work on repaired homes, which continued for years and generated litigation, is not quantified here.

pattern.mechanism: The state natural-disaster insurer took on managed repairs itself, contracted one construction firm to project-manage tens of thousands of jobs, and paid for it from a pre-funded disaster fund and reinsurance.
preconditions: A pre-funded public catastrophe fund with reinsurance
One contractor able to mobilise a regional workforce
Building inspection capacity to check repairs as they are signed off

records.title: Catastrophe bond payout after Hurricane Melissa
records.claim: Jamaica's government received confirmation in November 2025 of a full US$150 million payout under the catastrophe insurance it had bought from the World Bank, backed by a catastrophe bond issued in 2024 and renewing cover first placed in 2021, after Hurricane Melissa met the bond's parametric triggers in October 2025.

metric.name: Catastrophe bond payout to the Government of Jamaica

secondMetric.name: Total damage and losses from Hurricane Melissa (PIOJ estimate)

source.publisher: World Bank, press release 'Hurricane Melissa Triggers 100% Payout of $150 Million World Bank Catastrophe Bond for Jamaica', 7 November 2025

records.limits: The payout figure is the World Bank's announcement that the triggers were met; it does not say when the money reached the Treasury. The damage estimate is the Planning Institute of Jamaica's, reported by the Jamaica Information Service on 3 March 2026 (https://jis.gov.jm/total-loss-and-damage-from-hurricane-melissa-estimated-at-1-952-trillion/), and the payout covered about 1.2 percent of it (our division), so the record shows a pre-arranged instrument paying in full, not adequate protection. The bond is issued by the World Bank and priced by capital markets; Jamaica's institutional move is buying and renewing the cover and building the layered risk-financing strategy around it. Other layers (CCRIF, contingency funds, contingent credit) are not quantified here. The press release is the lender's own statement, which praises the government's strategy.

pattern.mechanism: The finance ministry bought parametric hurricane cover through the World Bank's bond programme, renewed it when it expired, and received a full payout within days of a storm that met the pressure and track triggers.
preconditions: A finance ministry with a written disaster risk financing strategy
Budget to pay premiums in years without a storm
An intermediary able to place the risk in capital markets

records.title: Central railway concession to the RITES-led Tanzania Railways Limited, and its collapse in 2011
records.claim: Tanzania concessioned the central railway network for 25 years to Tanzania Railways Limited, 51 percent owned by a consortium led by Rail India Technical and Economic Services, which took over operations in October 2007; freight fell from 470,000 tons in 2008 to 237,000 tons in 2010, and after a dispute the RITES shares were transferred to the government in 2011, leaving the operator fully state owned four years into the term.

metric.name: Freight carried by Tanzania Railways Limited on the central (metre gauge) network

secondMetric.name: Freight carried by Tanzania Railways Limited in its first full year of concession operation

source.publisher: World Bank, Project Appraisal Document, Tanzania Intermodal and Rail Development Project (P127241), Report No. 78925-TZ, April 2014, paragraphs 14 and 16

records.limits: The figures are in a PDF, on pages 16 and 17 of the appraisal document (printed pages 4 and 5), written by the World Bank as it prepared a new loan to the now state-owned operator, so the publisher had an interest in describing the concession as a failure. The PAD gives no date in 2011 for the share transfer and calls it amicable, and it is not consistent on the year: paragraph 16 (page 17) puts the transfer in 2011 and an annex (PDF page 116) says TRL took over in 2011, but another annex paragraph (PDF page 117, Annex paragraph 28) says the concession was terminated in 2010; the concession was not formally terminated by a court or an arbitral award in this source, so what ended was private participation, not the railway. The earlier completion report for the Central Transport Corridor Project (ICR00001299, June 2010, page 9) records the concession as performing poorly and the parties discussing termination, and adds (paragraph 94) that most of the traffic had already moved to road during the two years of bidding delay, from 1.2 to 0.5 million tons a year, before the concessionaire took over: the decline therefore began under public operation. The 2008 to 2010 fall also includes the 2009 to 2010 floods in the Kilosa to Gulwe section, which the PAD says halted services between Dar es Salaam and Dodoma, so not all of it is the concessionaire's doing. 2008 is the first full year of concession operation, not a demonstrated peak. The 1.5 million tons TRC carried in 2002, which the PAD also gives, is the public railway before the concession and is not used as the peak here.

pattern.mechanism: The government unbundled the railway into an asset-holding company and an operating company, sold 51 percent of the operator to a foreign rail consortium on a 25-year concession, and kept the track; when traffic, investment and maintenance fell short, the state bought back the private shares and ran the operator itself.
preconditions: A base load of bulk freight large enough to make a concession pay, which the central line had lost before the handover
Contract terms that oblige and finance track maintenance, which here sat between an asset holder and an operator
A short bidding and handover period, so traffic does not leak to road while the deal is negotiated
pattern.travelled: The Beira railway concession in Mozambique, signed in 2004 and terminated on 7 December 2011 according to its World Bank completion report, ended the same way in the same year (see moz-beira-railway).

records.title: Zambia Railways concession to Railway Systems of Zambia, and its cancellation in 2012
records.claim: Zambia concessioned its national railway, after a decade in which traffic halved from 1,072 million net ton kilometres in 1993 to 540 million in 1999, to the private operator Railway Systems of Zambia, which took over on 3 December 2003 and raised traffic by about 30 percent in net ton kilometres in 2004 against 2003; the World Bank later reported that the network and service kept deteriorating and that the concession was cancelled in September 2012.

metric.name: Increase in rail freight traffic (net ton kilometres) in the first year of the concession, 2004 against 2003

secondMetric.name: Concession fees paid to government by the concessionaire since takeover, per the concessionaire's auditors

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion Report, Zambia Railways Restructuring Project, Report No. 32520, December 2005

records.limits: The cited completion report was written two years into the concession and supports the start and the early gains only; it says the 30 percent rise came with a fall in tonnage as the operator dropped short hauls, and that the borrower disputed the concessionaire's fee compliance and Parliament set up a review in December 2005. The cancellation rests on a second World Bank document, the Country Partnership Strategy for FY13 to FY16 (Report No. 75089-ZM, February 2013, http://documents.worldbank.org/curated/en/182591468178437607/pdf/750890CORRIGEN0IC00IDA0R20130002703.pdf, PDF page 22, paragraph 49), which says the rail network condition and service continued to deteriorate and the concession was cancelled in September 2012 with a commitment to recapitalise the railway, and elsewhere (page 11) calls it a reversal of the railway concession that stakeholders saw as policy incoherence. Neither document gives traffic for the later concession years, so the record shows a delivered early gain and a cancellation, not a measured decline from a peak. Both documents come from the lender that financed the concession process and argued for privatisation. The figures are in PDFs (the 1993 and 1999 traffic on page 5, the fees on page 10, the 2004 traffic gain on page 19, the 20-year term on page 43). The concession was originally 20 years with possible extensions (Annex 10), so it ran about nine years of a 20-year term, a figure computed here.

pattern.mechanism: After two decades of falling traffic under the state railway, the government retrenched staff with World Bank money and let one private consortium run all freight and passenger services and the track under a vertically integrated concession; the operator lengthened hauls and paid fees for a few years, then a later government judged the network was still deteriorating and took the railway back.
preconditions: A concession agreement with enforceable investment and maintenance obligations and a monitoring body able to apply them
Bulk mining freight that the railway can win back from road
Political agreement across governments that private operation is the policy, which did not survive here

records.title: Urban water lease (affermage) with SEEG, and the return to public management after 2000
records.claim: Guinea ran its urban water service from 1989 under a ten-year lease in which the public asset company SONEG owned and financed the network and the privately led operator SEEG ran it, but after renegotiation failed the private operator withdrew in December 2000, the government decided in July 2003 to keep the service public, and revenue collected from private customers fell from US$5.8 million in 1998 to US$1.7 million in 2005.

metric.name: Revenue collection from private customers, urban water services

secondMetric.name: Revenue collection from private customers in the last full years of the lease

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion Report, Guinea Third Water Supply and Sanitation Project, Report No. 36083-GUI, June 2006, section 4.1

records.limits: The figures sit in a PDF (page 9, printed page 4; the ten-year lease ending in 1999 is on page 6). The World Bank financed the lease from its first project in 1989 and rated this follow-on project and the borrower unsatisfactory, so it has a view on who was to blame. The revenue figures are in US dollars, and the report says tariffs were frozen until 2005 and fell from US$0.86 to US$0.21 per cubic metre in real dollar terms, so much of the fall in dollar collections is a currency and tariff effect, not only worse collection; the same paragraph says SONEG's net income went from US$2.9 million in 1998 to a loss of US$0.5 million in 2005. 1998 is a year chosen by the report, not a demonstrated peak. The report also says 24 hour service and compliance with water quality standards, achieved under the earlier operation, were lost and service became intermittent, with no figure for when. SEEG's private shareholder is named only as SAUR, in passing, and the share structure is not given. The 1989 start is inferred from the ten-year lease ending in 1999 and the first supporting credit of May 1989; the report gives no signing date. The lease ended at the end of its term after two years of failed renegotiation and contract extensions, so this is a partnership that was not renewed rather than one terminated for breach.

pattern.mechanism: The state split the urban water utility into a public asset-holding company that owned and financed the network and a private-led operating company that ran it under a lease and was paid from tariffs; when the lease came up for renewal, tariffs were frozen, the private shareholder saw too much risk and left, and the public company took over operations it was not prepared to run.
preconditions: Tariffs set high enough and indexed so the operator's revenue does not erode in real terms
Renegotiation started well before the lease expires, with a deadline
A public asset company able to run operations itself if the private partner leaves

records.title: Maputo water lease to Aguas de Mocambique, and the public buyout of the operator in 2010
records.claim: Mozambique's water asset fund FIPAG leased Maputo's water service from 2000 to the private operator Aguas de Mocambique, whose lead shareholder SAUR pulled out in December 2001 and offered its stake to Aguas de Portugal for one euro; under the lease Maputo connections rose from 77,793 at the end of 2000 to 109,932 in March 2009, and in 2010 FIPAG bought out the Portuguese shareholder, leaving the operator primarily publicly owned.

metric.name: Maputo water connections served by the lease operator at project completion

secondMetric.name: Maputo water connections at the start of the lease (baseline)

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Mozambique Second National Water Development Project, Report No. ICR0000700, September 2009

records.limits: The connection counts are in a PDF (page 7, the results table; the SAUR withdrawal on page 18, paragraph 22), reported by the lender that designed and financed the lease. The end of private participation rests on a second World Bank document, the completion report for the Greater Maputo Water Supply Expansion Project (Report No. ICR00005527, February 2022, http://documents.worldbank.org/curated/en/306811653587372748/pdf/Mozambique-Greater-Maputo-Water-Supply-Expansion-Project.pdf, page 22, paragraph 37), which says the operator's performance fell well below expectations, relations with FIPAG deteriorated, FIPAG bought out the Portuguese partner's roughly 85 percent stake in 2010, and the renamed company, Aguas da Regiao de Maputo, has run the lease since then as a primarily public company, with the lease extended to 2019 and private partners for the regional utilities only scheduled for 2022. The two reports do not agree on the lease length (15 years in 2009, 14 years in 2022). The record shows growth in connections under the lease and the end of private ownership, not a fall in service: connections were not shown to decline after the buyout, so what eroded is the partnership, not access. The 2009 report rates the private operator's performance poorly through much of the period: the 2000 floods, SAUR's underbidding, and two years of renegotiation delayed the programme by about four years, and supply in 2009 averaged 14 hours a day against a target of continuous supply. Lease revenue to FIPAG stayed far below expectation (2022 report, paragraph 52).

pattern.mechanism: The state kept the water assets in a public fund and leased operation of the capital's system to a private consortium paid from tariffs, with a regulator able to order tariff reviews; when the lead foreign operator left and its successor underperformed, the asset fund bought the operating company itself and kept the lease structure with a public owner.
preconditions: Bids priced on reliable information about network condition, which the security situation prevented here
A lead operator whose corporate strategy commits it to the country for the contract term
A regulator with power to order tariff reviews, which existed (CRA) but could not save the original consortium

records.title: NAMFISA Regulatory Sandbox, microlending cohort
records.claim: Namibia's non-bank financial regulator NAMFISA launched its Regulatory Sandbox in May 2023, received 10 applications for its first, microlending cohort, and had admitted three participants (ReferredBy Financial Solutions, Ergo Analytics trading as Verime, and the microlender Express Credit) with a fourth application under review by its 2025 annual report.

metric.name: Participants admitted to the NAMFISA Regulatory Sandbox (cumulative)

secondMetric.name: Applications received for the first (microlending) cohort

source.publisher: Namibia Financial Institutions Supervisory Authority (NAMFISA), Annual Report 2025

records.limits: NAMFISA is reporting on its own programme. Both figures are inside PDFs: the three admitted participants and the fourth applicant are on printed pages 87 to 88 of the Annual Report 2025 (PDF page 100), with the same count in the risk section ('three active participants and a fourth in an advanced stage'); the 10 applications are in the Annual Report 2024 (printed page 81, PDF page 48, https://www.namfisa.com.na/download/annual-report-2024/), whose chart of successful against unsuccessful applications prints labels that cannot be read reliably as counts, so the record does not use it. The reporting year ends 31 March 2025, but the text calls the third participant 'recently admitted', so the asOf is the report year, not a day. The same report's division summary for the Market Conduct and Operations function says that in the first cohort two participants were actively regulated and monitored during 2024/25, which fits the third, Express Credit, being admitted late in the year and still in mobilisation. The count is cumulative admissions over about two years, not admissions in one year, and no firm is reported as having completed or exited the sandbox; the 2024 report notes one selected entity whose start was delayed for market readiness. Three firms in a population of about three million is small, and it covers only the non-bank sector NAMFISA supervises: the Bank of Namibia's separate FinTech innovation framework publishes no participant count and is not included. A second cohort for crowdfunding and peer-to-peer lending closed applications on 23 February 2026 with no admissions published yet.

pattern.mechanism: The non-bank supervisor opens industry-specific cohorts, admits licensed firms and start-ups to test a product under supervision where current legislation would not otherwise allow it, and feeds what it learns into regulation, with a FinTech Square event as its engagement channel.
preconditions: A supervisor with power to grant conditions or exemptions to the entities it licenses
A cohort design narrow enough for a small supervisory team to monitor
A pipeline of local fintech applicants, here built partly through the FinTech Square events
pattern.travelled: NAMFISA plans to re-establish the sandbox under the Financial Institutions and Markets Act (FIMA) once it commences; the Bank of Namibia runs a parallel framework for banking and payments with no published participant count.

records.title: Federal strategic stock of protective masks, and its dismantling
records.claim: The Federal Public Service Public Health held a strategic stock of masks for pandemic influenza in military warehouses in Namur from 2006, sized at 32 million surgical masks when the Bioethics Committee reviewed the pandemic plan in 2009. It destroyed the expired masks in operations in late 2015 and late 2018 without replacing them, so Belgium entered the COVID-19 crisis in early 2020 with no strategic mask stock.

metric.name: Federal strategic stock of masks at the start of the COVID-19 crisis

secondMetric.name: Strategic stock of surgical masks referred to in the 2009 review of the pandemic plan

source.publisher: Chambre des représentants de Belgique, Rapport de la Commission spéciale COVID-19, DOC 55 1394/002, 13 September 2021

records.limits: The zero is not a counted figure. It is our reading of the committee's prose statement that no strategic mask stock existed when the crisis began. The 32 million is the stock named in the 2009 bioethics advice and the plan's target; the report never gives an audited count of masks actually held in any year. Some of the stock was probably unusable before it was destroyed: the report records that the Namur warehouses lost their heating in 2012 and the masks stayed in unheated storage. The dates of destruction (late 2015 and late 2018) come from a chronology entry built from hearing testimony, which the committee marks as contradicted by other witnesses, not from a finding of its own. Responsibility for the decision not to replace the stock is disputed in the report itself between the former health minister and the experts heard. A mask stock is one narrow input to pandemic preparedness. It says nothing about the pandemic plan, testing, hospital surge capacity or the later rebuilding of a stock.

pattern.mechanism: From 2006 the federal health administration stored a national reserve of masks under its pandemic plan, then destroyed expired stock in 2015 and 2018 without a replacement contract, so the reserve ran down to nothing between two pandemics.
preconditions: A pandemic plan that names a stock size but no owner for rotating and replacing it
Storage borrowed from another department (Defence), with conditions that degraded the stock

records.title: BE-Alert
records.claim: The National Crisis Centre of the Federal Public Service Interior has run BE-Alert, the national system that lets municipalities and provinces alert the population by SMS, including location-based SMS, and information screens, since 2017. By 1 September 2025, 537 of 565 municipalities, covering 95 percent of Belgian territory, were affiliated, 1,369,659 citizen addresses were registered, and the system had been used 273 times in 2025.

metric.name: Municipalities affiliated to BE-Alert

secondMetric.name: Citizen addresses registered in BE-Alert

source.publisher: Centre de Crise National, SPF Intérieur, 'Toutes les communes flamandes sont affiliées à BE-Alert', 16 September 2025

records.limits: This is the crisis centre's own news release, not a statistic or an audit. Affiliation means a municipality can send alerts, not that it does so well or in time: the release gives no measure of how fast or how accurately any alert reached people in a real emergency. The 273 uses in 2025 mix real alerts, vigilance messages and tests, and the release does not split them. One person can register up to five addresses, so the count is not people. Location-based SMS reaches unregistered phones, but this page gives no reach figure for it. Coverage took eight years to reach 95 percent of territory, and 28 Walloon municipalities were still outside it in 2025. The page says nothing about the July 2021 floods in Wallonia, the largest recent test of national warning, so it cannot show that the system works when a major shock arrives. A warning channel is one part of preparedness and says nothing about recovery.

pattern.mechanism: The federal crisis centre built one national alerting platform and offered it to municipalities and provinces, which keep the legal power to warn. It added channels over time (registered SMS, location-based SMS, screens) and runs an annual national test.
preconditions: Emergency-planning powers held by mayors and governors, so a federal tool needs local uptake to work
Mobile operators obliged or willing to send location-based messages
A federal budget for a platform that municipalities can join voluntarily

records.title: Rogun hydropower plant
records.claim: The Government of Tajikistan resumed construction of the Soviet-era Rogun hydropower plant in 2007 from the state budget, signed the main dam contract in 2016 and commissioned two temporary units (400 MW) in 2018 and 2019. It invested about US$3.3 billion in 2007 to 2022, and in November 2024 the World Bank put the cost to complete the plant at US$6.29 billion, with construction completion moved to 2033 and full reservoir impoundment not before 2039, 63 years after construction first began in 1976.

metric.name: Estimated cost to complete the Rogun HPP programme

secondMetric.name: Government of Tajikistan investment in Rogun HPP, 2007 to 2022

source.publisher: World Bank, Project Appraisal Document PAD00208, Sustainable Financing for Rogun Hydropower Project (P181029), 19 November 2024

records.limits: No cost overrun can be computed: the appraisal document gives no original budget or baseline completion date to set the US$6.29 billion against, so the gap's unit (percent overrun) is not met. The US$6.29 billion is a forward estimate of remaining cost with contingencies, not an outturn, and adding it to the US$3.3 billion already spent is our arithmetic, not the Bank's. The schedule slip is our reading of milestone dates: construction began in 1976, the Soviet works stopped in 1992, and completion is now 2033 with impoundment in 2039. The Bank itself expects 'some further delays' to the March 2024 milestones. It attributes slow progress to financing shortfalls. The source is the lender's appraisal for its own grant, written to justify financing. The project is now financed by ten development partners, so delivery after 2024 is shared rather than purely Tajik. Spending close to 39 percent of GDP and a US$500 million Eurobond left the country at high risk of debt distress. 'Operating' means two temporary units run, not that the 3,780 MW plant is built.

pattern.mechanism: The Tajik government restarted a stalled Soviet megaproject from its own budget and a Eurobond, brought two temporary turbines online early to earn revenue during construction, then used World Bank-backed safety and environmental studies to draw in a donor financing package for the rest.
preconditions: A site with Soviet-era works, surveys and tunnels already in place
A state willing to divert a large share of GDP to one project for over a decade
Riparian water agreements and an independent dam-safety review credible enough for international lenders

records.title: Work permits for Syrian refugees under the Jordan Compact, and the end of the fee waiver
records.claim: After the February 2016 London conference, Jordan's Ministry of Labour opened formal work permits to Syrian refugees and waived their fees. Annual permits issued rose from 36,788 in 2016 to a peak of 90,152 in 2023. In July 2024 the waiver was not extended for flexible or employer-sponsored permits, and issuance fell to 54,586 in 2024.

metric.name: Work permits issued to Syrian refugees in Jordan

secondMetric.name: Work permits issued to Syrian refugees in Jordan at the 2023 peak

source.publisher: UNHCR Jordan, Economic Inclusion of Syrian Refugees factsheet (June 2025), from Ministry of Labour data

records.limits: The construct is how fast rules and programmes change when conditions change, but a permit count measures uptake. The speed of the 2016 rule change is shown only by the timeline and the 2016 bar. The annual figures are chart labels in a one-page UNHCR factsheet, and the factsheet credits them to the Ministry of Labour. They count permits, not people: renewals, short-term and retroactive permits are all counted, so 340,000 cumulative permits overstates the number of refugees who ever held one. The World Bank and UNHCR copies disagree slightly (45,000 against 47,762 for 2019). The waiver ended in July 2024, so 2024 is only half a post-change year. The 2025 figure (35,702 to July) is partial and is not annualised here. Fall in permits is not fall in work: refugees may have moved back into informal jobs, and the series cannot show that.

pattern.mechanism: Jordan's Ministry of Labour turned a donor compact into labour-law changes: it waived permit fees, created flexible permits not tied to one employer, and let cooperatives and trade unions act as sponsors. When the donor-funded waiver lapsed in July 2024, it charged Syrians full foreign-worker fees, and issuance fell by about 40 percent.
preconditions: Concessional financing tied to the refugee response that paid for the waived fees
A labour ministry able to issue and track permits at volume, with intermediaries such as agricultural cooperatives and unions
Domestic tolerance for refugee labour in sectors open to foreigners, which is what came under fiscal and political pressure later
pattern.travelled: Ethiopia's 2019 refugee proclamation and Turkey's 2016 work-permit regulation followed the same compact logic. Both kept permit numbers low relative to their refugee populations.

records.title: Kvalitetsfonden hospital building programme (supersygehuse), and its overruns
records.claim: Denmark set up Kvalitetsfonden in 2007 to fund a new hospital structure. Through it the regions are building or rebuilding 16 hospitals with a combined investment frame of about DKK 57 billion (2023 prices). Rigsrevisionen reported in November 2023 that the programme's largest overrun, Nyt Hospital Nordsjælland, had its budget raised by DKK 2.3 billion, or 44 percent, and was expected six years later than planned.

metric.name: Budget increase over the grant frame, Nyt Hospital Nordsjælland (largest overrun in the programme)

secondMetric.name: Schedule delay, Nyt Hospital Nordsjælland, expected completion end of 2026 against plan

source.publisher: Rigsrevisionen (National Audit Office of Denmark), Beretning 4/2023 om byggeriet af Nyt Hospital Nordsjælland, November 2023

records.limits: The headline 44 percent belongs to one project, the worst in the programme, so it is not the programme's cost performance. The report gives no programme-wide overrun in its text. Figure 2 of the same report lists original and latest budgets in 2009 prices for 15 of the 16 projects, leaving out Nyt Hospital Bispebjerg, whose budget had not been published. Summed by hand, the 15 come to about DKK 43.9 billion against frames of DKK 39.2 billion, roughly 12 percent over. That is our calculation from chart labels, not a published figure. Several projects held their frame partly by cutting scope through savings catalogues, which Rigsrevisionen criticised in Beretning 11/2019 and its follow-ups. A frame that holds after cuts is not a delivery on time and on specification. 2007 is the year the fund was set up. Grants were confirmed project by project afterwards (2013 for Nordsjælland), so construction started years after 2007. The programme is unfinished: Rigsrevisionen's January 2025 follow-up still counted seven projects under construction, six of them under heightened ministry supervision, so final outturns are not known. The figure is a budget forecast in 2023 prices and is reported as a region's estimate, not an audited final account.

pattern.mechanism: Parliament created a state fund that gave each region a fixed, inflation-indexed grant frame per hospital and made the regions carry any overrun. The health ministry supervised changes against the grant conditions, and Rigsrevisionen audited the projects repeatedly while they were being built.
preconditions: A 2007 structural reform that created five regions large enough to act as client for a multi-billion-krone building
A national decision to concentrate acute care in fewer, larger hospitals, which fixed the scope in advance
An audit office and a parliamentary audit committee that report on projects while they are still under construction
pattern.travelled: Norway's hospital trusts and the Netherlands' hospital rebuild programmes used fixed regional frames in a similar way. In the Danish case the largest single-site projects still ran over.

records.title: Modernizace dálnice D1 (D1 motorway modernisation, Mirošovice to Kývalka)
records.claim: Czechia's Road and Motorway Directorate (ŘSD) rebuilt 160.8 km of the D1 motorway between Mirošovice and Kývalka in 20 sections from April 2013, reopening the last sections in October 2021, three years later than the 2012 schedule, with costs projected at CZK 29.844 billion including the Šmejkalka bridge against CZK 28.208 billion planned.

metric.name: Slip in reopening the whole modernised motorway, measured against the 2012 schedule
metric.asOf: August 2021 schedule update, audited to November 2022

secondMetric.name: Projected total cost including the Šmejkalka bridge, against CZK 28.208 billion in the 2012 investment plan

source.publisher: Nejvyšší kontrolní úřad (Supreme Audit Office of the Czech Republic), audit conclusion 21/37 on the D1 motorway modernisation

records.limits: The cost figure looks good only because of the baseline it is compared with. The 2012 plan of CZK 28.208 billion was never approved: the audit office says the Ministry of Transport rejected the summary investment plan and approved 20 separate section projects, with no binding overall budget or schedule. The roughly 6 percent overrun is our computation from two published totals, in nominal crowns, with no inflation adjustment. The final cost is unknown. The audit office says the figure is not final, several sections had not been financially settled, and the Šmejkalka bridge cost is a forecast for work planned from 2022 to 2026. Against an earlier baseline the project looks worse. The audit office's 2017 release (audit 16/06) gave the expected total as CZK 20.5 billion and found unit costs up 73 percent, from CZK 74 to 128 million per km, between the 2013 sections and those begun in 2015 and 2016. The three-year slip is measured to the August 2021 schedule, which ŘSD revised 73 times. In November 2022 eight sections still lacked final approval, and nine bridges and three overpasses were in poor or very poor condition. The audit says the modernisation is not complete, so a later finish date would lengthen the slip. This is a rebuild of an existing motorway kept open to traffic, not a new build. The audit looked closely at only five sections, worth CZK 6.792 billion, and a cyber attack on ŘSD's systems limited what auditors could see. The figures are ŘSD's own, reviewed by the auditor, not independently measured.

pattern.mechanism: The Road and Motorway Directorate rebuilt the country's main Prague to Brno motorway section by section with traffic still running. The Ministry of Transport approved 20 separate section projects instead of one programme budget, and EU cohesion funds paid CZK 14.0 billion of the cost.
preconditions: EU Operational Programme Transport co-financing for two budget periods, which paid half the cost
A road agency able to tender and supervise many concurrent section contracts, and a ministry that never set a binding overall schedule or budget
A permit appeal process that averaged 444 days per contested section, which set the pace more than construction did

records.title: Lae Port Development Project (Lae Tidal Basin, phase 1)
records.claim: Papua New Guinea's Independent Public Business Corporation, using ADB and OPEC Fund loans, built the first phase of the Lae tidal basin, a new berth and container terminal at the port of Lae, between April 2012 and December 2014. It was about four years later than planned and cost $310.4 million, against a $154 million project at the 2007 approval.

metric.name: Total project cost at completion

secondMetric.name: Delay in completing the civil works against the appraisal schedule

source.publisher: Asian Development Bank, Independent Evaluation Department, Validation Report: Papua New Guinea, Lae Port Development Project (PVR-540), December 2017

records.limits: The headline 7 percent overrun is against a 2011 revised estimate that had already absorbed $137.4 million of design changes found by later geotechnical work. Against the $154 million package approved in 2007 the increase is about 100 percent. That is our computation and is not like for like, because the scope grew. The validation reports civil works costs up 116 percent and involuntary resettlement costs up 3,590 percent against appraisal. Figures are nominal US dollars. The evaluator is the lender's own evaluation department, validating a completion report the lender wrote. It rated the project less than successful overall, less than effective, less than efficient and less than likely sustainable. The validation attributes the four-year delay to the combination of post-approval design changes and resettlement: 482 settler households on government marshland and a landing site used by three Labu villages, for which a supplementary resettlement plan acceptable to the affected communities had to be prepared. The contractors were foreign: a Korean design-build consultant and China Harbour Engineering. The national institutions' role was procurement, finance and resettlement. A post-completion audit found siltation back to 11 m below chart datum, from the dredged 14 m, at the basin's western entrance. The source says it appeared to have stabilised and does not report lost berth capacity. We have not treated it as an eroded delivery, but a reviewer could. The validation finds handling capacity of 2.0 million revenue tons a year, above the 1.4 million target, so the cost and delay bought a working asset. One project says nothing about PNG's record on other major works.

pattern.mechanism: The government had its state enterprise holding company, IPBC, borrow concessionally from ADB and the OPEC Fund. IPBC procured a single design-and-build contract for reclamation, berth and terminal, and the Morobe Provincial Administration ran the livelihood programme for displaced settlers and the Labu community.
preconditions: Multilateral lenders willing to add $89 million of financing in 2011 when geotechnical findings broke the original design
A resettlement plan acceptable to settler households on government land and to the Labu villages
A state port company with tariff revenue to service the debt, which the validation doubted

records.title: Second-wave motorway concessions (Central E-65, Olympia Odos, Moreas), and their reset
records.claim: Greece procured 744 km of motorway as three PPP concessions that commenced in 2008; after works were suspended in 2011 and the contracts were renegotiated in 2013 and 2015, the European Court of Auditors found the three projects delayed by four years on average, their combined cost per km up 36 percent, from 9.1 to 12.4 million euro, and the planned road length cut to 486 km.

metric.name: Increase in total project cost per km across the three audited motorway concessions, initial plan to post-reset
metric.asOf: Post-reset position as audited in 2017, published March 2018

secondMetric.name: Average construction delay of the three motorways against their initial completion dates

source.publisher: European Court of Auditors, Special Report 09/2018, Public Private Partnerships in the EU: Widespread shortcomings and limited benefits (paragraphs 34(d), 37-40, Tables 2 and 3)

records.limits: This is a record of poor cost and schedule performance, not of good delivery, and it is filed because the gap asks for exactly that figure. The 36 percent is a cost per km, and it mixes two movements: the absolute cost of the Central motorway fell (2,375 to 1,594 million euro) while its length was cut by 55 percent, and Olympia's length was cut by 45 percent, so per-km cost rises partly because fixed and financial costs were spread over fewer kilometres. It is not a like-for-like overrun on a fixed scope. Table 3 of the report shows the combined total project cost of the three concessions falling from 6,743 million euro (2,375 + 2,825 + 1,543) to 6,004 million euro (1,594 + 2,619 + 1,791) as length fell from 744 to 486 km, so the 36 percent per-km increase coincides with an absolute cost about 11 percent lower on a 35 percent smaller scope. The ECA computed the figures from information provided by the Greek authorities and audited only three of the five second-wave concessions (Aegean and Nea Odos are not covered). The completion dates in Table 2 are labelled estimated/actual as of the audit, so the four-year average includes forecasts for the Central and Olympia sections due in August 2017. The ECA attributes much of the cost to the 2009 financial crisis, under which traffic fell around 50 percent below the lenders' worst case, and to the public partner's poor preparation (archaeology, environmental permits, expropriation): the record cannot separate those causes. The deferred northern and southern sections of E-65 and the deferred Olympia stretches were taken out of these contracts; whatever was built later under other contracts is not in this number. The report is from 2018. The ECA also records that Greece's PPP route procured 744 km in three tenders where the earlier 82 km of Olympia took up to 20 years and 31 procurements, which is the strongest point in the programme's favour.

pattern.mechanism: The Greek state bundled several hundred kilometres of motorway into three design-build-finance-operate concessions, transferred traffic risk to the concessionaires, and paid toll-backed private finance plus EU co-financing; when traffic collapsed the state renegotiated, deferred sections and paid about 1.2 billion euro more rather than stop the works.
preconditions: Access to EU cohesion co-financing large enough to fill a renegotiated financing gap
A parliament willing to ratify concession contracts in the absence of a general concession law
Contracts signed before archaeology, permits and land expropriation were settled, which is what turned the crisis into public liability
pattern.travelled: Spain's A-1 and C-25 concessions, audited in the same report, were renegotiated soon after signature at a public cost of about 300 million euro, a smaller version of the same pattern.

records.title: Bildungskarenz with Weiterbildungsgeld, and its abolition
records.claim: Austria's Public Employment Service (AMS) paid Weiterbildungsgeld from 1998 to employees taking up to a year of educational leave, an average of about 14,000 recipients in 2021 at a cost that rose from 236 million euros in 2019 to 646 million in 2024, until the Nationalrat ended the benefit on 31 March 2025 in a budget consolidation law.

metric.name: Average Weiterbildungsgeld recipients on educational leave

secondMetric.name: Total spending on Bildungskarenz in its last full year before abolition

source.publisher: Rechnungshof Österreich (Austrian Court of Audit), report Bildungskarenz, Reihe Bund 2023/11

records.limits: The recipient count is an annual average of people on leave at once, not a share of adults who trained in a year, so it cannot be set against the indicator's unit. The Court of Audit found the training requirements so weak that the leave could fund low-value courses or plain time out of work, and that uptake skewed toward people already highly educated, so the programme's peak is partly a peak in subsidised leave rather than in learning. The 2024 spending figure is the parliament's summary of the government's justification, it includes social insurance contributions, and it is a cost, not a participation number. Abolition is not the end of state support for training leave: a successor Weiterbildungszeit with a Weiterbildungsbeihilfe capped at 150 million euros a year took effect in January 2026 with stricter eligibility (PK0907, 16 October 2025), so a reviewer could call this erosion rather than dismantling. The record documents that the benefit ended by decision; it does not show that adult learning participation in Austria fell as a result.

pattern.mechanism: The federal government let employees suspend their contract for training and had the AMS pay an unemployment-benefit-level allowance out of the unemployment insurance fund; parliament then cut the allowance outright when costs tripled and evaluations found weak employment effects.
preconditions: An unemployment insurance fund large enough to carry a training benefit without a separate appropriation
Labour law that lets an employee suspend a contract by agreement and return to the job
Loose eligibility on course content, which drove both growth and the case for abolition
pattern.travelled: The successor scheme keeps the leave but caps the budget at 150 million euros a year, tightens eligibility and makes higher-earning employees' employers co-fund the allowance, which is the targeting the Court of Audit asked for in 2023.

records.title: Third Highway Project: M4 Baku-Shamakhi and M3 Yenikend-Shorsulu motorways
records.claim: Azerbaijan's road administration upgraded 94 km of the M4 Baku-Shamakhi highway to a four-lane road and built 48 km of new M3 motorway under the World Bank-financed Third Highway Project, at US$2.47 million per km against US$2.96 million estimated at appraisal, with the loan closing in March 2021 instead of March 2015.

metric.name: Actual cost per km of the upgraded M4 Baku-Shamakhi highway (appraisal estimate US$2.96 million per km)

secondMetric.name: Slip of the actual loan closing date against the original closing date

source.publisher: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR00005553, Azerbaijan Third Highway Project (P118023)

records.limits: The completion report is the lender's own evaluation of its loan, drafted with the borrower's data. The cost saving is not mainly efficiency: the report says the lower dollar outcome is mainly attributable to the manat losing more than half its value in 2015 to 2017 while works contracts were priced in local currency, so in local terms the project may have overrun. The 72-month slip is computed here from the two closing dates; the scope also changed twice (the M3 section added, part of the M4 dropped in a landslide zone), and the report concedes the final extension may have been avoidable, so not all of it is construction delay. The efficiency rating is only Modest. It is one corridor of 142 km, with a lender supervising procurement, so it is weak evidence about Azerbaijan's road programme outside donor projects.

pattern.mechanism: The road administration borrowed from the World Bank for a defined corridor, accepted the lender's procurement and engineering review, held to the original alignment instead of the ministry's costlier viaduct proposal, and reused savings by adding a motorway section through restructuring.
preconditions: Access to multilateral lending with appraisal estimates that create a published baseline
A road agency able to procure and supervise several works contracts at once
Works contracts in local currency, which turned a devaluation into a dollar saving

records.title: Central Bank of Azerbaijan regulatory sandbox
records.claim: The Central Bank of the Republic of Azerbaijan began testing its first regulatory sandbox participant in December 2024 and admitted three more whose testing began in 2026, out of 14 applicants.

metric.name: Firms whose sandbox testing began in 2026, counted from the registry

secondMetric.name: Applicants to the sandbox since launch

source.publisher: Central Bank of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Regulatory Sandbox Registry

records.limits: The year count of three is computed from testing start dates in the registry; the central bank publishes only undated cumulative counters (14 applicants, 4 participants), so the series has no official annual figure and earlier years cannot be reconstructed if entries are removed. The registry's completed projects section shows no entries although the first test was scheduled to end in February 2026 and is still listed as current, so firms completing the regime, half of what the indicator asks for, cannot be counted. Only one regulator is covered. A sandbox of four firms is not a national flagship in the sense of a programme policymakers name first; it is filed because it evidences this gap's construct literally.

pattern.mechanism: The central bank wrote rules on a special regulation regime that exempt participants from licensing, opened cohort application windows, and admitted a handful of banks and crypto firms to test products with capped users under its supervision.
preconditions: A central bank that is also the integrated financial regulator, so one body can grant the exemption
Demand for products the existing licence categories do not cover, here Islamic finance and crypto exchange

records.title: Defence against the June 2013 Danube flood
records.claim: During the June 2013 Danube flood, which crested at a record 891 cm in Budapest, the government declared an emergency and Hungary's national disaster management directorate ran six days of intensive defence along 807.4 km of levees; of 206,000 people the flood directly endangered, 1,570 had to be evacuated.

metric.name: People directly endangered by the flood

secondMetric.name: People evacuated

source.publisher: Belügyminisztérium Országos Katasztrófavédelmi Főigazgatóság (Ministry of Interior, National Directorate General for Disaster Management)

records.limits: The source is the agency that ran the defence, writing about itself six days after the crest, so it is self-reporting with no independent verification. The page gives no count of deaths, injuries or damage cost, and no recovery figure, so it evidences the preparing and defending half of the construct and not the recovering half. A low evacuation count could reflect where the river happened to break out (47,285 hectares, mostly forest and farmland, were flooded) as much as the defence. Much of the protection is a stock of levees rather than a 2013 move, and 36,780 civilian volunteers, 19,515 civil guards and 8,306 soldiers took part, so the outcome is not the directorate's alone. This is one event; it says nothing about the capacity against other hazards such as the 2010 Ajka red sludge spill. The 206,000 is a rounded figure.

pattern.mechanism: The government declared an emergency by river section, and the national disaster management directorate, unified under the interior ministry, took over command of the defence from mayors in 81 settlements and drew soldiers, police, students, public-works employees and volunteers onto the levees.
preconditions: A national levee system built and maintained over generations by the water directorates
A single disaster management body with legal power to take command from local authorities in an emergency
Upstream gauge readings that gave days of warning before the crest reached Budapest

records.title: Belene nuclear power plant, and its cancellation
records.claim: Bulgaria's state utility NEK ordered long-lead reactor equipment for the Belene nuclear plant from Atomstroyexport in 2008. The project was cancelled before any unit was completed, and on 6 December 2016 the Ministry of Energy transferred 601,617,133 euros to NEK so it could pay the damages awarded against it in ICC arbitration case 18086/GZ/MHM.

metric.name: State financial assistance transferred to NEK to pay the Belene arbitration award to Atomstroyexport

secondMetric.name: Costs incurred on the Belene construction to date, as stated by the Minister of Energy

source.publisher: Ministry of Energy of the Republic of Bulgaria, press release of 6 December 2016

records.limits: Belene never produced electricity, so this record documents a delivery that failed before it operated, not a capability that eroded. The headline number is a termination cost, the arbitration damages for equipment ordered in 2008, and not a cost overrun against a budget: the record carries no official baseline budget or schedule for the 2008 phase. The 1.4 billion leva of costs incurred comes from a minister speaking in a television interview. The ministry republished the transcript without a printed date; the 2016 year is inferred from the special assistance law the interview discusses. It is not an audited figure. The project was decided in April 2005, cancelled in March 2012, and revived by a National Assembly decision of 7 June 2018 and a Council of Ministers decision of 29 June 2018. Later decisions on the site and the equipment are not covered by these sources. The 601.6 million euros was advanced to NEK as repayable assistance, not a grant, so the final fiscal loss is not shown here. The later disposal or reuse of the equipment the payment bought is not covered.

pattern.mechanism: NEK, the state utility, ordered long-lead reactor equipment from a single foreign vendor in 2008 before financing or a final contract price was settled. The government cancelled the project in 2012, the Ministry of Energy advanced NEK repayable assistance in 2016 to pay the vendor's arbitration claim, and the project was revived in 2018.
preconditions: A state utility allowed to commit to equipment orders before the project's financing was closed
Political control of the decision that changed with each government
A single-vendor contract enforceable in international arbitration

records.title: Belarusian nuclear power plant (BelAES), delivered behind schedule
records.claim: Belarus started building its first nuclear power plant at Ostrovets in November 2013, a two-unit WWER-1200 plant totalling 2,400 MW. Its regulator's 2019 report scheduled unit 1 for 2019 and unit 2 for 2020. Unit 1 was commissioned in 2021 and unit 2 in October 2023, three years after the 2019 schedule.

metric.name: Year power unit No. 2 entered commercial operation

secondMetric.name: Year power unit No. 2 was scheduled for commissioning in the 2019 national report

source.publisher: Gosatomnadzor, Ministry for Emergency Situations of the Republic of Belarus, National Report on the implementation of the Convention on Nuclear Safety (2025)

records.limits: This is a schedule figure only. The record carries no official budget or final cost for the plant, so cost performance is unknown. The slip is measured against a schedule that the 2019 report itself calls 'updated'. This record uses the 2019 schedule because it is the one stated in an official source. The schedule is given in years, not months, so the three-year slip for unit 2 is approximate. The 2019 schedule speaks of commissioning while the 2023 figure is the start of commercial operation, so the two milestones may not be identical. Both figures come from the Belarusian regulator reporting on its own country's flagship project. The plant was built turnkey on a Russian design, financed from the republican budget and a Russian state export credit, as the 2019 national report states. The delivery is therefore only partly attributable to Belarusian institutions: they decided, licensed, supervised, financed and now operate it. The source does not show capacity factors or outages after commissioning.

pattern.mechanism: The Belarusian state chose a single foreign state vendor to build a reference design turnkey, and built up a domestic regulator and operator in parallel under a sequence of IAEA review missions, accepting slippage on the vendor's schedule.
preconditions: A strategic partner state willing to supply design, construction and credit together
A centralised state able to hold a decade-long build through political and diplomatic opposition
A reference plant of the same design already being built abroad (Leningrad NPP-2)

records.title: Bishkek-Osh road rehabilitation, third phase
records.claim: The Kyrgyz Ministry of Transport and Communications completed the third and final phase of the Bishkek-Osh road rehabilitation in July 2007, bringing the rehabilitated length of the only internal surface connection between Bishkek and Osh to 463 km, with a 31.7 percent cost overrun on base cost items and civil works finished 33 months after the October 2004 appraisal schedule.

metric.name: Cost overrun on base cost items, Third Road Rehabilitation Project

secondMetric.name: Civil works completion delay (appraisal schedule October 2004, actual July 2007)

source.publisher: Asian Development Bank, Independent Evaluation Department, Validation Report PCV: KGZ 2009-40, Third Road Rehabilitation Project (Loan 1853)

records.limits: The record covers phase three only: 120 km of the Bishkek-Osh road and 125 km of secondary roads, not the two earlier phases. The 31.7 percent is on base cost items and is driven by the secondary roads and an added bridge ($7.6 million of the $13.6 million); main-road civil works ran 11.6 percent over per km, and total project cost rose from $50.0 million to $57.1 million, about 14 percent, because contingencies and currency gains absorbed part of the overrun. The 33 months is computed from two dates in the text, and 22 of the delay months came before construction, in loan effectiveness and bidding against a 7-month plan; one civil works contract was terminated and the supervision consultant was sanctioned. The road was 80 percent financed by an ADB concessional loan, and the validation is ADB's evaluation office reviewing ADB's own completion report; it rated the project 'less effective' pending a later performance evaluation that this record does not carry. Traffic grew about 4 percent a year against a forecast of 6 to 7, accidents rose in number and severity after the works, and the road maintenance funding covenants were not met until 2007, so nothing here shows the condition of the road today.

pattern.mechanism: The Kyrgyz government, through the Ministry of Transport and Communications and a project implementation unit staffed by local consultants experienced on the earlier phases, rehabilitated its only north-south trunk road in phases over a decade, financing each phase with an ADB concessional loan and a counterpart share.
preconditions: A concessional lender willing to finance the same corridor three times in succession
An implementation unit staffed by local consultants experienced on the earlier phases
Counterpart and maintenance funding from a small budget, which arrived late and only after the works ended
